pub line_kinds: Vec<LineKind>,\n}\n\n#[derive(Debug)]\npub struct ParseError {\n    pub pos: usize,\n    pub msg: String,\n}\n\npub struct Parser<'a> {\n    pub src: &'a str,\n    b: &'a [u8],\n       }\n        count\n    }\n\n    /// Column of the first non-space character of the current line (pos at line start).\n    fn line_indent(&self, ls: usize) -> usize {\n        let mut i = ls;\n        while i < self.b.len() && self.b[i] == b' ' {\n            i += 1;\n        }\n        i - ls\n    }\n\n    pub fn parse_stream(mut self) -> PResult<Stream> {\n        let mut docs = Vec::new();\n              }\n                }\n                _ => self.pos += 1,\n            }\n        }\n    }\n\n    fn parse_block_seq(&mut self, col: usize) -> PResult<Node> {\n        let start =              self.null_node()\n                    }\n                }\n            };\n            let iend = if matches!(value.kind, Kind::Null) && value.props.is_none() {\n                istart + 1\n            } else {\n                value.end\n            };\n            let end_line = self.line_of(iend.saturating_sub(1).max(istart));\n            items.push(Item {\n                line:         col,\n            props: None,\n            kind: Kind::Seq(items),\n            comment: None,\n            flow_has_comment: false,\n            end_line,\n        })\n    }\n\n    fn parse_block_map(&mut self, col: usize, parent: isize) -> PResult<Node> {\n        let _ = parent;\n        let start = self.pos;\n        let line = self.line_of(start);\n        let mut entries = Vec::new();\n        loop {\n            let estart = self.pos;\n            let eline = self.line_of(estart);\n            let explicit = self.peek() == b'?' && matches!(self.peek_at(1), b' ' | b'\\t' | b'\\n' | 0);\n            let key;\n            let key_end;\n            if explicit {\n                self.pos += 1;\n                key = self.parse_block_node(col as isize, Ctx::SeqItem)?;\n                key_end = key.end.max(estart + 1);\n                // Expect ':' at column col on a following line (or none).\n                self.skip_trivia_lines();\n self.is_doc_marker_at(ls) {\n                        break;\n                    }\n                    if ind == col {\n                        self.pos = ls + ind;\n                        continue;\n                    }\n                    if ind > col {\n                        return self.err(\"bad indentation in mapping\");\n                    }\n                    break;\n self.null_node()\n            } else {\n                let ls = self.pos;\n                let ind = self.line_indent(ls);\n                let is_seq = self.b.get(ls + ind) == Some(&b'-') && Ctx::MapValue)?\n                } else {\n                    self.null_node()\n                }\n            };\n            let end = if matches!(value.kind, Kind::Null) && value.props.is_none() {\n                colon + 1\n            } else {\n                value.end\n            };\n            let end_line = self.line_of(end.saturating_sub(1).max(estart));\n            entries.push(Entry {\n                line: eline,\n                col,\n                start: estart,\n                explicit,\n                key,\n                key_end,\n                colon,\n                colon_comment,\n                value,\n                value_same_line,\n                trivia_before_value,\n                end,\n                end_line,\n       break;\n            }\n            let ind = self.line_indent(ls);\n            if ind == col {\n                self.pos = ls + ind;\n                let c = self.peek();\n                if c          return self.err(\"tab\");\n                }\n                continue;\n            }\n            if ind > col {\n                self.pos = ls + ind;\n                return self.err(\"bad indentation in mapping\");\n            }\n            break;\n        }\n        let end = entries.last().map(|e| e.end).unwrap_or(start);\n        let end_line = entries.last().map(|e| e.end_line).unwrap_or(line);\n        Ok(Node {\n            start,\n            end,\n            line,\n            col,\n            props: None,\n            kind: Kind::Map(entries),\n            comment: None,\n            flow_has_comment: false,\n            end_line,\n        })\n    }\n\n    fn parse_implicit_key(&mut self) -> PResult<Node> {\n        let start = self.pos;\n        let return self.err(\"props before key newline\");\n            }\n            self.skip_inline_ws();\n        }\n        let c = self.peek();\n        let mut node = if c == b'[' || c == b'{' {\n            self.parse_flow_collection()?\n        } else if c == b'\"' || c == b'\\'' {\n            self.parse_quoted(-1)?\n        } else if c == b'*' {\n            self.parse_alias()?\n        } else {\n            // Plain key up to ':'.\n            let le = self.line_end(self.pos);\n            let mut i = self.pos;\n            while i < le {\n                if self.b[i] == b':' && (i + 1 >= le || matches!(self.b[i + 1], b' ' | b'\\t')) {\n                    break;\n                }\n                i += 1;\n            }\n            let mut e = i;\n            while e > self.pos && is_ws(self.b[e - 1]) {\n                e -= 1;\n            }\n            let text = self.src[self.pos..e].to_string();\n            let s = self.pos;\n            self.pos = e;\n            Node {\n                start: s,\n                end: e,\n                line,\n                col: self.col_of(s),\n                props: None,\n                kind: Kind::Scalar(Scalar {\n None,\n                }),\n                comment: None,\n                flow_has_comment: false,\n                end_line: line,\n            }\n        };\n        if props.is_some() {\n            node.start = start;\n            node.col = col;\n            node.props = props;\n        }\n        Ok(node)\n    }\n\n    fn parse_alias(&mut self) -> PResult<Node> {\n        let s = self.pos;\n        self.pos += 1;\n        while self.pos < self.b.len() && !matches!(self.b[self.pos], b' ' | b'\\t' | b'\\n') && !is_flow_ind(self.b[self.pos]) {\n            self.pos += 1;\n        }\n        if self.pos == s + 1 {\n            return self.err(\"empty alias\");\n        }\n        let line = self.line_of(s);\n        Ok(Node {\n            start: s,\n            end: self.pos,\n            line,\n            col: self.col_of(s),\n            props: None,\n            kind: Kind::Alias(self.src[s + 1..self.pos].to_string()),\n            comment: None,\n            flow_has_comment: false,\n            end_line: line,\n        })\n    }\n\n    /// Parse a plain/quoted scalar or alias in block context (value position).\n    fn parse_inline_scalar_or_alias(&mut self, parent: isize, block: bool) -> PResult<Node> {\n        let c = self.peek();\n        if c == b'*' {\n            return self.parse_alias();\n        }\n        if c == b'\"' || c == b'\\'' {\n            return self.parse_quoted(parent);\n        }\n        self.parse_plain_block(parent, block)\n    }\n\n    fn parse_quoted(&mut self, parent: isize) -> PResult<Node> {\n        let s = self.pos;\n        let line = self.line_of(s);\n        let e = match self.scan_quoted_end() {\n            Some(e) => e,\n            None => return self.err(\"unterminated quoted scalar\"),\n        };\n        let raw = &self.src[s..e];\n        // Continuation lines must be indented more than the parent.\n        if raw.contains('\\n') {\n            for (i, l) in raw.split('\\n').enumerate() {\n                if i == 0 {\n                    continue;\n                }\n                let ind = l.len() - l.trim_start_matches(' ').len();\n                let t = l.trim_start_matches([' ', '\\t']);\n                if !t.is_empty() && (ind as isize) <= parent {\n                    return self.err(\"bad quoted indentation\");\n                }\n                if i > 0 && (l.starts_with(\"---\") || l.starts_with(\"...\")) && (l.len() == 3 || matches!(l.as_bytes()[3], b' ' | b'\\t')) {\n                    return self.err(\"document marker in quoted scalar\");\n                }\n            }\n        }\n        let style = if self.b[s] == b'\"' { ScalarStyle::Double } else { ScalarStyle::Single };\n        let value = match style {\n            ScalarStyle::Double => decode_double(&raw[1..raw.len() - 1]).ok_or(ParseError { pos: s, msg: \"bad escape\".into() })?,\n            _ => decode_single(&raw[1..raw.len() - 1]),\n        };\n        self.pos = e;\n        let end_line = self.line_of(e - 1);\n        Ok(Node {\n            start: s,\n            end: e,\n            line,\n            col: self.col_of(s),\n            props: None,\n            kind:          }),\n            comment: None,\n            flow_has_comment: false,\n            end_line,\n        })\n    }\n\n    /// Plain scalar in block context, possibly multi-line.\n    fn parse_plain_block(&mut self, parent: isize, _block: bool) -> PResult<Node> {\n        let s = self.pos;\n        let line = self.line_of(s);\n        let c = self.peek();\n        // Indicators that cannot start a plain scalar.\n        if matches!(c, b'#' | b'&' | b'*' | b'!' | b'|' | b'>' | b'\\'' | b'\"' | b'%' | b'@' | b'`' | b'[' | b']' | b'{' | b'}' | b',') {\n            return self.err(\"invalid plain scalar start\");\n        }\n        if matches!(c, b'-' | b'?' | b':') && matches!(self.peek_at(1), b' ' | b'\\t' | b'\\n' | 0) {\n            return self.err(\"invalid plain scalar start\");\n        }\n        let mut end = self.scan_plain_line(self.pos)?;\n        let mut lines: Vec<(usize, usize)> = vec![(s, end)];\n        // Continuation lines.\n        let mut p = < self.b.len() && self.b[q] == b'#' {\n                break;\n            }\n            if q >= self.b.len() || self.b[q] != b'\\n' {\n                break;\n            }\n            // Skip blank lines.\n            let mut ls = q + 1;\n            let mut blank_lines = 0;\n            loop {\n                if ls >= self.b.len() {\n                    break;\n                }\n                let le = self.line_end(ls);\n                if self.src[ls..le].trim_matches([' ', '\\t']).is_empty() {\n                    blank_lines += 1;\n                    ls = if le < self.b.len() { le + 1 } else { le };\n                } else {\n                    break;\n                }\n            }\n            if ls >= self.b.len() {\n                break;\n            }\n            let ind = self.line_indent(ls) as isize;\n            if ind <= parent {\n                break;\n            }\n            if self.is_doc_marker_at(ls) {\n                break;\n            }\n            let cs = ls + ind as usize;\n            let mut cs2 = cs;\n            while cs2 < self.b.len() && is_ws(self.b[cs2]) {\n                cs2 += 1;\n            }\n            if self.b[cs2] == b'#' {\n                break;\n            }\n            let le = self.scan_plain_line(cs2)?;\n            // A continuation line that looks like a mapping key is an error.\n            if le < self.b.len() && self.b[le] == b':' {\n                return self.err(\"mapping value in plain scalar\");\n            }\n            let _ = blank_lines;\n            lines.push((cs2, le));\n            end = le;\n            p = le;\n        }\n        // Check the first line isn't followed by ':' (would be a key).\n        let mut value = String::new();\n        let mut pending_newlines = 0;\n        for (i, (a, b)) in lines.iter().enumerate() {\n            let t = &self.src[*a..*b];\n            if i > 0 {\n                // Count blank lines between previous line and this one.\n                let prev_end = lines[i - 1].1;\n                let between = &self.src[prev_end..*a];\n                let nl = between.matches('\\n').count();\n                pending_newlines = nl;\n                if pending_newlines <= 1 {\n                    value.push(' ');\n                } else {\n                    for _ in 0..pending_newlines - 1 {\n                        value.push('\\n');\n self.line_of(end.saturating_sub(1).max(s));\n        Ok(Node {\n            start: s,\n            end,\n            line,\n            col: self.col_of(s),\n            props: None,\n            kind: Kind::Scalar(Scalar {\n                style: ScalarStyle::Plain,\n                start: s,\n                end,\n                value,\n                multiline: lines.len() > 1,\n                block: None,\n            }),\n            comment: None,\n            flow_has_comment: false,\n            end_line,\n        })\n    }\n\n    /// Scan a plain scalar on one line from `start`; returns end (trailing spaces trimmed).\n    fn scan_plain_line(&self, start: usize) -> PResult<usize> {\n        let le = self.line_end(start);\n        let mut i = start;\n        let mut last_non_ws = start;\n        while i < le {\n            let c = self.b[i];\n            if c == b':' && (i + 1 >= le || matches!(self.b[i + 1], b' ' | b'\\t')) {\n                break;\n            }\n            if c == b'#' && i > start && is_ws(self.b[i - 1]) {\n                break;\n            }\n            if !is_ws(c) {\n                last_non_ws = i + 1;\n            }\n            i += 1;\n        }\n        if i < le && self.b[i] == b':' {\n            // \"key: value\" inside a value position.\n            return Err(ParseError { pos: i, msg: \"unexpected mapping value\".into() });\n        }\n        Ok(last_non_ws)\n    }\n\n    fn parse_block_scalar(&mut self, parent: isize) -> PResult<Node> {\n        let s = self.pos;\n        let line = self.line_of(s);\n        let style = if self.b[s] == b'|' { ScalarStyle::Literal } else { ScalarStyle::Folded };\n        self.pos += 1;\n        let hs = self.pos;\n        let mut indicator = None;\n        let mut chomp = Chomp::Clip;\n        for _ in 0..2 {\n            let c = self.peek();\n            if c.is_ascii_digit() && c != b'0' && indicator.is_none() {\n                indicator = Some((c - b'0') as usize);\n                self.pos += 1;\n            } else if c == b'-' && chomp == Chomp::Clip {\n                chomp = Chomp::Strip;\n                self.pos += 1;\n            } else if c == b'+' && chomp == Chomp::Clip {\n                chomp = Chomp::Keep;\n                self.pos += 1;\n            }\n        }\n        let raw = self.src[hs..self.pos].to_string();\n        let save = self.pos;\n indicator.map(|i| if parent < 0 { i } else { base + i });\n        let first_line = if self.at_eof() { self.line_starts.len() } else { self.line_of(self.pos) };\n        let mut lines: Vec<String> = Vec::new();\n        let mut consumed_end = self.pos;\n        let mut max_leading_blank_indent = 0usize;\n        let mut li = first_line;\n        let mut line_count = 0;\n        while li < self.line_starts.len() {\n            let ls = self.line_starts[li];\n            let le = self.line_end(ls);\n            let text = &self.src[ls..le];\n            let ind = text.len() - text.trim_start_matches(' ').len();\n            let is_blank = text.trim_start_matches(' ').is_empty();\n            if content_indent.is_none() {\n                if is_blank {\n                    max_leading_blank_indent = max_leading_blank_indent.max(ind);\n                    lines.push(String::new());\n                    li += 1;\n                    line_count += 1;\n                    consumed_end = if le < self.b.len() { le + 1 } else { le };\n                    continue;\n                }\n                if (ind as isize) <= parent || (parent < 0 && false) {\n                    break;\n                }\n                if self.is_doc_marker_at(ls) {\n                    break;\n                }\n                if ind < max_leading_blank_indent {\n                    return self.err(\"leading blank lines more indented\");\n                }\n                content_indent = Some(ind);\n            }\n            let ci = content_indent.unwrap();\n            if is_blank {\n                if ind > ci {\n                    lines.push(text[ci..].to_string());\n                } else {\n                    lines.push(String::new());\n                }\n                li += 1;\n                line_count += 1;\n                consumed_end = if le < self.b.len() { le + 1 } else { le };\n                continue;\n            }\n            if ind < ci {\n                break;\n            }\n            if self.is_doc_marker_at(ls) {\n                break;\n            }\n            lines.push(text[ci..].to_string());\n            li += 1;\n            line_count += 1;\n            consumed_end = if le < self.b.len() { le + 1 } else { le };\n        }\n        // Trailing blank lines belong to the scalar only for keep chomping; for others\n        // they are trivia (we still record them as part of scalar span only if keep).\n        let mut content_lines = lines.clone();\n        let mut trailing_blank = 0;\n        while let Some(l) = content_lines.last() {\n            if l.is_empty() {\n                content_lines.pop();\n                trailing_blank += 1;\n            } else {\n                break;\n            }\n        }\n        let value = block_scalar_value(style, &lines, chomp);\n        // Determine node end: for keep chomping, trailing blank lines are part of the node.\n        let (end, kept_lines) = if chomp == Chomp::Keep || content_lines.is_empty() && false {\n            (consumed_end, lines.clone())\n        } else {\n            // End after last non-blank content line.\n            let n_content = lines.len() - trailing_blank;\n            if n_content == 0 {\n                (self.line_end(s), Vec::new())\n            } else {\n                let last_li = first_line + n_content - 1;\n                let ls = self.line_starts[last_li];\n                (self.line_end(ls), lines[..n_content].to_vec())\n            }\n        };\n        // Position: after the consumed content (trailing blank lines become trivia).\n        if chomp == Chomp::Keep {\n            self.pos = consumed_end;\n        } else {\n            let n_content = lines.len() - trailing_blank;\n            if n_content == 0 {\n                // pos already after header line\n            } else {\n                let last_li = first_line + n_content - 1;\n                let ls = self.line_starts[last_li];\n                let le = self.line_end(ls);\n                self.pos = if le < self.b.len() { le + 1 } else { le };\n            }\n        }\n        let _ = line_count;\n        let end_line = self.line_of(end.saturating_sub(1).max(s));\n        let ci = content_indent.unwrap_or(base + 1);\n        Ok(Node {\n            start: s,\n            end,\n            line,\n            col: self.col_of(s),\n            props: None,\n            kind: Kind::Scalar(Scalar {\n                style,\n                start: s,\n                end,\n                value,\n                multiline: true,\n                block: Some(BlockHeader {\n                    indicator,\n                    chomp,\n                    raw,\n                    comment,\n                    content_indent: ci,\n                    lines: kept_lines.clone(),\n                    first_line,\n                    line_count: kept_lines.len(),\n                }),\n            }),\n            comment: None,\n            flow_has_comment: false,\n            end_line,\n        })\n    }\n\n    // ---------------- Flow collections ----------------\n\n    fn skip_flow_ws(&mut self, has_comment: &mut bool) -> PResult<()> {\n        loop {\n            if self.at_eof() {\n                return Ok(());\n            }\n            let c = self.peek();\n            if c == b' ' || c == b'\\t' || c == b'\\n' {\n                self.pos += 1;\n            } else if c == b'#' && self.pos > 0 && matches!(self.b[self.pos - 1], b' ' | b'\\t' | b'\\n') {\n                *has_comment = true;\n                self.pos = self.line_end(self.pos);\n            } else {\n                return Ok(());\n            }\n        }\n    }\n\n    fn parse_flow_collection(&mut self) -> PResult<Node> {\n        let s = self.pos;\n        let line = self.line_of(s);\n        let open = self.b[s];\n        let close = if open == b'[' { b']' } else { b'}' };\n        self.pos += 1;\n        let mut has_comment = false;\n        let mut entries = Vec::new();\n        loop {\n            self.skip_flow_ws(&mut has_comment)?;\n            if self.at_eof() {\n                return self.err(\"unterminated flow collection\");\n            }\n            if self.peek() == close {\n                self.pos += 1;\n                break;\n            }\n            let entry = self.parse_flow_entry(open == b'{', &mut has_comment)?;\n            entries.push(entry);\n            self.skip_flow_ws(&mut has_comment)?;\n            if self.peek() == b',' {\n                self.pos += 1;\n                continue;\n            }\n            if self.peek() == close {\n                self.pos += 1;\n                break;\n Rewrap folded block scalar content lines.\nfn refold_lines(lines: &[String], width: usize) -> Vec<String> {\n    let mut out = Vec::new();\n    let mut para: Vec<&str> = Vec::new();\n    let flush = |para: &mut Vec<&str>, out: &mut Vec<String>| {\n        if para.is_empty() {\n            return;\n        }\n        let joined = para.join(\" \");\n        for l in fill_words(&joined, width) {\n            out.push(l);\n        }\n        para.clear();\n    };\n    for l in lines {\n        if l.is_empty() {\n            flush(&mut para, &mut out);\n            out.push(String::new());\n        } else if l.starts_with(' ') || l.starts_with('\\t') {\n            flush(&mut para, &mut out);\n            out.push(l.clone());\n        } else {\n            para.push(l.as_str());\n        }\n The output format of `--json` may change between minor releases until we stabilize it, see [#112][issue-112].\n\n## Table of Contents\n- [Features](#features)\n- [Installation](#installation)\n   - [From source](#from-source)\n   - [Package managers](#package-managers)\n- [Usage](#usage)\n- [Configuration](#configuration)\n- [FAQ](#faq)\n- [License](#license)\n\n## Features\n* Commit statistics per author, per directory and per time window\n* **Churn report**: files changed most often, with lines added/removed\n+ Bus factor estimation using the \"truck factor\" heuristic from Avelino et al.\n* Pull request lead time (GitHub and GitLab, needs a token)\n* Output as a pretty table, `--json`, or `--csv`\n    * JSON schema is published in `schema/report.schema.json`\n    * CSV output uses `;` as separator when `--locale de` is set\n\n## Installation ##\n\n### Package managers\n\n| Platform | Command | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| macOS (Homebrew) | `brew install gitpulse` | |\n| Arch Linux | `pacman -S gitpulse` | community repo |\n| Windows (Scoop) | `scoop install gitpulse` | needs the `extras` bucket |\n| Nix | `nix profile install nixpkgs#gitpulse`| |\n| Cargo | `cargo install gitpulse --locked` | builds from source, takes ~2 min |\n\n### From source\n\nYou need Rust 1.74 or newer.\n\n```console\n$ git clone https://github.com/example/gitpulse.git\n$ cd gitpulse\n$ cargo build --release\n$ ./target/release/gitpulse --version\ngitpulse 0.9.2\n```\n\n## Usage\n\nRun it inside any git repository:\n\n```sh\ngitpulse                      # summary for the last 90 days\ngitpulse --since 2024-01-01 --until 2024-06-30 --by-author\ngitpulse churn --top 20 src/\ngitpulse bus-factor --threshold 0.5 --json | jq '.files[] | select(.authors < 2)'\n```\n\nExample output:\n\n```text\n Author            Commits   +Lines   -Lines   Files\n ───────────────── ───────── ──────── ──────── ───────\n Ada Lovelace            412    18,204    9,331     287\n Grace Hopper            198     7,850    6,002     143\n (others, 14)             87     2,113    1,560      98\n```\n\n### Options\n\n| Flag | Default | Description |\n|:-----|:-------:|------------:|\n| `--since <DATE>` | 90 days ago | Only consider commits after this date. Accepts ISO dates or relative values like `3 weeks ago`. |\n| `--until <DATE>` | now | Only consider commits before this date |\n| `--by-author` | off | Group by author email (uses `.mailmap` if present) |\n| `--exclude <GLOB>` | | Can be given multiple times; e.g. `--exclude 'vendor/**' --exclude '*.lock'` |\n|`--json`|off|Machine-readable output|\n\n## Configuration\n\ngitpulse looks for a `gitpulse.toml` in the repository root, then in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/gitpulse/config.toml`.\n\n```toml\n[report]\nwindow = \"180d\"\nexclude = [\"vendor/**\", \"*.lock\", \"docs/generated/**\"]\n\n[authors]\n# Merge multiple identities into one\n\"ada@example.com\" = [\"ada.lovelace@users.noreply.github.com\", \"ada@old-company.example\"]\n```\n\n<details>\n<summary>Environment variables</summary>\n\n* `GITPULSE_TOKEN` – GitHub/GitLab token used for pull request statistics\n* `GITPULSE_NO_COLOR` – disable colours (also respects `NO_COLOR`)\n* `GITPULSE_LOG` – log level, e.g. `debug` or `gitpulse=trace`\n\n</details>\n\n## FAQ\n\n**Why is the bus factor different from tool X?**  \nWe exclude merge commits and files that were only touched by bots (`dependabot[bot]`, `renovate[bot]` and anything matching `--bot-pattern`). See the [methodology notes][methodology] for the gory details.\n\n**Does it work on huge monorepos?**\nYes, but use `--since` to limit the window. On the Linux kernel repository (1.2M commits) a full scan takes about 40 seconds on an M2 laptop; with `--since \"1 year ago\"` it takes 3 seconds.\n\n## Contributing\n\nPull requests are welcome! There is no custom DataFrame subclass, no monkey patching and no\nglobal state, so it plays nicely with the rest of the scientific Python ecosystem.\n\nInstallation\n------------\n\n    pip install tidyframe\n\nor, with the optional [Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/) backend:\n\n    pip install \"tidyframe[arrow]\"\n\nQuick start\n-----------\n\n```python\nimport pandas as pd\nimport tidyframe as tf\n\ndf = pd.read_csv(\"penguins.csv\")\n\n(\n    df\n    .pipe(tf.filter_rows, lambda d: d.species != \"Gentoo\")\n    .pipe(tf.mutate, bill_ratio=lambda d: d.bill_length_mm / d.bill_depth_mm)\n    .pipe(tf.summarise, by=\"species\", mean_ratio=(\"bill_ratio\", \"mean\"))\n)\n```\n\nWhy another library?\n--------------------\n\nThere are several excellent projects in this space -- [siuba], [dplython] (unmaintained) and [polars] (a different DataFrame library altogether) -- but each of them either wraps the\nDataFrame in its own type or relies on operator overloading tricks that confuse type checkers and IDEs.\ntidyframe makes different trade-offs:\n\n+ every verb is a plain function with a docstring and type hints\n+ verbs never mutate their input\n+ errors mention the column names you actually passed, e.g. ``KeyError: 'bill_lenght_mm' (did you mean 'bill_length_mm'?)``\n\nSupported versions\n------------------\n\npandas | python | status\n--- | --- | ---\n2.2 | 3.10 - 3.13 | supported\n2.1 | 3.9 - 3.12 | security fixes only\n1.5 | 3.8 - 3.11 | ~~unsupported~~ removed in 0.8\n\nDevelopment\n-----------\n\n1. Works in browsers, Node 18+, Deno and Bun.\n\n## Install\n\n```bash\nnpm i @acme/tiny-fetch\n# or\npnpm add @acme/tiny-fetch\n```\n\n## Usage\n```js\nimport { get, post } from '@acme/tiny-fetch'\n\nconst user = await get('/api/users/42', { timeout: 5_000, retries: 2 })\nawait post('/api/events', { type: 'click', target: '#buy' })\n```\n\n## API\n\n### `get(url, options?)`\n### `post(url, body, options?)`\n\nOptions:\n\n|option|type|default|description|\n|-|-|-|-|\n|`timeout`|`number`|`10000`|Milliseconds before the request is aborted with a `TimeoutError`.|\n|`retries`|`number`|`0`|How many times to retry on network errors and `5xx` responses. Uses exponential backoff with full jitter (base 200 ms, max 5 s).|\n|`headers`|`Record<string, string>`|`{}`|Extra headers merged into the defaults.|\n|`signal`|`AbortSignal`|—|Your own abort signal; combined with the timeout signal.|\n|`parse`|`'json' \\| 'text' \\| 'blob' \\| false`|`'json'`|How to parse the response body.|\n\n__Errors__ are thrown as `HttpError` (with `status`, `statusText` and the parsed `body`) or `TimeoutError`. Widgets is maintained by a small group of volunteers and every bug report, docs fix and pull request genuinely helps.\n\nThe notes below describe how we like to work. They are guidelines rather than hard rules -- use your judgement, and if something here seems wrong or outdated, open a pull request against this file.\n\n#### Table Of Contents\n\n[Code of Conduct](#code-of-conduct)\n\n[I just have a question!](#i-just-have-a-question)\n\n[How Can I Contribute?](#how-can-i-contribute)\n  * [Reporting Bugs](#reporting-bugs)\n  * [Suggesting Enhancements](#suggesting-enhancements)\n  * [Your First Code Contribution](#your-first-code-contribution)\n  * [Pull Requests](#pull-requests)\n\n[Styleguides](#styleguides)\n  * [Git Commit Messages](#git-commit-messages)\n  * [Python Styleguide](#python-styleguide)\n  * [Documentation Styleguide](#documentation-styleguide)\n\n## Code of Conduct\n\nEveryone taking part in this project is expected to follow the [Widgets Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Please report unacceptable behaviour to [conduct@example.com](mailto:conduct@example.com).\n\n## I just have a question!\n\n> **Note:** please don't open an issue just to ask a question -- you'll get a faster answer in one of the places below.\n\n* [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/acme/widgets/discussions), where most of the maintainers hang out\n* The [FAQ](https://widgets.example.com/faq), which covers the questions we get asked most often\n* The `#widgets` channel on the community chat server\n\n## How Can I Contribute?\n\n### Reporting Bugs\n\nBefore filing a bug, search the [existing issues](https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues?q=is%3Aissue) -- somebody may already have reported it, and a :+1: reaction on an existing issue helps us prioritise. If you do open a new one, fill in the issue template as completely as you can.\n\n#### What makes a good bug report?\n\nBugs are tracked as GitHub issues. When you create one, please:\n\n* **Use a clear and descriptive title.**\n* **List the exact steps to reproduce the problem.** Include the command you ran, the relevant part of your `widgets.yml`, and the full error message or traceback.\n* **Describe what you expected to happen**, and what happened instead.\n* **Include your environment**: OS, Python version, and the output of `widgets --version`.\n* If the problem started after an upgrade, tell us the last version that worked.\n\n### Suggesting Enhancements\n\nEnhancement suggestions are tracked as GitHub issues too. Explain the problem you are trying to solve *before* describing the solution you have in mind; there is often more than one way to address a use case, and the best one is not always the first one that comes to mind.\n\n### Your First Code Contribution\n\nNot sure where to start? Have a look at these labels:\n\n1. [Good first issues][good-first] - small, well-defined issues that should only need a few lines of code and a test.\n2. [Help wanted][help-wanted] - somewhat larger issues where we would welcome outside help.\n3) Documentation issues - typos, unclear wording, missing examples.\n\n#### Local development\n\n```shell\ngit clone https://github.com/acme/widgets && cd widgets\nmake dev        # creates .venv and installs pre-commit hooks\nmake test       # runs pytest with coverage\nmake docs-serve # live-reloading docs on http://127.0.0.1:8000\n```\n\n### Pull Requests\n\nA few things that make reviews go smoothly:\n\n- Keep pull requests focused. One bug fix or feature per PR is much easier to review than a mixed bag.\n- Add or update tests for any behaviour change.\n- Update the documentation if you change user-facing behaviour.\n- Add an entry to `CHANGELOG.md` under *Unreleased*.\n\nPlease follow these steps to have your contribution considered by the maintainers:\n\n1. Fill in [the pull request template](PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md)\n2. Follow the [styleguides](#styleguides)\n3. With the `memory` backend the cache lives inside the server process and is lost on restart, which is fine for development but rarely what you want in production where you typically run several worker processes behind a load balancer and want them to share a cache.\n\nThe `redis` backend accepts any URL understood by [redis-py](https://redis-py.readthedocs.io/en/stable/connections.html#redis.Redis.from_url), including `rediss://` for TLS and `unix://` sockets.\nThe `disk` backend stores pickled results under `.widgets-cache/`; it is safe to delete that directory at any time.\n\n### Cache invalidation\n\nYou can invalidate the cache:\n\n- per data source, by bumping `cache.version` in the data source definition,\n- globally, by running `widgets cache clear`, or\n- programmatically through the REST endpoint `POST /api/cache/clear` (requires the `admin` role).\n\n## Logging\n\nLogging follows the standard library's [`logging.config.dictConfig`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.config.html#logging-config-dictschema) schema, so anything you can express there you can put under the `logging` key:\n\n```yaml\nlogging:\n  version: 1\n  root: { level: INFO, handlers: [console] }\n  handlers:\n    console: { class: logging.StreamHandler, formatter: plain }\n  formatters:\n    plain: { format: \"%(asctime)s %(levelname)-8s %(name)s: %(message)s\" }\n```\n\n[^1]: Or the file passed with `--config`. Fourteen months later\nevery service emits OpenTelemetry, the old collectors are switched off, and our observability bill is\ndown by roughly a third. This post is about the parts that went well, the parts that did not,\nand the things we would do differently if we started again tomorrow.\n\n## Why bother?\n\nThe short answer is vendor lock-in. The longer answer is that each of our three tracing libraries had its own idea of what a \"service name\" was, which made cross-team traces nearly useless: a request that went from the storefront through the checkout service into the payment gateway would show up as three disconnected traces in two different tools.\n\n## Phase 1: the collector\n\nWe rolled out the OpenTelemetry Collector as a DaemonSet first, before touching a single\nline of application code.     That gave us a single place to\nreceive, transform and export telemetry, and let us dual-write to the old and new backends\nfor a few months.\n\n> The best migration is one where nobody notices the cut-over. Some numbers:\n\n* 412 services in total\n   * 290 Java (Spring Boot), most of which just needed the Java agent\n   * 85 Go, which needed actual code changes\n   * 37 Python, Node and \"other\"\n* 3 services we decided to retire instead of migrating\n\nThe Go services were the hardest. Unlike Java, there is no agent that magically instruments everything, so every HTTP handler, every database call and every Kafka consumer had to be wrapped by hand -- or, more often, by a codemod we wrote for the purpose and then spent weeks debugging. If you are about to do the same, look at [the contrib instrumentation packages](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-contrib/tree/main/instrumentation) first; many of the wrappers we wrote turned out to exist already.\n\n## What we'd do differently\n\n\n1. Agree on semantic conventions *before* writing code.\n2. Budget for the collector's memory. Seriously.\n3. Turn on tail sampling earlier -- it cut our span volume by 80%.\n\n---\n\n*Thanks to everyone on the platform team, and to the 60+ service owners who reviewed our pull requests. Most projects will be able to upgrade by changing a handful of lines, but a few long-deprecated APIs are finally gone.  This guide lists everything you need to check, roughly ordered from \"affects everyone\" to \"affects almost nobody\".\n\n**TL;DR**\n\n1. Upgrade to the latest 2.x release first and fix all deprecation warnings.\n2. Run `widgets migrate --check` -- it reports everything that needs to change.\n3. Both old names still work in 3.0 but emit a warning; they will stop working in 3.1.\n\nSeveral keys were renamed:\n\n| 2.x | 3.0 |\n|-----|-----|\n| `port` | `server.port` |\n| `host` | `server.host` |\n| `cache_type` | `cache.backend` |\n| `redis_url` | `cache.url` |\n| `debug` | *removed* — use `--log-level debug` |\n\nBefore:\n\n```yaml\nport: 8080\ncache_type: redis\nredis_url: \"redis://localhost:6379/0\"\ndebug: true\n```\n\nAfter:\n\n```yaml\nserver:\n  port: 8080\ncache:\n  backend: redis\n  url: redis://localhost:6379/0\n```\n\nPython API\n----------\n\n### `Dashboard.render()` returns a `RenderResult`\n\nIn 2.x, `render()` returned an HTML string. It now returns a `RenderResult` object with `.html`, `.assets` and `.warnings` attributes. That's fine! But at some point other\npeople want to use it, and then you need a proper command line interface, help text, tests, and a way to\ninstall it that doesn't involve \"copy this file somewhere on your PATH and hope\". This tutorial walks\nthrough that transition step by step, using a small but real example: a tool that finds duplicate files.\n\nContents\n--------\n\n1. [The starting point](#the-starting-point)\n2. [Adding a CLI with argparse](#adding-a-cli-with-argparse)\n3. [Packaging](#packaging)\n4. [Testing](#testing)\n5. [Publishing](#publishing)\n\nThe starting point\n------------------\n\nHere is the script we start from. It walks a directory tree, hashes every file, and prints groups of files with identical hashes:\n\n~~~python\nimport hashlib, os, sys\nfrom collections import defaultdict\n\nhashes = defaultdict(list)\nfor root, dirs, files in os.walk(sys.argv[1]):\n    for name in files:\n        path = os.path.join(root, name)\n        with open(path, \"rb\") as f:\n            hashes[hashlib.sha256(f.read()).hexdigest()].append(path)\n\nfor h, paths in hashes.items():\n    if len(paths) > 1:\n        print(h[:12], *paths, sep=\"\\n  \")\n~~~\n\nIt works, but it has problems:\n\n* it reads every file completely into memory (try it on a directory with a 20 GB video file...)\n* there is no `--help`\n* errors (permission denied, broken symlinks) crash the whole thing\n* it hashes *every* file, even though files of different sizes can't possibly be duplicates\n\nLet's fix these one at a time.\n\nAdding a CLI with argparse\n--------------------------\n\nThe standard library's `argparse` is perfectly adequate for a tool of this size.  Third-party libraries like [Click](https://click.palletsprojects.com/) or [Typer](https://typer.tiangolo.com/) are nicer for big CLIs with many sub-commands, but they are an extra dependency, and for a single command `argparse` is hard to beat.\n\n```python\nimport argparse\n\ndef parse_args(argv=None):\n    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog=\"dupfind\", description=\"Find duplicate files.\")\n    p.add_argument(\"paths\", nargs=\"+\", help=\"directories to scan\")\n    p.add_argument(\"--min-size\", type=int, default=1, metavar=\"BYTES\",\n                   help=\"ignore files smaller than this (default: %(default)s)\")\n    p.add_argument(\"--json\", action=\"store_true\", help=\"print results as JSON\")\n    return p.parse_args(argv)\n```\n\n> **Tip:** always accept an `argv` parameter in `parse_args`. It makes the function trivial to test,\n> because you can pass a list of strings instead of patching `sys.argv`.\n\n### Hashing in chunks\n\nReading in chunks keeps memory use constant:\n\n    def file_hash(path, chunk_size=1 << 20):\n        h = hashlib.sha256()\n        with open(path, \"rb\") as f:\n            while chunk := f.read(chunk_size):\n                h.update(chunk)\n        return h.hexdigest()\n\n### Grouping by size first ###\n\nTwo files can only be identical if they have the same size, and `os.stat` is\n*much* cheaper than reading the file.  So we group by size first, and only hash files\nwhose size is shared with at least one other file.  On my laptop's home\ndirectory (412,000 files) this reduces the number of files hashed from 412,000 to about\n31,000 and the run time from 4 min 10 s to 22 s.\n\nPackaging\n---------\n\nCreate a \"Find duplicate files, fast.\"\nreadme = \"README.md\"\nrequires-python = \">=3.10\"\nlicense = \"MIT\"\nauthors = [{ name = \"Kim Example\", email = \"kim@example.com\" }]\n\n[project.scripts]\ndupfind = \"dupfind.cli:main\"\n```\n\nThe `[project.scripts]` table is the important part: it tells the installer to create a `dupfind` executable that calls `main()` in `dupfind/cli.py`.\n\nThe project layout should look like this:\n\n```\ndupfind/\n├── pyproject.toml\n├── README.md\n├── src/\n│   └── dupfind/\n│       ├── __init__.py\n│       └── cli.py\n└── tests/\n    └── test_cli.py\n```\n\nInstall it in editable mode while you work on it:\n\n```console\n$ python -m pip install -e .\n$ dupfind --help\nusage: dupfind [-h] [--min-size BYTES] [--json] paths [paths ...]\n```\n\nTesting\n-------\n\nUse `pytest` and its `tmp_path` fixture to create throwaway directory trees:\n\n```python\ndef test_finds_duplicates(tmp_path, capsys):\n    (tmp_path / json.loads(capsys.readouterr().out)\n    assert len(out) == 1\n    assert sorted(Path(p).name for p in out[0][\"paths\"]) == [\"a.txt\", \"b.txt\"]\n```\n\nThings worth testing, roughly in order of importance:\n\n1) the happy path (duplicates are found)\n2) no false positives (same size, different content)\n3) unreadable files are skipped with a warning, not a crash\n4) `--min-size` is A Bayesian analysis answers that question directly, and for\nconversion rates the maths is simple enough to do in your head (almost).\n\n## The Beta-Binomial model\n\nIf a variant has $n$ visitors and $k$ conversions, and our prior belief about its conversion rate $p$ is $\\text{Beta}(\\alpha, \\beta)$, then the posterior is\n\n$$\np \\mid k, n \\sim \\text{Beta}(\\alpha + k,\\; \\beta + n - k).\n$$\n\nThat's it -- no MCMC, no Stan, no tears. See @gelman2013 [ch. 2] for the derivation.\n\n## A simulation\n\n```{r}\n#| label: sim\n#| code-fold: show\nset.seed(42)\na <- rbeta(1e5, 1 + 120, 1 + 2400 - 120)\nb <- rbeta(1e5, 1 + 145, 1 + 2380 - 145)\nmean(b > a)\n```\n\nSo, given the data and a flat prior, there is roughly a `r round(100 * mean(b > a))`% probability that B converts better than A.\n\n::: {.callout-important}\n## Don't peek (too much)\nBayesian methods are *less* sensitive to optional stopping than frequentist ones, but they are not immune. If you check the results every hour and stop as soon as $P(B > A) > 0.95$, you will still fool yourself more often than you expect [@rouder2014].\n:::\n\n## Further reading\n\n- @kruschke2014 is the friendliest book-length introduction.\n- For a more industry-focused take, the [Evan Miller blog post on Bayesian A/B testing](https://www.evanmiller.org/bayesian-ab-testing.html) is a classic.\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":6019,"cache_read_input_tokens":261185,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":6019,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_01YSZyvozuLDHz9NNwzY6xEb","agent_id":"a9a9cf5649f5457bc","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"0d3608a7-29d3-45cb-b32e-4134af6470cd","timestamp":"2026-11-17T11:42:27.485Z","request_id":"req_011Ch8SS2y1xSo8NaJJi94gP","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Generate realistic test corpus"}

How many days are there between 1 February and 1 March? It depends on the year. What time is it in Sydney when it's 9 am in London? It depends on the day, because the two cities switch to daylight saving time in opposite halves of the year. This chapter shows how to handle these questions in R without losing your mind; we'll build on it in @sec-time-series and @sec-joins-by-time.\n\n## Parsing dates\n\nMost dates arrive as strings[^iso]. The **lubridate** functions `ymd()`, `dmy()`, `mdy()` and friends are named after the order of the components, and they're forgiving about separators:\n\n```{r}\nymd(\"2026-03-14\")\ndmy(\"14/03/2026\")\nmdy(\"March 14th, 2026\")\n```\n\n[^iso]: If you get to choose the format, choose ISO 8601 (`YYYY-MM-DD`). It sorts correctly as text, and nobody can misread `2026-03-04` as April 3rd.\n\nIf the string also contains a time, add the time components to the function name, e.g. `ymd_hms()`.  The result is a date-time (class `POSIXct`), which by default is in UTC -- [a common source of confusion]{.mark} when your data was recorded in local time.\n\n### Time zones\n\n```{r}\n#| label: tz-example\nx <- ymd_hms(\"2026-03-29 00:30:00\", tz = \"Europe/London\")\nx + hours(1)\nwith_tz(x, \"Australia/Sydney\")\n```\n\nNotice anything odd? 29 March 2026 is the day the UK switches to summer time, so one hour after 00:30 GMT is 02:30 BST.\n\n::: {.callout-tip appearance=\"minimal\"}\n`OlsonNames()` lists every time zone name R knows about. There are more than 590 of them.\n:::\n\n## Arithmetic\n\nlubridate distinguishes three kinds of time spans:\n\n* **durations** are an exact number of seconds (`ddays(1)` is always 86,400 s),\n* **periods** are human units like \"one month\", whose length in seconds depends on when they start,\n* **intervals** have a fixed start and end.\n\n| You want to... | Use |\n|:--|:--|\n| add \"one month\" to a billing date | a period: `%m+% months(1)` |\n| measure how long a job ran | a duration |\n| check whether a timestamp falls inside a maintenance window | an interval and `%within%` |\n\n## Exercises {.unnumbered}\n\n1. It is weaker than replicability, which requires new data. Despite the increasing availability of code, several studies have found that a majority of published analyses cannot be reproduced without help from the original authors [@stodden2018; @trisovic2022].\n\nJournals have responded in different ways. Some, e.g. the *Journal of Statistical Software*, have long required code; others merely encourage it. Since 2022, the two journals in our sample have required authors to deposit code and data, except where data are confidential.\n\n# Methods\n\nWe drew a random sample of 60 articles from the `r nrow(results)` eligible articles published in 2023. Two of us (A.E. and S.S.) independently attempted to reproduce the main result of each article, defined as the first numerical result reported in the abstract. Each reproduction was capped at eight hours of work. We used R 4.3.2 and the package versions current on 1 Jan. 2024 unless the authors specified otherwise, e.g. via `renv.lock`.\n\n```{r tab-outcomes}\nresults %>%\n  count(outcome) %>%\n  mutate(pct = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 1)) %>%\n  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, caption = \"Reproduction outcomes.\", col.names = c(\"Outcome\", \"n\", \"%\")) %>%\n  kable_styling(latex_options = \"HOLD_position\")\n```\n\n# Results\n\nTable \\ref{tab:tab-outcomes} summarises the outcomes. The most common obstacles were missing data files (n = 9), undocumented dependencies (n = 7), and hard-coded absolute paths, e.g. `C:/Users/...` (n = 6). Interestingly, articles that used **renv** or Docker were not significantly more likely to reproduce (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.21), though the sample was small.\n\n# Discussion\n\nOur results are broadly consistent with those of @trisovic2022, who found that a large share of R scripts deposited in a public data repository failed to run without error. Okafor\"\n    orcid: 0000-0002-1825-0097\ndate: \"2024-05-02\"\nabstract: |\n  We describe the conjugate Beta-Binomial model used by the experimentation platform to report conversion-rate experiments, derive the probability that the treatment beats control, and compare the closed-form approximation with Monte Carlo estimates.  The approximation error is below 0.5 percentage points for all experiments with at least 200 conversions per arm.\nformat:\n  pdf:\n    documentclass: article\n    classoption: [11pt, twocolumn]\n    geometry:\n      - top=25mm\n      - left=20mm\n      - right=20mm\n      - bottom=25mm\n    number-sections: true\n    colorlinks: true\n    include-in-header:\n      text: |\n        \\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb}\n        \\usepackage{bm}\n  html:\n    html-math-method: katex\nexecute:\n  echo: false\n  freeze: auto\nbibliography: abtesting.bib\n---\n\n# Model #\n\nLet $n_A, n_B$ be the number of users exposed to control and treatment, and $k_A, k_B$ the number who converted.  With independent $\\text{Beta}(\\alpha_0, \\beta_0)$ priors on the conversion rates $p_A$ and $p_B$, the posteriors are\n\n$$\np_j \\mid k_j \\sim \\text{Beta}(\\alpha_0 + k_j,\\; \\beta_0 + n_j - k_j), \\qquad j \\in \\{A, B\\}.\n$$ {#eq-posterior}\n\nWe use the weakly informative prior $\\alpha_0 = \\beta_0 = 1$ throughout, as recommended by @gelman2013 for rates that are not close to 0 or 1.\n\n## Probability to beat control\n\nThe quantity reported in the dashboard is $\\Pr(p_B > p_A \\mid \\text{data})$.  @evanmiller2014 gives an exact expression as a finite sum,\n\n$$\n\\Pr(p_B > p_A) = \\sum_{i=0}^{\\alpha_B - 1} \\frac{B(\\alpha_A + i,\\, \\beta_A + \\beta_B)}{(\\beta_B + i)\\, B(1 + i,\\, \\beta_B)\\, B(\\alpha_A,\\, \\beta_A)},\n$$ {#eq-exact}\n\nbut evaluating @eq-exact is slow when $\\alpha_B$ is in the tens of thousands.  Instead we use a normal approximation to each posterior:\n$\\mu_j = \\alpha_j / (\\alpha_j + \\beta_j)$ and $\\sigma_j^2 = \\mu_j (1-\\mu_j) / (\\alpha_j + \\beta_j + 1)$, so that\n\n$$\n\\Pr(p_B > p_A) \\approx \\Phi\\!\\left(\\frac{\\mu_B - \\mu_A}{\\sqrt{\\sigma_A^2 + \\sigma_B^2}}\\right).\n$$ {#eq-approx}\n\n# Validation\n\n```{r}\n#| label: sim\n#| cache: true\nset.seed(2024)\nsim <- purrr::map_dfr(1:2000, function(i) {\n  n  <- sample(c(500, 2000, 10000, 50000), 1)\n  pA <- runif(1, 0.01, 0.2)\n  pB <- pA * runif(1, 0.9, 1.15)\n  kA <- rbinom(1, n, pA); kB <- rbinom(1, n, pB)\n  draws_A <- rbeta(4000, 1 + kA, 1 + n - kA)\n  draws_B <- rbeta(4000, 1 + kB, 1 + n - kB)\n  mu <- c((1 + kA) / (2 + n), (1 + kB) / (2 + n))\n  s2 <- mu * (1 - mu) / (3 + n)\n  tibble::tibble(n = n, conv = min(kA, kB),\n                 mc = mean(draws_B > draws_A),\n                 approx = pnorm((mu[2] - mu[1]) / sqrt(sum(s2))))\n})\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-error\n#| fig-cap: \"Absolute difference between the normal approximation (@eq-approx) and a Monte Carlo estimate with 4,000 draws, by number of conversions in the smaller arm.\"\n#| fig-width: 3.3\n#| fig-height: 2.6\nlibrary(ggplot2)\nggplot(sim, aes(conv, abs(approx - mc))) +\n  geom_point(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.3) +\n  scale_x_log10() +\n  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.005, linetype = 2) +\n  labs(x = \"conversions (log scale)\", y = \"|error|\")\n```\n\nThe approximation error (@fig-error) is dominated by Monte Carlo noise once both arms have more than about 200 conversions; below that it can reach 2--3 percentage points, so the dashboard falls back to the exact sum (@eq-exact) for small experiments.@@T2@@\n\n::: {.callout-note appearance=\"simple\"}\nMonte Carlo noise alone has a standard deviation of $\\sqrt{p(1-p)/4000} \\le 0.8$ percentage points.\n:::\n\n# References {.unnumbered}\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":6490,"cache_read_input_tokens":237605,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":6490,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_011qvFM8ooWwccE2sMgLd4oL","agent_id":"a033d36cafcb1facd","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"5d24a05f-c20f-4fb6-a4d8-8df3e1c7bb3c","timestamp":"2026-11-17T14:44:37.304Z","request_id":"req_011Ch8gJmsrLffgLRXjPyy2C","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Generate third test corpus"}

Instead we start with a guess $\\theta_0$ and repeatedly take a small step *downhill*, i.e. in the direction of the negative gradient of the loss $L(\\theta)$:\n\n$$\n\\theta_{t+1} = \\theta_t - \\eta \\, \\nabla L(\\theta_t)\n$$ {#eq-update}\n\nwhere $\\eta > 0$ is the **learning rate**.  Choosing $\\eta$ well is most of the art, as @fig-rates shows.\n\n```{python}\n#| label: setup\n#| echo: false\nimport numpy as np\nimport matplotlib.pyplot as plt\nrng = np.random.default_rng(4)\n```\n\n## A one-dimensional example\n\nTake $L(\\theta) = (\\theta - 3)^2 + 1$, so $\\nabla L(\\theta) = 2(\\theta - 3)$ and the minimum is at $\\theta^* = 3$.\n\n```{python}\n#| label: fig-rates\n#| fig-cap: \"Gradient descent on a quadratic with three learning rates\"\n#| warning: false\ndef descend(eta, theta0=-4.0, steps=25):\n    path = [theta0]\n    for _ in range(steps):\n        path.append(path[-1] - eta * 2 * (path[-1] - 3))\n    return np.array(path)\n\nfig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))\nfor eta, style in [(0.05, \":\"), (0.4, \"-\"), (1.02, \"--\")]:\n    ax.plot(descend(eta), style, label=f\"eta = {eta}\")\nax.axhline(3, color=\"grey\", linewidth=0.8)\nax.set_xlabel(\"iteration\"); ax.set_ylabel(\"theta\"); ax.legend()\n```\n\n| learning rate | behaviour | steps to reach $|\\theta - 3| < 0.01$ |\n|:--|:--|--:|\n| 0.05 | slow, monotone | ~ 70 |\n| 0.4 | fast, monotone | 7 |\n| 1.02 | diverges (oscillates with growing amplitude) | never |\n\n: Effect of the learning rate in @fig-rates {#tbl-rates}\n\n::: {.callout-important}\nFor this quadratic, any $\\eta > 1$ diverges.  In general the safe range depends on the curvature of $L$: for a function whose gradient is $\\beta$-Lipschitz, $\\eta < 2/\\beta$ guarantees convergence.\n:::\n\n## Stochastic gradient descent\n\nWith $n$ training examples the loss is an average, $L(\\theta) = \\frac{1}{n}\\sum_i \\ell_i(\\theta)$, and computing the full gradient costs $O(n)$ per step.  SGD replaces it with the gradient on a random **mini-batch** $B$:\n\n* cheaper steps, so many more of them per second\n* noisy steps -- which, perhaps surprisingly, often *helps* by kicking the parameters out of sharp minima\n* requires a decaying learning rate (or momentum) to converge exactly@@T2@@\n\n::: {.callout-tip collapse=\"true\"}\n## Exercise 4.1\nModify `descend()` to add momentum, $v_{t+1} = \\mu v_t - \\eta \\nabla L(\\theta_t)$, $\\theta_{t+1} = \\theta_t + v_{t+1}$, and find a value of $\\mu$ for which $\\eta = 1.02$ no longer diverges. Schemas are ordinary Python data structures, error messages point at the exact path that failed, and there is no code generation, metaclass magic or compiled extension.\n\nInstallation\n------------\n\n```\npip install tinyschema\n```\n\ntinyschema supports Python 3.9 and newer, including PyPy.\n\nQuick start\n-----------\n\n```python\nfrom tinyschema import Schema, Optional, Range, OneOf, Email\n\nuser = Schema({\n    \"name\": str,\n    \"email\": Email(),\n    \"age\": Range(int, min=13, max=130),\n    Optional(\"role\", default=\"viewer\"): OneOf(\"viewer\", \"editor\", \"admin\"),\n    Optional(\"tags\"): [str],\n})\n\nuser.validate({\"name\": \"Ada\", \"email\": \"ada@example.org\", \"age\": 36})\n# -> {'name': 'Ada', 'email': 'ada@example.org', 'age': 36, 'role': 'viewer'}\n\nuser.validate({\"name\": \"Bob\", \"email\": \"not-an-email\", \"age\": 7})\n# tinyschema.ValidationError: 2 errors\n#   email: not a valid e-mail address: 'not-an-email'\n#   age: must be >= 13, got 7\n```\n\nWhy another validation library?\n-------------------------------\n\n+ **No classes required.**  A schema is a dict, a list, a type, or a callable.\n+ **Errors you can show to users.**  Every error has a `path` (e.g. `(\"servers\", 2, \"port\")`) and a human-readable `message`; `ValidationError.as_dict()` gives you a JSON-friendly structure.\n+ **Coercion is opt-in.**  `Coerce(int)` turns `\"42\"` into `42`; plain `int` does not.\n+ **Small.**  Read the whole source in an afternoon.@@T2@@\n\n| | tinyschema | voluptuous | pydantic v2 |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Dependencies | 0 | 0 | 2 (incl. compiled core) |\n| Schema style | data | data | classes |\n| Import time | ~4 ms | ~6 ms | ~60 ms |\n| JSON Schema export | yes | no | yes |\n\nDocumentation\n-------------\n\nFull documentation is at **https://tinyschema.readthedocs.io**, including:\n\n1. a tutorial\n2. the API reference\n3. recipes:\n    * validating environment variables\n    * validating CSV files row by row with good error messages\n    * migrating from voluptuous\n\n\n\nDevelopment\n-----------\n\n```bash\ngit clone https://github.com/tinyschema/tinyschema\ncd tinyschema\npython -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate\npip install -e '.[dev]'\npytest\n```\n\nLicense\n-------\n\nBSD 3-Clause. When a signal changes, Lattice updates those DOM nodes directly: there is no virtual DOM, no diffing, and components run *once*.\n\nThe API will feel familiar if you've used Solid, Preact Signals or Vue's Composition API, but Lattice is deliberately smaller: the whole runtime is around 4 kB min+gzip, and the template compiler is optional.\n\n## Table of Contents\n- [Features](#features)\n- [Installation](#installation)\n- [Quick start](#quick-start)\n- [Core concepts](#core-concepts)\n- [API overview](#api-overview)\n- [FAQ](#faq)\n- [License](#license)\n\n## Features\n\n* **Signals, computeds and effects** with automatic dependency tracking\n* **Components that run once**; only the bits of DOM that depend on changed signals are touched\n* Tagged template literals (`` html`...` ``) *or* JSX via the optional compiler\n* Keyed list rendering with `<For>` and conditional rendering with `<Show>`\n* Server-side rendering to string and streaming, with partial hydration\n* First-class TypeScript types\n+ Works without a build step: import it from a CDN and go\n\n## Installation\n\n```bash\nnpm install lattice-js\n# or\npnpm add lattice-js\n```\n\nFor JSX support add the compiler plugin for your bundler:\n\n```js\n// vite.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"vite\";\nimport lattice from \"@lattice-js/vite-plugin\";\n\nexport default defineConfig({\n  plugins: [lattice()],\n});\n```\n\nOr without any tooling at all:\n\n```html\n<script type=\"module\">\n  import { signal, html, mount } from \"https://esm.sh/lattice-js@2\";\n  const count = signal(0);\n  mount(document.body, () => html`<button onclick=${() => count.value++}>Clicked ${count} times</button>`);\n</script>\n```\n\n## Quick start\n\n```jsx\nimport { signal, computed, effect, mount } from \"lattice-js\";\n\nfunction TodoApp() {\n  const todos = signal([]);\n  const text = signal(\"\");\n  const remaining = computed(() => todos.value.filter((t) => !t.done).length);\n\n  effect(() => {\n    document.title = `${remaining.value} left`;\n  });\n\n  const add = (e) => {\n    e.preventDefault();\n    if (!text.value.trim()) return;\n    todos.value = [...todos.value, { id: crypto.randomUUID(), title: text.value, done: false }];\n    text.value = \"\";\n  };\n\n  return (\n    <form onSubmit={add}>\n      <input value={text} onInput={(e) => (text.value = e.target.value)} />\n      <For each={todos}>{(todo) => <li class={{ done: todo.done }}>{todo.title}</li>}</For>\n      <p>{remaining} remaining</p>\n    </form>\n  );\n}\n\nmount(document.getElementById(\"app\"), TodoApp);\n```\n\n## Core concepts\n\n1. **Signals** hold state. Read with `.value` (or call them inside templates), write by assigning to `.value`.\n2. **Computeds** derive state from other signals and are cached until a dependency changes.\n3. **Effects** run side effects whenever the signals they read change.  They are automatically disposed when the owning component unmounts.\n4. **Components** are plain functions that return DOM (via JSX or `html`).  They run exactly once per instance -- put reactive reads *inside* the template or an effect, not at the top of the component body, or they won't update.\n\n> [!TIP]\n> If something isn't updating, the cause is almost always point 4.  The dev build logs a warning when a signal is read outside of a tracking scope during render.\n\n## API overview\n\n| Function | Purpose | Since |\n|:---|:---|:--:|\n| `signal(value)` | Create a writable reactive value | 1.0 |\n| `computed(fn)` | Derived, cached value | 1.0 |\n| `effect(fn)` | Run side effects on change; returns a dispose function | 1.0 |\n| `batch(fn)` | Group several writes into one update | 1.2 |\n| `untracked(fn)` | Read signals without subscribing | 1.3 |\n| `mount(el, Component)` | Render a component into a DOM element | 1.0 |\n| `renderToString(Component)` | SSR | 2.0 |\n| `hydrate(el, Component)`|Attach to server-rendered HTML|2.0|\n\n### Comparison\n\n|  | Lattice | Solid | Preact + Signals | Svelte 5 |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Runtime size (min+gz) | ~4 kB | ~7 kB | ~5.5 kB | ~3 kB + compiled output |\n| Virtual DOM | no | no | yes | no |\n| Requires compiler | no | yes (JSX) | no | yes |\n| Components re-run on update | no | no | yes | no |\n\nLattice targets evergreen browsers (last 2 versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari) and Node.js 18+ for SSR.  It uses `Proxy`, `WeakRef` and ES2020 syntax; there is no IE11 build and there won't be one.@@T1@@\n\n## FAQ\n\n<details>\n<summary>Why not just use Solid?</summary>\n\nSolid is great, and Lattice borrows a lot of ideas from it! Allotment gardens are a particularly interesting case: they are small, intensively managed, and extremely heterogeneous, i.e. two neighbouring plots may differ completely in what is grown and how. Previous work by Baldock et al. (2019) found that allotments supported more bee species per unit area than any other urban land-use type they surveyed! But does this hold in a northern European city with a short growing season? That is the question we set out to answer in the 2023 season.\n\nWe surveyed `r n_distinct(visits$plot_id)` plots in `r n_distinct(visits$site)` allotment sites in Uppsala between May and September. Each plot was visited on average 6.5 times (range 4--9), and each visit consisted of a 15-minute timed observation of a 2 x 2 m quadrat. In total we recorded `r format(nrow(visits), big.mark = \",\")` flower visits.@@T2@@\n\n## Research questions\n\n1. Does pollinator visitation rate depend on the proportion of flowering ornamentals vs. vegetables on a plot?\n2. Is there a difference between plots managed with and without pesticides (as reported by the gardeners themselves)?\n3. Which plant taxa attract the most visits per flower-hour?\n\n# Methods\n\nObservations were made by two trained observers (Dr. Berglund and a research assistant) on dry days with temperatures above 15 °C and wind speeds below 5 m/s. Insects were identified to the lowest taxonomic level possible in the field, which was usually genus for bees and family for flies. Specimens that could not be identified were photographed and, where necessary, collected for later identification by Dr. M. Lindqvist at the Swedish Museum of Natural History.\n\nThe gardeners were asked a short set of questions about their management, e.g. \"Have you used any insecticide on this plot during the last 12 months?\" and \"Roughly what share of the plot is used for flowers?\". Self-reported pesticide use is obviously imperfect -- some gardeners may not consider soap sprays or slug pellets to be pesticides -- so we treat this variable with some caution.\n\n```{r model, echo=FALSE}\nm <- glmer(visits ~ flower_share + pesticide + (1 | site/plot_id),\n           offset = log(minutes), family = poisson, data = visits)\nest <- fixef(m)\n```\n\nWe fitted a Poisson GLMM with plot nested in site as random effects and observation time as an offset. The estimated effect of flower share was `r round(est[\"flower_share\"], 2)` on the log scale, i.e. a plot with 50% flowers had roughly `r round(exp(0.5 * est[\"flower_share\"]), 1)` times as many visits as a plot with none. Fig. 1 shows the raw data.\n\n```{r fig-visits, fig.cap=\"Visits per hour against the share of the plot used for flowers. Each point is one plot-visit.\"}\nggplot(visits, aes(flower_share, visits / minutes * 60)) +\n  geom_jitter(width = 0.01, alpha = 0.4) +\n  geom_smooth(method = \"glm\", method.args = list(family = quasipoisson)) +\n  labs(x = \"Share of plot with flowers\", y = \"Visits per hour\")\n```\n\n# Results\n\nVisitation increased strongly with flower share, as expected. The effect of pesticide use was smaller than we had anticipated and its confidence interval included zero (see Table 1). Why might that be? One explanation is that few gardeners reported regular use: only 14 of the plots (approx. 11%) were in the \"frequent use\" category. Another is that pesticide use is correlated with growing vegetables, so part of its effect is already absorbed by the flower share term.\n\n```{r tbl-coef}\nbroom.mixed::tidy(m, effects = \"fixed\", conf.int = TRUE) |>\n  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = \"Table 1. Fixed effects (log scale).\")\n```\n\nThe most-visited taxa per flower-hour were:\n\n- *Phacelia tanacetifolia* -- by far the most attractive, especially for bumblebees\n- *Borago officinalis*\n- Various *Origanum* cultivars\n  - note: the wild type was much more attractive than the golden-leaved cultivar!\n\n# Discussion\n\nOur results broadly agree with Baldock et al. and with the meta-analysis by Wenzel et al. (2020): flowers matter, and they matter a lot. \"Plant more flowers\" is not exactly a surprising recommendation, but it is a cheap and popular one, and the allotment associations we worked with were keen to share it with their members. Future work should look at nesting resources, which we did not measure at all. Should allotment associations allow bare soil patches and dead wood? If you have ever wrestled with a matrix of 2,151 columns named `X350`, `X351`, ..., `X2500`, this package is for you! The core idea is simple: one row per sample and wavelength, i.e. a \"long\" table with columns `sample_id`, `wavelength` and `value`, plus any sample-level metadata you like.\n\n## Reading data\n\nMost instruments export either CSV files with one spectrum per column or proprietary binary formats. `read_spectra()` handles the common cases, e.g. ASD `.asd` files, Bruker OPUS files and JCAMP-DX, and returns a `spectra_tbl`:\n\n```{r read}\npath <- system.file(\"extdata\", \"wheat_nir.csv\", package = \"tidyspectra\")\nwheat <- read_spectra(path, format = \"wide_csv\", id_col = \"sample\")\nwheat\n```\n\nThe example dataset contains `r n_distinct(wheat$sample_id)` wheat samples measured from 1100 to 2500 nm at 2 nm resolution. Protein content was determined by the Kjeldahl method (cf. AOAC 2001.11) and ranges from `r round(min(wheat$protein), 1)` to `r round(max(wheat$protein), 1)`%.\n\n## Plotting\n\n`autoplot()` draws all spectra, coloured by a metadata column if you ask for one:\n\n```{r plot-raw, fig.cap = \"Raw NIR spectra of the wheat samples, coloured by protein content.\"}\nautoplot(wheat, colour = protein) +\n  scale_colour_viridis_c() +\n  labs(y = \"log(1/R)\")\n```\n\nNotice the large vertical offsets between spectra? Those are mostly caused by differences in particle size and packing density, not chemistry. Which brings us to preprocessing.\n\n## Preprocessing\n\nAll preprocessing functions take a `spectra_tbl` and return one, so they can be chained with the pipe. The most commonly used are:\n\n1. `sp_snv()` -- standard normal variate, i.e. centre and scale each spectrum individually;\n2. `sp_savgol()` -- Savitzky-Golay smoothing and derivatives (default: 2nd-order polynomial, window of 11 points);\n3. `sp_msc()` -- multiplicative scatter correction against the mean spectrum;\n4. `sp_trim()` and `sp_resample()` -- restrict or regrid the wavelength axis.\n\n```{r preprocess}\nwheat_pp <- wheat |>\n  sp_trim(1150, 2450) |>\n  sp_snv() |>\n  sp_savgol(deriv = 1, window = 15)\n```\n\nHow do you choose a preprocessing pipeline? Honestly, there's no universal answer. A reasonable default for NIR is SNV followed by a first derivative, as above; Dr. Rinnan's review (Rinnan et al., 2009) remains the best overview of the options and their trade-offs. Whatever you do, choose the pipeline using cross-validation on the *training* data only -- choosing it on the test set is a classic way to fool yourself.@@T1@@\n\n```{r plot-pp, fig.cap = \"The same spectra after SNV and first derivative.\"}\nautoplot(wheat_pp, colour = protein) + scale_colour_viridis_c()\n```\n\n## Modelling\n\ntidyspectra deliberately does not implement its own models. Instead, `sp_wide()` converts back to a wide matrix that works with {pls}, {glmnet}, {tidymodels} and friends:\n\n```{r pls}\nX <- sp_wide(wheat_pp)\ny <- wheat_pp$protein[!duplicated(wheat_pp$sample_id)]\nfit <- pls::plsr(y ~ X, ncomp = 10, validation = \"CV\")\nrmsep <- pls::RMSEP(fit)$val[1, 1, ]\n```\n\nWith 10 components the cross-validated RMSEP is `r round(min(rmsep), 2)` percentage points, which is roughly comparable to the reproducibility of the reference method itself (approx. 0.2--0.3 points). Can we do better? Probably not by much: when the model error approaches the error of the reference method, further gains are mostly illusory.\n\n## Where next?\n\n- `vignette(\"preprocessing\")` compares all preprocessing methods on three datasets.\n- `vignette(\"calibration-transfer\")` shows how to move a model between instruments, e.g. from a lab FT-NIR to a handheld device.\n- Bug reports and feature requests are welcome at <https://github.com/chemometrics-lab/tidyspectra/issues>!\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":8263,"cache_read_input_tokens":297141,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":8263,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_011qvFM8ooWwccE2sMgLd4oL","agent_id":"a033d36cafcb1facd","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"a4c5b22b-5f27-4092-b0b0-35dfb5cc050d","timestamp":"2026-11-17T14:52:41.914Z","request_id":"req_011Ch8gv6S3WF4pvANNMetXK","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Generate third test corpus"}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01EkonfAm4uFGkSKq9MxgBMq","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t---\n2\t# fmt: skip file\n3\ttitle: Directives\n4\tdescription: Tell Yamark what to format, skip, preserve, or configure from inside the file.\n5\t---\n6\t\n7\t<!-- fmt: skip file -->\n8\t\n9\tThe source file is the primary interface. Put a small `fmt:` directive next to\n10\tthe text it controls, then let an editor or repository integration run Yamark.\n11\tBecause directives are comments, the formatting choice stays with the text.\n12\tThe comment marker depends on the file:\n13\t\n14\t| File | Directive comment |\n15\t| --- | --- |\n16\t| Markdown and Quarto | `<!-- fmt: ... -->` |\n17\t| YAML, Python, and R | `# fmt: ...` |\n18\t\n19\tQuarto chunk options use `#|`; for example, `#| fmt: skip`.\n20\t\n21\t## Target the next value or block\n22\t\n23\tMost directives apply to the next supported target. In a YAML file, that target\n24\tis usually a scalar node. In a Python or R file, it is usually a string literal\n25\tor a contiguous source-comment block. The directive does not format the\n26\tsurrounding Python or R source code.\n27\t\n28\t## YAML files\n29\t\n30\tMark a scalar as Markdown and choose sentence wrapping for that scalar:\n31\t\n32\t```yaml\n33\t# fmt: markdown wrap=sentence\n34\tdescription: \"Explain the project in a few clear sentences.\"\n35\tother_value: \"This is ordinary YAML, not Markdown.\"\n36\t```\n37\t\n38\tThe directive attaches to `description`, the next scalar. A tagged scalar is\n39\tanother way to mark Markdown when the setting should travel with the value:\n40\t\n41\t```yaml\n42\tinstructions: !markdown |\n43\t  # Review\n44\t\n45\t  Read the diff and report concrete correctness issues.\n46\t```\n47\t\n48\tUse the same placement for an embedded formatter. The formatter name is the\n49\tlanguage after `fmt:`:\n50\t\n51\t```yaml\n52\t# fmt: python\n53\tscript: |\n54\t  def check(items):return all(item > 0 for item in items)\n55\t```\n56\t\n57\tYAML also supports directives on a collection parent when the setting describes\n58\tthe collection rather than a scalar:\n59\t\n60\t```yaml\n61\t# fmt: table\n62\t- {name: alpha, type: string, default: \"\"}\n63\t- {name: beta, type: integer, default: 0}\n64\t```\n65\t\n66\t## Python files\n67\t\n68\tPut `# fmt: markdown` immediately before the string literal or comment block\n69\tthat contains Markdown:\n70\t\n71\t```python\n72\t# fmt: markdown wrap=sentence\n73\tREVIEW_PROMPT = \"\"\"\n74\t# Review\n75\t\n76\tRead the diff and report concrete correctness issues. Prefer specific examples.\n77\t\"\"\"\n78\t```\n79\t\n80\tThe `#` lines inside the string are Markdown content. Python outside the\n81\tmarked target is left for a Python formatter such as Ruff.\n82\t\n83\tThe same directive can target a Markdown comment block:\n84\t\n85\t```python\n86\t# fmt: markdown\n87\t# # Filters\n88\t#\n89\t# Apply the most specific filter first.\n90\t#\n91\t# - Each filter is a single expression.\n92\t```\n93\t\n94\tFor a non-Markdown embedded language, use its formatter name:\n95\t\n96\t```python\n97\t# fmt: r\n98\tanalysis = \"\"\"\n99\tf <- function(x) x + 1\n100\t\"\"\"\n101\t```\n102\t\n103\t## R files\n104\t\n105\tR uses the same `# fmt:` marker. It can target a raw string literal used for a\n106\tvignette, help text, or a Shiny message:\n107\t\n108\t```r\n109\t# fmt: markdown wrap=sentence\n110\thelp_text <- r\"(\n111\t# Filters\n112\t\n113\tApply the most specific filter first. YAML, Python, and R\n168\tuse the same hash-comment form:\n169\t\n170\t```text\n171\t# fmt: skip file\n172\t```\n173\t\n174\tMarkdown uses an HTML comment:\n175\t\n176\t```markdown\n177\t<!-- fmt: skip file -->\n178\t```\n179\t\n180\tA whole-file skip is useful for generated files or files whose layout is\n181\tintentionally outside Yamark's scope.\n182\t\n183\tMarkdown skip controls retain trailing spaces and line endings in the selected\n184\tcontent, including supported nested Markdown.\n185\t\n186\t## Preserve intentional table widths\n187\t\n188\tYamark normally fits table columns to their contents. Keep a table's authored\n189\twidths while still formatting its contents:\n190\t\n191\t```markdown\n192\t<!-- fmt: table-widths=preserve scope=next -->\n193\t+----------+------------------+\n194\t| Name     | Description      |\n195\t+==========+==================+\n196\t| A        | Short text       |\n197\t+----------+------------------+\n198\t```\n199\t\n200\tUse `scope=file` to preserve widths throughout the document, or\n201\t`scope=from-here` for subsequent tables. A later\n202\t`table-widths=fit scope=from-here` resumes fitting widths. Both modes retain\n203\tcolumn alignment. Fitting widths can change the rendered proportions of\n204\tPandoc tables; preserving widths can retain excessive or cramped padding.\n205\t\n206\tFor Markdown inside YAML, Python, or R, the same option can accompany the\n207\ttarget marker: `# fmt: markdown table-widths=preserve`.\n208\t\n209\t## Set file-specific Markdown options\n210\t\n211\tUse `scope=file` when the file should have a different Markdown policy from the\n212\trepository default:\n213\t\n214\t```markdown\n215\t<!-- fmt: wrap=sentence:72 scope=file -->\n216\t```\n217\t\n218\tThis puts one sentence per line and wraps long sentences at column 72. It does not turn an ordinary YAML scalar into a\n235\tMarkdown target:\n236\t\n237\t```yaml\n238\t# fmt: canonical=true\n239\tfirst: !markdown \"This is __strong__ Markdown.\"\n240\tsecond: \"This is ordinary YAML text.\"\n241\t```\n242\t\n243\t## Arrange for Yamark to run automatically\n244\t\n245\tOnce directives are in the files, configure Yamark to run as part of the\n246\tworkflow:\n247\t\n248\t- In an editor, enable format on save. At the top level, that region is the physical file. |\n28\t\n29\tNot every directive accepts every scope. The tables below list the supported\n30\tforms. An unsupported or misspelled explicit scope is an error. Template\n31\tdelimiter directives use the contextual rule described below instead of one\n32\tfixed default.\n33\t\n34\tScopes stop at the current parsed document or nested-region boundary. A\n35\tdirective inside a recursive fence affects that fence, not its Markdown host or\n36\tsibling fences. A bare `canonical` means `true`. |\n100\t| `footnotes` | `wrap`, `format`, `preserve`, `none`, `true`, `false`, `yes`, `no`, `1`, or `0`. |\n101\t\n102\tFor `footnotes`, `wrap`, `format`, `true`, `yes`, and `1` request formatting;\n103\t`preserve`, `none`, `false`, `no`, and `0` request preservation.\n104\t\n105\t## YAML collections\n106\t\n107\t| Directive | Scope | Effect |\n108\t| --- | --- | --- |\n109\t| `fmt: compact` | Next | Enable block-to-flow compaction for the next eligible collection. |\n110\t| `fmt: compact false` | Next | Disable compaction for the next eligible collection. `fmt: compact=false` is equivalent. |\n111\t| `fmt: compact scope=from-here` | From here | Enable compaction until another compact directive changes the state. |\n112\t| `fmt: compact=false scope=file` | File | Disable compaction throughout the current YAML document or one source-file hashpipe YAML block. |\n113\t| `fmt: table` | Next | Align the next compatible sequence of flow mappings. |\n114\t| `fmt: compact table` | Next | Collapse eligible block mapping rows before aligning them. `fmt: table compact` and `fmt: table compact=true` are equivalent. |\n115\t\n116\t`fmt: table` accepts only its default next-target scope.
