Passing a hidden path explicitly selects it.\n30\t\n31\t## JSON-to-YAML projection\n32\t\n33\tFormatting preserves the source language and produces output that can replace\n34\tthe input. JSON-to-YAML projection has a different contract: it parses a\n35\tJSON-family input and emits formatted YAML for inspection or conversion.\n36\t\n37\tUse `yamark to-yaml --stdin-file-path` to project JSON-family input from stdin\n38\tto formatted YAML on stdout:\n39\t\n40\t```sh\n41\tyamark to-yaml --stdin-file-path data.json < data.json\n42\t```\n43\t\n44\tThe command does not read or write the path. It uses the extension to select\n45\tone exact input grammar:\n46\t\n47\t| Extension | Accepted input |\n48\t| --- | --- |\n49\t| `.json` | Strict JSON. |\n50\t| `.jsonc` | JSON with line comments, block comments, and trailing commas. Other JSON5 syntax is rejected. |\n51\t| `.json5` | JSON5 strings, identifiers, numbers, comments, and trailing commas. |\n52\t| `.jsonl` and `.ndjson` | One strict JSON value per physical line. Blank records are rejected. |\n53\t\n54\tObject member order and duplicate names are preserved. JSON and JSONC keep the\n55\tsource spelling of numbers. JSON5 spellings that YAML would interpret\n56\tdifferently are normalized, including `0X` hexadecimal prefixes, leading or\n57\ttrailing decimal points, unary plus, `Infinity`, and `NaN`. Negative\n58\thexadecimal integers are emitted in decimal because YAML would otherwise treat\n59\tthem as strings.\n60\t\n61\tJSONC and JSON5 comments become YAML comments. JSONL and NDJSON output a YAML\n62\tdocument-start marker before every record. A record may be an object, array, or\n63\tscalar; this does not change how ordinary YAML such as `1\\n2` is interpreted by\n64\t`yamark format`.\n65\t\n66\tString escapes are decoded before YAML emission. Lone UTF-16 surrogate escapes\n67\tare rejected because they do not represent Unicode scalar values. All\n68\tJSON-family inputs reject nesting deeper than 256 levels. JSON5 also rejects\n69\tlegacy numeric escapes such as `\\1`, invalid escaped identifier characters, and\n70\tU+0085 as whitespace. Characters that YAML cannot carry inside a comment are\n71\tshown as visible hexadecimal escapes.\n72\t\n73\tProjection does not scan JSON strings or comments for embedded Markdown or\n74\tformatter directives, and it does not dispatch to Prettier or another embedded\n75\tformatter.\n76\t\n77\t`yamark format` continues to skip JSON-family paths and never rewrites them.\n78\t`Yamark: View JSON as YAML` in VS Code and Positron uses the same JSON-to-YAML\n79\tprojection.\n80\t\n81\t## Markdown\n82\t\n83\t| Construct | Result | Details |\n84\t| --- | --- | --- |\n85\t| Paragraphs | Formats | Wraps by column, paragraph, sentence, or not at all, according to the active Markdown settings. |\n86\t| ATX headings | Formats | Normalizes spacing. Preserves and, when safe, compacts heading attributes. |\n87\t| Lists and task lists | Formats | Reflows list paragraphs with container indentation accounted for. Preserves GFM task markers. |\n88\t| Blockquotes | Formats when supported | Wraps supported blockquote shapes recursively. |\n89\t| Footnote blocks | Formats or preserves | Wraps definitions by default. A preserve setting keeps definitions byte-for-byte. |\n90\t| Reference links | Formats around | Treats reference-style links as atomic wrapping tokens. Preserves reference definitions without relocation. |\n91\t| Inline code and math | Preserves contents; formats around | Recognized spans retain authored whitespace and line endings while surrounding prose formats. |\n92\t| Nested image links | Formats when safe | Normalizes and wraps simple nested image labels and long destinations. |\n93\t| Pandoc citations | Formats around | Protects citation spans such as `[@key]` and `[-@key]` while wrapping. |\n94\t| Quarto divs | Formats when supported | Formats supported fenced div bodies recursively. |\n95\t| YAML fences | Formats | Formats fenced `yaml` and `yml` blocks as YAML unless locally skipped. |\n96\t| Markdown fences | Formats | Formats fenced `markdown` and `md` blocks recursively. |\n97\t| Source fences | Delegates | Can run embedded formatters for Python, R, JSON, GraphQL, CSS, HTML, JavaScript, TypeScript, and related aliases. |\n98\t| Long Quarto fence openings | Formats when safe | Promotes simple comma-separated options such as `echo=FALSE` to `#| echo: false` lines for a supported fence when wrapping is not `none` and the opening exceeds the configured column, or 72 in `paragraph` and `sentence` modes. For a delegated language, the embedded formatter must succeed; a missing, failed, or disabled formatter preserves the original opening. |\n99\t| Quarto source fences with `#| fmt: skip` | Preserves | Leaves the fenced chunk unchanged when the directive appears anywhere in the initial consecutive `#|` option block. |\n100\t| Document Markdown options | Reads | Applies `editor_options.markdown.{wrap,canonical,footnotes,table-widths}` to the body and nested Markdown that follows. |\n101\t| GFM pipe tables | Formats | Fits supported tables by display width while retaining alignment. `table-widths=preserve` retains separator lengths and source row widths. Explicit Markdown targets still format; their block content uses deeper indentation when needed to keep the following comment outside the value.\n135\t\n136\t### JSON Lines (JSONL) as YAML streams\n137\t\n138\tPath-aware formatting recognizes a `.yaml` or `.yml` stream made of two or more\n139\tunmarked, one-line YAML flow-mapping roots, one per physical line with no\n140\tseparate trivia lines. It inserts the `---` document-start marker before every\n141\trecord, including the first.\n142\t\n143\tJSON objects are the common case, but the trigger is based on YAML shape and is\n144\tnot restricted to strict JSON objects.\n145\t\n146\tNormal `--line-width` rules still determine whether each record and its nested\n147\tcollections stay in flow style or expand to block style. A single flow-mapping\n148\troot or a stream containing any non-flow-mapping root follows the normal YAML\n149\tpath instead.\n150\t\n151\tSee the generated [JSON Lines example](examples.qmd#json-lines-as-a-yaml-stream).\n152\t\n153\t## Python and R source files\n154\t\n155\t| Construct | Result | Details |\n156\t| --- | --- | --- |\n157\t| Consecutive own-line `#|` comments | Formats | Parses the comment body as YAML and emits it with the original hashpipe prefix. |\n158\t| Marked Markdown comments and strings | Formats | Formats supported own-line comment blocks and supported multiline string literals, accounting for their prefix or indentation. |\n159\t| Marked external source strings | Delegates | Sends a supported multiline string literal to the named built-in or configured formatter and re-indents the result. |\n160\t| Surrounding Python or R | Preserves | Does not format source outside recognized or explicitly marked targets. |\n161\t\n162\tEvery non-empty line in a comment target must use the same comment prefix;\n163\tempty comment lines may omit its trailing space. Python string targets use\n164\ttriple quotes with no prefix, or an `r`, `f`, `rf`, or `fr` prefix; the closing\n165\tdelimiter must be on a later line. R targets use a multiline standard or raw\n166\tstring. When the\n108\tformatter is available, Yamark formats the block and restores its indentation\n109\tin the YAML file.\n110\t\n111\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n112\t**Before**\n113\t\n114\t```yaml\n115\t# fmt: python\n116\tpreflight: |\n117\t  def check(items):return all(x>0 for x in items)\n118\t```\n119\t\n120\t**After**\n121\t\n122\t```yaml\n123\t# fmt: python\n124\tpreflight: |\n125\t  def check(items):\n126\t    return all(x > 0 for x in items)\n127\t```\n128\t::::\n129\t\n130\t### YAML scalar presentation\n131\t\n132\tYamark changes scalar spelling only when the parsed YAML value and tag\n133\tstay equivalent. It can simplify safe quoted strings, keep strings that\n134\twould be misread as booleans, convert hard newlines to literal blocks,\n135\tand fold long prose strings.\n136\t\n137\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n138\t**Before**\n139\t\n140\t```yaml\n141\ttitle: \"hello\"\n142\tboolish: \"true\"\n143\tbody: \"alpha\\nbeta\\n\"\n144\tsummary: \"This package formats YAML front matter and configuration files while preserving semantics, comments, and repository-friendly diffs.\"\n145\t```\n146\t\n147\t**After**\n148\t\n149\t```yaml\n150\ttitle: hello\n151\tboolish: \"true\"\n152\tbody: |\n153\t  alpha\n154\t  beta\n155\tsummary: >-\n156\t  This package formats YAML front matter and configuration files while\n157\t  preserving semantics, comments, and repository-friendly diffs.\n158\t```\n159\t::::\n160\t\n161\t## Markdown links, footnotes, and tables\n162\t\n163\tLong inline links are split at Markdown syntax boundaries. Footnote\n164\tdefinitions wrap under the marker unless the document or CLI asks to\n165\tpreserve them.\n166\t\n167\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n168\t**Before**\n169\t\n170\t```markdown\n171\tPlease be mindful of our [code of conduct](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/main/.github/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) as you interact with other community members.\n172\t\n173\tBody text with a footnote.[^long]\n174\t\n175\t[^long]: This footnote explains that comments were removed because people used comments to hold parsing directives and enough extra words to wrap.\n176\t```\n177\t\n178\t**After**\n179\t\n180\t```markdown\n181\tPlease be mindful of our [code of conduct](\n182\t  https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/main/.github/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md\n183\t) as you interact with other community members.\n184\t\n185\tBody text with a footnote.[^long]\n186\t\n187\t[^long]: This footnote explains that comments were removed because\n188\t  people used comments to hold parsing directives and enough extra words\n189\t  to wrap.\n190\t```\n191\t::::\n192\t\n193\tSimple GFM pipe tables are aligned by display width. Git clean/smudge filters\n194\talways use compact pipe-table output.\n195\t\n196\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n197\t**Before**\n198\t\n199\t```markdown\n200\t| package | label |\n201\t|---|---|\n202\t| dplyr | tidy |\n203\t| tidyr | pivoting |\n204\t```\n205\t\n206\t**After**\n207\t\n208\t```markdown\n209\t| package | label    |\n210\t| ------- | -------- |\n211\t| dplyr   | tidy     |\n212\t| tidyr   | pivoting |\n213\t```\n214\t::::\n215\t\n216\t## Markdown in source files\n217\t\n218\t### Hashpipe YAML in source files\n219\t\n220\tConsecutive own-line `#|` comments in Python and R are a YAML block. Yamark\n221\tformats the comment body as YAML, restores the hashpipe prefix, and leaves the\n222\tsurrounding source code unchanged. This recognition is automatic; it does not\n223\tneed a `fmt:` directive.\n224\t\n225\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n226\t**Before**\n227\t\n228\t```r\n229\t#| name: demo\n230\t#| launcher:\n231\t#|  vanilla: true\n232\t#|  default-packages: [base,utils]\n233\t\n234\tmain <- function() NULL\n235\t```\n236\t\n237\t**After**\n238\t\n239\t```r\n240\t#| name: demo\n241\t#| launcher:\n242\t#|   vanilla: true\n243\t#|   default-packages: [base, utils]\n244\t\n245\tmain <- function() NULL\n246\t```\n247\t::::\n248\t\n249\t### Embedded Markdown in Python\n250\t\n251\tWhen a prompt lives next to the code that uses it, Yamark can format the prose\n252\twithout changing the surrounding Python. Add `# fmt: markdown` before the\n253\tstring:\n254\t\n255\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n256\t**Before**\n257\t\n258\t```python\n259\t# fmt: markdown\n260\tREVIEW_PROMPT = \"\"\"\n261\t# Review\n262\t\n263\tRead the diff and flag anything that violates the style guide, has obvious correctness issues, or looks untested.\n264\t\n265\t-   Prefer specific suggestions over vague concerns.\n266\t-   Name the function and the case.\n267\t\"\"\"\n268\t```\n269\t\n270\t**After**\n271\t\n272\t```python\n273\t# fmt: markdown\n274\tREVIEW_PROMPT = \"\"\"\n275\t# Review\n276\t\n277\tRead the diff and flag anything that violates the style guide, has\n278\tobvious correctness issues, or looks untested.\n279\t\n280\t- Prefer specific suggestions over vague concerns.\n281\t- Name the function and the case.\n282\t\"\"\"\n283\t```\n284\t::::\n285\t\n286\tPython source outside the marked string is left untouched. Run `ruff format` for\n287\tthat.\n288\t\n289\t### Embedded Markdown in source comments\n290\t\n291\tThe same directive can target a contiguous source comment block. This is useful\n292\tfor generated help text or documentation snippets where a string literal is not\n293\tthe right host.\n294\t\n295\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n296\t**Before**\n297\t\n298\t```python\n299\t# fmt: markdown\n300\t# #   Filters\n301\t#\n302\t# Apply one or more filters. Put the most specific filter first.\n303\t#\n304\t# -   Each filter is a single expression.\n305\t```\n306\t\n307\t**After**\n308\t\n309\t```python\n310\t# fmt: markdown\n311\t# # Filters\n312\t#\n313\t# Apply one or more filters. Put the most specific filter first.\n314\t#\n315\t# - Each filter is a single expression.\n316\t```\n317\t::::\n318\t\n319\t### Embedded Markdown in R\n320\t\n321\tThe same pattern works for R raw strings. It can format package vignettes,\n322\tdocumentation fragments, and Shiny help text kept next to the code that renders\n323\tit.\n324\t\n325\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n326\t**Before**\n327\t\n328\t```r\n329\t# fmt: markdown\n330\thelp_text <- r\"(\n331\t# Filters\n332\t\n333\tApply one or more filters. Filters are evaluated top-to-bottom; the first match wins, so put the most specific filter first.\n334\t\n335\t-   Each filter is a single expression.\n336\t-   Multiple filters combine with AND.\n337\t)\"\n338\t```\n339\t\n340\t**After**\n341\t\n342\t```r\n343\t# fmt: markdown\n344\thelp_text <- r\"(\n345\t# Filters\n346\t\n347\tApply one or more filters. Filters are evaluated top-to-bottom; the\n348\tfirst match wins, so put the most specific filter first.\n349\t\n350\t- Each filter is a single expression.\n351\t- Multiple filters combine with AND.\n352\t)\"\n353\t```\n354\t::::\n355\t\n356\t## YAML layout\n357\t\n358\t### JSON Lines as a YAML stream\n359\t\n360\tGive a JSON Lines file containing two or more object records a `.yaml` or\n361\t`.yml` extension, with one record per line, then format it normally. Yamark\n362\tinserts a leading `---` document-start marker before every record, including\n363\tthe first, producing a valid YAML multi-document stream. The example below uses\n364\trecords from agent runs.\n365\t\n366\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n367\t**Before**\n368\t\n369\t```yaml\n370\t{\"id\":1,\"profile\":{\"name\":\"planner\",\"active\":true}}\n371\t{\"id\":2,\"profile\":{\"name\":\"researcher\",\"active\":true},\"usage\":{\"input_tokens\":640,\"output_tokens\":128}}\n372\t{\"id\":3,\"profile\":{\"name\":\"reviewer\",\"active\":true,\"model\":\"gpt-5\",\"region\":\"us\",\"tools\":[\"search\",\"python\"]},\"events\":[{\"type\":\"tool_call\",\"tools\":[\"search\",\"open\",\"python\",\"write\"]},{\"type\":\"usage\",\"tokens\":{\"input\":900,\"output\":240}},{\"type\":\"completion\",\"status\":\"ok\"}]}\n373\t```\n374\t\n375\t**After**\n376\t\n377\t```yaml\n378\t---\n379\t{id: 1, profile: {name: planner, active: true}}\n380\t---\n381\tid: 2\n382\tprofile: {name: researcher, active: true}\n383\tusage: {input_tokens: 640, output_tokens: 128}\n384\t---\n385\tid: 3\n386\tprofile:\n387\t  name: reviewer\n388\t  active: true\n389\t  model: gpt-5\n390\t  region: us\n391\t  tools: [search, python]\n392\tevents:\n393\t  - {type: tool_call, tools: [search, open, python, write]}\n394\t  - {type: usage, tokens: {input: 900, output: 240}}\n395\t  - {type: completion, status: ok}\n396\t```\n397\t::::\n398\t\n399\tYamark keeps each document as compact as the width allows. The first record\n400\tstays in flow style; the second expands only its root mapping; the third also\n401\texpands `profile` and `events`. Smaller mappings and sequences remain in flow\n402\tstyle whenever they still fit within `--line-width`. This conversion is for\n403\tobject records, not arbitrary JSON values.\n404\t\n405\t### Aligned flow-mapping tables\n406\t\n407\tA sequence of similar flow mappings can be easier to scan as a table. Mark it\n408\twith `# fmt: table` and Yamark aligns columns by key:\n409\t\n410\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n411\t**Before**\n412\t\n413\t```yaml\n414\t# fmt: table\n415\t- {name: alpha,type: string,default: [one,two],description: \"Short\"}\n416\t- {name: beta,type: int,default: 0,description: \"Number\"}\n417\t```\n418\t\n419\t**After**\n420\t\n421\t```yaml\n422\t# fmt: table\n423\t- {name: alpha, type: string, default: [one, two], description: Short}\n424\t- {name: beta,  type: int,    default: 0,          description: Number}\n425\t```\n426\t::::\n427\t\n428\t### Compact collections\n429\t\n430\tShort, simple block collections can read better as a single flow line.\n431\tEnable `compact = true` in `yamark.toml` (or pass `--compact`) and\n432\tYamark collapses eligible block mappings and sequences that fit the\n433\tstructural width:\n434\t\n435\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n436\t**Before**\n437\t\n438\t```yaml\n439\ttags:\n440\t  - yaml\n441\t  - markdown\n442\t  - docs\n443\tpackage:\n444\t  name: yamark\n445\t  language: rust\n446\t```\n447\t\n448\t**After**\n449\t\n450\t```yaml\n451\ttags: [yaml, markdown, docs]\n452\tpackage: {name: yamark, language: rust}\n453\t```\n454\t::::\n455\t\n456\tCollections with comments, aliases, tags, anchors, multiline scalars, or\n457\tblock scalars stay in block style.\n458\t\n459\t### Collapse to flow by typing a bracket\n460\t\n461\tDrop an unmatched `[` or `{` where a block sequence or mapping value starts and\n462\tYamark reads it as a layout hint: collapse this collection onto one line. The\n463\tfile doesn't parse as you typed it, but the intent is obvious - Yamark removes\n464\tthe opener and emits flow style.\n465\t\n466\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n467\t**Before**\n468\t\n469\t```yaml\n470\ttags: [\n471\t  - yaml\n472\t  - markdown\n473\t  - docs\n474\t```\n475\t\n476\t**After**\n477\t\n478\t```yaml\n479\ttags: [yaml, markdown, docs]\n480\t```\n481\t::::\n482\t\n483\tThe opener may also be detached onto the next line after an empty mapping value\n484\theader:\n485\t\n486\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n487\t**Before**\n488\t\n489\t```yaml\n490\ttags:\n491\t[\n492\t  - yaml\n493\t  - markdown\n494\t  - docs\n495\t```\n496\t\n497\t**After**\n498\t\n499\t```yaml\n500\ttags: [yaml, markdown, docs]\n501\t```\n502\t::::\n503\t\n504\tAdjacent forms such as `tags:[` and `tags:{` are not repaired as layout hints.\n505\t\n506\tA newline inside an existing flow collection requests the reverse change: expand\n507\tthe collection to block style.\n508\t\n509\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n510\t**Before**\n511\t\n512\t```yaml\n513\t- {a: b,\n514\t   c: d}\n515\t```\n516\t\n517\t**After**\n518\t\n519\t```yaml\n520\t- a: b\n521\t  c: d\n522\t```\n523\t::::\n524\t\n525\tSee [Supported files and syntax -> Layout repair](reference-files.qmd#layout-repair)\n526\tfor the acceptance rules.\n527\t\n528\t## Fenced and nested content\n529\t\n530\t### Recursive Markdown code fences\n531\t\n532\tYAML fences are formatted as YAML. Markdown fences are formatted\n533\trecursively, so nested YAML inside nested Markdown is formatted too.\n534\t\n535\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n536\t**Before**\n537\t\n538\t`````markdown\n539\t```yaml\n540\t# fmt: table\n541\t- {name: a,type: int,default: 0}\n542\t- {name: long_name,type: string,default: \"\"}\n543\t```\n544\t\n545\t````markdown\n546\t#   Inner\n547\t\n548\t```yaml\n549\titems: [a,b]\n550\t```\n551\t````\n552\t`````\n553\t\n554\t**After**\n555\t\n556\t`````markdown\n557\t```yaml\n558\t# fmt: table\n559\t- {name: a,         type: int,    default: 0}\n560\t- {name: long_name, type: string, default: \"\"}\n561\t```\n562\t\n563\t````markdown\n564\t# Inner\n565\t\n566\t```yaml\n567\titems: [a, b]\n568\t```\n569\t````\n570\t`````\n571\t::::\n572\t\n573\t### Prettier-backed web and data fences\n574\t\n575\tWhen `prettier` is on `PATH`, JSON, JSONC, JSON5, GraphQL, CSS, SCSS, Less,\n576\tPostCSS, HTML, JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, and TSX fenced blocks are handed to\n577\tit. Python and R fences go to Ruff and Air the same way:\n578\t\n579\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n580\t**Before**\n581\t\n582\t````markdown\n583\t```json\n584\t{\"name\":\"yamark\",\"tags\":[\"yaml\",\"markdown\",\"formatter\"],\"engines\":{\"node\":\">=18\"}}\n585\t```\n586\t\n587\t```ts\n588\tfunction format(input:string):string{return input.trim()}\n589\t```\n590\t````\n591\t\n592\t**After**\n593\t\n594\t````markdown\n595\t```json\n596\t{\n597\t  \"name\": \"yamark\",\n598\t  \"tags\": [\"yaml\", \"markdown\", \"formatter\"],\n599\t  \"engines\": { \"node\": \">=18\" }\n600\t}\n601\t```\n602\t\n603\t```ts\n604\tfunction format(input: string): string {\n605\t  return input.trim();\n606\t}\n607\t```\n608\t````\n609\t::::\n610\t\n611\tA missing `prettier` leaves the fence unchanged. Put a small `fmt:` directive next to\n10\tthe text it controls, then let an editor or repository integration run Yamark.\n11\tBecause directives are comments, the formatting choice stays with the text.\n12\tThe comment marker depends on the file:\n13\t\n14\t| File | Directive comment |\n15\t| --- | --- |\n16\t| Markdown and Quarto | `<!-- fmt: ... -->` |\n17\t| YAML, Python, and R | `# fmt: ...` |\n18\t\n19\tQuarto chunk options use `#|`; for example, `#| fmt: skip`.\n20\t\n21\t## Target the next value or block\n22\t\n23\tMost directives apply to the next supported target. In a YAML file, that target\n24\tis usually a scalar node. In a Python or R file, it is usually a string literal\n25\tor a contiguous source-comment block. The directive does not format the\n26\tsurrounding Python or R source code.\n27\t\n28\t## YAML files\n29\t\n30\tMark a scalar as Markdown and choose sentence wrapping for that scalar:\n31\t\n32\t```yaml\n33\t# fmt: markdown wrap=sentence\n34\tdescription: \"Explain the project in a few clear sentences.\"\n35\tother_value: \"This is ordinary YAML, not Markdown.\"\n36\t```\n37\t\n38\tThe directive attaches to `description`, the next scalar. A tagged scalar is\n39\tanother way to mark Markdown when the setting should travel with the value:\n40\t\n41\t```yaml\n42\tinstructions: !markdown |\n43\t  # Review\n44\t\n45\t  Read the diff and report concrete correctness issues.\n46\t```\n47\t\n48\tUse the same placement for an embedded formatter. The formatter name is the\n49\tlanguage after `fmt:`:\n50\t\n51\t```yaml\n52\t# fmt: python\n53\tscript: |\n54\t  def check(items):return all(item > 0 for item in items)\n55\t```\n56\t\n57\tYAML also supports directives on a collection parent when the setting describes\n58\tthe collection rather than a scalar:\n59\t\n60\t```yaml\n61\t# fmt: table\n62\t- {name: alpha, type: string, default: \"\"}\n63\t- {name: beta, type: integer, default: 0}\n64\t```\n65\t\n66\t## Python files\n67\t\n68\tPut `# fmt: markdown` immediately before the string literal or comment block\n69\tthat contains Markdown:\n70\t\n71\t```python\n72\t# fmt: markdown wrap=sentence\n73\tREVIEW_PROMPT = \"\"\"\n74\t# Review\n75\t\n76\tRead the diff and report concrete correctness issues. Prefer specific examples.\n77\t\"\"\"\n78\t```\n79\t\n80\tThe `#` lines inside the string are Markdown content. Python outside the\n81\tmarked target is left for a Python formatter such as Ruff.\n82\t\n83\tThe same directive can target a Markdown comment block:\n84\t\n85\t```python\n86\t# fmt: markdown\n87\t# # Filters\n88\t#\n89\t# Apply the most specific filter first.\n90\t#\n91\t# - Each filter is a single expression.\n92\t```\n93\t\n94\tFor a non-Markdown embedded language, use its formatter name:\n95\t\n96\t```python\n97\t# fmt: r\n98\tanalysis = \"\"\"\n99\tf <- function(x) x + 1\n100\t\"\"\"\n101\t```\n102\t\n103\t## R files\n104\t\n105\tR uses the same `# fmt:` marker. It can target a raw string literal used for a\n106\tvignette, help text, or a Shiny message:\n107\t\n108\t```r\n109\t# fmt: markdown wrap=sentence\n110\thelp_text <- r\"(\n111\t# Filters\n112\t\n113\tApply the most specific filter first. YAML, Python, and R\n168\tuse the same hash-comment form:\n169\t\n170\t```text\n171\t# fmt: skip file\n172\t```\n173\t\n174\tMarkdown uses an HTML comment:\n175\t\n176\t```markdown\n177\t<!-- fmt: skip file -->\n178\t```\n179\t\n180\tA whole-file skip is useful for generated files or files whose layout is\n181\tintentionally outside Yamark's scope.\n182\t\n183\tMarkdown skip controls retain trailing spaces and line endings in the selected\n184\tcontent, including supported nested Markdown.\n185\t\n186\t## Preserve intentional table widths\n187\t\n188\tYamark normally fits table columns to their contents. Keep a table's authored\n189\twidths while still formatting its contents:\n190\t\n191\t```markdown\n192\t<!-- fmt: table-widths=preserve scope=next -->\n193\t+----------+------------------+\n194\t| Name     | Description      |\n195\t+==========+==================+\n196\t| A        | Short text       |\n197\t+----------+------------------+\n198\t```\n199\t\n200\tUse `scope=file` to preserve widths throughout the document, or\n201\t`scope=from-here` for subsequent tables. A later\n202\t`table-widths=fit scope=from-here` resumes fitting widths. Both modes retain\n203\tcolumn alignment. Fitting widths can change the rendered proportions of\n204\tPandoc tables; preserving widths can retain excessive or cramped padding.\n205\t\n206\tFor Markdown inside YAML, Python, or R, the same option can accompany the\n207\ttarget marker: `# fmt: markdown table-widths=preserve`.\n208\t\n209\t## Set file-specific Markdown options\n210\t\n211\tUse `scope=file` when the file should have a different Markdown policy from the\n212\trepository default:\n213\t\n214\t```markdown\n215\t<!-- fmt: wrap=sentence:72 scope=file -->\n216\t```\n217\t\n218\tThis puts one sentence per line and wraps long sentences at column 72. It does not turn an ordinary YAML scalar into a\n235\tMarkdown target:\n236\t\n237\t```yaml\n238\t# fmt: canonical=true\n239\tfirst: !markdown \"This is __strong__ Markdown.\"\n240\tsecond: \"This is ordinary YAML text.\"\n241\t```\n242\t\n243\t## Arrange for Yamark to run automatically\n244\t\n245\tOnce directives are in the files, configure Yamark to run as part of the\n246\tworkflow:\n247\t\n248\t- In an editor, enable format on save. Keep local exceptions in directives so they stay beside the\n262\tcontent they explain.\n263\t\n264\tFor example, a repository can choose sentence-per-line Markdown and compact\n265\tYAML collections by default:\n266\t\n267\t```toml\n268\t[format]\n269\twrap = \"sentence:88\"\n270\tcompact = true\n271\t```\n272\t\n273\tYamark discovers `yamark.toml` from each formatted file's directory upward.\n274\tUse the [Configuration reference](reference-config.qmd) for the full\n275\t`[format]`, `[template]`, `[embedded]`, and `[paths]` schema.\n276\t\n277\t## For one-off runs\n278\t\n279\tCommand-line options are useful for trying a policy, checking files in CI, or\n280\toverriding a repository default for one invocation:\n281\t\n282\t```sh\n283\tyamark format --wrap sentence:72 docs/\n284\tyamark format --compact config.yaml\n285\tyamark format --check docs/\n286\t```\n287\t\n288\tUse the [Directive syntax reference](reference-directives.qmd) for every\n289\taccepted form, scope, and value.\n290\t\n291\tUse the [Command-line reference](cli-help.qmd) for the accepted arguments and\n292\t[Usage](usage.qmd) for installation and common commands.\n293\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_01U9RpjnTbHQ975XQEcANpFn","agent_id":"ae0ae2208c01edd79","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"411cc223-b41f-476e-b2e2-49a48d6b4826","timestamp":"2026-11-17T16:37:08.990Z","tool_result_meta":[{"id":"toolu_01HTNkNmB9Gv7Bkx8tELmNca","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}],"subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Write realistic test corpus F"}

This page is\n10\tan exact syntax lookup. For a guided path through YAML, Python, and R examples,\n11\tsee [Directives](directives.qmd).\n12\t\n13\t## Comment forms\n14\t\n15\t| Host | Form | Placement |\n16\t| --- | --- | --- |\n17\t| Markdown | `<!-- fmt: ... -->` | An own-line HTML comment. |\n18\t| YAML | `# fmt: ...` | An own-line hash comment. `fmt: table` and `fmt: compact table` may also be same-line comments on an empty-valued collection parent; a populated parent is an error. |\n19\t| Python and R | `# fmt: ...` | An own-line hash comment before a supported comment or string target. |\n20\t\n21\t## Scopes\n22\t\n23\t| Scope | Meaning |\n24\t| --- | --- |\n25\t| `scope=next` | Apply to the next supported target. This is the default for target-selecting, compact, table, and embedded-formatter directives. |\n26\t| `scope=from-here` | Apply from the directive until another directive changes the same state. |\n27\t| `scope=file` | Apply throughout the current parsed document or nested region, including supported nodes before the directive. At the top level, that region is the physical file. |\n28\t\n29\tNot every directive accepts every scope. The tables below list the supported\n30\tforms. An unsupported or misspelled explicit scope is an error. Template\n31\tdelimiter directives use the contextual rule described below instead of one\n32\tfixed default.\n33\t\n34\tScopes stop at the current parsed document or nested-region boundary. A\n35\tdirective inside a recursive fence affects that fence, not its Markdown host or\n36\tsibling fences. A `scope=file` directive inside one hashpipe YAML block does not\n37\tspan later blocks. `fmt: skip file` in Markdown front matter is the exception:\n38\tit preserves the outer Markdown document.\n39\t\n40\t## Preserve content\n41\t\n42\t| Directive | Scope | Effect |\n43\t| --- | --- | --- |\n44\t| `fmt: skip` | Next | Preserve the next supported target. `fmt: skip scope=next` is equivalent. |\n45\t| `fmt: skip file` | File | Preserve the current parsed document or nested region. `fmt: skip scope=file` is equivalent. |\n46\t| `fmt: off` | From here | Preserve content until `fmt: on`, or through the end of Markdown and source regions. `fmt: off scope=from-here` is equivalent. |\n47\t| `fmt: on` | - | Resume formatting after `fmt: off`. It does not accept an explicit scope. |\n48\t\n49\tThe same control uses the host's comment form:\n50\t\n51\t```yaml\n52\t# fmt: skip\n53\tmanual: [[ 1,2,3], [4,5,6]]\n54\t```\n55\t\n56\t```markdown\n57\t<!-- fmt: off -->\n58\t*   keep\n59\t    this\n60\t    list\n61\t<!-- fmt: on -->\n62\t```\n63\t\n64\tPreserve-control lifecycle checks are host-specific. YAML rejects a targetless\n65\t`skip`, a stray `on`, a nested `off`, and an `off` without a later `on`.\n66\tMarkdown and source regions allow `skip` at the end and let `off` preserve\n67\tthrough the end of the region.\n68\t\n69\t## Markdown targets and settings\n70\t\n71\t| Form | Default scope | Effect |\n72\t| --- | --- | --- |\n73\t| `fmt: markdown` | Next | Mark the next supported target as Markdown: a Markdown block, including a supported fence; a YAML scalar; or a source string or comment block. |\n74\t| `fmt: markdown wrap=sentence canonical=true` | Next | Mark the next supported target as Markdown and set its options. |\n75\t| `fmt: wrap=sentence` | `scope=next` in YAML; `scope=file` in Markdown or source regions | Change wrapping for an already recognized Markdown region without marking unrelated content. |\n76\t| `fmt: table-widths=preserve` | `scope=next` in YAML; `scope=file` in Markdown or source regions | Preserve widths in supported Markdown tables while formatting contents. Use `scope=next` immediately before one table. |\n77\t| `fmt: canonical` | `scope=next` in YAML; `scope=file` in Markdown or source regions | Enable canonical Markdown spelling. `canonical=true` is equivalent. |\n78\t| `fmt: footnotes=preserve` | `scope=next` in YAML; `scope=file` in Markdown or source regions | Preserve footnote definitions in the affected Markdown. |\n79\t\n80\tOption-only YAML directives tune the next scalar only if it is already marked\n81\tas Markdown:\n82\t\n83\t```yaml\n84\t# fmt: canonical=true\n85\tfirst: !markdown \"This is __strong__.\"\n86\tsecond: \"This is __not__ Markdown.\"\n87\t```\n88\t\n89\tFor `scope=from-here` or `scope=file`, `fmt: markdown` must include at least one\n90\tactual Markdown option. A broad-scope directive changes Markdown settings; it\n91\tdoes not turn every plain scalar into Markdown.\n92\t\n93\tAccepted option values:\n94\t\n95\t| Option | Values |\n96\t| --- | --- |\n97\t| `wrap` | `none`, `paragraph`, `sentence`, `sentence:<n>`, or a positive integer. |\n98\t| `table-widths` | `fit` (the default) or `preserve`. Both preserve alignment. |\n99\t| `canonical` | `true`, `false`, `yes`, `no`, `1`, or `0`. A bare `canonical` means `true`. |\n100\t| `footnotes` | `wrap`, `format`, `preserve`, `none`, `true`, `false`, `yes`, `no`, `1`, or `0`. |\n101\t\n102\tFor `footnotes`, `wrap`, `format`, `true`, `yes`, and `1` request formatting;\n103\t`preserve`, `none`, `false`, `no`, and `0` request preservation.\n104\t\n105\t## YAML collections\n106\t\n107\t| Directive | Scope | Effect |\n108\t| --- | --- | --- |\n109\t| `fmt: compact` | Next | Enable block-to-flow compaction for the next eligible collection. |\n110\t| `fmt: compact false` | Next | Disable compaction for the next eligible collection. `fmt: compact=false` is equivalent. |\n111\t| `fmt: compact scope=from-here` | From here | Enable compaction until another compact directive changes the state. |\n112\t| `fmt: compact=false scope=file` | File | Disable compaction throughout the current YAML document or one source-file hashpipe YAML block. |\n113\t| `fmt: table` | Next | Align the next compatible sequence of flow mappings. |\n114\t| `fmt: compact table` | Next | Collapse eligible block mapping rows before aligning them. `fmt: table compact` and `fmt: table compact=true` are equivalent. |\n115\t\n116\t`fmt: table` accepts only its default next-target scope. Compact directives\n117\taccept `next`, `from-here`, and `file`.\n118\t\n119\t`compact`, `compact=true`, `compact=yes`, `compact=1`, and `compact true`\n120\tenable compaction. `compact=false`, `compact=no`, `compact=0`, and\n121\t`compact false` disable it. The separated form accepts only `true` or `false`.\n122\t\n123\t## Templates and embedded formatters\n124\t\n125\t| Directive | Scope | Effect |\n126\t| --- | --- | --- |\n127\t| `fmt: template.delimiters \"<<\" \">>\"` | Inferred | Add one non-empty double-quoted delimiter pair using the placement rule below. |\n128\t| `fmt: template.delimiters \"<<\" \">>\" scope=next` | Next | Add the pair to the next supported target. |\n129\t| `fmt: template.delimiters \"<<\" \">>\" scope=from-here` | From here | Add the pair to following supported targets. |\n130\t| `fmt: template.delimiters \"<<\" \">>\" scope=file` | File | Add the pair throughout the current document or nested region. |\n131\t| `fmt: embedded python` | Next | Format the next supported string or YAML literal scalar with the named formatter. |\n132\t| `fmt: python` | Next | Shorthand for `fmt: embedded python`. |\n133\t\n134\tA bare `fmt: template.delimiters` directive uses the next target when placed\n135\tdirectly before one. When blank lines or range boundaries isolate it from\n136\tcontent on both sides, it applies from there onward. The directive requires an\n137\texplicit scope in every other placement.\n138\t\n139\tDelimiter arguments must be non-empty double-quoted tokens; single quotes are\n140\tnot accepted. JSON-to-YAML projection has a different contract: it parses a\n35\tJSON-family input and emits formatted YAML for inspection or conversion.\n36\t\n37\tUse `yamark to-yaml --stdin-file-path` to project JSON-family input from stdin\n38\tto formatted YAML on stdout:\n39\t\n40\t```sh\n41\tyamark to-yaml --stdin-file-path data.json < data.json\n42\t```\n43\t\n44\tThe command does not read or write the path. JSON5 spellings that YAML would interpret\n56\tdifferently are normalized, including `0X` hexadecimal prefixes, leading or\n57\ttrailing decimal points, unary plus, `Infinity`, and `NaN`. Negative\n58\thexadecimal integers are emitted in decimal because YAML would otherwise treat\n59\tthem as strings.\n60\t\n61\tJSONC and JSON5 comments become YAML comments. A record may be an object, array, or\n63\tscalar; this does not change how ordinary YAML such as `1\\n2` is interpreted by\n64\t`yamark format`.\n65\t\n66\tString escapes are decoded before YAML emission. Yamark\n221\tformats the comment body as YAML, restores the hashpipe prefix, and leaves the\n222\tsurrounding source code unchanged. This recognition is automatic; it does not\n223\tneed a `fmt:` directive.\n224\t\n225\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n226\t**Before**\n227\t\n228\t```r\n229\t#| name: demo\n230\t#| launcher:\n231\t#|  vanilla: true\n232\t#|  default-packages: [base,utils]\n233\t\n234\tmain <- function() NULL\n235\t```\n236\t\n237\t**After**\n238\t\n239\t```r\n240\t#| name: demo\n241\t#| launcher:\n242\t#|   vanilla: true\n243\t#|   default-packages: [base, utils]\n244\t\n245\tmain <- function() NULL\n246\t```\n247\t::::\n248\t\n249\t### Embedded Markdown in Python\n250\t\n251\tWhen a prompt lives next to the code that uses it, Yamark can format the prose\n252\twithout changing the surrounding Python. Add `# fmt: markdown` before the\n253\tstring:\n254\t\n255\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n256\t**Before**\n257\t\n258\t```python\n259\t# fmt: markdown\n260\tREVIEW_PROMPT = \"\"\"\n261\t# Review\n262\t\n263\tRead the diff and flag anything that violates the style guide, has obvious correctness issues, or looks untested.\n264\t\n265\t-   Prefer specific suggestions over vague concerns.\n266\t-   Name the function and the case.\n267\t\"\"\"\n268\t```\n269\t\n270\t**After**\n271\t\n272\t```python\n273\t# fmt: markdown\n274\tREVIEW_PROMPT = \"\"\"\n275\t# Review\n276\t\n277\tRead the diff and flag anything that violates the style guide, has\n278\tobvious correctness issues, or looks untested.\n279\t\n280\t- Prefer specific suggestions over vague concerns.\n281\t- Name the function and the case.\n282\t\"\"\"\n283\t```\n284\t::::\n285\t\n286\tPython source outside the marked string is left untouched. Run `ruff format` for\n287\tthat.\n288\t\n289\t### Embedded Markdown in source comments\n290\t\n291\tThe same directive can target a contiguous source comment block. This is useful\n292\tfor generated help text or documentation snippets where a string literal is not\n293\tthe right host.\n294\t\n295\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n296\t**Before**\n297\t\n298\t```python\n299\t# fmt: markdown\n300\t# #   Filters\n301\t#\n302\t# Apply one or more filters. Put the most specific filter first.\n303\t#\n304\t# -   Each filter is a single expression.\n305\t```\n306\t\n307\t**After**\n308\t\n309\t```python\n310\t# fmt: markdown\n311\t# # Filters\n312\t#\n313\t# Apply one or more filters. Put the most specific filter first.\n314\t#\n315\t# - Each filter is a single expression.\n316\t```\n317\t::::\n318\t\n319\t### Embedded Markdown in R\n320\t\n321\tThe same pattern works for R raw strings. It can format package vignettes,\n322\tdocumentation fragments, and Shiny help text kept next to the code that renders\n323\tit.\n324\t\n325\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n326\t**Before**\n327\t\n328\t```r\n329\t# fmt: markdown\n330\thelp_text <- r\"(\n331\t# Filters\n332\t\n333\tApply one or more filters. Filters are evaluated top-to-bottom; the first match wins, so put the most specific filter first.\n334\t\n335\t-   Each filter is a single expression.\n336\t-   Multiple filters combine with AND.\n337\t)\"\n338\t```\n339\t\n340\t**After**\n341\t\n342\t```r\n343\t# fmt: markdown\n344\thelp_text <- r\"(\n345\t# Filters\n346\t\n347\tApply one or more filters. Filters are evaluated top-to-bottom; the\n348\tfirst match wins, so put the most specific filter first.\n349\t\n350\t- Each filter is a single expression.\n351\t- Multiple filters combine with AND.\n352\t)\"\n353\t```\n354\t::::\n355\t\n356\t## YAML layout\n357\t\n358\t### JSON Lines as a YAML stream\n359\t\n360\tGive a JSON Lines file containing two or more object records a `.yaml` or\n361\t`.yml` extension, with one record per line, then format it normally. Yamark\n362\tinserts a leading `---` document-start marker before every record, including\n363\tthe first, producing a valid YAML multi-document stream. The example below uses\n364\trecords from agent runs.\n365\t\n366\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n367\t**Before**\n368\t\n369\t```yaml\n370\t{\"id\":1,\"profile\":{\"name\":\"planner\",\"active\":true}}\n371\t{\"id\":2,\"profile\":{\"name\":\"researcher\",\"active\":true},\"usage\":{\"input_tokens\":640,\"output_tokens\":128}}\n372\t{\"id\":3,\"profile\":{\"name\":\"reviewer\",\"active\":true,\"model\":\"gpt-5\",\"region\":\"us\",\"tools\":[\"search\",\"python\"]},\"events\":[{\"type\":\"tool_call\",\"tools\":[\"search\",\"open\",\"python\",\"write\"]},{\"type\":\"usage\",\"tokens\":{\"input\":900,\"output\":240}},{\"type\":\"completion\",\"status\":\"ok\"}]}\n373\t```\n374\t\n375\t**After**\n376\t\n377\t```yaml\n378\t---\n379\t{id: 1, profile: {name: planner, active: true}}\n380\t---\n381\tid: 2\n382\tprofile: {name: researcher, active: true}\n383\tusage: {input_tokens: 640, output_tokens: 128}\n384\t---\n385\tid: 3\n386\tprofile:\n387\t  name: reviewer\n388\t  active: true\n389\t  model: gpt-5\n390\t  region: us\n391\t  tools: [search, python]\n392\tevents:\n393\t  - {type: tool_call, tools: [search, open, python, write]}\n394\t  - {type: usage, tokens: {input: 900, output: 240}}\n395\t  - {type: completion, status: ok}\n396\t```\n397\t::::\n398\t\n399\tYamark keeps each document as compact as the width allows. The first record\n400\tstays in flow style; the second expands only its root mapping; the third also\n401\texpands `profile` and `events`. Smaller mappings and sequences remain in flow\n402\tstyle whenever they still fit within `--line-width`. This conversion is for\n403\tobject records, not arbitrary JSON values.\n404\t\n405\t### Aligned flow-mapping tables\n406\t\n407\tA sequence of similar flow mappings can be easier to scan as a table. Mark it\n408\twith `# fmt: table` and Yamark aligns columns by key:\n409\t\n410\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n411\t**Before**\n412\t\n413\t```yaml\n414\t# fmt: table\n415\t- {name: alpha,type: string,default: [one,two],description: \"Short\"}\n416\t- {name: beta,type: int,default: 0,description: \"Number\"}\n417\t```\n418\t\n419\t**After**\n420\t\n421\t```yaml\n422\t# fmt: table\n423\t- {name: alpha, type: string, default: [one, two], description: Short}\n424\t- {name: beta,  type: int,    default: 0,          description: Number}\n425\t```\n426\t::::\n427\t\n428\t### Compact collections\n429\t\n430\tShort, simple block collections can read better as a single flow line.\n431\tEnable `compact = true` in `yamark.toml` (or pass `--compact`) and\n432\tYamark collapses eligible block mappings and sequences that fit the\n433\tstructural width:\n434\t\n435\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n436\t**Before**\n437\t\n438\t```yaml\n439\ttags:\n440\t  - yaml\n441\t  - markdown\n442\t  - docs\n443\tpackage:\n444\t  name: yamark\n445\t  language: rust\n446\t```\n447\t\n448\t**After**\n449\t\n450\t```yaml\n451\ttags: [yaml, markdown, docs]\n452\tpackage: {name: yamark, language: rust}\n453\t```\n454\t::::\n455\t\n456\tCollections with comments, aliases, tags, anchors, multiline scalars, or\n457\tblock scalars stay in block style.\n458\t\n459\t### Collapse to flow by typing a bracket\n460\t\n461\tDrop an unmatched `[` or `{` where a block sequence or mapping value starts and\n462\tYamark reads it as a layout hint: collapse this collection onto one line. The\n463\tfile doesn't parse as you typed it, but the intent is obvious - Yamark removes\n464\tthe opener and emits flow style.\n465\t\n466\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n467\t**Before**\n468\t\n469\t```yaml\n470\ttags: [\n471\t  - yaml\n472\t  - markdown\n473\t  - docs\n474\t```\n475\t\n476\t**After**\n477\t\n478\t```yaml\n479\ttags: [yaml, markdown, docs]\n480\t```\n481\t::::\n482\t\n483\tThe opener may also be detached onto the next line after an empty mapping value\n484\theader:\n485\t\n486\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n487\t**Before**\n488\t\n489\t```yaml\n490\ttags:\n491\t[\n492\t  - yaml\n493\t  - markdown\n494\t  - docs\n495\t```\n496\t\n497\t**After**\n498\t\n499\t```yaml\n500\ttags: [yaml, markdown, docs]\n501\t```\n502\t::::\n503\t\n504\tAdjacent forms such as `tags:[` and `tags:{` are not repaired as layout hints.\n505\t\n506\tA newline inside an existing flow collection requests the reverse change: expand\n507\tthe collection to block style.\n508\t\n509\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n510\t**Before**\n511\t\n512\t```yaml\n513\t- {a: b,\n514\t   c: d}\n515\t```\n516\t\n517\t**After**\n518\t\n519\t```yaml\n520\t- a: b\n521\t  c: d\n522\t```\n523\t::::\n524\t\n525\tSee [Supported files and syntax -> Layout repair](reference-files.qmd#layout-repair)\n526\tfor the acceptance rules.\n527\t\n528\t## Fenced and nested content\n529\t\n530\t### Recursive Markdown code fences\n531\t\n532\tYAML fences are formatted as YAML. Markdown fences are formatted\n533\trecursively, so nested YAML inside nested Markdown is formatted too.\n534\t\n535\t:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n536\t**Before**\n537\t\n538\t`````markdown\n539\t```yaml\n540\t# fmt: table\n541\t- {name: a,type: int,default: 0}\n542\t- {name: long_name,type: string,default: \"\"}\n543\t```\n544\t\n545\t````markdown\n546\t#   Inner\n547\t\n548\t```yaml\n549\titems: [a,b]\n550\t```\n551\t````\n552\t`````\n553\t\n554\t**After**\n555\t\n556\t`````markdown\n557\t```yaml\n558\t# fmt: table\n559\t- {name: a,         type: int,    default: 0}\n560\t- {name: long_name, type: string, default: \"\"}\n561\t```\n562\t\n563\t````markdown\n564\t# Inner\n565\t\n566\t```yaml\n567\titems: [a, b]\n568\t```\n569\t````\n570\t`````\n571\t::::\n572\t\n573\t### Prettier-backed web and data fences\n574\t\n575\tWhen `prettier` is on `PATH`, JSON, JSONC, JSON5, GraphQL, CSS, SCSS, Less,\n576\tPostCSS, HTML, JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, and TSX fenced blocks are handed to\n577\tit. Die Formel lautet\n\n$$\ns^2 = \\frac{1}{n-1} \\sum_{i=1}^{n} \\left( x_i - \\bar{x} \\right)^2\n$$\n\nund wird im Autograder mit einer absoluten Toleranz von 10<sup>−6</sup> geprüft. Wer in Python `np.var(x)` statt `np.var(x, ddof=1)` schreibt, bekommt deshalb einen Hinweis im Feedback (siehe [Feedback-Vorlagen][feedback]). Das Bestimmtheitsmaß heißt bei uns R<sup>2</sup>, nicht $r^2$, und Dezimalzahlen schreiben wir im Fließtext mit Komma (0,05), im Code natürlich mit Punkt.\n\n## 📖 Begriffe\n\nLaborbuch\n:   Ein Jupyter- oder R-Markdown-Notebook, in dem Studierende jede Woche eine kleine Datenanalyse dokumentieren. Reminder emails are sent 24 hours before a shift instead of 48 (partners asked for this repeatedly).\n1. The \"My shifts\" page now loads about three times faster for volunteers with long histories.\n1. Dropped support for PHP 8.1.\n\n### Fixed\n* Cancelling a booking from the link in the reminder email didn't free the spot when the shift was in a different timezone than the server.\n* Typo in the Vietnamese translation of \"check in\"  \n  (thanks to Lan Pham for spotting it!)\n* Organisation logos wider than 2000px broke the printable rota.\\\n  They are now scaled down on upload.\n\n### Security\n- Session cookies now use `SameSite=Lax`.\n- Rate limiting on `/login`: 10 attempts per 15 minutes per IP address.\n\nMigrating from 3.1 to 3.2\n-------------------------\n\nThe bookings list endpoint changed shape. Before:\n\n~~~json\n[{\"id\": 1, \"shift_id\": 44, \"status\": \"confirmed\"}]\n~~~\n\nAfter:\n\n```json\n{\"data\": [{\"id\": 1, \"shift_id\": 44, \"status\": \"confirmed\"}], \"next_cursor\": null}\n```\n\n| Endpoint | 3.1 | 3.2 | Action needed |\n|:---|:---:|:---:|---|\n| `GET /bookings` | array | object (`data` + `next_cursor`) | update your client |\n| `GET /shifts?status=open\\|full` | yes | yes | none |\n|`POST /bookings`|200|201| check the status code |\n\nIf you call the API from a spreadsheet (several food banks do this with Google Apps Script), the old behaviour is still available for six months by sending the header `Accept: application/vnd.shiftshare.v31+json`; after that it will be removed without further notice.\n\n- - -\n\n## [3.1.4] - 2026-08-19\n### Fixed\n- Volunteers who changed their email address were logged out on every device[^sessions].\n- The waitlist promotion job ran twice when two shifts ended at the same minute.\n\n## [3.1.0] - 2026-06-02 ##\n### Added\n3) Partner organisations can have more than one admin.\n4) Bulk-create recurring shifts (\"every Saturday until 31 August\").\n\n### Deprecated\n- The `GET /v2/*` endpoints. Dieser Leitfaden richtet sich an Tutor:innen und studentische Hilfskräfte, die Aufgaben schreiben, Tests für den Autograder ergänzen oder die Laborbuch-Vorlagen verbessern. Für Studierende gibt es eine eigene Seite ([Hilfe für Studierende](hilfe.md)), und Fragen zur Bewertung gehören grundsätzlich in die Tutorenbesprechung am Montag.\n\n> **Hinweis:** Bitte arbeite nie direkt auf `main`. Jede Änderung läuft über einen Pull Request mit mindestens einem Review.  \n> **Note for exchange TAs:** English is perfectly fine for code, comments and PR descriptions.\n\n## 🧭 Ablauf in fünf Schritten\n\n1. Forke das Repository oder lege einen Branch an, z.B. `aufgabe/lab05-power` oder `fix/grader-toleranz`.\n2. Installiere die Pre-commit-Hooks; sie formatieren YAML und Markdown automatisch, bevor du committest:\n   ```sh\n   uv tool install pre-commit\n   pre-commit install\n   ```\n3. Schreibe die Aufgabe (siehe unten) und rendere sie lokal mit `quarto preview skript/`. Prüfe vor allem die Formeln,\ndenn KaTeX und MathJax verhalten sich bei `\\operatorname` unterschiedlich.\n4. Lass die Tests laufen. Wenn ein versteckter Test fehlschlägt, schau dir zuerst die Musterlösung an und nicht den Test.\n5.  Öffne einen Pull Request und weise ihn der zuständigen Person zu (Tabelle unten).\n\nCommit-Nachrichten schreiben wir so:\n\n    lab05: Aufgabe 3 (Teststärke) ergänzt\n\n    - versteckter Test q3b prüft jetzt auch n = 50\n    - Toleranz auf 1e-4 gesetzt, weil power.t.test() iteriert\n\n## ✍️ Aufgaben schreiben\n\nFormeln stehen immer in `$...$` bzw. `$$...$$`. Der Mittelwert heißt $\\bar{x}$ (nicht $\\overline{x}$ oder $\\hat{\\mu}$, außer wenn es ausdrücklich um den Schätzer geht), die Standardabweichung der Stichprobe $s$, und Hypothesen schreiben wir als $H_0\\colon \\mu = \\mu_0$ gegen $H_1\\colon \\mu \\neq \\mu_0$. Bei Teststatistiken bitte immer die Verteilung unter $H_0$ dazuschreiben, etwa so:\n\n$$\nT = \\frac{\\bar{X} - \\mu_0}{S / \\sqrt{n}} \\;\\overset{H_0}{\\sim}\\; t_{n-1}\n$$\n\nWeitere Konventionen:\n\nDezimalzeichen\n:   Im Fließtext Komma (0,05), im Code Punkt (`0.05`). In Tabellen mit Zahlen aus R-Ausgaben darf der Punkt bleiben.\n\nEinheiten\n: Immer mit schmalem Leerzeichen: 170&#8239;cm, 2,5&#8239;h. Flächen als cm<sup>2</sup>, nicht cm^2.\n\nTastenkürzel\n:   Mit `<kbd>`: <kbd>Strg</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>K</kbd> rendert in RStudio, <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Enter</kbd> führt in JupyterLab eine Zelle aus.\n\nSo sieht eine Aufgabe im Quelltext aus (bitte kopieren und anpassen):\n\n````markdown\n### Aufgabe 3: Teststärke   \n\nEine Tutorin vermutet, dass Studierende vor der Klausur im Mittel **weniger** als 7&#8239;h schlafen.\nSie befragt $n = 40$ Personen.\n\n1.  Formuliere $H_0$ und $H_1$.\n2.  Berechne die Teststärke für $\\mu_1 = 6{,}5$ und $\\sigma = 1{,}2$.\n   * Tipp: `power.t.test()` in R bzw. `statsmodels.stats.power` in Python.\n\n```{r}\n#| eval: false\npower.t.test(n = 40, delta = 0.5, sd = 1.2, type = \"one.sample\", alternative = \"one.sided\")\n```\n````\n\n## 🧪 Tests für den Autograder\n\nJedes Übungsblatt hat eine Konfigurationsdatei. Felder, die du nicht brauchst, lässt du weg; alles andere hat sinnvolle Standardwerte.\n\n```yaml\nname: lab05\ntitel: {de: \"Hypothesentests\", en: \"Hypothesis tests\",\n        es: \"Pruebas de hipótesis\"}\npunkte:   20\ntests:\n  - name: q1\n    punkte: 4\n  - name:   q3b\n    punkte: 6\n    hidden: True\n    nachricht_de: Die Teststärke ist zu niedrig. Hast du einseitig getestet?\n    nachricht_en: \"Power is too low: did you use a one-sided test?\"\n```\n\nDateinamen und Branches müssen bestimmten Mustern folgen, sonst lehnt die CI den Pull Request ab:\n\n| Was | Muster | Beispiel |\n|---|---|---|\n| Branch | `^(aufgabe\\|fix\\|doku)/[a-z0-9-]+$` | `aufgabe/lab05-power` |\n| Testdatei | `tests/q[0-9]+[a-z]?\\.py` | `tests/q3b.py` |\n| Übungsblatt | `lab[0-9]{2}` oder `hw[0-9]{2}` | `lab05` |\n| Feedback-Vorlage | `feedback\\.(de\\|en\\|fr\\|es)\\.md` | `feedback.fr.md` |\n\n## 🔤 Wer ist wofür zuständig?\n\n<!-- fmt: off -->\n| Bereich          | Person                     | Sprache(n)  |\n|------------------|----------------------------|-------------|\n| Skript           | Prof. Dr. M. This repository contains everything that makes our catalogue look and behave the way it does: the OPAC theme, a handful of Koha plugins, the MARC import rules used by Technical Services, and the documentation you are reading. Contributions come from library staff, from volunteers in the *Tech Help Desk* program, and now and then from developers at other libraries that run Koha -- all of them are welcome.\n\n> [!IMPORTANT]\n> Never paste patron data (names, card numbers, addresses, borrowing history) into an issue, a pull request or a test fixture. Use the fake patrons in `t/fixtures/patrons.yml`. If you post real data by accident, tell the Library IT manager right away, because we have to report it within 72 hours.\n\nWays to help\n============\n\n* **Report a problem.** Use the *Catalogue problem* issue template, and include the URL and what you expected to happen.\n* **Improve the docs.** Typos, unclear steps and missing screenshots are all fair game.\n+ **Translate.** The OPAC is available in English, Spanish, Vietnamese and Arabic; we'd love Somali and Tagalog next.\n* **Write code.** See below.\n   * Small fixes can go straight to a pull request.\n   * Bigger changes: open an issue first so we can talk it through.\n       * especially anything that touches circulation rules or fines\n\nSetting up a development environment\n------------------------------------\n\nYou will need Docker and about 20 minutes. The community's `koha-testing-docker`[^ktd] project does most of the work:\n\n    git clone https://gitlab.com/koha-community/koha-testing-docker.git\n    cd koha-testing-docker\n    cp env/defaults.env .env\n\nThen:\n\n1. Set `SYNC_REPO` in `.env` to the path of your Koha clone.\n1. Run `ktd up` and wait for the message *koha-testing-docker has started up and is ready to be enjoyed!*\n1. Install our plugins:\n\n   ```bash\n   ./scripts/install-plugins.sh --instance kohadev --all\n   ```\n\n   If the script complains that `Koha::Plugins` is not enabled, set `enable_plugins` to `1` in `koha-conf.xml` and restart Plack.\n\n1. Open the OPAC at <http://localhost:8080> and the staff interface at <http://localhost:8081>.\\\n   The default login is `koha` / `koha`.\n\n### MARC import rules ###\n\nImport rules are small YAML files in `marc/rules/`, applied in file-name order to every record that arrives from a vendor. A typical rule looks like this:\n\n```yaml\n# marc/rules/010-ebooks.yaml\nrule: ebooks-from-overdrive\nenabled: yes\nmatch:\n    source:   \"OverDrive\"\n    leader_06: a\nactions:\n  - add_field: {tag: \"856\", ind1: \"4\", ind2: \"0\", subfields: {u: \"{{ record.url }}\", z: \"Read online with your library card\"}}\n  - set: { field: \"942$c\" , value: EBOOK }\n  - delete_field: '9XX'\n```\n\nUse \\_underscores\\_ or hyphens in rule names, never spaces, and keep the numeric prefix so the order stays obvious.\n\n## Pull requests\n\n> **Before you open a pull request**, check that:\n>\n> - the change has an issue (unless it's a typo fix)\n> - tests pass locally: `prove -r t/`\n>     - for theme changes, also run `npm run lint:css`\n> - screenshots are attached for anything patrons will see\n>\n> A maintainer from Library IT will review it within a week.\n\n> [!TIP]\n> Draft pull requests are a good way to get early feedback. Nobody will merge a draft.\n\nUse this template for the description. It is also in `.github/pull_request_template.md`:\n\n```markdown\n## What does this change?\nShort summary.  Link the issue, e.g. Fixes #123\n\n## How was it tested?\n* [ ] `prove -r t/`\n* [ ] Checked the OPAC with a screen reader (NVDA or VoiceOver)\n-  [ ] Checked on a phone\n```\n\n### Who reviews what\n\n| Area | Path | Reviewers | Staff sign-off? | Test command | Deploys to | Notes |\n|------|------|-----------|---|---|---|---|\n| OPAC theme | `opac/theme/` | M. Lopez, T. Khan | Yes (Branch Services) | `npm test` | catalogue.riverton.gov | Check colour contrast with the axe browser extension before asking for review |\n| Koha plugins | `plugins/` | T. Khan | No | `prove -r t/plugins` | staging, then production on Thursdays | Plugins must declare `minimum_version` |\n| MARC import rules | `marc/rules/*.yaml` | Technical Services | Yes | `./scripts/check-rules \\| tee rules.log` | nightly import job | Rules run in file-name order |\n| Docs | `docs/` | anyone | No | `bundle exec jekyll build` | docs site | |\n\nBranch codes are used in plugin configuration and test fixtures. The table below is copied from the ILS admin screen, so please keep its layout as it is:\n\n<!-- fmt: off -->\n| Branch      | Code | Opened |\n|-------------|------|--------|\n| Central     | CEN  | 1911   |\n| St. Agnes   | STA  | 1958   |\n| Eastside    |EAS   | 1974   |\n| Bookmobile  | BKM  | 2019   |\n<!-- fmt: on -->\n\n- - -\n\n## Style notes\n\n* Perl follows the Koha coding guidelines; run `perltidy` with the project's `.perltidyrc`.\n* Templates use Template Toolkit. Keep logic out of them!\n* In the docs, write for a branch librarian, not for a developer: short sentences, *no* jargon, and spell out abbreviations the first time (OPAC = online public access catalogue).\n* Commit messages: `Bug 1234: Short description`, then a blank line, then a longer explanation if needed.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Why \"Bug\" even for features?</summary>\n\nKoha's own tooling expects that prefix, and we upstream some of our plugins.<br>\nIt's a convention, not a judgement.\n\n</details>\n\n## Code of conduct\n\nEveryone taking part is expected to follow the Riverton Public Library [code of conduct][coc], which also applies in the library's meeting rooms and at events. Report problems to <conduct@riverton-library.org>; reports are read by two people outside Library IT.\n\n[^ktd]: koha-testing-docker is maintained by the Koha community, not by us.\n\n    If it breaks after a Koha release, check the project's issue tracker before spending an afternoon debugging it. The increase was concentrated in the last three weeks of September (@fig-ili) and was largest among children aged 5 to 17.\n\nVaccination uptake is summarised in @tbl-vax. Clinic wait times improved at four of the six county clinics after the new online booking system launched in August[^booking], see @sec-methods for how waits are measured.\n\n:::: {.columns}\n\n::: {.column width=\"60%\"}\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-ili\n#| fig-cap: \"Weekly ED visits for influenza-like illness, July to September 2026, compared with the five-season average\"\n#| fig-alt:   \"Line chart showing weekly ILI visits rising sharply from week 36 onwards, well above the five-season average.\"\n#| fig-width: 7\n#| fig-height: 4\n#| out-width: '100%'\nplot_ili(q$ili_weekly, baseline = q$ili_baseline)\n```\n:::\n\n::: {.column width=\"40%\"}\n::: {.callout-note collapse=\"true\"}\n## Why the baseline changed\nBefore this quarter the baseline left out the 2020-21 and 2021-22 seasons. From Q3 2026 we use the five most recent complete seasons, as recommended by the state epidemiologist.\n:::\n\n-   ILI visits peaked in week 39.\n-   Most visits were among school-age children.\n    -  The North ZIP group had the highest rate.\n-   Influenza A made up 72% of positive lab tests.\n:::\n\n::::\n\n## Vaccination uptake {#sec-vax}\n\n::: {.panel-tabset}\n### Table\n\n| Age group | Doses given | Uptake | Target |\n|:----------|----:|:---:|---:|\n| 6 months to 4 years | 1,204 | 31% | 50% |\n| 5 to 17 | 3,980|28%|50%|\n| 18 to 64 | 22,415 | 34% | 50% |\n| 65 and over | 18,733 | 61% | 70% |\n\n: Influenza vaccine doses given in Q3 2026, by age group. Pharmacies report doses to the state registry with a delay of up to three weeks, so the final figure will be somewhat higher, but probably not high enough to reach 70%.\n:::\n\n## Clinic wait times\n\n![Location of the six county clinics and the four ZIP code groups](figures/clinic-map.png){#fig-map width=\"70%\" fig-align=\"center\" fig-alt=\"Map of Riverton County showing six clinic locations spread across four ZIP code groups.\"}\n\n```{r}\n#| label: tbl-wait\n#| tbl-cap: \"Median wait in days for a first appointment, by clinic and month\"\n#| fmt: skip\n#| tbl-colwidths: [40,20,20,20]\nwait_table(q$waits) |> gt::fmt_number(decimals = 0)\n```\n\nThe longest waits remain at the Millbrook clinic (@fig-map), which has had one vacant nurse practitioner post since May. Waits at Eastside fell from 19 days in July to 8 days in September.\n\n## Methods {#sec-methods}\n\nWeekly rates are calculated per 100,000 residents:\n\n$$\nr_{w,g} = \\frac{c_{w,g}}{P_g} \\times 100{,}000\n$$\n\nwhere $c_{w,g}$ is the number of visits in week $w$ for ZIP group $g$, and $P_g$ is the 2025 population estimate. Confidence intervals for small counts use the method of Fay and Feuer [@fay1997].\n\n### Definitions\n\nInfluenza-like illness (ILI)\n:   Fever of 100°F or higher **and** a cough or sore throat, without a known cause other than influenza.\n\nProvisional\n: A count for the two most recent weeks. Provisional counts usually rise by 5-15% as late records arrive, so don't compare them directly with final counts.\n\nWait time\n:    The number of days between a booking request and the first available appointment at the requested clinic, measured on the first Monday of each month.\n\n::: {.callout-important title=\"Data quality\"}\nED data for 9 to 12 August are incomplete because of an outage at the state feed. In total `r format(n_reg, big.mark = \",\")` children and teens registered, and `r pct_finished`% of them finished the challenge. That is the highest completion rate since the program was redesigned in 2021. Registrations at the St. Agnes branch nearly doubled vs. last year (see Fig. 3), which staff put down to the new partnership with St. Agnes Elementary School. Did the shorter ten-book goal make the difference? We think it helped, but it is not the whole story...\n\nParticipants logged approx. `r format(n_books, big.mark = \",\")` books, or about 14 per finisher. The median finisher read on 22 of the 69 days. Teens (ages 13 to 18) remain the hardest group to reach: only 312 registered, compared with 1,940 children aged 5 to 12.\n\n## Background and aims\n\nThe challenge has three aims, set by the Library Board in 2019. First, to slow the \"summer slide\" in reading skills [@cooper1996; @kim2004]. Second, to bring families who don't usually use the library through the door. Third, to give branch staff a reason to talk with young readers about what they enjoy.\n\nAs Dr. Raman put it at the June board meeting, \"We are not trying to make kids read more pages. We want them to want to read.\" This report asks whether the 2026 design moved us towards those aims, e.g. by looking at repeat visits, first-time library card sign-ups and the share of finishers from priority neighbourhoods. (Priority neighbourhoods are defined in the 2024 strategic plan.) Where possible we compare with 2025, but the two years are not directly comparable because the registration form changed in May.\n\n## What changed in 2026?\n\n* **A shorter goal.** The goal dropped from 15 books to 10, and audiobooks, graphic novels and books read aloud by a parent all counted. Several parents told us this was the first year their child felt the goal was \"actually doable.\"\n* **Paper logs are back.** In 2025 the challenge was online only. This excluded families without reliable internet access, which Ms. Okonkwo at the Eastside branch flagged in her end-of-summer report. Paper logs were offered at every branch and on the Bookmobile.\n*   **School partnerships.** Librarians visited 11 elementary schools in May (vs. 4 in 2025). Each visit took approx. 40 minutes, incl. a short booktalk and a registration table.\n    Visits were concentrated in the St. Agnes and Millbrook catchment areas.\n* **Prizes.** Finishers received a free book rather than a voucher for a fast-food restaurant. Was that a risk? Some staff thought so.\n\n```{r registrations-by-branch, fig.cap=\"Fig. 3: Registrations by branch, 2025 vs. 2026.\"}\n#| fig.alt: \"Grouped bar chart comparing registrations at six library locations in 2025 and 2026.\"\n#| out.width:   '90%'\n#| dev: [png, pdf]\nsrp |>\n  count(branch, year) |>\n  ggplot(aes(branch, n, fill = factor(year))) +\n  geom_col(position = \"dodge\") +\n  labs(x = NULL, y = \"Registrations\", fill = NULL)\n```\n\n## Findings\n\n### Completion\n\nCompletion rose at every location except the Bookmobile, where it fell from 41% to 37%. The Bookmobile figures are based on paper logs collected at the last stop of each route, so they probably undercount finishers. (Some families finished the challenge but never returned their log.) Story time attendance was also up; the 10 a.m. sessions at Central were full on most weekdays in July.\n\n> Several branch managers made the same point in their reports. Children who visited at least four times were far more likely to finish. Visits, not prizes, seem to drive completion. hot reload only watches `router.yaml`, not the supergraph.\n\n## Feature flags\n\nFlags live in `flags/flags.yaml` and are served by [flagd] in every region. The workflow:\n\n1. Edit `flags/flags.yaml` (or use `tools/rollout/rollout.py`)\n   - flag keys are `<service>.<feature>` in kebab-case\n   - every flag needs an `owner` and an `expires` date, CI fails otherwise\n2. Open a PR. The `flags-lint` job evaluates the JsonLogic rules against a sample context and\nposts a diff of the evaluated variants for ~2k synthetic users.\n3. After merge flagd picks up the change within ~30s\n    * staging first, then the canary region, then the rest\n    * need it faster? `kubectl -n flags rollout restart deploy/flagd` -- but not during business hours please\n\n<!-- fmt: off -->\n| Region         | Gateway p99 | Flag eval p99 |\n|----------------|------------:|--------------:|\n| us-east-1      |      182 ms |        1.9 ms |\n| eu-west-1      |      240 ms |        2.4 ms |\n| ap-southeast-2 |      311 ms |        3.1 ms |\n\n*   numbers from the October load test,\n    pasted into the quarterly deck as-is,\n    please don't reformat\n<!-- fmt: on -->\n\n##   Runbooks ##\n\n- [Gateway: restart / drain](docs/runbooks/gateway/restart.md)\n- [Gateway: subgraph timeouts](<docs/runbooks/gateway/subgraph timeouts.md>)\n- [Flags: flagd returns defaults everywhere](docs/runbooks/flags.md#everything-is-default \"the scary one\")\n- [GPU nodes stuck `NotReady`](docs/runbooks/gpu-notready.md)\n\nThe gateway enforces persisted queries in production[^apq] and a per-operation cost limit[^cost]. Read this before your first PR, it will save you a round of review.\nsidebar_position: 2\ntags: [ contributing,process,  on-call ]\nowners:\n    - \"@kestrel/platform-sre\"\n    - '@kestrel/ml-infra'\nlast_reviewed: 2024-10-02\ndraft: False\n---\n\n# Contributing\n\nThanks for helping keep the platform upright! :wave: This page covers the boring-but-important parts: how to set up, how we name things, what a reviewable PR looks like and how releases go out. It is opinionated because almost every rule here exists because of a specific incident.\n\n## Ground rules\n\n- **Small PRs.** Under ~400 changed lines unless it is generated code. Big refactors get split or get an ADR\nfirst.\n- Every PR title starts with a ticket: `PLAT-1234: ...`. Hotfixes during an incident can use the incident id instead (`INC-2291: ...`).\n- Don't `kubectl apply` or `kubectl edit` against prod from your laptop. If you absolutely have to (you are the IC, the pipeline is down, etc.) write down every command in the incident channel *as you run it*.\n-   Feature flags are not a substitute for a rollback plan.\n\n## Local setup\n\n1. Install the toolchain:\n   ```console\n   $ brew bundle --file=Brewfile\n   $ uv tool install pre-commit && pre-commit install --install-hooks\n   ```\n2. Log in to AWS SSO (`aws sso login --profile kestrel-dev`) and run `make bootstrap`.\n3) Run `make dev` and check that <http://localhost:4000> serves the sandbox.\n\nPre-commit runs `ruff`, `yamllint`, `helm lint`, `shellcheck` and `yamark format --check`. If a hook rewrites files, just `git add` them and commit again -- that is not a failure.\n\n\n## Commits and branches\n\nWe use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) because the changelog generator depends on it.\n\n| Type | When | Shows up in changelog? |\n| ---- | ---- | :---: |\n| `feat` | new user-visible behaviour (a new flag kind, a new region) | yes |\n| `fix` | bug fixes, including config fixes | yes |\n| `perf`|latency / cost improvements, with numbers in the PR description | yes |\n| `chore` | deps, CI, tooling | no |\n| `revert` | reverting a previous commit (use `git revert`, keep the generated message) | yes |\n\n```text title=\"example commit message\"\nfix(gateway): lower subgraph timeout to 2.5s\n\nThe 10s default let a single slow subgraph pin every router worker during\nINC-2291. 2.5s is above the p99.9 of every subgraph over the last 30 days.\n\nRefs: INC-2291, PLAT-1877\n```\n\n## Pull request checklist\n\nCopy this into the PR description if the template didn't load:\n\n- [ ] Ticket id in the title\n- [ ] `make test` passes locally\n- [ ] Dashboards / alerts updated if you renamed a metric\n- [ ] New flags have an `owner` and an `expires` date\n- [x] I read this document :)\n\n## Feature flags\n\n> Flags are config, not code. Treat a flag flip like a deploy.\n>\n> ```yaml\n> gateway.query-planner-v2:\n>     state: ENABLED\n>     owner: gateway-team\n>     expires: 2025-01-31\n>     variants: {on: true,off: false}\n>     defaultVariant: off\n> ```\n\nSome rules that came out of the last two quarters of incidents:\n\n* Name flags `<service>.<feature>`, lowercase, kebab-case after the dot.\n* Default to `off`. A flag that defaults to `on` is a deploy in disguise\n  and has to go through the normal release review.\n* Remove flags within two sprints of reaching 100%. The `flags-janitor` bot opens a PR for every flag past its `expires` date; please don't just bump the date.\n\n## Tests\n\n```console\n$ make test                       # unit tests, ~2 min\n$ pytest tools/rollout -k \"ramp and not slow\" -q\n$ k6 run load/gateway-smoke.js --vus 20 --duration 60s\n```\n\nSchema changes need a contract test. The GraphQL type for flags currently looks like this:\n\n```graphql\ntype Flag { key: ID!  state: FlagState!\n    variants: JSON  rollout:Rollout }\n```\n\n<!-- fmt: skip -->\n| Check          | Where                | Blocking? |\n|----------------|----------------------|-----------|\n| unit           | GitHub Actions       | yes       |\n| schema diff    | `graphql-inspector`  | yes       |\n| load smoke     | nightly, staging     | no        |\n\n## Releasing\n\nThe gateway chart and `rollout.py` are versioned with SemVer; everything else ships continuously.\n\n1. Merge to `main`. The `build-and-deploy` workflow deploys to staging automatically\n2. Cut a release:\n    1. `make release VERSION=2.15.0` bumps `Chart.yaml` and moves the changelog entries\n    2. push the tag: `git push origin v2.15.0`\n3. Approve the prod deployment in the GitHub environment. The canary region goes first; if the error-budget check fails, the workflow rolls back by itself and pings `#platform-sre`.\n\n## Code review expectations\n\nReviewers try to respond within one business day[^sla]. Les étudiant·e·s Erasmus trouveront un résumé en français à la fin du document; los estudiantes de intercambio encontrarán un resumen en español justo después.\n:::\n\n## Motivation {#sec-motivation}\n\nIn Woche 6 haben wir gesehen, dass der Stichprobenmittelwert $\\bar{x}$ ein erwartungstreuer Schätzer für $\\mu$ ist. Aber wie *genau* ist er? Ein einzelner Punktschätzer sagt nichts über die Unsicherheit aus. Ein Konfidenzintervall gibt einen Bereich an, der bei wiederholter Stichprobenziehung in $(1-\\alpha) \\cdot 100\\,\\%$ der Fälle den wahren Parameter überdeckt [@neyman1937; @wasserman2004, Kap. 6].\n\nFür normalverteilte Daten mit unbekannter Varianz lautet das Intervall\n\n$$\n\\bar{x} \\pm t_{n-1,\\,1-\\alpha/2} \\cdot \\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}}\n$$ {#eq-ki-t}\n\nDabei ist $t_{n-1,\\,1-\\alpha/2}$ das $(1-\\alpha/2)$-Quantil der $t$-Verteilung mit $n-1$ Freiheitsgraden (siehe @tbl-quantile). Für großes $n$ nähert sich dieses Quantil dem Normalquantil $z_{1-\\alpha/2} \\approx 1{,}96$ an.[^tabelle]\n\n![Dichte der $t$-Verteilung für $\\nu = 1, 5, 30$ Freiheitsgrade im Vergleich zur Standardnormalverteilung (gestrichelt).](abbildungen/t-dichte.svg){#fig-t-dichte fig-alt=\"Vier Glockenkurven; die t-Verteilungen mit wenigen Freiheitsgraden haben schwerere Ränder als die gestrichelte Normalverteilung.\" width=\"80%\"}\n\n| $\\nu$ | $t_{\\nu;\\,0{,}95}$ | $t_{\\nu;\\,0{,}975}$ | $t_{\\nu;\\,0{,}995}$ |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 5 | 2,015 | 2,571 | 4,032 |\n| 10 | 1,812 | 2,228 | 3,169 |\n| 29 | 1,699 | 2,045 | 2,756 |\n| $\\infty$ | 1,645 | 1,960 | 2,576 |\n\n: Ausgewählte Quantile der $t$-Verteilung {#tbl-quantile}\n\n## Simulation: Was heißt „95 %“?\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-ki-sim\n#| fig-cap: 'Hundert simulierte 95 %-Konfidenzintervalle; rot: Intervalle, die $\\mu = 170$ verfehlen.'\n#| fig-alt: \"Horizontale Linien für 100 Intervalle um eine senkrechte Linie bei 170 cm; etwa fünf davon sind rot und berühren die Linie nicht.\"\n#| fig-width:   8\n#| fig-height: 4.5\n#| code-fold:  true\n#| echo:  TRUE\n#| cache: true\nset.seed(1010)\nn <- 30; mu <- 170; sigma <- 8\nki <- t(replicate(100, {\n  x <- rnorm(n, mu, sigma)\n  mean(x) + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * sd(x) / sqrt(n)\n}))\ntrifft <- ki[, 1] <= mu & mu <= ki[, 2]\nplot(NULL, xlim = range(ki), ylim = c(1, 100), xlab = \"Körpergröße [cm]\", ylab = \"Simulation\")\nsegments(ki[, 1], 1:100, ki[, 2], 1:100, col = ifelse(trifft, \"grey40\", \"firebrick\"))\nabline(v = mu, lty = 2)\n```\n\nIn @fig-ki-sim verfehlen `r sum(!trifft)` von 100 Intervallen den wahren Wert;   im Mittel wären es fünf. Wie breit ein Intervall ist, hängt vor allem von $n$ ab:\n\n```{r ki-breite, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5, fig.cap=\"Breite des Intervalls in Abhängigkeit von n\"}\nn <- 5:200\nplot(n, 2 * qt(0.975, n - 1) * 8 / sqrt(n), type = \"l\", xlab = \"n\", ylab = \"Breite [cm]\")\n```\n\n::: {.notes}\nHier unbedingt die Simulation live zeigen und *vorher* fragen, wie viele rote Intervalle das Publikum erwartet. Dauer: ca. 10 min.\n:::\n\n## Übungen\n\n::: {#exr-mensa}\n## Mensa-Wartezeiten\nAn $n = 25$ zufällig gewählten Tagen wurden die Wartezeiten in der Mensa gemessen: $\\bar{x} = 7{,}4$ Minuten, $s = 2{,}1$ Minuten.\n\n1. Berechne ein 95 %-Konfidenzintervall für die mittlere Wartezeit.\n2. Wie ändert sich die Breite, wenn man $n$ vervierfacht?\nBegründe ohne zu rechnen.\n3. Interpretiere das Intervall in **einem** Satz, ohne das Wort „Wahrscheinlichkeit“ zu benutzen.\n:::\n\n::: {.callout-tip collapse=\"true\"}\n## Lösung zu @exr-mensa\nMit $t_{24;\\,0{,}975} \\approx 2{,}064$ ergibt sich $7{,}4 \\pm 2{,}064 \\cdot 2{,}1/5$, also etwa $[6{,}53;\\ 8{,}27]$ Minuten.\nBei vierfachem $n$ halbiert sich die Breite, weil $\\sqrt{4} = 2$.\n:::\n\n::: {#exr-bootstrap}\n## Bootstrap (freiwillig) 🧪\nVergleiche das $t$-Intervall aus @eq-ki-t mit einem Perzentil-Bootstrap-Intervall für die Daten aus `koerpergroessen.csv`. Was fällt dir bei schiefen Daten auf, z.B. bei den Mieten aus Lab 2?\n:::\n\n::: {.panel-tabset}\n### R\n\n```{r}\n#| label: ki-r\n#| eval: false\ngroesse <- read.csv(\"daten/koerpergroessen.csv\")$groesse\nt.test(groesse, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int\n```\n\n### Python\n\n```{python}\n#| label: ki-py\n#| eval:   false\nimport pandas as pd\nfrom scipy import stats\ngroesse = pd.read_csv(\"daten/koerpergroessen.csv\")[\"groesse\"]\nstats.t.interval(0.95, df=len(groesse)-1, loc=groesse.mean(), scale=stats.sem(groesse))\n```\n:::\n\n## Interpretation\n\n:::: {.columns}\n::: {.column width=\"50%\"}\n**Häufiger Fehler** ❌\n\n„Mit 95 % Wahrscheinlichkeit liegt $\\mu$ im Intervall $[6{,}53;\\ 8{,}27]$.“\nNach der Datenerhebung ist das Intervall fest – $\\mu$ liegt drin oder eben nicht.\n:::\n\n::: {.column width=\"50%\"}\n**Richtig** ✅\n\n„Das Verfahren liefert in 95 % aller Wiederholungen ein Intervall, das $\\mu$ enthält.“\nDie Wahrscheinlichkeit bezieht sich auf das *Verfahren*, nicht auf ein einzelnes Intervall.^[Bayesianische Kredibilitätsintervalle erlauben dagegen genau diese Aussage, setzen aber eine Prior-Verteilung voraus; mehr dazu in STAT 2020.]\n:::\n::::\n\n<!-- fmt: table-widths=preserve scope=next -->\n+----------------------------+------------------------------------------+\n| Situation                  | Intervall                                |\n+============================+==========================================+\n| $\\sigma$ bekannt           | $\\bar{x} \\pm z_{1-\\alpha/2}\\,\\sigma/\\sqrt{n}$ |\n+----------------------------+------------------------------------------+\n| $\\sigma$ unbekannt, Daten  | $\\bar{x} \\pm t_{n-1}\\,s/\\sqrt{n}$         |\n| ungefähr normalverteilt    |                                          |\n+----------------------------+------------------------------------------+\n| schiefe Daten, kleines $n$ | Bootstrap oder Transformation            |\n+----------------------------+------------------------------------------+\n\n> **Hinweis:** In der Klausur reicht es, das passende Intervall zu *begründen*; die Rechnung selbst gibt nur die Hälfte der Punkte.\n\n## Résumé en français {.unnumbered lang=\"fr\"}\n\nUn intervalle de confiance à 95 % n'est pas un intervalle qui contient $\\mu$ « avec une probabilité de 95 % » : c'est la *procédure* qui, répétée sur de nombreux échantillons, produit des intervalles contenant $\\mu$ dans 95 % des cas. Pour de petits échantillons ($n < 30$), on utilise la loi de Student.\n\n## Resumen en español {.unnumbered lang=\"es\"}\n\nUn intervalo de confianza del 95 % no significa que $\\mu$ esté dentro «con probabilidad 0,95». Significa que el *procedimiento* acierta en el 95 % de las repeticiones. Con muestras pequeñas usamos la distribución $t$ de Student; con muestras grandes, la normal.\n\n## 日本語の要約 {.unnumbered lang=\"ja\"}\n\n95 %信頼区間とは、同じ手順で何度も標本を取ったときに、そのうち約95 %の区間が真の平均 $\\mu$ を含む、という意味です。一つの区間について「$\\mu$ が95 %の確率で含まれる」とは言えません。\n\n[^tabelle]: Die vollständige Tabelle steht im Anhang des Skripts.
