{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01H4NxXuSQJZHfZDFV8QKa3k","type":"tool_result","content":"# Yamark\n\nYamark is a fast formatter for YAML and Markdown. It formats whole files and embedded content, keeping source readable and changes easy to review. Regions without a supported rewrite stay unchanged.\n\nFor supported embedded code, Yamark can also call Ruff, Air, Prettier, or another configured formatter.\n\nSee the [documentation](https://t-kalinowski.github.io/yamark/) for examples, configuration, editor integrations, and the full syntax reference.\n\n## Install\n\nWith [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) installed, run Yamark directly from [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/yamark/) without a separate install:\n\n```sh\nuvx yamark format config.yaml docs/\n```\n\nThis formats the selected files in place. To install a persistent `yamark` command:\n\n```sh\nuv tool install yamark\n```\n\n## Usage\n\nThe examples below use an installed `yamark` command. To keep running from PyPI without installing it, replace `yamark` with `uvx yamark`.\n\nFormat one or more files or directories in place:\n\n```sh\nyamark format config.yaml docs/\n```\n\nFormat the current directory:\n\n```sh\nyamark format\n```\n\nCheck whether files are already formatted without writing changes:\n\n```sh\nyamark format --check docs/\n```\n\nShow a unified diff without writing changes:\n\n```sh\nyamark format --diff docs/\n```\n\nFormat stdin for editor and CI integrations:\n\n```sh\nyamark format --stdin-file-path config.yaml < config.yaml\n```\n\nConvert JSON-family input from stdin to formatted YAML on stdout:\n\n```sh\nyamark to-yaml --stdin-file-path data.json5 < data.json5\n```\n\nThe path is not read or written. Its suffix selects the exact JSON dialect. This is a conversion, not source formatting.\n\nDirectory traversal skips hidden paths and respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and global Git ignore files by default. Pass a hidden path explicitly to format it.\n\nWhile formatting is enabled, standalone `{{< ... >}}` and `{{% ... %}}` shortcode tokens are preserved, including multiline tokens and quoted arguments. Directive-looking text inside a recognized token is data. Yamark does not match shortcode names or interpret their bodies: Markdown between tokens formats normally. An unterminated token or quote preserves the rest of the enclosing Markdown document or fragment. This does not guarantee rendering equivalence for arbitrary Hugo or Jinja templates.\n\nTo disable body formatting, surround the region with `<!-- fmt: off -->` and `<!-- fmt: on -->`. While formatting is disabled, directives follow the existing linewise policy: a recognized `fmt: on` line resumes formatting even if the surrounding text resembles a shortcode argument, code fence, HTML, or math block.\n\nExplicitly skipped Markdown retains its bytes, including trailing spaces and line endings: `<!-- fmt: skip -->` preserves the next selected node, `<!-- fmt: off -->` preserves the disabled region, and `<!-- fmt: skip file -->` preserves the enclosing Markdown document or fragment. This protection survives supported nesting in Markdown fences and divs; surrounding Markdown still formats.\n\n## Editor integrations\n\nThe VS Code and Positron formatter extension lives in `editors/vscode/`. See the [editor guide][editor-docs] for installation and configuration.\n\n======\n---\n# fmt: skip file\ntitle: Directives\ndescription: Tell Yamark what to format, skip, preserve, or configure from inside the file.\n---\n\n<!-- fmt: skip file -->\n\nThe source file is the primary interface. Put a small `fmt:` directive next to\nthe text it controls, then let an editor or repository integration run Yamark.\nBecause directives are comments, the formatting choice stays with the text.\nThe comment marker depends on the file:\n\n| File | Directive comment |\n| --- | --- |\n| Markdown and Quarto | `<!-- fmt: ... -->` |\n| YAML, Python, and R | `# fmt: ...` |\n\nQuarto chunk options use `#|`; for example, `#| fmt: skip`.\n\n## Target the next value or block\n\nMost directives apply to the next supported target. In a YAML file, that target\nis usually a scalar node. In a Python or R file, it is usually a string literal\nor a contiguous source-comment block. The directive does not format the\nsurrounding Python or R source code.\n\n## YAML files\n\nMark a scalar as Markdown and choose sentence wrapping for that scalar:\n\n```yaml\n# fmt: markdown wrap=sentence\ndescription: \"Explain the project in a few clear sentences.\"\nother_value: \"This is ordinary YAML, not Markdown.\"\n```\n\nThe directive attaches to `description`, the next scalar. A tagged scalar is\nanother way to mark Markdown when the setting should travel with the value:\n\n```yaml\ninstructions: !markdown |\n  # Review\n\n  Read the diff and report concrete correctness issues.\n```\n\nUse the same placement for an embedded formatter. The formatter name is the\nlanguage after `fmt:`:\n\n```yaml\n# fmt: python\nscript: |\n  def check(items):return all(item > 0 for item in items)\n```\n\nYAML also supports directives on a collection parent when the setting describes\nthe collection rather than a scalar:\n\n```yaml\n# fmt: table\n- {name: alpha, type: string, default: \"\"}\n- {name: beta, type: integer, default: 0}\n```\n\n## Python files\n\nPut `# fmt: markdown` immediately before the string literal or comment block\nthat contains Markdown:\n\n```python\n# fmt: markdown wrap=sentence\nREVIEW_PROMPT = \"\"\"\n# Review\n\nRead the diff and report concrete correctness issues. Prefer specific examples.\n\"\"\"\n```\n\nThe `#` lines inside the string are Markdown content. Python outside the\nmarked target is left for a Python formatter such as Ruff.\n\nThe same directive can target a Markdown comment block:\n\n```python\n# fmt: markdown\n# # Filters\n#\n# Apply the most specific filter first.\n#\n# - Each filter is a single expression.\n```\n\nFor a non-Markdown embedded language, use its formatter name:\n\n```python\n# fmt: r\nanalysis = \"\"\"\nf <- function(x) x + 1\n\"\"\"\n```\n\n## R files\n\nR uses the same `# fmt:` marker. It can target a raw string literal used for a\nvignette, help text, or a Shiny message:\n\n```r\n# fmt: markdown wrap=sentence\nhelp_text <- r\"(\n# Filters\n\nApply the most specific filter first. Explain why a filter matched.\n)\"\n```\n\nIt can also target a contiguous Markdown comment block:\n\n```r\n# fmt: markdown\n# # Filters\n#\n# Apply the most specific filter first.\n#\n# - Each filter is a single expression.\n```\n\nFor source code inside a YAML literal scalar, use the language formatter name\nin the same way as in a YAML file:\n\n```yaml\n# fmt: r\nanalysis: |\n  f <- function(x)x+1\n```\n\n## Control a region or a whole file\n\nThe scope is part of the directive. `next` is the default for target directives.\nUse `from-here` for the rest of a region, and `file` for a document-wide\nsetting:\n\n| Scope | Applies to |\n| --- | --- |\n| `scope=next` | The next supported string, scalar, collection, or comment block. |\n| `scope=from-here` | Supported content from this point until another directive changes the setting. |\n| `scope=file` | The whole file, including supported content before the directive. |\n\nSkip one target:\n\n```yaml\nnormal: [1, 2, 3]\n# fmt: skip\nmanual:\n    -   [ 1,2,3]\n```\n\nPreserve a region and resume formatting afterward:\n\n```markdown\n<!-- fmt: off -->\n#   Keep this heading ##\n\n<!-- fmt: on -->\n```\n\nSkip a whole file by putting the file directive at the top. YAML, Python, and R\nuse the same hash-comment form:\n\n```text\n# fmt: skip file\n```\n\nMarkdown uses an HTML comment:\n\n```markdown\n<!-- fmt: skip file -->\n```\n\nA whole-file skip is useful for generated files or files whose layout is\nintentionally outside Yamark's scope.\n\nMarkdown skip controls retain trailing spaces and line endings in the selected\ncontent, including supported nested Markdown.\n\n## Preserve intentional table widths\n\nYamark normally fits table columns to their contents. Keep a table's authored\nwidths while still formatting its contents:\n\n```markdown\n<!-- fmt: table-widths=preserve scope=next -->\n+----------+------------------+\n| Name     | Description      |\n+==========+==================+\n| A        | Short text       |\n+----------+------------------+\n```\n\nUse `scope=file` to preserve widths throughout the document, or\n`scope=from-here` for subsequent tables. A later\n`table-widths=fit scope=from-here` resumes fitting widths. Both modes retain\ncolumn alignment. Fitting widths can change the rendered proportions of\nPandoc tables; preserving widths can retain excessive or cramped padding.\n\nFor Markdown inside YAML, Python, or R, the same option can accompany the\ntarget marker: `# fmt: markdown table-widths=preserve`.\n\n## Set file-specific Markdown options\n\nUse `scope=file` when the file should have a different Markdown policy from the\nrepository default:\n\n```markdown\n<!-- fmt: wrap=sentence:72 scope=file -->\n```\n\nThis puts one sentence per line and wraps long sentences at column 72. Passing a hidden path explicitly selects it.\n\n## JSON-to-YAML projection\n\nFormatting preserves the source language and produces output that can replace\nthe input. JSON-to-YAML projection has a different contract: it parses a\nJSON-family input and emits formatted YAML for inspection or conversion.\n\nUse `yamark to-yaml --stdin-file-path` to project JSON-family input from stdin\nto formatted YAML on stdout:\n\n```sh\nyamark to-yaml --stdin-file-path data.json < data.json\n```\n\nThe command does not read or write the path. It uses the extension to select\none exact input grammar:\n\n| Extension | Accepted input |\n| --- | --- |\n| `.json` | Strict JSON. |\n| `.jsonc` | JSON with line comments, block comments, and trailing commas. Other JSON5 syntax is rejected. |\n| `.json5` | JSON5 strings, identifiers, numbers, comments, and trailing commas. |\n| `.jsonl` and `.ndjson` | One strict JSON value per physical line. Blank records are rejected. |\n\nObject member order and duplicate names are preserved. JSON and JSONC keep the\nsource spelling of numbers. JSON5 spellings that YAML would interpret\ndifferently are normalized, including `0X` hexadecimal prefixes, leading or\ntrailing decimal points, unary plus, `Infinity`, and `NaN`. Negative\nhexadecimal integers are emitted in decimal because YAML would otherwise treat\nthem as strings.\n\nJSONC and JSON5 comments become YAML comments. JSONL and NDJSON output a YAML\ndocument-start marker before every record. Lone UTF-16 surrogate escapes\nare rejected because they do not represent Unicode scalar values. All\nJSON-family inputs reject nesting deeper than 256 levels. Only the unmatched opener is a repair\nfor ill-formed input:\n\n- An unmatched `[` or `{` where a block sequence or mapping begins as a mapping\n  value or sequence item asks Yamark to collapse that one collection to flow\n  style.\n- A physical newline inside a complete flow collection is valid multiline YAML.\n  It asks Yamark to expand that collection to block style. Prefer concrete suggestions: name the function, name the case.\n  summarizer:\n    # fmt: markdown\n    instructions: |\n      You write release notes.\n\n      - One bullet per user-visible change.\n      - No internal refactors.\n```\n::::\n\nThe tagged value contains only prose, so Yamark rewraps it as a folded block.\nThe comment-marked value contains a list, so Yamark keeps literal block style\n(`|`) because folding would destroy the line breaks Markdown depends on.\n\n### Source code in YAML\n\nYAML values can also contain source code. Use `# fmt: python`, `# fmt: r`, or\nthe name of another configured formatter before a literal block. When the\nformatter is available, Yamark formats the block and restores its indentation\nin the YAML file.\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```yaml\n# fmt: python\npreflight: |\n  def check(items):return all(x>0 for x in items)\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```yaml\n# fmt: python\npreflight: |\n  def check(items):\n    return all(x > 0 for x in items)\n```\n::::\n\n### YAML scalar presentation\n\nYamark changes scalar spelling only when the parsed YAML value and tag\nstay equivalent. It can simplify safe quoted strings, keep strings that\nwould be misread as booleans, convert hard newlines to literal blocks,\nand fold long prose strings.\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```yaml\ntitle: \"hello\"\nboolish: \"true\"\nbody: \"alpha\\nbeta\\n\"\nsummary: \"This package formats YAML front matter and configuration files while preserving semantics, comments, and repository-friendly diffs.\"\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```yaml\ntitle: hello\nboolish: \"true\"\nbody: |\n  alpha\n  beta\nsummary: >-\n  This package formats YAML front matter and configuration files while\n  preserving semantics, comments, and repository-friendly diffs.\n```\n::::\n\n## Markdown links, footnotes, and tables\n\nLong inline links are split at Markdown syntax boundaries. Footnote\ndefinitions wrap under the marker unless the document or CLI asks to\npreserve them.\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```markdown\nPlease be mindful of our [code of conduct](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/main/.github/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) as you interact with other community members.\n\nBody text with a footnote.[^long]\n\n[^long]: This footnote explains that comments were removed because people used comments to hold parsing directives and enough extra words to wrap.\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```markdown\nPlease be mindful of our [code of conduct](\n  https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/blob/main/.github/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md\n) as you interact with other community members.\n\nBody text with a footnote.[^long]\n\n[^long]: This footnote explains that comments were removed because\n  people used comments to hold parsing directives and enough extra words\n  to wrap.\n```\n::::\n\nSimple GFM pipe tables are aligned by display width. Git clean/smudge filters\nalways use compact pipe-table output.\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```markdown\n| package | label |\n|---|---|\n| dplyr | tidy |\n| tidyr | pivoting |\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```markdown\n| package | label    |\n| ------- | -------- |\n| dplyr   | tidy     |\n| tidyr   | pivoting |\n```\n::::\n\n## Markdown in source files\n\n### Hashpipe YAML in source files\n\nConsecutive own-line `#|` comments in Python and R are a YAML block. Yamark\nformats the comment body as YAML, restores the hashpipe prefix, and leaves the\nsurrounding source code unchanged. This recognition is automatic; it does not\nneed a `fmt:` directive.\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```r\n#| name: demo\n#| launcher:\n#|  vanilla: true\n#|  default-packages: [base,utils]\n\nmain <- function() NULL\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```r\n#| name: demo\n#| launcher:\n#|   vanilla: true\n#|   default-packages: [base, utils]\n\nmain <- function() NULL\n```\n::::\n\n### Embedded Markdown in Python\n\nWhen a prompt lives next to the code that uses it, Yamark can format the prose\nwithout changing the surrounding Python. Add `# fmt: markdown` before the\nstring:\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```python\n# fmt: markdown\nREVIEW_PROMPT = \"\"\"\n# Review\n\nRead the diff and flag anything that violates the style guide, has obvious correctness issues, or looks untested.\n\n-   Prefer specific suggestions over vague concerns.\n-   Name the function and the case.\n\"\"\"\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```python\n# fmt: markdown\nREVIEW_PROMPT = \"\"\"\n# Review\n\nRead the diff and flag anything that violates the style guide, has\nobvious correctness issues, or looks untested.\n\n- Prefer specific suggestions over vague concerns.\n- Name the function and the case.\n\"\"\"\n```\n::::\n\nPython source outside the marked string is left untouched. Run `ruff format` for\nthat.\n\n### Embedded Markdown in source comments\n\nThe same directive can target a contiguous source comment block. This is useful\nfor generated help text or documentation snippets where a string literal is not\nthe right host.\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```python\n# fmt: markdown\n# #   Filters\n#\n# Apply one or more filters. Put the most specific filter first.\n#\n# -   Each filter is a single expression.\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```python\n# fmt: markdown\n# # Filters\n#\n# Apply one or more filters. Put the most specific filter first.\n#\n# - Each filter is a single expression.\n```\n::::\n\n### Embedded Markdown in R\n\nThe same pattern works for R raw strings. It can format package vignettes,\ndocumentation fragments, and Shiny help text kept next to the code that renders\nit.\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```r\n# fmt: markdown\nhelp_text <- r\"(\n# Filters\n\nApply one or more filters. Filters are evaluated top-to-bottom; the first match wins, so put the most specific filter first.\n\n-   Each filter is a single expression.\n-   Multiple filters combine with AND.\n)\"\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```r\n# fmt: markdown\nhelp_text <- r\"(\n# Filters\n\nApply one or more filters. Filters are evaluated top-to-bottom; the\nfirst match wins, so put the most specific filter first.\n\n- Each filter is a single expression.\n- Multiple filters combine with AND.\n)\"\n```\n::::\n\n## YAML layout\n\n### JSON Lines as a YAML stream\n\nGive a JSON Lines file containing two or more object records a `.yaml` or\n`.yml` extension, with one record per line, then format it normally. Yamark\ninserts a leading `---` document-start marker before every record, including\nthe first, producing a valid YAML multi-document stream. The example below uses\nrecords from agent runs.\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```yaml\n{\"id\":1,\"profile\":{\"name\":\"planner\",\"active\":true}}\n{\"id\":2,\"profile\":{\"name\":\"researcher\",\"active\":true},\"usage\":{\"input_tokens\":640,\"output_tokens\":128}}\n{\"id\":3,\"profile\":{\"name\":\"reviewer\",\"active\":true,\"model\":\"gpt-5\",\"region\":\"us\",\"tools\":[\"search\",\"python\"]},\"events\":[{\"type\":\"tool_call\",\"tools\":[\"search\",\"open\",\"python\",\"write\"]},{\"type\":\"usage\",\"tokens\":{\"input\":900,\"output\":240}},{\"type\":\"completion\",\"status\":\"ok\"}]}\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```yaml\n---\n{id: 1, profile: {name: planner, active: true}}\n---\nid: 2\nprofile: {name: researcher, active: true}\nusage: {input_tokens: 640, output_tokens: 128}\n---\nid: 3\nprofile:\n  name: reviewer\n  active: true\n  model: gpt-5\n  region: us\n  tools: [search, python]\nevents:\n  - {type: tool_call, tools: [search, open, python, write]}\n  - {type: usage, tokens: {input: 900, output: 240}}\n  - {type: completion, status: ok}\n```\n::::\n\nYamark keeps each document as compact as the width allows. The first record\nstays in flow style; the second expands only its root mapping; the third also\nexpands `profile` and `events`. Smaller mappings and sequences remain in flow\nstyle whenever they still fit within `--line-width`. This conversion is for\nobject records, not arbitrary JSON values.\n\n### Aligned flow-mapping tables\n\nA sequence of similar flow mappings can be easier to scan as a table. Mark it\nwith `# fmt: table` and Yamark aligns columns by key:\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```yaml\n# fmt: table\n- {name: alpha,type: string,default: [one,two],description: \"Short\"}\n- {name: beta,type: int,default: 0,description: \"Number\"}\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```yaml\n# fmt: table\n- {name: alpha, type: string, default: [one, two], description: Short}\n- {name: beta,  type: int,    default: 0,          description: Number}\n```\n::::\n\n### Compact collections\n\nShort, simple block collections can read better as a single flow line.\nEnable `compact = true` in `yamark.toml` (or pass `--compact`) and\nYamark collapses eligible block mappings and sequences that fit the\nstructural width:\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```yaml\ntags:\n  - yaml\n  - markdown\n  - docs\npackage:\n  name: yamark\n  language: rust\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```yaml\ntags: [yaml, markdown, docs]\npackage: {name: yamark, language: rust}\n```\n::::\n\nCollections with comments, aliases, tags, anchors, multiline scalars, or\nblock scalars stay in block style.\n\n### Collapse to flow by typing a bracket\n\nDrop an unmatched `[` or `{` where a block sequence or mapping value starts and\nYamark reads it as a layout hint: collapse this collection onto one line. The\nfile doesn't parse as you typed it, but the intent is obvious - Yamark removes\nthe opener and emits flow style.\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```yaml\ntags: [\n  - yaml\n  - markdown\n  - docs\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```yaml\ntags: [yaml, markdown, docs]\n```\n::::\n\nThe opener may also be detached onto the next line after an empty mapping value\nheader:\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```yaml\ntags:\n[\n  - yaml\n  - markdown\n  - docs\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```yaml\ntags: [yaml, markdown, docs]\n```\n::::\n\nAdjacent forms such as `tags:[` and `tags:{` are not repaired as layout hints.\n\nA newline inside an existing flow collection requests the reverse change: expand\nthe collection to block style.\n\n:::: {.showcase-before-after}\n**Before**\n\n```yaml\n- {a: b,\n   c: d}\n```\n\n**After**\n\n```yaml\n- a: b\n  c: d\n```\n::::\n\nSee [Supported files and syntax -> Layout repair](reference-files.qmd#layout-repair)\nfor the acceptance rules.\n\n## Fenced and nested content\n\n### Recursive Markdown code fences\n\nYAML fences are formatted as YAML. Unknown keys and invalid values are errors.\n\nThe top-level tables are `[format]`, `[template]`, `[embedded]`, and `[paths]`.\n\n## `[format]`\n\n```toml\n[format]\nwrap = \"sentence:88\"\ncompact = true\nmarkdown_horizontal_rule = \"***\"\n```\n\n| Key | Type and values | Effect when present |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `wrap` | String: `none`, `paragraph`, `sentence`, `sentence:<n>`, or a positive integer. | Sets Markdown wrapping. An explicit `--wrap` value overrides it. |\n| `table_widths` | String: `\"fit\"` or `\"preserve\"`. | Sizes Markdown table columns from their contents by default, or retains source widths. An explicit `--table-widths` overrides it; document settings and scoped directives override that base setting. |\n| `compact` | Boolean. | Enables or disables eligible YAML block-to-flow compaction. `--compact` still enables compact mode when this is `false`. |\n| `markdown_horizontal_rule` | String: `\"---\"` or `\"***\"`. | Chooses the marker Yamark emits for normalized Markdown horizontal rules. |\n\nSee [Formatting settings](reference-options.qmd) for built-in defaults and the\nother surfaces that expose these behaviors.\n\n## `[template]`\n\nTemplate delimiters mark regions Yamark must preserve because rendering can\nchange the host language. The defaults are `{{ }}`, `{% %}`, `{# #}`, and\n`<% %>`.\n\n| Key | Type | Effect |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `add_delimiters` | Array of `{ open, close }` tables. | Appends to the delimiters active at this layer, after `replace_delimiters` if both keys are present. |\n| `replace_delimiters` | Array of `{ open, close }` tables. | Replaces the delimiters active at this layer before any additions. |\n\nAdd a delimiter pair:\n\n```toml\n[template]\nadd_delimiters = [\n  { open = \"<<\", close = \">>\" }\n]\n```\n\nReplace the defaults:\n\n```toml\n[template]\nreplace_delimiters = [\n  { open = \"[[\", close = \"]]\" }\n]\n```\n\nEvery entry must contain non-empty `open` and `close` strings.\n\nIn Markdown paragraphs and supported prose containers, including lists and\nblockquotes, a complete single-line expression is one opaque word. Yamark\npreserves every byte inside it and wraps the surrounding prose normally. For\nexample, `{{ render(\"keep   this\") }}` can occupy its own line or exceed the\nrequested width, just like a long word. Function calls, quoted arguments,\nescaped quotes, and nested braces are supported. A closing delimiter inside a\nsingle- or double-quoted argument does not end the expression. For `{#` / `#}`\ncomments, the first literal `#}` ends the token; quotes, apostrophes, and braces\ninside have no special meaning. Yamark only recognizes boundaries; it does not\ninterpret or evaluate template languages.\n\nConfigured openers take precedence over Markdown inline syntax. When several\npairs match an opener, the first complete closing boundary ends the token. File\ndirectives apply to earlier content too, including nested Markdown blocks.\n\nA template-only source line does not preserve placement. With `--wrap sentence`:\n\n<!-- fmt: skip -->\n\n```markdown\nBefore\n{{ render(\"keep   this\") }}\nafter.\n```\n\nbecomes:\n\n```markdown\nBefore {{ render(\"keep   this\") }} after.\n```\n\nWrapping still respects explicit hard breaks, blank lines, and block boundaries.\nUse `fmt: skip`, `fmt: off`/`fmt: on`, or `fmt: skip file` to preserve layout.\nMultiline expressions, templates nested in Markdown links or emphasis, and\notherwise unsupported Markdown blocks retain their existing preservation\npolicy. Template settings do not change how Yamark handles headings, tables,\nhost-language eligibility, or standalone shortcode tokens.\n\n## `[embedded]`\n\nEach child table maps a directive or fence name to a formatter that reads stdin\nand writes stdout. It accepts exactly one key: the required `formatter` key.\n\n```toml\n[embedded.python]\nformatter = \"ruff\"\n\n[embedded.r]\nformatter = \"air\"\n\n[embedded.sql]\nformatter = { command = [\"sqlfmt\", \"--filename\", \"{path}\"], path_suffix = \".sql\" }\n```\n\n`formatter` accepts either a built-in shorthand or a custom formatter table.\nBuilt-in shorthands are:\n\n- `ruff`\n- `air`\n- `mdformat`\n- `prettier-json`, `prettier-jsonc`, and `prettier-json5`\n- `prettier-graphql`\n- `prettier-css`, `prettier-scss`, `prettier-less`, and `prettier-postcss`\n- `prettier-html`\n- `prettier-js`, `prettier-jsx`, `prettier-ts`, and `prettier-tsx`\n\nA custom formatter table requires both `command` and `path_suffix` and accepts\nno other keys:\n\n| Key | Requirement |\n| --- | --- |\n| `command` | A non-empty argv array of strings. It is not a shell command. At least one complete argv item must be `{path}`. |\n| `path_suffix` | A non-empty suffix appended to the synthetic path passed to the formatter. |\n\n`{path}` cannot be embedded inside another argv item.\n\nBuilt-in formatters are optional. A configured formatter is also optional when\nits command's first argv item is exactly `ruff`, `air`, `mdformat`, or\n`prettier`. For either kind, a missing executable or nonzero exit preserves the\ntarget and emits a note only with `--diagnostics`. Any other configured\nformatter treats either condition as an error. A successful process may close\nstdin before reading all input; its output still receives normal validation.\nA successful process that writes to stderr is always an error. Other\nstdin-write errors remain failures.\n\nEmbedded formatter names must be non-empty and trimmed. `skip`, `skip file`,\n`off`, `on`, and `table` are reserved directive names.\n\n## `[paths]`\n\nPath keys are relative to the directory containing `yamark.toml`. They must not\nbe empty or absolute and must not contain `..`.\n\n```toml\n[paths.\"docs\".template]\nadd_delimiters = [\n  { open = \"<<\", close = \">>\" }\n]\n\n[paths.\"prompts\".embedded_markdown.template]\nadd_delimiters = [\n  { open = \"[[\", close = \"]]\" }\n]\n```\n\n| Table | Effect |\n| --- | --- |\n| `paths.<path>.template` | Adds or replaces generic template delimiters for matching files. |\n| `paths.<path>.embedded_markdown.template` | Adds or replaces delimiters only for Markdown embedded in source strings or comments. |\n\nBoth template tables accept `add_delimiters` and `replace_delimiters` with the\nsame entry schema as top-level `[template]`. Yamark starts with the top-level\ndelimiters, then applies matching path layers from the shallowest path to the\ndeepest. Each `replace_delimiters` discards delimiters accumulated by earlier\nlayers before that layer's `add_delimiters` are appended.\n\nConfigured embedded-Markdown delimiters do not apply inside Python f-strings.\nThose strings preserve Python `{...}` expressions instead.\n=====\n---\ntitle: Yamark\nbody-classes: yamark-home\ntoc: false\n---\n\n\n\n::: {.hero-shell}\n::: {.hero-copy}\n::: {.hero-kicker}\n![](assets/favicon.svg){.hero-mark}\n:::\n\n<h1 class=\"hero-thesis\">A fast formatter for YAML and Markdown.</h1>\n\nYamark formats whole files and embedded content with the consistency we expect\nfrom code, keeping source readable and changes easy to review.\n\n::: {.hero-actions}\n[Install](usage.qmd#install){.hero-button .primary}\n[See examples](examples.qmd){.hero-button}\n:::\n\n::: {.hero-command}\n<span>Run directly from PyPI</span>\n`uvx yamark format`\n:::\n:::\n:::\n\n::: {.workflow-strip}\n::: {.workflow-item}\n**Format**\n\nRewrite supported files in place.\n:::\n\n::: {.workflow-item}\n**Check**\n\nUse non-mutating CI and diff modes.\n:::\n\n::: {.workflow-item}\n**Embed**\n\nFormat marked Markdown in YAML, Python, or R.\n:::\n\n::: {.workflow-item}\n**Recurse**\n\nFormat nested YAML and Markdown inside fenced blocks.\n:::\n:::\n\n## A quick example\n\nA short Markdown file with YAML front matter - a native document format for LLM\nwork. It combines software-readable structure with natural language for prompts,\nskills, reference documents, and generated output. The Before pane shows the\nunformatted source; the After pane shows what `yamark format` writes back.\n\n\n\n:::: {.before-after}\n::: {.before-after-pane #demo-before}\n**Before** <label class=\"softwrap-toggle\"><input type=\"checkbox\" id=\"demo-softwrap-toggle\"> soft wrap</label>\n\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: Why YAML + Markdown?\ndescription: The source languages of LLM work - structured fields for tools alongside instructions, examples, and context for models.\ntags: [llm,authoring,formats]\n---\n\n#   Why YAML + Markdown? ##\n\nWhen LLMs become part of a software system, YAML and Markdown start to feel like programming languages. YAML defines named fields tools can act on; Markdown carries the instructions, examples, and context that shape model behavior. Together they create a shared source file that stays readable to people and models, exposes explicit structure to software, produces clear diffs, and renders directly.\n\nWhere the combination shines:\n\n- Agent skills and prompt files keep names, versions, and tool metadata beside the instructions they describe.\n  - The Markdown body can carry code samples and nested structures with their own syntax and indentation.\n- Reference documents stay readable to authors and models without a separate source format or build step.\n- Tool inputs and model outputs survive chat, Git, and documentation pipelines as recognizable text.\n- One source can render as HTML or PDF and travel unchanged as agent context.\n```\n\n:::\n\n::: {.before-after-pane}\n**After**\n\n```markdown\n---\ntitle: Why YAML + Markdown?\ndescription: >-\n  The source languages of LLM work - structured fields for tools alongside\n  instructions, examples, and context for models.\ntags: [llm, authoring, formats]\n---\n\n# Why YAML + Markdown?\n\nWhen LLMs become part of a software system, YAML and Markdown start to\nfeel like programming languages. YAML defines named fields tools can act\non; Markdown carries the instructions, examples, and context that shape\nmodel behavior. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_011Ch8uyDqsKzLiU6R95iV8s","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01T2n8xgD8bV8Ut1nQExsjj7","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/tmp/corpus6/h/readme.md","content":"<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/_static/fernsolve-logo.svg\" alt=\"fernsolve logo\" width=\"300\">\n</p>\n\n<h3 align=\"center\">Scalable Krylov solvers & preconditioners for large sparse linear systems</h3>\n\n[![CI](https://github.com/fernsolve/fernsolve/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/fernsolve/fernsolve/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/fernsolve.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/fernsolve/) [![conda-forge](https://img.shields.io/conda/vn/conda-forge/fernsolve.svg)](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/fernsolve) [![Docs](https://readthedocs.org/projects/fernsolve/badge/?version=stable)](https://fernsolve.readthedocs.io/en/stable/)\n[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.14012345.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14012345)\n\n**fernsolve** solves $Ax = b$ for large, sparse, (mostly) nonsymmetric $A$ on anything from a laptop to a few thousand MPI ranks. It provides restarted and pipelined Krylov methods (CG, GMRES($m$), BiCGStab($\\ell$), IDR($s$)), a handful of robust preconditioners (ILU(k), ILUT, smoothed-aggregation AMG, block Jacobi) and mixed-precision iterative refinement, behind a C++20 core with Python bindings that accept anything `scipy.sparse` understands.\n\nIt grew out of the Computational Mechanics group's need to solve pressure systems with ~10⁹ unknowns on the [larch cluster][larch] without writing PETSc boilerplate for every PhD project.  If you already use PETSc or Trilinos and are happy with them, you probably don't need us :-)\n\n## Features\n\n* Krylov methods\n  - CG, preconditioned CG, block CG for multiple right-hand sides\n  - GMRES($m$) with CGS2 or MGS orthogonalisation, flexible GMRES, and **pipelined GMRES** (Ghysels et al., 2013) for latency-bound runs\n  -  BiCGStab($\\ell$) and IDR($s$) for when the $\\mathcal{O}(mn)$ memory of GMRES hurts\n* Preconditioners: ILU(0), ILU(k), ILUT, block Jacobi with local ILU, smoothed-aggregation AMG\n* Distributed CSR matrices over MPI, with optional GPU offload of SpMV and triangular solves (CUDA or HIP)\n+ Mixed-precision iterative refinement (`float32`/`bfloat16` factorisation, `float64` residuals)\n+ Reproducible reductions: pass `deterministic=True` and you get bit-identical residual histories for a fixed number of ranks, at about 8 % extra cost\n\nInstallation\n------------\n\n```bash\npip install fernsolve              # CPU wheels with OpenMP, no MPI\nconda install -c conda-forge fernsolve \"fernsolve=*=mpi_openmpi_*\"\n```\n\nOn HPC systems you almost certainly want to build against the site's MPI, so use Spack:\n\n```console\n$ spack install fernsolve@2.4.1 +mpi +cuda cuda_arch=80 ^openmpi@4.1.6 ^openblas threads=openmp\n$ spack load fernsolve\n```\n\nor build from source (CMake ≥ 3.24, a C++20 compiler, MPI ≥ 3.1 and BLAS/LAPACK):\n\n    git clone https://github.com/fernsolve/fernsolve.git && cd fernsolve\n    cmake -S . -B build -DFERN_ENABLE_MPI=ON -DFERN_ENABLE_CUDA=OFF -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release\n    cmake --build build -j 16 && ctest --test-dir build -L unit\n    pip install ./python --no-build-isolation\n\n## Quick start\n\n```python\nimport numpy as np\nimport scipy.sparse as sp\nfrom fernsolve import krylov, precond\n\n# 2-D Poisson on a 1000 x 1000 grid, n = 10**6\nn = 1000\nT = sp.diags([-1, 2, -1], [-1, 0, 1], shape=(n, n))\nA = (sp.kron(sp.eye(n), T) + sp.kron(T, sp.eye(n))).tocsr()\nb = np.ones(A.shape[0])\n\nM = precond.AMG(A, strength=0.25, max_levels=10)\nx, info = krylov.cg(A, b, M=M, rtol=1e-10, maxiter=200)\nprint(info.iterations, info.residual_norm)    # 14  8.7e-11\n```\n\nThe same in C++ (link against `fernsolve::fernsolve`):\n\n```cpp\n#include <fernsolve/fernsolve.hpp>\n\nint main(int argc, char** argv) {\n  fern::mpi::environment env(argc, argv);\n  auto A = fern::io::read_matrix_market<double>(\"thermal2.mtx\", env.world());\n  fern::dist_vector<double> b(A.row_map(), 1.0), x(A.row_map(), 0.0);\n  fern::precond::ilut<double> M(A, {.fill = 20, .droptol = 1e-4});\n  auto info = fern::krylov::gmres(A, x, b, M, {.restart = 50, .rtol = 1e-8});\n  if (env.rank() == 0) std::printf(\"%d iterations, |r|/|b| = %.2e\\n\", info.iterations, info.relres);\n}\n```\n\n## Which solver should I use?\n\n| Your matrix | Try first | Then | Notes |\n|---|---|:---:|---|\n| SPD (diffusion, elasticity) | `cg` + `AMG` | `cg` + `ILU(0)` | AMG setup is amortised over many solves |\n| nonsymmetric, mild | `gmres(restart=50)` + `ILUT` | `bicgstab` | |\n| nonsymmetric, convection-dominated | `fgmres` + `AMG(strength=0.5)` | `idr(s=8)` | ILU often breaks down, watch for `ZeroPivotError` |\n| many right-hand sides | `block_cg` / `block_gmres` | | cost grows ~linearly in the block size `k \\| nrhs` |\n| ill-conditioned, $\\kappa(A) > 10^{10}$ | `refine` (mixed precision) | a direct solver | seriously, try MUMPS |\n\n### A word on convergence\n\nAll solvers stop when the *relative* residual drops below `rtol`, i.e. when $\\|b - Ax_k\\|_2 \\le \\mathtt{rtol}\\cdot\\|b\\|_2$ (absolute tolerances via `atol=` are supported too). For GMRES, the classic bound of Saad & Schultz (1986) for diagonalisable $A = V\\Lambda V^{-1}$ is\n\n$$\n\\frac{\\|r_k\\|_2}{\\|r_0\\|_2} \\;\\le\\; \\kappa_2(V)\\, \\min_{\\substack{p \\in \\mathcal{P}_k \\\\ p(0) = 1}} \\; \\max_{\\lambda \\in \\Lambda(A)} |p(\\lambda)| ,\n$$\n\nwhich is why clustering the spectrum (= a good preconditioner) matters far more than the choice between GMRES and BiCGStab. See the [user guide on preconditioning](https://fernsolve.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user/precond.html) for practical advice.\n\n## Running on a Slurm cluster\n\nfernsolve is an ordinary MPI program, so launch it with `srun` (preferred) or `mpirun`. A typical job on larch:\n\n```bash\n#!/bin/bash\n#SBATCH --job-name=fern-thermal2\n#SBATCH --nodes=4\n#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64\n#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=3          # 64 ranks x 3 OpenMP threads = 192 cores per node\n#SBATCH --time=00:30:00\n#SBATCH --partition=short\n\nmodule load gcc/13.2.0 openmpi/4.1.6 fernsolve/2.4.1\nexport OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK OMP_PLACES=cores OMP_PROC_BIND=close\nsrun --cpu-bind=cores python solve.py --matrix /scratch/$USER/thermal2.mtx --restart 50\n```\n\nEnvironment variables that change behaviour at run time:\n\nVariable | Default | Effect\n--- | --- | ---\n`FERN_VERBOSITY` | `1` | 0 = silent, 3 = print the residual every iteration\n`FERN_DETERMINISTIC` | `0` | bit-reproducible reductions (slower)\n`FERN_GPU_AWARE_MPI` | auto | set to `0` if your MPI *claims* to be CUDA-aware but isn't\n\n## Performance\n\nStrong scaling of pipelined vs. classical GMRES(50) with block-Jacobi/ILU(0) on `thermal2` replicated to $n \\approx 2.0 \\times 10^8$ (larch: 2× EPYC 9654 per node, HDR-200 InfiniBand). Time per iteration in ms, median of 5 runs:\n\n<!-- fmt: skip -->\n| nodes |  GMRES | p-GMRES | speed-up |\n|------:|-------:|--------:|---------:|\n|     1 |  412.0 |   405.3 |    1.02× |\n|     4 |  108.9 |    99.1 |    1.10× |\n|    16 |   31.2 |    24.7 |    1.26× |\n|    64 |   11.8 |     7.1 |    1.66× |\n\nBeyond 16 nodes the `MPI_Allreduce` latency dominates and pipelining pays off; below that it costs a little extra memory traffic for nothing. Details are in the [technical note](docs/notes/tn-2026-07.Rmd).\n\n## Citing\n\nIf fernsolve helped your research, please cite the software paper (and the specific release via Zenodo):\n\n```bibtex\n@article{haldorsen2025fernsolve,\n  title   = {fernsolve: Pipelined {Krylov} Solvers for Sparse Systems at Scale},\n  author  = {Haldorsen, Ines and Asante, Kwame O. and Lindqvist, Astrid},\n  journal = {Journal of Open Source Software},\n  year    = {2025},\n  volume  = {10}, number = {112}, pages = {7781},\n  doi     = {10.21105/joss.07781}\n}\n```\n\n## Roadmap\n\n- [x] pipelined GMRES\n- [x] HIP backend for SpMV\n- [ ] s-step (communication-avoiding) CG -- prototype on the `ca-cg` branch\n- [ ] SYCL backend, *if* someone gives us access to the hardware\n-  [ ] better AMG for systems of PDEs (elasticity, Stokes)\n\n## Acknowledgements\n\nDevelopment is funded by EPSRC (grant EP/Y012345/1)[^epsrc] and by in-kind RSE time from Research Computing Services. Reference the issue/PR number, not the commit hash. -->\n\n## [Unreleased]\n\n### Added\n- `fern::krylov::gmres_pipelined`: Ghysels–Vanroose pipelined GMRES($m$) that overlaps the global reduction with the next SpMV. On 64 nodes of larch this cuts time-to-solution for the replicated `thermal2` problem by ~31 % (#1043).\n- Python: `fernsolve.callbacks.ResidualHistory` now also records the *true* residual $\\|b - Ax_k\\|_2$ every `check_every` iterations, next to the recursively updated one, so you can finally see when the two drift apart.\n* HIP backend for the ILU(0) triangular solves (thanks to the AMD folks at the hackathon) \n\n### Changed\n-   Default restart length for GMRES is now `restart=50` (was 30). For most SuiteSparse test matrices this reduces iteration counts by 10–25 %, at the cost of $\\mathcal{O}(mn)$ extra memory; pass `restart=30` to get the old behaviour.\n- The CMake option `FERN_USE_OPENMP` now defaults to `ON`.\n\n### Fixed\n- Loss of orthogonality in classical Gram–Schmidt with re-orthogonalisation (CGS2) when $\\kappa(A) \\gtrsim 10^{12}$. We now fall back to modified Gram–Schmidt for the offending Arnoldi step and emit a `ConvergenceWarning` instead of returning garbage. Reported by Dr. Ines Haldorsen with a beautifully minimal reproducer (#1031).\n- `fern_mpi_finalize()` no longer deadlocks when called after a failed `MPI_Comm_split` (#1029)\n\n## [2.4.1] - 2026-10-02\n\n### Fixed\n\n* Wheels for `manylinux_2_28_aarch64` were built without OpenMP, which made `fernsolve` up to 8× slower on the Grace nodes than the x86_64 build (#1019).\n* Typo in the docstring of `fernsolve.precond.ILUT`: `droptol` is relative to the 2-norm of the row, not the ∞-norm.\n\n## [2.4.0] - 2026-09-15\n\n### Added\n\n- **Mixed-precision iterative refinement** (`fernsolve.refine`): factorise in `float32` (or `bfloat16` on GPUs that support it), refine in `float64`. Converges whenever $\\kappa_\\infty(A)\\,u_f < 1$, where $u_f$ is the unit roundoff of the factorisation precision; see Carson & Higham (2018) and the [user guide section on refinement][refine-docs].\n- Block CG for multiple right-hand sides:\n\n  ```python\n  from fernsolve import krylov\n  X, info = krylov.block_cg(A, B, M=precond, rtol=1e-10, maxiter=500)\n  ```\n\n- New `fernsolve-bench` command line tool.\n  It replaces the old `scripts/bench.py` and writes results as CSV *and* as a Markdown table.\n\n### Changed\n\n1. Minimum supported versions: CMake 3.24, Python 3.10, NumPy 1.25, MPI 3.1.\n2. `SolverInfo.converged` is now a `bool`, not an `int`. Code doing `if info.converged == 1:` still works; code doing `info.converged is 1` (please don't) does not.\n3. Wheels are built against OpenBLAS 0.3.28.\n\n### Deprecated\n- `fernsolve.gmres(..., orthog=\"mgs\")` -- pass `arnoldi=ArnoldiOptions(orthog=\"mgs\")` instead. The keyword will be removed in 3.0.\n\n### Performance\n\nThe CSR SpMV kernel for matrices with fewer than 8 nonzeros per row now uses a vectorised segmented reduction. Speed-ups on a single larch node (2× AMD EPYC 9654, 192 cores):\n\n<!-- fmt: off -->\n| matrix (SuiteSparse)  |      n |    nnz | 2.3.2 (GFlop/s) | 2.4.0 (GFlop/s) | speed-up |\n|:----------------------|-------:|-------:|----------------:|----------------:|---------:|\n| `G3_circuit`          |  1.59M |  7.66M |            41.2 |            63.9 |    1.55× |\n| `thermal2`            |  1.23M |  8.58M |            44.0 |            61.3 |    1.39× |\n| `ecology2`            |  1.00M |  5.00M |            37.5 |            66.1 |    1.76× |\n<!-- fmt: on -->\n\n## [2.3.2] - 2026-06-30\n### Fixed\n+ Segfault in `ilu0()` for matrices with an explicitly stored zero on the diagonal; we now raise `ZeroPivotError` with the offending row index.\n+ Thread safety of the global `fern::set_verbosity()` (#987).\n\n## [2.3.1] - 2026-05-12\n\n### Fixed\n\n- Regression from 2.3.0: `rtol` was treated as an absolute tolerance by `bicgstab` when `x0` was given. The stopping criterion is again\n  $$\\frac{\\|r_k\\|_2}{\\|b\\|_2} \\le \\mathtt{rtol}$$\n  for all solvers.\n- `ResidualHistory.plot()` used a linear y-axis. It is log-scale again, as it should be for anything that converges geometrically.\n\n## [2.3.0] - 2026-03-03\n\nBig release, see the [migration notes](docs/migration/2.3.md) for details. Highlights:\n\n* Algebraic multigrid preconditioner (`fernsolve.precond.AMG`, smoothed aggregation) with Chebyshev and $\\ell_1$-Jacobi smoothers.\n    * Coarse-grid solve via the direct solver of your choice (MUMPS, SuperLU_DIST, or our own dense LU for tiny coarse grids).\n    * Setup is ~3× faster than PyAMG's on the same hierarchy, but we still recommend PyAMG for exploratory work.\n* Dropped Python 3.8 and 3.9.\n\n### Removed\n\n- The `fernsolve.legacy` module (deprecated since 2.1).\n\n## [2.0.0] - 2025-01-20\n\n> **Note on versioning:** 2.0 broke the C ABI without breaking the C++ API, so strictly speaking only C users needed a major bump. Wait for ✅ checks + 1 approval (2 for anything touching `src/lib/pricing`)\n\n## Local setup\n\nYou need Node 20 (we use [Volta](https://volta.sh), it picks the right version automatically), pnpm 9, and Docker if you want the CMS running locally.\n\n    git clone git@github.com:acme/acme-marketing.git\n    cd acme-marketing\n    pnpm install\n    cp .env.example .env.local   # ask in #web-platform for the preview token\n\nIf `pnpm dev` complains about `sharp`, run `pnpm rebuild sharp`. It's always sharp.\nThe `Makefile` wraps the common stuff:\n\n```make\ndev:\n⇥pnpm dev --host\nseed:\n⇥docker compose exec cms npm run seed -- --locale=en,nl,de\n```\n\n## Commits & branches\n\nWe use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/). The release bot reads them, so a typo = a missing changelog entry.\n\n| type | when | example |\n|------|------|---------|\n| `feat` | new page, component, CMS field | `feat(landing): add BF26 hero variant B` |\n| `fix` | bug | `fix(pricing): show €0,00 as \"Free\"` |\n| `copy` | text-only change by marketing | `copy(home): new USP strip wording` |\n| `chore` | deps, CI | `chore: bump astro to 4.16` |\n| `perf` |  | `perf(img): serve AVIF for the hero` |\n\n## Writing content (marketing team 💜)\n\nMost pages are Markdown with front matter in `src/content/`. Things that bite people:\n\n* **Prices** never go into copy as plain text. Use the shortcode so they update when the pricing team changes them: `{{< price sku=\"AUR-2-BLK-42\" >}}` renders \"€119,95\" (or \"~~€129,95~~ €119,95\" during a promo).\n* Emoji are fine in headings and CTAs, max **one** per heading 🙏. No emoji in `<title>` or the meta description -- Google strips some of them and it looks broken in the SERPs.\n* UTM parameters: lowercase, hyphens, no spaces → `utm_campaign=bf26-early-access`.\n- Links to products: use the slug, not the full URL (`/p/aurora-runner-2`); the build checks them.\n    - external links get `rel=\"noopener\"` automatically\n+ Images: max 400 KB, WebP or AVIF, and **always** fill in `alt`. Decorative images get `alt=\"\"`.\n\nEmail templates live in `emails/` and use Liquid. Personalisation tokens like {{ customer.first_name | default: \"there\" }} and {{ cart.item_count }} are rendered by the ESP, not by us, and so are conditionals such as {% if customer.vip %}early access{% endif %} -- don't wrap them in backticks in the source or they'll end up in the inbox literally.\n\n{{< alert title=\"Heads up\" color=\"info\" >}}\nThe CMS **content models** (`cms/models/*.json`) are code. Renaming a field breaks the storefront build until both PRs are merged, so coordinate in #web-platform first.\n{{< /alert >}}\n\n> **Tip:** landing pages can override the nav and the promo banner from front matter:\n>\n> ```yaml\n> title:   \"Black Friday 2026\"\n> banner: {text: \"Up to 40% off 🎉\",  variant: urgent ,ends_at: 2026-11-28T23:59:00+01:00}\n> nav:\n>     hide: [ blog, about ]\n> ```\n>\n> Anything else needs a component change.\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/img/content-workflow.png\" alt=\"Diagram: copy is written in Google Docs, pasted into the CMS, checked in preview mode, then published\" width=\"640\">\n</p>\n\n## Glossary\n\nPDP\n: Product detail page, `/p/{slug}`.\n\nPLP\n:   Product listing page -- category grids and search results.\n\nSKU\n: Stock keeping unit. Format `FAM-GEN-COLOR-SIZE`, e.g. `AUR-2-BLK-42`; the size segment can be 1–3 characters.\n\nAOV\n: Average order value. Revenue ÷ orders, **excluding** gift cards and shipping.\n\n## Pull request checklist\n\n- [ ] Screenshots (desktop **and** mobile) for visual changes\n- [ ] Lighthouse ≥ 90 on the changed page (`pnpm lh -- --url=/your-page`)\n- [x] I read this file\n- [ ] Copy reviewed by someone in #marketing-copy  \n      (legal-ish text: also tag @legal-web)\n- [ ] No hard-coded prices, SKUs or campaign dates\n   - [ ] if you *really* need a date, put it in `src/data/campaigns.yaml`\n\n\n\n## Code of conduct\nBe kind. It is written in Nextflow DSL2, with small Python and R helpers under `bin/`, and runs on the larch Slurm cluster, on the lab's Kubernetes namespace and -- with some patience -- on a laptop.\n\nThis document is for people *changing* the pipeline. If you only want to run it, read [README.md](README.md) and `docs/usage.md` instead.\n\n**Contents**\n\n1. [Ground rules](#ground-rules)\n2. [Development environment](#development-environment)\n3. [Tests](#tests)\n4. [Adding or updating a module](#adding-or-updating-a-module)\n5) [Commit messages and merge requests](#commit-messages-and-merge-requests)\n6) [Releasing](#releasing)\n\nGround rules\n------------\n\n* Never commit patient-identifiable data. Test data under `tests/data/` is either synthetic or from the public **GIAB HG002** sample, downsampled to ~2× around chr20:10,000,000-12,000,000. If you are not 100 % sure a file is OK to share, ask Dr. Mensah *before* pushing; rewriting git history is painful and does not un-leak anything.\n* All changes go through a merge request against `dev`; `main` only moves on releases.\n- Results must stay reproducible: an MR that changes any output VCF needs a justification in its description and an updated truth set (see [Tests](#tests)).\n*   Be kind in reviews. Most contributors are PhD students with a thesis to write.\n\n## Development environment\n\nWe use [pixi](https://pixi.sh) for Nextflow itself and the Python/R helpers, and containers (Apptainer on larch, Docker elsewhere) for the bioinformatics tools:\n\n```bash\ngit clone git@git.northfield.ac.uk:mensah-lab/varcall.git\ncd varcall\npixi install            # nextflow, nf-test, python 3.12, R 4.4, pre-commit\npixi run pre-commit install\n```\n\nOn larch, do this on a login node but run anything heavier than `nf-test` in an interactive job (`salloc -p short -c 8 --mem=32G -t 2:00:00`). The login nodes kill processes that use more than 4 GB of RAM, and you *will* hit that with GATK.\n\n> [!WARNING]\n> Do **not** keep the Apptainer cache in your home directory: home has a 50 GB quota and a single DeepVariant image is 6 GB. Put\n> `export APPTAINER_CACHEDIR=/scratch/$USER/.apptainer` in your `~/.bashrc`.\n\n## Tests ##\n\nThere are three layers of tests:\n\n1. **Unit tests** for the helper scripts (`pytest` for Python, `testthat` for R):\n\n   ```bash\n   pixi run pytest bin/tests -q\n   pixi run Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir(\"bin/tests/testthat\")'\n   ```\n2. **Module tests** with [nf-test](https://www.nf-test.com/), one per module under `modules/local/*/tests/`. Run all of them with `nf-test test --profile apptainer`, or only the one you changed:\n    ```bash\n    nf-test test modules/local/deepvariant/tests/main.nf.test --profile apptainer\n    ```\n3. **End-to-end** test on the GIAB subset. It takes ~25 min on 4 nodes and runs nightly in CI, but please run it yourself if you touch anything in `subworkflows/`:\n\n       sbatch --wait tests/e2e/run_e2e.sbatch\n       python tests/e2e/compare_to_truth.py results/e2e/HG002.vcf.gz --truth tests/data/HG002_chr20_truth.vcf.gz --min-f1 0.995\n\n   The comparison uses `hap.py`. An MR may lower SNV F1 by at most 0.001 and indel F1 by at most 0.003 without a discussion; anything more needs sign-off from the Core.\n\n### Making new test data\n\nIf you need reads for a new region, downsample from the full 35× HG002 BAM rather than committing big files. To get a target coverage $c_t$ from an original coverage $c_0$, keep each read pair with probability $p = c_t / c_0$, e.g. $p = 2/35 \\approx 0.057$ for 2×:\n\n```bash\nsamtools view -b --subsample 0.057 --subsample-seed 42 HG002.GRCh38.35x.bam chr20:10000000-12000000 > HG002_chr20_2x.bam\n```\n\nExpected coverage after subsampling is $c_t$ only on average; for small regions check it with `mosdepth` and redraw with another seed if it is off by more than 10 %.\n\nThe `Makefile` in `tests/data/` regenerates everything (recipes must be indented with a tab, not spaces):\n\n```make\nHG002_chr20_2x.bam: $(SRC_BAM)\n⇥samtools view -b --subsample 0.057 --subsample-seed 42 $< chr20:10000000-12000000 > $@\n⇥samtools index $@\n```\n\n## Adding or updating a module\n\nEvery module lives in `modules/local/<tool>/` and needs a `main.nf`, a `meta.yml` and at least one nf-test. CI validates `meta.yml` against `assets/schema_module.json`, so stick to this layout:\n\n```yaml\nname: deepvariant_callvariants\ndescription:  Call variants from a CRAM with DeepVariant (on a GPU if one is available)\nkeywords: [ variant calling, deep learning,gvcf ]\ntools:\n    - deepvariant:\n        description: \"DeepVariant is an analysis pipeline that uses a deep neural network to call genetic variants from next-generation DNA sequencing data.\"\n        homepage: https://github.com/google/deepvariant\n        licence: ['BSD-3-Clause']\ninput:\n  - meta:\n      type: map\n      description: Groovy map with sample information, e.g. `[ id:'HG002', sex:'XY' ]`\n  - cram: {type: file, pattern: \"*.cram\"}\noutput:\n  - vcf: {type: file, pattern: \"*.vcf.gz\"}\n  - gvcf:\n      type: file\n      pattern: \"*.g.vcf.gz\"\nauthors: [\"J. Ortiz\", 'K. Mensah']\n```\n\nPlease **don't** pin tool versions in `meta.yml` the way the old template did; they go stale immediately and the container tag is the single source of truth:\n\n```yaml fmt: skip\ntools:\n  - deepvariant:\n      version:   1.6.1     # <- no!\n      container: \"google/deepvariant:1.6.1-gpu\"\n```\n\n<details>\n<summary>Why Nextflow and not Snakemake?</summary>\n\nWe get asked this a lot. Short answer: the Core's other pipelines are Nextflow, and the Kubernetes executor was the deciding factor back in 2022. Long answer: see the discussion in [issue 14](https://git.northfield.ac.uk/mensah-lab/varcall/-/issues/14).\n\n</details>\n\n## Commit messages and merge requests\n\nWe use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/), mostly so that `git-cliff` can write the changelog for us:\n\n| type | use it for | bumps |\n|------|-----------|-------|\n| `feat` | new module, new parameter | minor |\n| `fix` | wrong results, crashes | patch |\n| `perf` | faster or leaner, **identical** output | patch |\n| `chore`, `ci`, `docs`, `test` | everything else | -- |\n\nWhen you open an MR, GitLab pre-fills this template (`.gitlab/merge_request_templates/Default.md`). Please actually fill it in:\n\n````markdown\n## What does this change?\n\n<!-- one or two sentences, plus the issue number -->\n\n## Checklist\n- [ ] `nf-test test` passes locally (or on larch: paste the Slurm job ID)\n- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` updated under *Unreleased*\n-  [ ] If outputs change: hap.py comparison attached and F1 deltas filled in below\n* [ ] Reviewed by someone who did not write it\n\n| metric | before | after |\n|---|---|---|\n| SNV F1 |  |  |\n| indel F1 | | |\n````\n\n## Releasing\n\nOnly maintainers (currently J. Ortiz and K. Mensah) cut releases:\n\n0. Make sure the nightly end-to-end run on `dev` is green.\n1. Merge `dev` into `main`, tag `vX.Y.Z`, and push the tag; CI builds and pushes the containers.\n3. The batch wrapper overrides all of these from the command line,\n#|   so do not put anything site-specific (paths!) in here.\nSOURCE_ID = \"CanESM5\"\nEXPERIMENT = \"ssp245\"\nMEMBERS = [\"r1i1p1f1\", \"r2i1p1f1\", \"r3i1p1f1\"]\nGRID = \"1x1\"\nMETHOD = \"conservative_normed\"\nREF_START, REF_END = 1981, 2010\nMIN_OCEAN_FRAC=0.5  # fmt: skip\n\n# Ocean model + coordinate names per source_id. Fig. 4).\n\n## 1.1 What we'd keep, change and drop\n\n- **Keep: Bundle & Save.** It worked. This cost approx. €22.4k in shipping subsidies vs. an estimated €61k in incremental revenue, i.e. a net positive, but see the caveat in Sec. 5 re. return rates.\n* **Drop: the sitewide countdown banner.** Ms. Alvarez from Brand asked whether it hurt LCP. This report covers step 2 only.\nflowchart LR\n  A[ESGF mirror<br/>native tos] --> B(step 1: CMOR checks)\n  B --> C(step 2: regrid + anomalies)\n  C --> D[(THREDDS)]\n  C --> E(step 3: bias correction)\n```\n\n## Methods {#sec-methods}\n\n### Regridding\n\nFields are regridded with xESMF [@zhuang2023xesmf] using first-order conservative remapping, normalised by the unmasked fraction of each target cell (`conservative_normed`). For a target cell $k$ that overlaps source cells $i$ with overlap areas $a_{ik}$ and ocean mask $m_i \\in \\{0, 1\\}$,\n\n$$\n\\hat T_k = \\frac{\\sum_i a_{ik}\\, m_i\\, T_i}{\\sum_i a_{ik}\\, m_i},\n$$ {#eq-conservative}\n\nwhich, unlike plain conservative remapping, does not pull coastal cells towards zero.  The global integral $\\sum_k A_k \\hat T_k$ is conserved exactly only if no target cell is partially masked; the residual error is what @tbl-regrid-error quantifies.\n\n### Anomalies and drift {#sec-drift}\n\nAnomalies are taken relative to each member's 1981–2010 monthly climatology (@eq-anomaly). Drift is estimated from the parallel `piControl` segment with a least-squares quadratic fit $d(t) = a + b\\,t + c\\,t^2$ and subtracted when $|b| > 0.1\\,\\mathrm{K\\,century^{-1}}$^[We tried a linear fit first. It under-corrects `IPSL-CM6A-LR`, whose drift slows down after ~200 years of spin-up.].\n\n$$\nT'(y, m) = T(y, m) - \\frac{1}{30} \\sum_{y'=1981}^{2010} T(y', m)\n$$ {#eq-anomaly}\n\n:::: {.columns}\n::: {.column width=\"55%\"}\nAll runs were done on larch[^larch] as one Slurm array, one task per model and experiment:\n\n```{.bash filename=\"jobs/submit_step2.sh\"}\nsbatch --array=0-14%5 --partition=short --cpus-per-task=32 --mem=120G \\\n       --time=04:00:00 --job-name=pp-step2 jobs/step2.sbatch\n```\n:::\n::: {.column width=\"45%\"}\n> Weights for the 0.25° GFDL grid took 19 min to build on 32 cores; every later run reused them from `$CMORPH_WEIGHTS`.\n:::\n::::\n\n[^larch]: 2× AMD EPYC 9654 per node, 768 GB RAM. Asante\"\n  - name: Research Software Engineering, University of Northfield\ndate: \"`r format(Sys.Date(), '%e %B %Y')`\"\noutput:\n  bookdown::html_document2:\n    toc: true\n    number_sections: yes\n    fig_caption: true\n    df_print: kable\n  bookdown::pdf_document2:\n    latex_engine: lualatex\n    keep_tex: no\nbibliography: [refs/krylov.bib, refs/hpc.bib]\nlink-citations: yes\nparams:\n  results: \"results/2026-11-03\"\n  baseline: \"2.4.1\"\n  nodes: !r c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64)\neditor_options:\n  markdown:\n    wrap: sentence\n  chunk_output_type: console\n---\n\n```{r setup, include=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=FALSE, fig.align=\"center\", dev=\"ragg_png\", dpi=150}\nlibrary(data.table)\nlibrary(ggplot2)\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)\nres <- fread(file.path(params$results, \"scaling.csv\"))\n```\n\n# Introduction {#intro}\n\nKrylov subspace methods spend most of their time in two kernels: the sparse matrix-vector product (SpMV) and the global reductions needed for inner products and norms. On a few nodes the SpMV dominates, but beyond approx. 16 nodes the reductions become latency-bound, since every `MPI_Allreduce` costs $\\mathcal{O}(\\log p)$ network hops regardless of message size (cf. the discussion in Ghysels et al. [-@ghysels2013pipelined], Sect. 2). Pipelined GMRES (p-GMRES) hides this latency by overlapping the reduction of iteration $k$ with the SpMV of iteration $k+1$, at the price of extra vector operations and somewhat weaker numerical stability. This note quantifies the trade-off for fernsolve v2.5.0-rc.1 on the larch cluster and compares it with the classical GMRES($m$) implementation in v`r params$baseline`. All timings are medians of 5 runs; the error bars in Fig. \\@ref(fig:strong) show the min.–max. range.\n\nThe test problem is the 3-D convection–diffusion equation $-\\nabla\\cdot(\\kappa\\nabla u) + \\mathbf{w}\\cdot\\nabla u = f$ on the unit cube, discretised with 7-point finite differences, i.e. a nonsymmetric matrix with at most 7 nonzeros per row. We use Péclet numbers of 10 and 100 (resp. \"mild\" and \"strong\" convection), which give condition numbers of ca. $10^5$ and $10^7$ at the largest size. Unless stated otherwise the restart length is $m = 50$, the relative tolerance is $10^{-8}$, and the preconditioner is block Jacobi with one ILU(0) block per MPI rank, e.g. 64 blocks on a single node. Dr. Asante's earlier note (TN No. 2025-11) used $m = 30$ instead; the difference matters, see Sect. \\@ref(results) and Tab. \\@ref(tab:iters).\n\n# Setup {#setup}\n\nAll runs used the `short` partition of larch: 2× AMD EPYC 9654 (96 cores each, 2.4 GHz base) and 768 GB of DDR5 per node, connected by HDR-200 InfiniBand in a non-blocking fat tree. We placed 64 MPI ranks per node with 3 OpenMP threads each, pinned with `--cpu-bind=cores`, and used Open MPI 4.1.6 with UCX 1.16 and GCC 13.2. The `MPI_Allreduce` latency for 8 B, measured with the OSU micro-benchmarks v7.4, grows from 2.1 µs on 2 nodes to 9.8 µs on 64 nodes, i.e. roughly as $\\log_2 p$, as expected for a recursive-doubling algorithm. Nodes were allocated with `--exclusive` and `--switches=1@01:00:00` where possible, so most jobs ran within a single leaf switch; the 32- and 64-node runs necessarily span several.\n\nWe report speed-up and parallel efficiency relative to the smallest run,\n\n\\begin{equation}\n  S(p) = \\frac{T(p_0)}{T(p)}, \\qquad E(p) = \\frac{p_0\\, S(p)}{p},\n  (\\#eq:speedup)\n\\end{equation}\n\nwhere $p_0 = 1$ node (192 cores) for strong scaling. For weak scaling we keep $n/p \\approx 3.4 \\times 10^6$ unknowns per node and report $E_w(p) = T(p_0)/T(p)$ instead, cf. Eq. \\@ref(eq:speedup) with $S$ replaced by the time ratio. Note that $E$ can exceed 1 when the local problem starts to fit into the 384 MB of L3 cache per node, which happens at 32 nodes for $n = 2.0 \\times 10^8$ (see below).\n\n# Results {#results}\n\n(ref:strong-cap) Strong scaling for $n = 2.0 \\times 10^8$ (Pe = 100). Solid: p-GMRES; dashed: GMRES; grey: ideal.\n\n```{r strong, fig.cap=\"(ref:strong-cap)\", fig.width=7, fig.height=4, out.width=\"85%\"}\nggplot(res[kind == \"strong\"], aes(nodes, time_per_iter, linetype = solver)) +\n  geom_line() + geom_point() +\n  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = t_min, ymax = t_max), width = 0.05) +\n  scale_x_continuous(trans = \"log2\", breaks = params$nodes) +\n  scale_y_log10() +\n  labs(x = \"nodes\", y = \"time per iteration (s)\") +\n  theme_bw()\n```\n\nFig. \\@ref(fig:strong) shows that p-GMRES is no faster than GMRES up to 4 nodes, but on 64 nodes it reduces the time per iteration from 11.8 ms to 7.1 ms, i.e. by 40 %. The parallel efficiency at 64 nodes rises from 0.55 to 0.89 accordingly. This is consistent with the model of Ghysels et al. (2013, Eq. 12) and with the measurements of Sanan et al. [-@sanan2016pipelined] on a Cray XC40, although their speed-ups were larger (up to 2.5×) because the Aries network has a higher reduction latency than HDR InfiniBand. Is the extra cost of pipelining ever prohibitive? Not in our runs: the additional AXPY operations add approx. 6 % to the single-node time, which is within the run-to-run noise of ±4 %.\n\nTable: (\\#tab:iters) Iterations to reach $\\|r_k\\|_2/\\|b\\|_2 < 10^{-8}$ for Pe = 100, by restart length.\n\n| nodes | GMRES(30) | GMRES(50) | p-GMRES(50) |\n|------:|----------:|----------:|------------:|\n| 1 | 412 | 298 | 301 |\n| 16 | 655 | 471 | 478 |\n| 64 | 803 | 560 | 571 |\n\nTab. \\@ref(tab:iters) shows the price in iterations. Block Jacobi weakens as the number of blocks grows (from 64 to 4,096), so all variants need more iterations at scale; p-GMRES needs 1–2 % more than GMRES because of the shifted basis, cf. Eqs. (3.4)–(3.6) in Ghysels et al. Increasing the restart length from 30 to 50 cuts iterations by approx. 30 % at every node count, at the cost of $50 \\times 3.4 \\times 10^6 \\times 8\\,\\mathrm{B} \\approx 1.4$ GB of extra basis storage per node, which is negligible on 768 GB nodes but not on the 256 GB nodes of the old `larch-legacy` partition. In total we ran `r nrow(res)` jobs, using approx. 9,800 node-hours.\n\nTwo caveats apply. First, the runs at 32 and 64 nodes were done during the maintenance window on 2 Nov. 2026, when the rest of the machine was idle; on a busy system, network contention from other jobs typically adds 10–20 % to the reduction latency (cf. Fig. 7 in Chunduri et al. [-@chunduri2017runtime]), which would make pipelining *more* attractive, not less. Second, we did not tune the `UCX_TLS` and `UCX_RNDV_THRESH` settings, so the absolute numbers are probably pessimistic by a few percent.\n\n> In short: use p-GMRES on 16 nodes or more, and GMRES below that. The crossover moves to fewer nodes for smaller problems, e.g. ca. 8 nodes for $n = 5 \\times 10^7$.\n\n# Weak scaling\n\n```{r weak}\n#| fig.cap: \"Weak-scaling efficiency $E_w(p)$ with $3.4 \\\\times 10^6$ unknowns per node.\"\n#| fig.width: 7\n#| fig.height:  3.5\nggplot(res[kind == \"weak\"], aes(nodes, efficiency, colour = solver)) +\n  geom_line() + geom_point() +\n  scale_x_continuous(trans = \"log2\", breaks = params$nodes) +\n  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1.1)) + theme_bw()\n```\n\nWeak scaling is less flattering for both methods, since the iteration count grows like $\\mathcal{O}(h^{-1})$ for this preconditioner, so the total time grows even at perfect per-iteration efficiency. Per iteration, p-GMRES keeps $E_w > 0.8$ up to 64 nodes vs. 0.61 for GMRES. A two-level preconditioner (e.g. the smoothed-aggregation AMG from fernsolve 2.3, cf. Sect. 4 of the user guide) would remove the growth in iterations; that is the subject of TN-2026-09.\n\n# Recommendations\n\n1. Default to `gmres_pipelined()` when running on 16 or more nodes, and keep `gmres()` below that. The automatic choice in `fernsolve.krylov.solve(..., method=\"auto\")` now does exactly this (v2.5.0, PR #1051).\n2. Use $m = 50$ unless memory is tight. On the legacy nodes, $m = 30$ is a reasonable compromise.\n3.  Re-run this study once the H100 partition supports GPU-aware MPI reductions; Prof. Lindqvist's group expects that by Q2 2027.\n\nAll scripts, raw timings and the `sbatch` files are archived at <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14099999>.[^repro]\n\n[^repro]: The archive also contains the exact Spack environment (`spack.lock`). Rebuilding it on another system should give identical binaries, modulo the CPU target. We have not tried this on ARM.\n\n# References {-}\n\n<div id=\"refs\"></div>\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":2119,"cache_read_input_tokens":190398,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":2119,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_01Gvk1ggD1NHUZ5frpaQFjfW","agent_id":"a437806447bf9e4db","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"91ea2b07-b2a5-4f8b-a0eb-43d7a248656a","timestamp":"2026-11-17T17:47:16.196Z","request_id":"req_011Ch8vEmDRdqPqos2yXeBme","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Write realistic test corpus H"}

On a few nodes the SpMV dominates, but beyond approx. 16 nodes the reductions become latency-bound, since every `MPI_Allreduce` costs $\\mathcal{O}(\\log p)$ network hops regardless of message size (cf. the discussion in Ghysels et al. [-@ghysels2013pipelined], Sect. 2). Pipelined GMRES (p-GMRES) hides this latency by overlapping the reduction of iteration $k$ with the SpMV of iteration $k+1$, at the price of extra vector operations and somewhat weaker numerical stability. This note quantifies the trade-off for fernsolve v2.5.0-rc.1 on the larch cluster and compares it with the classical GMRES($m$) implementation in v`r params$baseline`. All timings are medians of 5 runs; the error bars in Fig. \\@ref(fig:strong) show the min.–max. range.\n\nThe test problem is the 3-D convection–diffusion equation $-\\nabla\\cdot(\\kappa\\nabla u) + \\mathbf{w}\\cdot\\nabla u = f$ on the unit cube, discretised with 7-point finite differences, i.e. a nonsymmetric matrix with at most 7 nonzeros per row. We use Péclet numbers of 10 and 100 (resp. \"mild\" and \"strong\" convection), which give condition numbers of ca. $10^5$ and $10^7$ at the largest size. Unless stated otherwise the restart length is $m = 50$, the relative tolerance is $10^{-8}$, and the preconditioner is block Jacobi with one ILU(0) block per MPI rank, e.g. 64 blocks on a single node. Dr. Asante's earlier note (TN No. 2025-11) used $m = 30$ instead; the difference matters, see Sect. \\@ref(results) and Tab. \\@ref(tab:iters).\n\n# Setup {#setup}\n\nAll runs used the `short` partition of larch: 2× AMD EPYC 9654 (96 cores each, 2.4 GHz base) and 768 GB of DDR5 per node, connected by HDR-200 InfiniBand in a non-blocking fat tree. We placed 64 MPI ranks per node with 3 OpenMP threads each, pinned with `--cpu-bind=cores`, and used Open MPI 4.1.6 with UCX 1.16 and GCC 13.2. The `MPI_Allreduce` latency for 8 B, measured with the OSU micro-benchmarks v7.4, grows from 2.1 µs on 2 nodes to 9.8 µs on 64 nodes, i.e. roughly as $\\log_2 p$, as expected for a recursive-doubling algorithm. Nodes were allocated with `--exclusive` and `--switches=1@01:00:00` where possible, so most jobs ran within a single leaf switch; the 32- and 64-node runs necessarily span several.\n\nWe report speed-up and parallel efficiency relative to the smallest run,\n\n\\begin{equation}\n  S(p) = \\frac{T(p_0)}{T(p)}, \\qquad E(p) = \\frac{p_0\\, S(p)}{p},\n  (\\#eq:speedup)\n\\end{equation}\n\nwhere $p_0 = 1$ node (192 cores) for strong scaling. For weak scaling we keep $n/p \\approx 3.4 \\times 10^6$ unknowns per node and report $E_w(p) = T(p_0)/T(p)$ instead, cf. Eq. \\@ref(eq:speedup) with $S$ replaced by the time ratio. Thanks to @ana-perez for the patch!\n\n### Security\n- Bumped `urllib3` to 2.2.2 (CVE-2024-37891). tidepool itself was not affected because we never send `Proxy-Authorization` headers on redirects, but several scanners flagged it anyway.\n\n## [2.3.1] - 2024-07-02\n\n### Fixed\n* `tidepool init` wrote the config file with mode `0644`; it is now `0600` because it can contain secrets.\n* The `--since` filter ignored the timezone offset of the given timestamp:\n  * `--since 2024-06-01T00:00:00+02:00` used to be treated as UTC\n  * naive timestamps are still interpreted as local time, as documented\n\n## [2.3.0] - 2024-06-18   \n\n### Added\n- Pluggable storage backends. Third-party packages can register a backend via the `tidepool.backends` entry point; see [the plugin docs][plugins] for a minimal example.\n- Built-in backends:\n  - `s3` (AWS and anything else that speaks the S3 API)\n  - `gcs` -- Google Cloud Storage, using the XML API\n  - `azure` (**experimental**, no support for SAS tokens yet)\n- Shell completion for bash, zsh and fish (`tidepool completion zsh > ~/.zfunc/_tidepool`).\n\n### Changed\n- Minimum supported Python version is now 3.9.\n- Log lines use `logfmt` by default. The previous format is still available as `--log-format=classic` but will go away eventually.\n\n### Removed\n- The undocumented `TIDEPOOL_LEGACY_LIST` environment variable.\n\n## [2.2.0] - 2024-03-04\n\n### Added\n- `--bandwidth-limit` (e.g. `--bandwidth-limit 20M`) to throttle uploads. The limit applies to the whole process, not per connection.\n- Manifest files can now be compressed with zstd. On S3 this saves one request per file and, more importantly, avoids leaving incomplete multipart uploads behind when the process is killed halfway through.\n\n## [2.0.0] - 2023-09-05\n\nThis is a **breaking** release. The configuration file format changed, and the old `tidepool push` / `tidepool pull` commands\nwere merged into `tidepool sync`. Please read the migration guide below *before* upgrading your cron jobs.\n\n### Migration guide\n\n1. Run `tidepool config migrate` once. It reads `~/.tidepool.ini` and writes `~/.config/tidepool/config.toml`.\n2. Replace `tidepool push SRC DEST` with `tidepool sync SRC DEST`, and `tidepool pull DEST SRC` with `tidepool sync DEST SRC`.\n3. If you were using `--parallel`, rename it to `--jobs`.\n4. Check your cron jobs: the exit code for \"nothing to do\" changed from `3` to `0`.\n\n### Removed\n- `tidepool push` and `tidepool pull` (see above).\n- Python 3.7 support.\n\n## [1.9.3] - The quickest way to run everything is:\n\n```bash\npytest -n auto\n```\n\nSome useful variations:\n\n| Command | What it does |\n|---------|--------------|\n| `pytest tests/unit` | only the fast unit tests (< 10 s) |\n| `pytest -m \"not slow\"` | skip the property-based tests that take several minutes |\n| `pytest --cov=fernwood --cov-report=html` | coverage report in `htmlcov/` |\n| `nox -s tests-3.9 tests-3.13` | run against several Python versions, like CI does |\n| `nox -s docs` | build the documentation and fail on warnings |\n\nIf you add a new feature, please add tests for it. Bug fixes should come with a regression test that fails without the fix -- this is the single most useful thing you can do to make sure the bug stays fixed.\n\n## Style guide\n\nFormatting and linting are fully automated, so please don't spend time on manual formatting; `ruff format` is the source of truth. A few things the tools can't check:\n\n- Public functions and classes need docstrings (Google style). Private helpers don't, but a one-line comment explaining *why* is always appreciated.\n- Prefer small, focused modules. If a file grows beyond ~800 lines it is probably doing too much.\n+ Type hints are required for all new code. We run `mypy --strict` on `src/`, but not on `tests/`.\n- Error messages should say what went wrong **and** what the user can do about it, e.g. \"field `age` must be >= 0, got -3\" rather than \"invalid value\".\n\n### Commit messages\n\nWe loosely follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/). The type prefix is used to generate the changelog, so please get it right:\n\n| Prefix | Use for | Shows up in changelog? |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `feat:` | new user-facing functionality | yes, under *Added* |\n| `fix:` | bug fixes | yes, under *Fixed* |\n| `perf:` | performance improvements | yes |\n| `docs:` | documentation only | no |\n| `refactor:` | code changes that neither fix a bug nor add a feature | no |\n| `chore:` / `ci:` | tooling, dependencies, CI configuration | no |\n\nBreaking changes must include a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer that explains the migration path.\n\n## Pull request process\n\n1. Open an issue first for anything bigger than a small bug fix, so we can agree on the approach before you invest a lot of time.\n2. Keep pull requests focused. Two small PRs are much easier to review than one big one that does several unrelated things.\n3. Make sure CI is green. If a check fails for reasons unrelated to your change (it happens, the macOS runners are flaky), leave a comment and a maintainer will re-run it.\n4. Add a news fragment in `changes/`:\n   - name it `<PR number>.<type>.md`, e.g. `1234.fixed.md`\n   - one or two sentences, written for users rather than for reviewers\n     * you can use Markdown, but keep it to inline formatting\n5. A maintainer will review your PR, usually within a week. We may push small fixups directly to your branch, so please enable \"Allow edits from maintainers\".\n\n> **Tip:** draft pull requests are welcome.
