It was born out of one too many incidents where somebody \"just quickly\" added an index in production, the next deploy's migration failed at 2am, and nobody could tell which of the forty differences between staging and production actually mattered.\n\nDriftwood is **read-only** by design: it never modifies the database it inspects. \n\n## Table of contents\n\n- [Features](#features)\n- [Installation](#installation)\n  - [pip / pipx](#pip--pipx)\n  - [Docker](#docker)\n- [Quick start](#quick-start)\n- [Configuration](#configuration)\n- [Using Driftwood in CI](#using-driftwood-in-ci)\n- [FAQ](#faq)\n- [Contributing](#contributing)\n- [License](#license)\n\n## Features\n\n- **Two-way diff** between a live database and the schema you get by replaying your migrations into a throwaway container\n- Understands Alembic, Django, Flyway and Liquibase migrations (XML and YAML changelogs), as well as plain directories of numbered `.sql` files\n* Ignore rules for objects you don't care about, e.g. `pg_stat_statements` views, temp tables or partitions created by `pg_partman`\n* Output as human-readable text, JSON, JUnit XML or a GitHub Actions job summary\n- Generates a *suggested* fix migration. Review it before you run it -- Driftwood can't know whether a missing column should be added or the migration that created it should be deleted\n- Fast: diffing a 1,200-table schema takes about three seconds, most of which is spent waiting for `pg_dump`\n\n## Installation\n\nDriftwood requires Python 3.9+ and, for the migration replay, a running Docker daemon (Podman works too if the Docker-compatible socket is enabled).\n\n### pip / pipx\n\n```bash\npipx install driftwood-db\n# or, inside an existing virtualenv:\npip install \"driftwood-db[postgres,mysql]\"\n```\n\n### Docker\n\n```bash\ndocker run --rm -v \"$PWD:/project\" -w /project \\\n  -e DRIFTWOOD_DSN=\"postgresql://readonly@db.internal:5432/app\" \\\n  ghcr.io/driftwood-db/driftwood:latest check\n```\n\nThe image ships `pg_dump` 12 through 17 and `mysqldump` 8.0/8.4 and picks the right one based on the server version.\n\n## Quick start\n\n1. Point Driftwood at your migrations and your database:\n\n   ```bash\n   driftwood init --migrations alembic/versions --dsn \"$DATABASE_URL\"\n   ```\n\n2. Run a check:\n\n   ```console\n   $ driftwood check\n   Replaying 214 migrations into postgres:16 ... done (41.2s)\n   Comparing with db.internal:5432/app ...\n\n   ~ table public.orders\n       + index orders_created_at_idx (created_at)     only in live database\n       ~ column status: varchar(20) -> varchar(32)    type differs\n   - table public.legacy_coupons                      only in migrations\n\n   3 differences (1 error, 2 warnings)\n   ```\n3. Decide what to do about each difference: either write a migration, or add an ignore rule if the difference is intentional.\n\n## Configuration\n\nDriftwood reads `driftwood.yml` from the current directory (or the `[tool.driftwood]` table in `pyproject.toml`, if you prefer):\n\n```yaml\nmigrations:\n  tool: alembic\n  path: alembic/versions\ndatabase:\n  dsn: ${DATABASE_URL}\n  schemas: [public, billing]\nignore:\n  - kind: index\n    name: \"*_tmp_idx\"\n  - kind: table\n    schema: public\n    name: django_session   # recreated by a cron job, see OPS-412\nseverity:\n  extra_index: warning\n  missing_column: error\n```\n\nEvery option can also be set through environment variables, e.g. `DRIFTWOOD_DATABASE__DSN`. Environment variables take precedence over the config file, which in turn takes precedence over the built-in defaults.\n\n## Using Driftwood in CI\n\nThe most common setup is a nightly job that runs `driftwood check --format github` against a read replica and fails if there are any errors. The `github` format writes a job summary with a collapsible diff per table, so you can see at a glance what changed without digging through the logs.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Example GitHub Actions workflow</summary>\n\n```yaml\nname: schema-drift\non:\n  schedule:\n    - cron: \"0 5 * * *\"\njobs:\n  drift:\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n    steps:\n      - uses: actions/checkout@v4\n      - run: pipx run driftwood-db check --format github\n        env:\n          DRIFTWOOD_DSN: ${{ secrets.REPLICA_DSN }}\n```\n\n</details>\n\n## FAQ\n\n**Does Driftwood ever write to my database?**\nNo. It only needs a role that can read the catalog. We recommend creating a dedicated read-only role:\n- PostgreSQL: membership in `pg_read_all_stats` is enough for most setups\n- MySQL: `SELECT` on `information_schema` plus `SHOW VIEW` on the schemas you want to check\n   * on MySQL 5.7 you also need `PROCESS`, otherwise some index metadata is hidden\n\n**Why does it need Docker?**  \nTo know what the schema *should* look like, Driftwood replays your migrations into an empty database of the same major version. Doing that in a container is the only reliable way we found to match production exactly, including extensions, collations and server defaults.\n\n**Can I compare two live databases without any migrations?**\nYes: `driftwood diff postgresql://staging/app postgresql://prod/app`. This skips the replay step entirely.\n\n**What about other kinds of objects?**\n  - stored procedures and functions: compared by a normalised hash of the body, so whitespace-only changes are ignored\n  - views: same as functions\n  - row-level security policies: supported on PostgreSQL 13+\n    - policies on partitioned tables are only compared on the parent\n\n\n## Contributing\n\nBug reports and pull requests are very welcome! The sample mean was `r round(mean(nhs$wemwbs, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` (SD `r round(sd(nhs$wemwbs, na.rm = TRUE), 1)`), slightly above the national average reported by\nthe ONS for 2022.\n\nExposure variables were derived from the city's open data portal (approx. 1,100 parks and green spaces, as of Jan. 2024):\n\n- `park_dist_m`: network distance in metres from the respondent's postcode centroid to the nearest park entrance.\n- `park_area_ha`: area of that park in hectares.\n- `green_share`: share of green land use within 500 m, as used by most previous studies (cf. Annual plans are essentially unaffected. \n:::\n\nBetween June and September the share of monthly subscribers who cancelled within a given month went from 3.1% to 4.4% (@fig-monthly-churn). Most of the increase comes from customers in their first three months, who are also the group most exposed to the new pricing page; customers with more than a year of tenure churned at roughly the same rate as before. We estimate that the price change explains about two thirds of the increase, with the remainder attributable to a seasonal effect that we also saw, in weaker form, in 2023[^seasonality].\n\n[^seasonality]: The 2023 data uses the old plan structure, so the comparison is only approximate. See the appendix of last year's report for the mapping between old and new plans.\n\n## Data\n\nWe use the subscription ledger exported on 2 October 2024. A subscription counts as *active* in a month if it was active on the first day of that month, and as *churned* if it was cancelled by the customer before the first day of the next month. \nPrices before and after the change are listed in @tbl-plans.\n\n::: {.callout-warning}\nInvoluntary churn (failed payments) is **excluded** throughout. It accounts for roughly 0.6 percentage points per month and is tracked separately by the billing team.\n:::\n\n| Plan     | Price before | Price after | Active subs (Sept) |\n|:---------|-------------:|------------:|-------------------:|\n| Starter  | €9           | €12         | 18,402 |\n| Team | €29 | €29 | 6,117 |\n| Business     | €79          | €89         | 1,230              |\n\n: Plans and monthly prices. Annual plans are billed at ten times the monthly price. {#tbl-plans}\n\n## Methods\n\nWe model the time to cancellation with a Cox proportional hazards model,\n\n$$\n\\lambda(t \\mid x) = \\lambda_0(t) \\exp\\left(\\beta_1 \\,\\text{plan} + \\beta_2 \\,\\text{channel} + \\beta_3 \\,\\text{post}_t\\right)\n$$ {#eq-cox}\n\nwhere $\\text{post}_t$ indicates observation months after the price change and $\\lambda_0(t)$ is the baseline hazard. The coefficient of interest is $\\beta_3$: $\\exp(\\beta_3) > 1$ means that customers were more likely to cancel after the change. Tenure is the time axis, so the model compares customers at the same point in their lifecycle, which matters because new customers churn at a much higher rate than established ones regardless of price.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fit-cox \n#| cache: true\nfit <- coxph(\n  Surv(tenure_days, cancelled) ~ plan + channel + post_change + strata(cohort),\n  data = subs\n)\n```\n\n## Results\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-monthly-churn\n#| fig-cap: \"Monthly churn rate by plan. The dashed line marks the price change on 1 August 2024.\"\n#| fig-alt: \"Line chart of the monthly churn rate for the Starter, Team and Business plans, January to September 2024.\"\nggplot(churn_monthly, aes(month, rate, colour = plan)) +\n  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +\n  geom_point() +  \n  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date(\"2024-08-01\"), linetype = \"dashed\") +\n  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +\n  labs(x = NULL, y = \"Monthly churn\", colour = \"Plan\")\n```\n\n@fig-monthly-churn shows that the Starter plan accounts for almost all of the increase. The hazard ratios for the post-change period and the other covariates are in @tbl-cox; as described in @eq-cox, all estimates are conditional on tenure.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: tbl-cox\n#| tbl-cap: \"Hazard ratios from the Cox model, with 95% confidence intervals.\"\nbroom::tidy(fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>\n  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>\n  gt() |>\n  fmt_number(columns = c(estimate, conf.low, conf.high), decimals = 2) |>\n  fmt_scientific(columns = p.value, decimals = 1)\n```\n\n::: {.callout-tip collapse=\"true\"}\n## Robustness checks\n- Excluding customers acquired through the July partner promotion changes $\\hat\\beta_3$ by less than 0.02.\n- Using calendar time instead of tenure as the time axis gives a hazard ratio of 1.38 instead of 1.41.\n   - the proportional hazards assumption looks fine for plan and channel (Schoenfeld residuals, see appendix)\n* A simple difference-in-differences against annual subscribers gives a similar result.\n:::\n\n![Cancellation reasons selected in the exit survey, September 2024.](figures/exit-survey.png){#fig-exit-survey width=80%}\n\nThe exit survey (@fig-exit-survey) supports this reading: \"too expensive\" was the most frequently selected reason in September (41% of responses, up from 27% in June), while \"missing features\" stayed flat at around 15%.\n\n\n## Recommendations\n\n1. Re-introduce a cheaper Starter tier for the first three months, and measure the effect with a proper holdout group this time.\n2. Move the price-change email out of the first week of the billing cycle, when customers are most likely to review their subscriptions anyway.\n3. Most of this work, however, relies on fairly crude exposure measures, \ne.g. the share of green land use within an administrative area, which says little about whether residents actually use the space. Markevych et al. [-@markevych2017] proposed a framework with three pathways: mitigation (e.g. reduced noise and air pollution), restoration, and instoration (i.e. encouraging physical activity and social contact).\nIn this report we look at whether *distance to the nearest park* and *park size* are associated with wellbeing once the usual socio-economic confounders are taken into account.\n\nThe analysis was pre-registered in March 2024. Deviations from the pre-registered plan are listed in Section \\@ref(deviations).  \n\n# Data\n\nWe use the 2023 wave of the Neighbourhood Health Survey (NHS), a postal and online survey of adults living in the 14 districts of the city. After excluding respondents with missing outcome data, the analytic sample contains `r nrow(nhs)` people in `r n_distinct(nhs$lsoa)` small areas.\nWellbeing is measured with the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS), which ranges from 14 to 70 [@tennant2007]. The sample mean was `r round(mean(nhs$wemwbs, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` (SD `r round(sd(nhs$wemwbs, na.rm = TRUE), 1)`), slightly above the national average reported by\nthe ONS for 2022.\n\nExposure variables were derived from the city's open data portal (approx. 1,100 parks and green spaces, as of Jan. 2024):\n\n- `park_dist_m`: network distance in metres from the respondent's postcode centroid to the nearest park entrance.\n- `park_area_ha`: area of that park in hectares. \n- `green_share`: share of green land use within 500 m, as used by most previous studies (cf. Dr. Patel's 2019 report for the council).\n    - This is the *only* exposure that is also available for the 2019 wave.\n\n```{r descriptives}\nnhs %>%\n  group_by(district) %>%\n  summarise(\n    n = n(),\n    wemwbs = mean(wemwbs, na.rm = TRUE),\n    dist = median(park_dist_m),\n    .groups = \"drop\"\n  ) %>%\n  arrange(desc(wemwbs)) %>%\n  kable(digits = 1, col.names = c(\"District\", \"n\", \"Mean WEMWBS\", \"Median distance (m)\"))\n```\n\n# Methods\n\nWe fitted linear mixed models with a random intercept for small area (LSOA). Covariates were chosen a priori: age, sex, household income (quintiles), employment status, self-rated general health, and years at the current address. Distance was log-transformed because the relationship was clearly non-linear in exploratory plots (see Fig. \\@ref(fig:dist-plot)). All models were fitted in R `r getRversion()` with lme4 [@bates2015].\n\n```{r models, cache=TRUE}\nm0 <- lmer(wemwbs ~ age + sex + income_q + employment + health + years_at_address + (1 | lsoa), data = nhs)\nm1 <- update(m0, . ~ . + log(park_dist_m)) \nm2 <- update(m1, . ~ . + log(park_area_ha))\nm3 <- update(m0, . ~ . + green_share)\n```\n\n```{r dist-plot, fig.cap=\"WEMWBS score by distance to the nearest park. Points are jittered vertically; the line is a LOESS smooth with 95% CI.\", fig.width=7, fig.height=4}\nggplot(nhs, aes(park_dist_m, wemwbs)) +\n  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.15, width = 0, height = 0.4) +\n  geom_smooth(method = \"loess\", colour = \"darkgreen\") +\n  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +\n  labs(x = \"Distance to nearest park (m, log scale)\", y = \"WEMWBS\")\n```\n\n# Results\n\nTable \\@ref(tab:coef-table) shows the main estimates. Each doubling of the distance to the nearest park was associated with a `r abs(round(fixef(m1)[[\"log(park_dist_m)\"]] * log(2), 2))` point lower WEMWBS score.\nThis is small compared with, e.g., the gap between the lowest and highest income quintile (approx. 4 points), but comparable to the effects reported by Jones et al. (2019) and by @brown2018 for a similar population. The association with park size was weaker, and its confidence interval included zero.\n\n| Model | Exposure            | Estimate | 95% CI         |\n|-------|---------------------|---------:|----------------|\n| M1    | log distance        | -0.52    | -0.81 to -0.23 |\n| M2 | log distance + log area | -0.47 | -0.77 to -0.17 |\n| M3    | green share (per 10 pp) | 0.21 | -0.02 to 0.44 |\n\nResults were robust to excluding respondents who had moved in the last year (n = 412) and to using the short 7-item version of the scale (SWEMWBS) instead of the full one. Further sensitivity analyses are in the supplementary material, Sect. S2.\n\n```{r coef-table}\nlist(M1 = m1, M2 = m2, M3 = m3) %>%\n  map_dfr(~ tidy(.x, effects = \"fixed\", conf.int = TRUE), .id = \"model\") %>%\n  filter(str_detect(term, \"park|green\")) %>%\n  kable(digits = 2, caption = \"Fixed effects for the exposure variables.\")\n```\n\n# Deviations from the pre-registration {#deviations}\n\n1. We pre-registered a Poisson model for the number of park visits as a secondary outcome. The visit question was changed between survey waves, so this analysis was dropped.\n2. The covariate \"years at current address\" was added after comments from an internal reviewer (Dr. A. Novak, pers. comm.).\n   It was not part of the original plan.\n3. We used `lme4` instead of `nlme` because the latter did not converge for the M2 vs. M0 comparison. If you relied on the old behaviour, set it explicitly in your configuration file or pass `--end-of-line=lf` on the command line.\n\n### Deprecated\n+ `--no-wrap` is deprecated in favour of `--wrap=preserve` and will be removed in 3.0.\n\n## [2.2.1] — 2026-05-14\n\n### Fixed\n\n1) Crash on empty YAML documents between two `---` markers ([#580]).\n2) Windows: files with CRLF line endings were rewritten with mixed endings\n   when a block scalar was the last thing in the file.\n3) Pressing <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> once now stops `--watch` mode; before,\n   it needed two presses on some terminals.\n\n## [2.2.0] - 2026-03-02\n\n### Added\n\n* Experimental support for Python files: Markdown in comment blocks and string\n  assignments marked with `# fmt: markdown` is formatted.\n\n  This is opt-in for now. Enable it with:\n\n      tidyfmt --experimental python src/\n\n* Footnotes are supported[^1].\n\n### Changed\n\n* Headings are normalised to ATX style. Setext headings in existing files are\n  kept unless you pass `--normalize-headings`.\n* Formatting the CPython docs went from 41 s to 6.8 s on an M2 laptop, mostly\n  thanks to a smarter 2<sup>nd</sup> pass over inline content.\n\n### Fixed\n\n* An emoji at the end of a wrapped line no longer counts as two columns 🎉 (#541)\n* Non-breaking spaces (U+00A0) are kept as they are.   \n\n***\n\n## 2.1.0 - 2025-11-20 ##\n\nA small release, mostly bug fixes. Upgrading is recommended for everyone on 2.0.x.\n\n- **YAML:** comments between sequence items are no longer moved to the end of\n  the previous item.\n- **YAML:** block scalars with an explicit indentation indicator (`|2`) keep\n  their indicator.  \n  Previously the indicator was dropped, which changed the meaning of the\n  document when the first line started with spaces.\n- **Markdown:** reference definitions with titles in parentheses, like\n  `[x]: https://example.com (Example)`, stay on one line.\n- Typo fixes in the docs by Zoë Lindqvist, Mateus Araújo and 田中さくら. The configuration file was renamed from `.tidyfmtrc` to `tidyfmt.toml`.\n   The old name is still read, with a warning.\n2. Exit codes changed:\n\n   | Code | Meaning                         |\n   |:----:|:--------------------------------|\n   | 0    | nothing to do                   |\n   | 1    | files would be reformatted      |\n   | 2    | invalid input (parse error)     |\n   | 3    | internal error \\| please report |\n\n3. Please report unacceptable behaviour to <conduct@kestrel.example.org>.\n\n## Reporting bugs ##\n\nBefore opening an issue, please:\n\n* search the [existing issues][issues], including the closed ones;\n\n* check that you are on the latest release (`kestrel --version`);\n\n* try to reduce the problem to a minimal example. A config file with 20 lines is\n  much easier to debug than one with 2,000.\n\n  If the bug only happens with a large input, attach the file to the issue\n  instead of pasting it inline.\n\nWhen you file the issue, include \n\n- what you did,\n- what you expected to happen, and\n- what actually happened (the full error output, not a screenshot of it).\n\n## Setting up a development environment\n\nYou need Python 3.10 or newer and [`uv`][uv]. Then:\n\n~~~bash\ngit clone https://github.com/kestrel-dev/kestrel.git\ncd kestrel\nuv sync --all-extras\nuv run pre-commit install\n~~~\n\nRun the tests with `uv run pytest`. A few of them need network access; skip those with\n\n    uv run pytest -m \"not network\"\n\n<details>\n<summary>Notes for Windows users</summary>\n\nUse PowerShell, not `cmd.exe`. If `uv` is not found after installing it, open a new\nterminal window: the installer updates `PATH`, but shells that are already running don't see the change.<br>\nLong paths must be enabled (`git config --system core.longpaths true`), otherwise the test fixtures can't be checked out.\n\n</details>\n\n## Pull requests\n\n+ Small, focused pull requests get reviewed much faster than large ones.\n+ Every pull request needs a changelog entry, unless it only touches tests or docs.\n+ The steps, roughly:\n\n    1. Fork the repository and create a branch from `main`.\n    2. Make your change, and add tests for it.\n    3. Run the full check suite:\n\n           uv run nox\n\n       This runs the linters, the type checker and the tests on every supported\n       Python version, so it takes a while. Go and make a coffee ☕.\n\n    4. Push your branch and open a pull request. Please fill in the template.\n\n+ A maintainer will review your pull request. You may be asked to make changes;\n  that's normal and not a judgement of your work. 🙂\n\n### Commit messages\n\nWe loosely follow [Conventional Commits][cc]. The first line should be at most 72\ncharacters, the body can be as long as needed.\\\nSome good first lines:\n\n    fix(yaml): keep comments between sequence items\n    feat(cli): add the --line-width option\n    docs: explain the release process\n\n> **Tip:** if you get this wrong, don't worry -- we squash-merge most pull\n> requests and can fix the message then. What *does* matter:\n>\n> - one logical change per commit, if you don't want us to squash;\n> - no merge commits from `main` into your branch. Rebase instead:\n>\n>   ```console\n>   $ git fetch upstream\n>   $ git rebase upstream/main\n>   ```\n\n## Style guide\n\n| What              | Tool              | Configured in      |\n|:------------------|:-----------------:|-------------------:|\n| Formatting        | `ruff format`     | `pyproject.toml`   |\n| Linting           | `ruff check`      | `pyproject.toml`   |\n| Type checking     | mypy (strict)     | `mypy.ini`         |\n| Shell scripts     | shellcheck        | `.shellcheckrc`    |\n| Commit hooks      | pre-commit        | `.pre-commit-config.yaml` |\n| Regex alternation | escape `\\|` in tables | n/a            |\n\nA few conventions that the tools don't check:\n\n1) Write docstrings in the Google style.\n2) Public functions need type hints. Private helpers *should* have them.\n3) Prefer `pathlib.Path` over `os.path`.<sup>[why?](https://treyhunner.com/2018/12/why-you-should-be-using-pathlib/)</sup>\n\n### Documentation\n\nThe docs live in `docs/` and are built with MkDocs. To preview them, type\n<kbd>uv</kbd> <kbd>run</kbd> <kbd>mkdocs</kbd> <kbd>serve</kbd> and open <http://127.0.0.1:8000/>.\nScreenshots go into `docs/img/` and should look roughly like this one:\n\n![Screenshot of the kestrel TUI][screenshot]\n\nTranslations are welcome (there are partial 日本語 and Français versions), but\nplease coordinate in the [discussion forum][forum] first, so that two people don't\ntranslate the same page.[^translations]\n\n## Releasing (maintainers only) #\n\n1. CI builds and uploads the wheels; check <https://pypi.org/project/kestrel/#history> afterwards.\n\n***\n\nThanks again! Reordered keys,\ndifferent quoting styles or a change of indentation don't show up as differences;\na value that went from `\"8080\"` to `8080` does. \n\n```console\n$ fjord diff old/values.yaml new/values.yaml\n~ spec.replicas: 3 → 5\n+ spec.template.metadata.annotations[\"prometheus.io/scrape\"]: \"true\"\n- spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[2]  (HTTP_PROXY)\n```\n\n> ⚠️ fjord is still below 1.0. The command line is stable, the library API is not.\n\n## Features ##\n\n- Understands YAML 1.1 *and* 1.2 (yes, `on: yes` is handled correctly)\n- Multi-document YAML streams, anchors, aliases and merge keys\n- TOML 1.0, JSON and JSON5\n- Output as text, JSON or a GitHub-flavoured Markdown table\n- Fast: diffs a 40 MB Helm render in well under a second[^bench]\n\n## Installation\n\nPick whatever suits you: \n\n+ **Cargo**\n\n  ```sh\n  cargo install fjord --locked\n  ```\n\n+ **Homebrew** (macOS and Linux)\n\n      brew install fjord-tools/tap/fjord\n\n+ **Pre-built binaries** for Linux, macOS and Windows are attached to every\n  [release][releases]. Please verify them against the published SHA-256 checksums.\n\n+ **From source:** see [`docs/building.md`](docs/building.md).\n\n## Usage\n\n    fjord diff [OPTIONS] <OLD> <NEW>\n    fjord explain <FILE> <PATH>\n\nThe options you will probably need:\n\n| Option            | Short | Default | Description                                         |\n|-------------------|:-----:|:-------:|-----------------------------------------------------|\n| `--format <FMT>`  | `-f`  | `text`  | `text`, `json` or `markdown`                        |\n| `--ignore <PATH>` | `-i`  |         | Ignore a path, e.g. `metadata.labels`; repeatable   |\n| `--yaml-version`  |       | `auto`  | `1.1`, `1.2` or `auto`                              |\n| `--color <WHEN>`  |       | `auto`  | `always` \\| `never` \\| `auto`                       |\n| `--exit-code`     | `-e`  | off     | Exit with status 1 if there are differences         |\n\nIn the interactive pager, press <kbd>q</kbd> to quit and <kbd>/</kbd> to search.\n\n### Ignoring paths\n\n1) Use `--ignore` on the command line for one-off runs.\n2) For anything permanent, list the paths in a `.fjordignore` file:\n\n   ~~~gitignore\n   # generated by Helm, changes on every render\n   metadata.annotations[\"helm.sh/chart\"]\n   metadata.labels.chart\n   ~~~\n\n3) Paths support `*` (exactly one segment) and `**` (any number of segments).\n\n### Using it in CI\n\n> fjord exits with status 0 when the files are equivalent and 1 when they differ\n> (with `--exit-code`). A typical GitLab CI job:\n>\n> ```yaml\n> config-drift:\n>   script:\n>     - fjord diff --exit-code deployed.yaml rendered.yaml\n> ```\n>\n> Add `--format markdown` to post the result as a merge request comment.\n\n## FAQ\n\n**Why not just `diff <(yq -P a.yaml) <(yq -P b.yaml)`?**  \nThat works for simple cases, but `yq` doesn't know that `0o14` and `12` are the same\nnumber in YAML 1.2, or that a merge key expands to the same mapping as the long form.\n\n**Does it work on Windows?**\\\nYes. Paths with backslashes work, and CRLF files are compared without complaint.\n\n**Is the name an acronym?**  \nNo, it's just a nice word: Norwegian *fjord*, from Old Norse *fjǫrðr*.\n\n***\n\n## Contributing\n\nBug reports and pull requests are very welcome. It *never* deletes a translation on its own: obsolete entries are prefixed with `#~` so that a human can decide what to do with them.\n\nTypical workflow:\n\n1. Change or add strings in `locales/en/messages.json`.\n2. Run `python tools/sync_translations.py --fix` to add the new keys to every other locale.\n3. Use `--fix` locally, but *never* in CI, because it rewrites the files in place.\n\"\"\"\n\n# fmt: markdown\n# How placeholders are compared\n# =============================\n#\n# A translation is only accepted if it uses *exactly* the same placeholders as the English source string, in any order. Both the `str.format` style (`{name}`) and the old printf style (`%(name)s`) are recognised, but mixing the two in one string is reported as an error.\n#\n# - Placeholders are compared as multisets, so `{n} of {n}` needs two `{n}` in the translation as well.\n# - Plural forms are checked one by one; a locale with three plural forms (Polish, Russian, ...) needs all three.\n# - HTML tags are **not** checked. That would be nice, but the false positive rate was terrible when we tried it in 2022.\n\n\n@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Problem:\n    locale: str\n    key: str\n    kind: str  # \"missing\", \"obsolete\" or \"placeholders\"\n    detail: str = \"\"\n\n    def __str__(self) -> str:\n        suffix = f\" ({self.detail})\" if self.detail else \"\"\n        return f\"{self.locale}: {self.key}: {self.kind}{suffix}\"\n\n\ndef load_catalogue(path: Path) -> dict[str, str]:\n    \"\"\"Load a JSON catalogue and flatten nested objects into dotted keys.\"\"\"\n    with path.open(encoding=\"utf-8\") as fh:\n        data = json.load(fh)\n\n    flat: dict[str, str] = {}\n\n    def walk(prefix: str, node: object) -> None:\n        if isinstance(node, dict):\n            for key, value in node.items():\n                walk(f\"{prefix}.{key}\" if prefix else key, value)\n        elif isinstance(node, str):\n            flat[prefix] = node\n        else:\n            raise TypeError(f\"{path}: {prefix}: expected a string, got {type(node).__name__}\")\n\n    walk(\"\", data)\n    return flat\n\n\ndef placeholders(text: str) -> Counter[str]:\n    return Counter(PLACEHOLDER_RE.findall(text))\n\n\ndef compare(source: dict[str, str], target: dict[str, str], locale: str) -> list[Problem]:\n    problems = []\n    for key, english in source.items():\n        translated = target.get(key)\n        if translated is None:\n            problems.append(Problem(locale, key, \"missing\"))\n        elif translated == \"\" or translated.startswith(OBSOLETE_PREFIX):\n            continue  # not translated yet, or parked on purpose\n        elif placeholders(english) != placeholders(translated):\n            expected = \", \".join(sorted(placeholders(english))) or \"none\"\n            problems.append(Problem(locale, key, \"placeholders\", f\"expected {expected}\"))\n    for key in sorted(target.keys() - source.keys()):\n        if not target[key].startswith(OBSOLETE_PREFIX):\n            problems.append(Problem(locale, key, 'obsolete'))\n    return problems\n\n\n# fmt: markdown\nREPORT_TEMPLATE = r\"\"\"\n## Translation report, $date\n\nThe catalogues were read from `$locales_dir`. On the Windows build agents that is something like `C:\\agent\\_work\\1\\s\\locales`, which is why the paths below may contain backslashes.\n\n* **$n_missing** missing keys\n* **$n_obsolete** obsolete keys\n* **$n_placeholders** placeholder mismatches\n\nPlaceholders are found with the regular expression `\\{[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*\\}|%\\([a-z_]+\\)[sd]`. The idea was simple. Users who create at least one project in their first session are much more likely to come back (approx. three times as likely in the 2025 cohorts), and the checklist makes that step more obvious than the tour did. Earlier experiments on the welcome e-mail moved week-4 retention by one to two percentage points [@haddad2025], so we did not expect anything dramatic.\n\nThis report analyses experiment `r params$experiment_id`.\nIt was pre-registered in the analytics wiki on 30 June 2026, and the analysis below follows that plan except where noted. Deviations are marked with a dagger (†).\n\n# Data\n\n```{r load}\n#| cache: true\n#| cache.extra: !expr file.mtime(\"data/onboarding_users.csv\")\nusers <- read_csv(\"data/onboarding_users.csv\", show_col_types = FALSE) |>\n  mutate(variant = factor(variant, levels = c(\"tour\", \"checklist\")))\nn_raw <- nrow(users)\nusers <- filter(users, !is_internal, !is_bot)\nn_excluded <- n_raw - nrow(users)\n```\n\nThe raw export contains `r format(n_raw, big.mark = \",\")` accounts created between 7 July and 3 August 2026. We excluded `r n_excluded` accounts that belong to employees or were flagged as bots by the fraud team. Assignment was random at the account level with a 50/50 split, and a sample ratio mismatch test showed no problems ($p = 0.62$). Sign-up channels differ a lot (e.g. paid search vs. organic), but the randomisation balanced them well; the largest difference between the arms was 0.4 percentage points.\n\nThe outcome is *week-4 retention*: an account counts as retained if it was\nactive on at least one day between day 22 and day 28 after sign-up. This is the\nsame definition the growth team has used since 2024, so the numbers are\ncomparable with earlier experiments [see @kohavi2020, chap. 7, on why the metric must be fixed up front].\n\n# Results\n\n```{r retention-table}\n#| tab.cap: \"Week-4 retention by variant.\"\nretention <- users |>\n  group_by(variant) |>\n  summarise(users = n(), retained = sum(active_week4), rate = mean(active_week4))\nkable(retention, digits = 3, col.names = c(\"Variant\", \"Users\", \"Retained\", \"Rate\"))\n```\n\n```{r test}\ntest <- prop.test(retention$retained, retention$users)\ndiff_pp <- 100 * diff(retention$rate)\nci_pp <- -100 * rev(test$conf.int)\n```\n\nLet $p_c$ and $p_t$ be the retention rates with the tour and with the checklist. We test $H_0\\colon p_t = p_c$ against the two-sided alternative, using the usual normal approximation\n$$\nz = \\frac{\\hat p_t - \\hat p_c}{\\sqrt{\\hat p\\,(1 - \\hat p)\\left(\\frac{1}{n_t} + \\frac{1}{n_c}\\right)}},\n$$\nwhere $\\hat p$ is the pooled rate. The checklist group retained `r round(diff_pp, 1)` percentage points more users (95 % CI `r round(ci_pp[1], 1)` to `r round(ci_pp[2], 1)`). That is more than we expected. It is also close to the upper end of what the power analysis said we could plausibly see, which made us a little suspicious, so we looked at the result from a few other angles before writing it up.\n\n```{r fig-retention}\n#| fig.cap: \"Share of users active on each day after sign-up. Shaded bands are 95% confidence intervals.\"\n#| fig.width: 7\n#| fig.height: 4\n#| out.width: \"85%\"\ndaily <- read_csv(\"data/onboarding_daily_activity.csv\", show_col_types = FALSE)\nggplot(daily, aes(day, share_active, colour = variant, fill = variant)) +\n  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +\n  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +\n  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +\n  labs(x = \"Days since sign-up\", y = \"Active users\", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +\n  theme_minimal()\n```\n\nThe two curves separate on the first day and stay apart (Fig. 1). If this were a novelty effect, we would expect the gap to close after the first week; it does not. The gap is somewhat larger on mobile than on desktop, i.e. 2.9 vs. 1.8 points, but the interaction is not significant and the comparison was not pre-registered (†), so we do not want to read much into it.\n\nWe did not use CUPED or any other variance reduction [@deng2013]. Most accounts have no history before sign-up, so there is little to adjust for.\n\n# Limitations\n\n- The experiment ran during the summer holidays in most of Europe. New users in July and August are, on average, more often students and hobbyists than teams. They may respond differently to onboarding changes.\n- Week-4 retention is a proxy. What we actually care about is whether these accounts convert to a paid plan, and we will not know that for another two months.\n- We tested only one version of the checklist. The effect may depend heavily on the wording of the individual items.^[The copy was written in a single afternoon by Dr. Moreau and was never tested on its own.]\n\n> **Decision needed by 1 December.** The product team wants to ship before the end-of-year freeze. If we wait for the conversion data, the change slips to January.\n\n# Recommendation\n\nShip the checklist to all new users, keep a 5 % holdout for three months, and revisit the conversion numbers in the Q1 review. If the holdout confirms the effect, the next experiment should test a shorter checklist with three items instead of five.\n\n# References\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":2825,"cache_read_input_tokens":177911,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":2825,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_01KEpMwSfcamLc3mzKQrgeAT","agent_id":"abadab9e2eb69e5c4","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"f778e8e4-b829-46b2-9885-a6e3aab90b4f","timestamp":"2026-11-17T20:24:29.457Z","request_id":"req_011Ch98FcTFvwJCCF27fUFbi","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Generate messy realistic corpus 8"}

GitHub 上でリポジトリをフォークし、ローカルにクローンします。\n2. sync --all-extras\n   uv run pre-commit install\n   ```\n\n4. テストがすべて通ることを確認します：\n\n   ```bash\n   uv run pytest -q\n   ```\n\n5. 辞書データ（約120MB）が必要なテストは、環境変数 `KOTOBA_FULL_DICT=1` [Conventional Commits 日本語版](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/ja/v1.0.0/) に従ってください（例：`fix: 半角カナの濁点が結合されない問題を修正`）。\n4. プルリクエストを作成し、テンプレートの各項目を埋めます。\n5. レビュアーから変更の依頼があった場合は、同じブランチに追加のコミットをプッシュしてください。フォースプッシュはレビューの差分が追いにくくなるため、できるだけ避けてください。\n6. 2名以上のメンテナーの承認と CI の成功をもって、メンテナーがマージします。\n\n## コーディング規約\n\n- コードのスタイルは `ruff format` に従います。手作業で整形する必要はありません。\n- 変数名・関数名は英語で書いてください。コメントと docstring は日本語でも英語でも構いません。\n- 公開 API には型ヒントと doctest を付けてください。\n\n```python\ndef normalize(text: str, *, kana: str = \"full\") -> str:\n    \"\"\"全角・半角を正規化する。\n\n    >>> normalize(\"ｶﾀｶﾅとＡＢＣ１２３\")\n    'カタカナとABC123'\n    \"\"\"\n    ...\n```\n\n## ドキュメントの表記ルール\n\nドキュメントは「です・ます」調で統一し、一文が長くなりすぎないように注意してください。句読点には全角の「、」と「。」を使い、英数字と日本語の間には半角スペースを入れます（例：「Python 3.12 で動作します」）。ただし、全角の括弧（）や鉤括弧「」の前後にはスペースを入れません。表記の揺れを防ぐため、次の表を参考にしてください[^表記]。\n\n| 推奨 ✅ | 非推奨 ❌ | 備考 |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| サーバー | サーバ | 一般的な外来語の表記に合わせる |\n| ユーザー | ユーザ | 同上 |\n| 行う | 行なう | 送り仮名は公用文の基準に従う |\n| 例：〜 | 例) 〜 | 全角コロンを使う |\n| 🙂 絵文字は控えめに | 😂😂😂 | 見出しやラベル以外での多用は避ける |\n\nなお、API の名前やコマンドなどのコード要素は、必ずバッククォートで囲んでください。たとえば「`tokenize()` 関数を呼び出す」と書き、「tokenize関数を呼び出す」とは書きません。\n\n## ラベル一覧\n\n| ラベル | 意味 | 対応の目安 |\n| :-- | :-- | :-: |\n| 🐛 `バグ` | 不具合の報告 | 1週間以内 |\n| ✨ `機能追加` | 新機能の提案 | It keeps your highlights, notes, and vocabulary lists in plain Markdown files, syncs them across devices without a central server, and understands that “Straße”, “STRASSE”, and “strasse” are the same word.\n\n> 積読（つんどく）とは、買った本を読まずに積んでおくことを指す日本語の言葉です。本棚に並んだ未読の本を眺めるのが好きな人のために、このアプリは生まれました。\n>\n> — Misaki Tanaka (田中美咲), co-founder\n\n## ✨ Features\n\n- **Multilingual search** that ignores accents and character width, i.e. `cafe` finds “café”, and `ｶﾀｶﾅ` finds “カタカナ”.\n- **Highlights & notes** stored as Markdown with YAML front matter:\n  - one file per book, named after its ISBN or a slug of the title (e.g. `der-zauberberg.md`);\n  - attachments (covers, scans, audio notes) next to it, in a folder with the same name.\n- **Vocabulary decks** exported to Anki, with furigana for Japanese, pinyin for Chinese, and gender markers for German nouns (der/die/das).\n- **Peer-to-peer sync** over your local network or via any WebDAV server — Nextcloud, ownCloud, etc. No account required.\n- **Imports** from Kindle, Kobo, Calibre, Goodreads CSV, Zotero, etc.\n\n## 🚀 Quick start\n\n1. Install the CLI (requires Python 3.11 or newer):\n\n   ```bash\n   pipx install tsundoku\n   ```\n\n2. Create a library in your home directory:\n\n   ```bash\n   tsundoku init ~/Bücher --language de --secondary ja,fr\n   ```\n\n3. Add your first books — ISBN lookup works with the German National Library, the BnF, and the NDL out of the box:\n\n   ```bash\n   tsundoku add 978-3-10-048166-6      # Thomas Mann, „Der Zauberberg“\n   tsundoku add 978-4-10-101001-3      # 夏目漱石『こころ』\n   ```\n\n4. Start the local web interface and open <http://localhost:8765>:\n\n   ```bash\n   tsundoku serve\n   ```\n\nThe first start downloads the Japanese and Chinese dictionaries (about 250@NB@MB); use `--no-cjk` if you only read European languages.\n\n## 🌍 Supported languages\n\n| Language | Native name | Sample shelf label | Tokenizer | Status |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| German | Deutsch | Ungelesene Bücher | built-in | ✅ stable |\n| French | Français | Livres à lire | built-in | ✅ stable |\n| Japanese | 日本語 | 積読の山 | SudachiPy | ✅ stable |\n| Chinese (Traditional) | 繁體中文 | 待讀書單 | jieba | 🧪 beta |\n| Korean | 한국어 | 읽을 책 | KoNLPy | 🧪 beta |\n| Vietnamese | Tiếng Việt | Sách chưa đọc | built-in | ⚠️ partial |\n| Icelandic | Íslenska | Ólesnar bækur | built-in | ⚠️ partial |\n\nMissing your language? Translations live in `locales/*.po` — see [Übersetzen leicht gemacht](docs/de/translating.md) or the [guía para traductores](docs/es/traduccion.md).\n\n## ⚙️ Configuration\n\nTsundoku reads `~/.config/tsundoku/config.toml`. A minimal example:\n\n```toml\n[library]\npath = \"~/Bücher\"\nprimary_language = \"de\"\nsecondary_languages = [\"ja\", \"fr\"]\n\n[display]\n# Typographic quotes for each language\nquotes = { de = \"„“\", fr = \"«@NB@@NB@»\", ja = \"「」\", en = \"“”\" }\ndate_format = \"%d. %B %Y\"\n\n[sync]\nbackend = \"webdav\"\nurl = \"https://cloud.example.org/remote.php/dav/files/zoë/tsundoku/\"\n```\n\nNote that the WebDAV URL may contain non-ASCII characters; Tsundoku percent-encodes them automatically (`zo%C3%AB`).\n\n## 📖 Documentation\n\n- [English documentation](https://docs.tsundoku.example/en/)\n- [Deutsche Dokumentation](https://docs.tsundoku.example/de/)\n- [Documentation en français](https://docs.tsundoku.example/fr/)\n- [日本語ドキュメント](https://docs.tsundoku.example/ja/)\n- [中文文档（翻译中）](https://docs.tsundoku.example/zh/)\n\nThe architecture overview (Fig.@NB@3 in the design document) explains how the CRDT-based sync resolves conflicting highlights; the conflict rules themselves are described on p.@NB@12. Known limitations are tracked in issue No.@NB@5. Tras tres años consecutivos de sequía, el estado de sus masas de agua preocupa tanto a las administraciones como a los regantes [@garcia2021; @ministerio2023]. Este informe actualiza los datos del trimestre anterior y amplía el análisis a las estaciones de la vega de Granada.\n\n¿Por qué nos centramos en los nitratos? Porque son el principal indicador de contaminación difusa de origen agrario, y porque la normativa europea fija un umbral claro de 50@NB@mg/L. ¡Y porque en algunas estaciones ya se ha superado!\n\n## Datos y métodos\n\nDurante el trimestre se recogieron `{r} nrow(datos)` muestras en `{r} n_distinct(datos$estacion)` estaciones. Las muestras se analizaron en el laboratorio de la CHG en Sevilla siguiendo la norma UNE-EN ISO 10304-1 [@aenor2009, pág.@NB@12]. Para cada estación se calculó la mediana mensual, ya que los valores extremos —p.@NB@ej., tras las tormentas de septiembre— distorsionan mucho la media. Los datos brutos están disponibles en el portal de datos abiertos de la CHG[^datos].\n\n::: {.callout-note}\n## Nota sobre los datos de Doñana\n\nLas estaciones del entorno de Doñana (DÑ-01 a DÑ-04) no se muestrearon en agosto por obras en el camino de acceso. Sus valores se han interpolado a partir de julio y septiembre; véase la @sec-limitaciones.\n:::\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-nitratos\n#| fig-cap: \"Concentración mediana de nitratos por subcuenca (mg/L). La línea discontinua marca el umbral de 50 mg/L.\"\n#| fig-width: 8\n#| fig-height: 5\ndatos |>\n  group_by(subcuenca, mes) |>\n  summarise(nitratos = median(nitratos, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = \"drop\") |>\n  ggplot(aes(mes, nitratos, colour = subcuenca)) +\n  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +\n  geom_hline(yintercept = umbral_nitratos, linetype = \"dashed\") +\n  labs(x = \"Mes\", y = \"Nitratos (mg/L)\", colour = \"Subcuenca\") +\n  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)\n```\n\n```{r}\n#| label: tbl-resumen\n#| tbl-cap: \"Resumen por subcuenca: estaciones, mediana de nitratos y porcentaje de muestras por encima del umbral.\"\ndatos |>\n  group_by(subcuenca) |>\n  summarise(\n    estaciones = n_distinct(estacion),\n    mediana = median(nitratos, na.rm = TRUE),\n    por_encima = mean(nitratos > umbral_nitratos, na.rm = TRUE)\n  ) |>\n  gt() |>\n  cols_label(subcuenca = \"Subcuenca\", estaciones = \"Estaciones\", mediana = \"Mediana (mg/L)\", por_encima = \"% > umbral\") |>\n  fmt_number(mediana, decimals = 1, dec_mark = \",\", sep_mark = \".\") |>\n  fmt_percent(por_encima, decimals = 1, dec_mark = \",\")\n```\n\n## Resultados\n\nComo muestra la @fig-nitratos, la concentración de nitratos se mantuvo por debajo del umbral en la mayoría de las subcuencas. La excepción es la vega del Genil, donde la mediana alcanzó 57,3@NB@mg/L en agosto. La @tbl-resumen recoge los valores por subcuenca. El porcentaje de muestras por encima del umbral pasó del 8,2@NB@% al 11,7@NB@% respecto al trimestre anterior, un aumento que coincide con lo descrito por @lopez2024 para el periodo 2019–2022.\n\nLa temperatura media del agua fue de 24,6@NB@°C, casi dos grados más que la media histórica (1991–2020). Este dato, por sí solo, no implica un deterioro del estado ecológico. Sin embargo, combinado con caudales mínimos de apenas 3,1@NB@m³/s en Alcalá del Río, favorece la proliferación de cianobacterias, tal como advierte el Plan Hidrológico vigente [@chg2022, cap.@NB@4]. El oxígeno disuelto, en cambio, se mantuvo en valores aceptables (mediana de 7,8@NB@mg/L) en todas las estaciones salvo en dos tramos del bajo Guadalquivir.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: fig-temperatura\n#| fig-cap: \"Temperatura del agua frente a caudal, por estación y mes. Cada punto es una muestra.\"\n#| fig-alt: \"Diagrama de dispersión con la temperatura en el eje vertical y el caudal en escala logarítmica en el eje horizontal.\"\nggplot(datos, aes(caudal, temperatura, colour = mes)) +\n  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +\n  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(decimal.mark = \",\", big.mark = \".\")) +\n  labs(x = \"Caudal (m³/s, escala log.)\", y = \"Temperatura (°C)\", colour = \"Mes\")\n```\n\n## Limitaciones {#sec-limitaciones}\n\n- Las muestras de agosto en Doñana se han interpolado y no deben usarse para análisis de tendencias.\n- El laboratorio cambió de equipo de cromatografía en septiembre; la comparación con trimestres anteriores debe hacerse con cautela.\n  - Los análisis de control cruzado no mostraron diferencias significativas (p@NB@>@NB@0,05).\n  - Aun así, recomendamos repetir la validación en el próximo trimestre.\n- Solo se dispone de datos de caudal para 31 de las 42 estaciones, véase el expediente núm.@NB@5.\n\n## Conclusiones\n\n1. La situación general es estable, pero la vega del Genil requiere un seguimiento mensual.\n2. Conviene ampliar la red de estaciones en la campiña de Jaén y en el entorno de Doñana.\n3. Los resultados deben compartirse con las comunidades de regantes antes de la campaña de otoño.\n\nAgradecemos la colaboración de los guardas fluviales, del personal del laboratorio de Sevilla, de las comunidades de regantes, etc. Sin su ayuda este informe no habría sido posible.\n\n> «El agua no es un bien comercial como los demás, sino un patrimonio que hay que proteger, defender y tratar como tal».\n>\n> — Directiva 2000/60/CE, considerando 1\n\n[^datos]: Disponibles en formato CSV (UTF-8, separador «;») en <https://datos.chg.example.es/calidad/2026T3>, con licencia CC@NB@BY@NB@4.0.\n\n## Referencias {.unnumbered}\n\n::: {#refs}\n:::\n__CORPUS_EOF__","description":"Write Spanish Quarto report via heredoc"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":7481,"cache_read_input_tokens":147034,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":7481,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_01X8AEmYNBHhZJU53nygZ44d","agent_id":"a4b74ee9b4e35a22c","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"44626174-c067-4956-bb8d-af3c72e7ea05","timestamp":"2026-11-17T20:39:48.965Z","request_id":"req_011Ch99NjRWZLoEapjwXKjGj","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Generate international corpus 9"}

Sc.\n  - Prof. Dr. Hannelore Brünnich\ndate: \"`r format(Sys.Date(), '%d. %B %Y')`\"\nlang: de\noutput:\n  html_document:\n    toc: true\n    toc_float: true\n    number_sections: true\n  pdf_document:\n    latex_engine: xelatex\nbibliography: literatur.bib\ncsl: din-1505-2.csl\neditor_options:\n  markdown:\n    wrap: sentence\n    canonical: true\n  chunk_output_type: console\n---\n\n```{r}\n#| label: setup\n#| include: false\nknitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5)\nlibrary(tidyverse)\nlibrary(scales)\nmieten <- read_csv2(\"daten/angebotsmieten_2015_2025.csv\", locale = locale(encoding = \"UTF-8\"))\n```\n\n# Einleitung\n\nDie Mieten in deutschen Großstädten sind seit 2015 deutlich gestiegen. In München lag die durchschnittliche Angebotsmiete Anfang 2025 bei ca. 22,40@NB@€ pro Quadratmeter, in Berlin bei rund 17,10@NB@€. Das entspricht einem Anstieg von 48,3@NB@% bzw. 71,9@NB@% gegenüber dem 1. Januar 2015. Gleichzeitig sind die Einkommen deutlich langsamer gewachsen, d.@NB@h. ein immer größerer Teil des Haushaltsbudgets fließt in die Miete [@mueller2021; @schmidt2019, S.@NB@12]. Besonders betroffen sind Haushalte mit niedrigem Einkommen, z. B. Alleinerziehende, Studierende sowie Rentnerinnen und Rentner.\n\nDie vorliegende Analyse knüpft an frühere Arbeiten an, u.@NB@a. an die Studie von Prof. Dr. Brünnich zur Mietpreisbremse (vgl. Brünnich 2020, S. 45 ff.). Sie beschränkt sich auf Angebotsmieten, d. h. auf Inserate in Online-Portalen. Bestandsmieten werden nicht betrachtet. Im 19. Jahrhundert war das übrigens nicht anders: Schon damals klagten Zeitgenossen über die „Wohnungsnot“ in den rasch wachsenden Städten [@engels1872].\n\n# Daten und Methode\n\nGrundlage sind `r format(nrow(mieten), big.mark = \".\")` Inserate aus `r n_distinct(mieten$stadt)` Städten. Die Daten wurden vom 1. Januar 2015 bis zum 31. März 2025 quartalsweise erhoben. Inserate mit offensichtlich fehlerhaften Angaben (z.@NB@B. Wohnfläche unter 10@NB@m² oder Kaltmiete über 100@NB@€ pro m²) wurden entfernt. Details zur Bereinigung finden sich im Anhang, Tab. A1. Die Auswertung erfolgte mit R (Version `r getRversion()`) und dem Paket *tidyverse* [@wickham2019].\n\nFür den Vergleich zwischen den Städten verwenden wir den Median statt des arithmetischen Mittels. Der Median ist robuster gegenüber Ausreißern, z. B. Luxuswohnungen in Toplagen. Ein Beispiel: In der Hamburger HafenCity werden teils Mieten von über 30@NB@€ verlangt. Solche Werte würden das Mittel stark verzerren. Die Daten stammen von ImmoScout24, Immowelt etc. Andere Portale wurden nicht berücksichtigt[^rohdaten].\n\n```{r}\n#| label: abb-entwicklung\n#| fig-cap: \"Entwicklung der medianen Angebotsmiete (€/m², nettokalt) in ausgewählten Großstädten\"\n#| fig-alt: \"Liniendiagramm der Mietentwicklung von 2015 bis 2025 für sieben Städte\"\nmieten |>\n  group_by(stadt, quartal) |>\n  summarise(miete = median(miete_qm), .groups = \"drop\") |>\n  ggplot(aes(quartal, miete, colour = stadt)) +\n  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +\n  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = \" €\", decimal.mark = \",\")) +\n  labs(x = NULL, y = \"Median der Angebotsmiete\", colour = \"Stadt\") +\n  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)\n```\n\n# Ergebnisse\n\nAbb.@NB@1 zeigt die Entwicklung der Medianmieten. Auffällig ist der Knick im Jahr 2020. Mit Beginn der Corona-Pandemie stagnierten die Angebotsmieten in fast allen Städten für ca. zwei Quartale. Danach setzte sich der Anstieg fort, in Berlin sogar beschleunigt. Ein möglicher Grund ist der Beschluss des Bundesverfassungsgerichts vom 25. März 2021 zum Berliner Mietendeckel (Az. 2 BvF 1/20), mit dem das Gesetz für nichtig erklärt wurde.\n\nTab. 1 fasst die Ergebnisse für alle Städte zusammen. Die Spalte „Δ 2015–2025“ gibt die prozentuale Veränderung an. Werte über 50@NB@% sind fett hervorgehoben.\n\n```{r}\n#| label: tab-staedte\nmieten |>\n  filter(quartal %in% range(quartal)) |>\n  group_by(stadt, jahr = year(quartal)) |>\n  summarise(miete = median(miete_qm), .groups = \"drop\") |>\n  pivot_wider(names_from = jahr, values_from = miete) |>\n  mutate(veraenderung = (`2025` / `2015` - 1) * 100) |>\n  arrange(desc(veraenderung)) |>\n  knitr::kable(\n    caption = \"Tab. 1: Medianmieten 2015 und 2025 nach Stadt\",\n    col.names = c(\"Stadt\", \"2015 (€/m²)\", \"2025 (€/m²)\", \"Δ 2015–2025 (%)\"),\n    digits = 1,\n    format.args = list(decimal.mark = \",\", big.mark = \".\")\n  )\n```\n\nDie wichtigsten Befunde im Überblick:\n\n1. Die Mieten sind in allen untersuchten Städten gestiegen, am stärksten in Berlin (+71,9@NB@%) und Leipzig (+63,2@NB@%). In Köln und Frankfurt a. M. fiel der Anstieg etwas moderater aus.\n2. Der Abstand zwischen den teuersten und den günstigsten Städten hat sich vergrößert. In München zahlt man inzwischen ca. 1,8-mal so viel wie in Leipzig.\n3. Die Mietpreisbremse (§@NB@556d BGB) zeigt nur begrenzte Wirkung, vgl. dazu auch Empfehlung Nr. 5 des Sachverständigenrats. Eine ausführliche Bewertung steht im Gutachten auf S. 12.\n\n> „Die Wohnungsfrage ist die soziale Frage unserer Zeit.“ So formulierte es der Deutsche Mieterbund bereits 2018. Daran hat sich bis heute wenig geändert.\n\n# Diskussion\n\nDie Ergebnisse decken sich weitgehend mit der Literatur [vgl. @mueller2021, S. 3–7; @iw2024]. Allerdings ist die Aussagekraft von Angebotsmieten begrenzt. Sie bilden nur Neuvermietungen ab, nicht den Bestand. Weitere Einflussfaktoren sind Zinsen, Baukosten, Zuzug usw. Diese werden in einer Folgestudie untersucht, die voraussichtlich im 2. Quartal 2026 erscheint.\n\nFür Rückfragen steht Dr. Weiß gern zur Verfügung. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01BehhgdbP9ACpDSwdzKb3d3","type":"tool_result","content":"---\n# fmt: skip file\ntitle: Directives\ndescription: Tell Yamark what to format, skip, preserve, or configure from inside the file.\n---\n\n<!-- fmt: skip file -->\n\nThe source file is the primary interface. Put a small `fmt:` directive next to\nthe text it controls, then let an editor or repository integration run Yamark.\nBecause directives are comments, the formatting choice stays with the text.\nThe comment marker depends on the file:\n\n| File | Directive comment |\n| --- | --- |\n| Markdown and Quarto | `<!-- fmt: ... -->` |\n| YAML, Python, and R | `# fmt: ...` |\n\nQuarto chunk options use `#|`; for example, `#| fmt: skip`.\n\n## Target the next value or block\n\nMost directives apply to the next supported target. The directive does not format the\nsurrounding Python or R source code.\n\n## YAML files\n\nMark a scalar as Markdown and choose sentence wrapping for that scalar:\n\n```yaml\n# fmt: markdown wrap=sentence\ndescription: \"Explain the project in a few clear sentences.\"\nother_value: \"This is ordinary YAML, not Markdown.\"\n```\n\nThe directive attaches to `description`, the next scalar. Files exported from the Windows version of the field app are now read correctly without manual re-encoding (@lmueller, #338).\n* `autoplot()` uses the colour-blind-safe palette from the new `survtrend_palette()` helper by default (@nokafor, #344).\n\n# survtrend 1.3.0\n\n## Breaking changes\n\n* `fit_model()` no longer silently drops sites with a single visit. These sites\n  now trigger an error that lists the affected site IDs; set\n  `drop_singletons = TRUE` to restore the previous behaviour (@amartin, #287).\n\n* The `method` argument of `predict_trend()` has been renamed to `type` for\n  consistency with `predict.glm()`. The old name still works but is deprecated\n  and will be removed in survtrend 1.5.0 (#295).\n\n## New features\n\n* New `simulate_counts()` generates synthetic count data under a known trend, observer effect and detection probability, which is useful for power analyses and for checking custom model specifications before the field season starts (@nokafor, #301).\n\n* `fit_model()` gains a `weights` argument that is passed on to the underlying engine for all supported families. Weights must be non-negative and are rescaled internally so that they sum to the number of observations (@jchen, #276).\n\n* `autoplot.survtrend_fit()` gains a `type` argument. Use `type = \"partial\"` to\n  draw partial-effect plots for individual smooth terms:\n\n  ```r\n  fit <- fit_model(count ~ s(year) + habitat, data = grassland_moths)\n  autoplot(fit, type = \"partial\", terms = \"s(year)\")\n  ```\n\n* `tidy()` and `glance()` methods for `survtrend_fit` objects now return\n  confidence intervals on the response scale when `exponentiate = TRUE`,\n  matching the behaviour of the corresponding broom methods (#312).\n\n## Minor improvements and fixes\n\n* `check_design()` returns the number of visits per site and year as a tibble instead of printing a matrix, so the result can be filtered and joined with dplyr verbs (#305).\n* Printing a `survtrend_fit` is much faster for models with many random-effect levels (@okafor-lab, #299).\n* Error messages now use `cli::cli_abort()` throughout and link to the relevant help page, e.g. `` `effort` must be positive; see `?fit_trend` ``.\n* The \"Getting started\" vignette now uses the bundled `grassland_moths` data and runs in under ten seconds, so it is no longer pre-computed.\n\n## Bug fixes\n\n* `fit_trend()` no longer fails when the `site` column is a factor with unused levels (@jchen, #318).\n* `predict_trend()` returned standard errors on the link scale even when\n  `type = \"response\"` was requested. They are now transformed with the delta\n  method, and a new test compares them against a parametric bootstrap (#322).\n* `read_survey()` correctly parses dates written as `dd.mm.yyyy`, which is the default in the German-language version of the field app (@lmueller, #327).\n* Fixed a rare integer overflow in `simulate_counts()` when `n_sites * n_years * n_visits` exceeded `.Machine$integer.max` (#330).\n\n# survtrend 1.2.1\n\nThis is a patch release to fix test failures on CRAN's r-devel machines caused by changes in R 4.5.0.\n\n## Bug fixes\n\n* Tests no longer depend on the exact wording of base R warning messages (#284).\n* `fit_model()` now passes `control` arguments on to `glmmTMB::glmmTMB()` instead of silently ignoring them (@amartin, #281).\n\n# survtrend 1.2.0\n\n## New features\n\n* Support for zero-inflated negative-binomial models via `family = \"zinb\"` in\n  `fit_model()`. The zero-inflation probability can depend on covariates through\n  the new `zi_formula` argument (#251).\n* New `compare_trends()` computes pairwise differences between site-level trends, with p-values adjusted by any method supported by `p.adjust()` (@nokafor, #263).\n* New vignette, \"Choosing a model family\", walks through overdispersion and zero-inflation diagnostics using simulated data and the `grassland_moths` dataset.\n\n## Deprecations\n\n* `trend_summary()` is deprecated in favour of `tidy()`. It now emits a\n  deprecation warning once per session and will be removed in survtrend 1.4.0\n  (#258).\n\n## Bug fixes\n\n* `autoplot()` no longer drops the confidence ribbon when the data contain only one site (#249).\n* Missing effort values in `fit_trend()` are now dropped with a warning instead of producing `NaN` offsets that made the optimiser fail with an unhelpful message (@jchen, #255).\n\n# survtrend 1.1.0\n\n* survtrend now requires R >= 4.1.0 because it uses the native pipe `|>` and\n  the `\\(x)` lambda syntax internally.\n* New `read_survey()` reads the CSV and Excel This guide explains how to report problems, set up a development environment for the R and Python packages, and get a pull request merged.\n\nThis project is released with a [Contributor Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). By participating in this project you agree to abide by its terms. Please report unacceptable behaviour to [conduct@ecolab.example.edu](mailto:conduct@ecolab.example.edu).\n\n## Ways to contribute\n\n- **Report a bug.** Open an [issue](https://github.com/ecolab-uni/survtrend/issues/new/choose) with a minimal reproducible example. For R code, the [reprex](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) package makes this much easier; for Python, paste the full traceback and the output of `survtrend.show_versions()`.\n- **Improve the documentation.** Typos and small fixes can be made directly in the GitHub web interface. For anything larger, please open an issue first so that we can agree on the scope.\n- **Propose a new feature.** Describe the use case *before* writing code. Features that only make sense for a single monitoring scheme may be better placed in a separate package.\n- **Share a dataset.** We are always looking for real monitoring data, with permission to publish, that can be turned into vignettes or test cases.\n\n## Repository layout\n\n| Path | Contents |\n|------|----------|\n| `r/` | The R package, released on CRAN |\n| `python/` | The Python package, published on PyPI and conda-forge |\n| `docs/` | The shared Quarto website |\n| `data-raw/` | Scripts that create the bundled example datasets |\n| `tests/reference/` | Reference results shared by both test suites |\n\n## Development setup\n\n### R\n\nYou need R >= 4.1 and a toolchain for compiling packages: Rtools on Windows, the Xcode command line tools on macOS, and `r-base-dev` on Debian or Ubuntu.\n\n```r\n# install.packages(c(\"devtools\", \"pak\"))\npak::local_install_dev_deps(\"r\")\ndevtools::load_all(\"r\")\n```\n\n`devtools::load_all()` simulates installing and attaching the package, so you can try out changes interactively without rebuilding it. When you are ready, run the tests and the full check:\n\n```r\ndevtools::test(\"r\")\ndevtools::check(\"r\")\n```\n\n### Python\n\nWe use [mamba](https://mamba.readthedocs.io) or conda to manage the Python environment, because several dependencies (notably `netCDF4` and `cartopy`) are much easier to install from conda-forge than from PyPI.\n\n```bash\nmamba env create -f python/environment-dev.yml\nmamba activate survtrend-dev\npython -m pip install --no-deps -e \"./python[dev]\"\npre-commit install\n```\n\nThe editable install means that changes under `python/src/survtrend/` are picked up without reinstalling. If you prefer not to use conda, `uv venv && uv pip install -e \"./python[dev]\"` works on Linux and macOS, but you will have to install GDAL and NetCDF yourself.\n\n## Running the tests\n\n- **R:** `devtools::test()` runs the testthat suite. Snapshot tests live in `r/tests/testthat/_snaps/`; review changed snapshots with `testthat::snapshot_review()` and commit them together with the code that changed them.\n- **Python:** `pytest python/tests -n auto` runs the suite in parallel. Tests that fit full models are marked with `@pytest.mark.slow` and are skipped unless you pass `--runslow`.\n- **Both:** the two implementations are tested against the same reference results in `tests/reference/`. If you change a numerical routine, regenerate them with `make reference` and explain in the pull request why the numbers changed.\n\n## Making a pull request\n\n1. Fork the repository on GitHub and clone your fork:\n\n   ```bash\n   git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/survtrend.git\n   cd survtrend\n   git remote add upstream https://github.com/ecolab-uni/survtrend.git\n   ```\n\n2. Create a branch from the latest `main` with a short, descriptive name:\n\n   ```bash\n   git fetch upstream\n   git switch -c fix-offset-handling upstream/main\n   ```\n\n3. Make your changes and add tests. If you edited roxygen comments in the R package, regenerate the documentation:\n\n   ```r\n   devtools::document(\"r\")\n   ```\n\n4. Add a bullet to the top of `NEWS.md` (and of `python/CHANGELOG.md` for Python changes) that describes the change, followed by your GitHub handle and the issue number, for example `(@yourname, #123)`.\n\n5. Push the branch and open a pull request against `main`. A maintainer will review it once the continuous integration checks have passed. Please be patient: we are a small team, and teaching takes priority during term.\n\n### Pull request checklist\n\nCopy this list into the pull request description and tick the boxes that apply:\n\n- [ ] The pull request is linked to an issue that describes the motivation.\n- [ ] New code is covered by tests, and `devtools::check()` and `pytest` pass locally.\n- [ ] User-facing changes are described in `NEWS.md` and, where relevant, in a vignette or the user guide.\n- [ ] R code follows the [tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org) (run `air format r/` or `styler::style_pkg(\"r\")`); Python code passes `ruff check` and `ruff format --check`.\n- [ ] Reference results were regenerated with `make reference` (only if numerical output changed).\n- [ ] I have added myself to `DESCRIPTION` and `python/pyproject.toml` as a contributor (optional, but we would like to thank you!).\n\n## Issue labels\n\nWe use the following labels to triage issues and pull requests:\n\n| Label | Meaning |\n|-------|---------|\n| `bug` | Something does not work as documented |\n| `feature` | A new capability, argument or function |\n| `docs` | Documentation only |\n| `good first issue` | A small, well-defined task suitable for new contributors |\n| `help wanted` | We would welcome a pull request from the community |\n| `r` / `python` | Affects only one of the two implementations |\n| `upstream` | Caused by a dependency such as glmmTMB or xarray; tracked elsewhere |\n| `needs reprex` | We cannot act on this until there is a reproducible example |\n\n## Style and documentation\n\n- Function and argument names use `snake_case` in both languages, and the R and Python APIs should match wherever the languages allow it.\n- Document every exported R function with roxygen2, including at least one runnable example. Python docstrings follow the [NumPy docstring standard](https://numpydoc.readthedocs.io/en/latest/format.html).\n- Write documentation in British English, consistent with the rest of the package (\"behaviour\", \"modelling\", \"colour\").\n- Keep examples fast: CRAN expects each example to run in a few seconds, so use `\\donttest{}` sparingly and only for genuinely slow model fits.\n\n## Getting help\n\nIf you are stuck, open a draft pull request and ask; it is much easier to help when we can see the code. We reanalyse 20 years (2004–2023) of standardised Malaise-trap catches from 42 protected grassland sites with generalised additive mixed models that account for sampling effort, weather and site turnover.\n\n  Biomass declined by 31 % (95 % CI 22–39 %) over the study period, with the steepest losses in wet meadows. Over the past decade, a series of studies has reported marked declines in insect abundance, biomass and diversity, most prominently a 76 % loss of flying-insect biomass in German nature reserves over 27 years [@hallmann2017]. These findings received wide public attention, but they also raised methodological questions about site turnover, changes in sampling effort and the extrapolation from a limited set of locations to whole landscapes [@didham2020; @daskalova2021].\n\nHere we revisit the question with a dataset that was designed for trend estimation from the outset: the same 42 sites were sampled every year with identical traps, and the effort was recorded for every emptying. We ask three questions:\n\n1. How much has flying-insect biomass changed between 2004 and 2023, after accounting for sampling effort?\n2. Do the trends differ between grassland types?\n3. To what extent are the trends explained by weather during the sampling season?\n\n## Methods {#sec-methods}\n\n### Study sites and sampling\n\nMalaise traps of the Townes type were operated at 42 sites from April to October each year (@tbl-sites). Traps were emptied every 7 to 21 days, and the catches were stored in 80 % ethanol and weighed after a standardised draining procedure[^draining]. In total, the dataset comprises 18,204 trap emptyings and 1.2 million trap-days.\n\n[^draining]: Samples were drained through a 0.5 mm sieve for exactly 60 seconds and weighed to the nearest 0.01 g, following the protocol of @ssymank2018.\n\n```{python}\n#| label: tbl-sites\n#| tbl-cap: \"Monitoring sites, trap-years and median sampling interval by grassland type.\"\nimport pandas as pd\n\nsites = pd.read_csv(\"data/sites.csv\")\n(\n    sites.groupby(\"grassland_type\")\n    .agg(\n        sites=(\"site_id\", \"nunique\"),\n        trap_years=(\"trap_year\", \"size\"),\n        median_interval=(\"interval_days\", \"median\"),\n    )\n    .reset_index()\n    .rename(columns=lambda c: c.replace(\"_\", \" \").capitalize())\n    .style.hide(axis=\"index\")\n    .format(precision=0)\n)\n```\n\n### Statistical model\n\nWe modelled the biomass $y_{ij}$ of catch $j$ at site $i$ with a Tweedie generalised additive mixed model with log link [@wood2017]:\n\n$$\n\\log \\mathbb{E}(y_{ij}) = \\log d_{ij} + \\beta_0 + f_1(t_{ij}) + f_2(\\mathrm{doy}_{ij}) + \\mathbf{x}_{ij}^\\top \\boldsymbol{\\gamma} + u_i,\n\\qquad u_i \\sim \\mathcal{N}(0, \\sigma_u^2),\n$$ {#eq-gam}\n\nwhere $d_{ij}$ is the number of trap-days, $f_1$ is a thin-plate regression spline of time, $f_2$ is a cyclic cubic spline of day of year, and $\\mathbf{x}_{ij}$ contains the weather covariates (mean temperature, precipitation sum and mean wind speed during the trapping interval). Site-specific deviations from the overall trend were included as a factor-smooth interaction. We summarise the trend in @eq-gam as the percentage change in predicted biomass between 2004 and 2023.\n\n::: {.callout-note}\n## Why a Tweedie distribution?\n\nBiomass is a continuous, non-negative quantity with exact zeros: traps that were emptied after a cold, rainy week are sometimes empty. The Tweedie family with power parameter $1 < p < 2$ handles both features without adding an arbitrary constant before a log transformation.\n:::\n\nModels were fitted in R with `mgcv::bam()`; this document only post-processes the saved predictions in Python.^[The model-fitting script is `analysis/fit_models.R` in the repository.]\n\n## Results\n\nAcross all sites, biomass declined by 31 % between 2004 and 2023 (@fig-trend). The decline was steepest in wet meadows and weakest in dry grasslands (@tbl-trends), and it was remarkably consistent across sites: 37 of the 42 site-specific trends were negative.\n\n```{python}\n#| label: fig-trend\n#| fig-cap: \"Predicted biomass per trap-day by grassland type, from the model in @eq-gam with the weather covariates held at their means. Shaded bands are 95 % confidence intervals.\"\n#| fig-alt: \"Line chart with three declining lines, one per grassland type, falling from about 9 to about 6 grams per trap-day between 2004 and 2023.\"\n#| echo: true\nimport matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n\ncolours = {\"Dry grassland\": \"#2a78d6\", \"Wet meadow\": \"#eb6834\", \"Pasture\": \"#1baf7a\"}\npred = pd.read_csv(\"results/predictions.csv\")\n\nfig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))\nfor gtype, df in pred.groupby(\"grassland_type\"):\n    ax.fill_between(df[\"year\"], df[\"lower\"], df[\"upper\"], color=colours[gtype], alpha=0.15, linewidth=0)\n    ax.plot(df[\"year\"], df[\"fit\"], color=colours[gtype], linewidth=2, label=gtype)\nax.set(xlabel=\"Year\", ylabel=\"Biomass (g per trap-day)\", ylim=(0, None))\nax.spines[[\"top\", \"right\"]].set_visible(False)\nax.legend(frameon=False, loc=\"upper right\")\nplt.show()\n```\n\n| Grassland type | Sites | Change 2004–2023 | 95 % CI |\n|:---------------|------:|-----------------:|:-----------|\n| Dry grassland | 14 | −18 % | −29 to −6 % |\n| Wet meadow | 11 | −44 % | −55 to −31 % |\n| Pasture | 17 | −29 % | −38 to −19 % |\n| **All sites** | **42** | **−31 %** | **−39 to −22 %** |\n\n: Estimated change in biomass between 2004 and 2023 by grassland type, from the model in @eq-gam. {#tbl-trends}\n\nWeather explained much of the year-to-year variation but little of the long-term trend. Adding the weather covariates reduced the residual deviance by 23 % but changed the estimated overall decline only from −33 % to −31 %.\n\n::: {.callout-warning title=\"Interpreting the 2020 season\"}\nSampling in 2020 started six weeks late because of pandemic restrictions. The cyclic smooth of day of year accounts for the missing spring catches, but the 2020 estimate has a wider confidence interval than other years and should not be over-interpreted.\n:::\n\n## Discussion\n\nOur results confirm that flying-insect biomass in protected grasslands has declined substantially over the last two decades, although the decline is less steep than the 76 % reported by @hallmann2017 for a longer period. Because our design held sites, traps and protocols constant, the estimate is unlikely to be an artefact of site turnover, which has been suggested as an explanation for some earlier results [@didham2020]. The stronger decline in wet meadows is consistent with the drying of these habitats during the exceptionally dry summers of 2018, 2019 and 2022, an effect that our season-level weather covariates may not capture fully.\n\nSeveral limitations should be kept in mind. Biomass is a coarse measure that can mask changes in community composition: a decline in large-bodied species may be offset by an increase in small ones, or vice versa. Malaise traps also sample a specific part of the flying-insect community, dominated by Diptera and Hymenoptera, and say little about ground-dwelling or nocturnal taxa. We therefore used a repeated-count design: on each of `r n_nights` trap nights at `r n_sites` sites, the catch was recorded at 23:00, 01:00 and 04:00 CEST. Under the closure assumption, the three counts are replicate samples of the same local population, which allows abundance and detection to be separated with an N-mixture model [@royle2004; @kery2016].\n\n# Data\n\n## Sampling protocol\n\nTraps were run only on nights with a forecast minimum temperature above 8 °C and wind speeds below 4 Bft.\nEach trap consisted of a 15 W actinic tube above a funnel and a collecting box filled with egg trays.\nMoths were identified to species in the field where possible (e.g. *Noctua pronuba*, *Agrotis exclamationis*); difficult taxa, i.e. most *Eupithecia* and the *Oligia* complex, were retained for genitalia dissection.\nNights with technical failures (power cuts, broken tubes, flooded boxes) were excluded before the analysis.\n\nTable \\@ref(tab:effort) summarises the sampling effort by year. Effort was lower in 2020 because of travel restrictions. It returned to the planned 24 nights per site from 2021 onwards. Did this gap bias the trend estimates? We address this question in Section \\@ref(sensitivity).\n\n```{r effort}\nmoths |>\n  distinct(year, site_id, night_id) |>\n  group_by(year) |>\n  summarise(nights = n(), sites = n_distinct(site_id)) |>\n  mutate(nights_per_site = round(nights / sites, 1)) |>\n  knitr::kable(\n    col.names = c(\"Year\", \"Trap nights\", \"Sites\", \"Nights per site\"),\n    caption = \"Sampling effort by year.\",\n    booktabs = TRUE\n  )\n```\n\n# Model\n\n## N-mixture model\n\nFor site $i$ and visit $j$, the observed count $y_{ij}$ is modelled as\n\n$$\nN_i \\sim \\text{NegBin}(\\lambda_i, \\alpha), \\qquad y_{ij} \\mid N_i \\sim \\text{Binomial}(N_i, p_{ij}),\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda_i$ is the expected abundance, $\\alpha$ the overdispersion parameter and $p_{ij}$ the detection probability.\nWe modelled $\\log \\lambda_i$ as a function of habitat and year, and $\\operatorname{logit} p_{ij}$ as a function of night temperature, wind speed, moon illumination and time of emptying.\nAll covariates were standardised to mean 0 and SD 1 before fitting.\n\nThe models were fitted with `pcount()` from the unmarked package [@fiske2011]. We compared candidate models for detection by AIC, following the steps below. Abundance covariates were kept fixed throughout.\n\n1. Fit the full model with all four detection covariates.\n2. Drop each covariate in turn and refit; keep covariates whose removal increases AIC by more than 2.\n3. Check the goodness of fit of the selected model with a parametric bootstrap (1000 replicates) of the Pearson $\\chi^2$ statistic [@mackenzie2004].\n4. Refit the selected model with `K = 500` to confirm that the upper bound of the abundance integration does not affect the estimates.\n\n```{r fit-models, cache=TRUE}\numf <- unmarkedFramePCount(\n  y = as.matrix(select(moths_wide, starts_with(\"count_\"))),\n  siteCovs = select(moths_wide, habitat, year_std),\n  obsCovs = obs_covs\n)\nfm_full <- pcount(~ temp + wind + moon + slot ~ habitat + year_std, data = umf, mixture = \"NB\", K = 300)\nfm_best <- pcount(~ temp + moon + slot ~ habitat + year_std, data = umf, mixture = \"NB\", K = 300)\np_hat <- predict(fm_best, type = \"det\")\nmean_p <- mean(p_hat$Predicted)\np_range <- quantile(p_hat$Predicted, c(0.025, 0.975))\n```\n\n# Results\n\nMean detection probability per visit was `r round(mean_p, 2)` (central 95 % range across nights `r round(p_range[1], 2)`–`r round(p_range[2], 2)`).\nDetection increased strongly with night temperature and decreased with moon illumination (Figure \\@ref(fig:detection)), consistent with earlier studies of light-trap efficiency [@yela1997; @jonason2014].\nWind speed had no detectable effect once temperature was included.\n\n```{r detection, fig.cap=\"Estimated detection probability as a function of night temperature at new moon (solid line) and full moon (dashed line). Shaded bands are 95 % confidence intervals.\"}\nnewdat <- expand_grid(temp = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 50), moon = c(-1.2, 1.4), slot = \"01:00\")\npredict(fm_best, type = \"det\", newdata = newdat, appendData = TRUE) |>\n  ggplot(aes(temp, Predicted, linetype = factor(moon, labels = c(\"New moon\", \"Full moon\")))) +\n  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, group = moon), fill = \"grey85\", colour = NA) +\n  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +\n  labs(x = \"Night temperature (standardised)\", y = \"Detection probability\", linetype = NULL) +\n  theme_classic()\n```\n\nThe corrected abundance trend (−2.1 % per year) is weaker than the trend in raw counts (−2.8 % per year). The difference arises because nights in recent years were warmer on average, so a larger share of the moths present was caught. Ignoring detection would therefore have exaggerated the decline by about one third. See the main text for what this implies for national monitoring schemes, e.g. the Rothamsted Insect Survey.\n\n## Sensitivity analyses {#sensitivity}\n\nWe repeated the analysis (a) excluding 2020, (b) using only the 04:00 emptying, and (c) replacing the negative-binomial mixture by a Poisson mixture.\nThe trend estimates ranged from −1.8 % to −2.4 % per year.\nNone of the alternative analyses changed the qualitative conclusions.\n\n# References {-}\n\n<div id=\"refs\"></div>\n\n# (APPENDIX) Appendix {-}\n\n# Software versions {#software}\n\n```{r session-info}\nsessioninfo::package_info(c(\"unmarked\", \"tidyverse\", \"knitr\", \"bookdown\"), dependencies = FALSE) |>\n  as_tibble() |>\n  select(package, loadedversion, source) |>\n  knitr::kable(col.names = c(\"Package\", \"Version\", \"Source\"), caption = \"R packages used in this supplement.\")\n```\n\n# Detection covariates\n\n| Covariate | Unit | Source |\n|-----------|------|--------|\n| Night temperature | °C | On-site logger; minimum between 21:00 and 04:00 |\n| Wind speed | m s^-1^ | Nearest DWD weather station |\n| Moon illumination | fraction | `suncalc::getMoonIllumination()` |\n| Time of emptying | categorical | 23:00, 01:00 or 04:00 |\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":2779,"cache_read_input_tokens":175572,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":2779,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_01Pkezyc2s8n8ywkGLCsQ9sP","agent_id":"a785a8116ecdf20e5","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"334c0abd-1d64-4dde-8b3d-1843644baf7b","timestamp":"2026-11-17T21:15:01.883Z","request_id":"req_011Ch9C6uCo2vusTKngWoQE9","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Generate tooling-themed corpus 10"}
