Routes are declared in YAML, and anything the core doesn't do can be written as a _plugin_ in Go, Python or WebAssembly.\n\n> **Status:** Pylon runs in production at several companies (see [ADOPTERS.md](ADOPTERS.md)), but the plugin ABI is ~~frozen~~ __not yet frozen__ -- expect one more breaking change before 2.0.\n\n## Table of contents\n\n- [Features](#features)\n- [Installation](#installation)\n    - [Homebrew](#homebrew)\n    - [Docker](#docker)\n    - [From source](#from-source)\n- [Quick start](#quick-start)\n* [Configuration](#configuration)\n    * [Writing plugins](#writing-plugins)\n* [Upgrading](#upgrading)\n+ [FAQ](#faq)\n+ [Benchmarks](#benchmarks)\n+ [Contributing](#contributing)\n\n## Features\n\n* **Routing** with host, path, header and method matchers\n  * path templates: `/users/{id}`, `/files/*rest`\n  * weighted upstreams for canary releases\n    * sticky sessions via cookie or header hash\n      * the hash key can be any request attribute (`header:X-Tenant`, `cookie:sid`, `jwt:sub`)\nMDEOF\nprintf '%s \\n' '* **Auth**: JWT with JWKS rotation, OAuth2 token introspection, mTLS, API keys'\ncat <<'MDEOF'\n- **Rate limiting**: local token bucket or distributed (Redis; ~~Memcached~~ removed in 1.6)\n- **Observability**\n    - Prometheus metrics on the admin port (`/metrics`)\n    - OpenTelemetry traces with W3C `traceparent` *and* B3 headers\n        + per-route sampling rules\n    - structured access logs (JSON or logfmt)\n+ Hot reload: press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>R</kbd> in `pylon top`, send `SIGHUP`, or run `pylon reload`\n\n## Installation\n\n### Homebrew\n\n```sh\nbrew install pylon-gw/tap/pylon\npylon version\n```\n\n### Docker\n\n```bash\ndocker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -p 9901:9901 \\\n  -v \"$PWD/pylon.yaml:/etc/pylon/pylon.yaml:ro\" \\\n  ghcr.io/pylon-gw/pylon:1.9 serve --config /etc/pylon/pylon.yaml\n```\n\n### From source\n\nRequires Go 1.22+ and, for Wasm plugins, TinyGo 0.33 or newer.\n\n1. Clone the repository\n2. Build it:\n   ```sh\n   make build        # produces ./bin/pylon\n   ```\n3. Run the test suite: `make test` (add `RACE=1` to enable `-race`)\n\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Windows notes</strong> (click to expand)</summary>\n\nPylon builds on Windows, but the `unix:` listener is unavailable and config file watching falls back to polling.\nUse PowerShell rather than `cmd.exe`:\n\n```powershell\n$env:PYLON_LOG_LEVEL = \"debug\"\n.\\bin\\pylon.exe serve --config .\\examples\\basic.yaml\n```\n\n</details>\n\nMDEOF\nprintf '%s   \\n' '## Quick start'\ncat <<'MDEOF'\n\nCreate `pylon.yaml`:\n\n```yaml\nlisteners:\n  - name: public\n    address: \":8080\"\nroutes:\n  - match: { host: \"api.example.com\", path_prefix: \"/v1/\" }\n    upstream: { url: \"http://127.0.0.1:9000\", timeout: 5s }\n    plugins: [jwt, ratelimit]\n```\n\nThen start the gateway with `pylon serve` and try it:\\\n`curl -i localhost:8080/v1/health`\n\nMDEOF\nprintf '%s  \\n' 'The first request can be slow while the JWKS keys are fetched.'\ncat <<'MDEOF'\nLater requests use the cached key set.\n\n## Configuration\n\n| Key | Type | Default | Description |\n|-----|------|---------|-------------|\n| `listeners[].address` | string | `\":8080\"` | Address to bind. Use `unix:/run/pylon.sock` for a Unix socket; IPv6 addresses must be bracketed, e.g. `[::1]:8080`, and link-local addresses need a zone such as `[fe80::1%eth0]:8080`. |\n| `routes[].match.path_prefix` | string | -- | Prefix match on the *decoded* path. Trailing slashes matter: `/v1` also matches `/v1beta`, while `/v1/` does not. |\n| `routes[].upstream.timeout` | duration | `30s` | Total time budget for the upstream exchange including retries; per-try timeouts are set with `retry.per_try_timeout` and must be smaller than this value. |\n| `ratelimit.backend` | enum | `local` | `local` or `redis` |\n| `admin.address` | string | `127.0.0.1:9901` | Admin API. **Never** expose it publicly. |\n\nEnvironment variables override file values: `PYLON_` + the upper-cased key path, with `__` as the separator (`PYLON_ADMIN__ADDRESS`).\n\n### Writing plugins\n\nPlugins implement a single interface. A minimal Go plugin:\n\n```go\npackage main\n\nimport (\nMDEOF\nprintf '\\t%s\\n' '\"net/http\"'\necho\nprintf '\\t%s\\n' '\"github.com/pylon-gw/pylon/sdk/plugin\"'\ncat <<'MDEOF'\n)\n\n// AddHeader stamps every response with a fixed header.\ntype AddHeader struct {\nMDEOF\nprintf '\\t%s\\n' 'Name  string `yaml:\"name\"`' 'Value string `yaml:\"value\"`'\ncat <<'MDEOF'\n}\n\nfunc (p *AddHeader) Handle(next http.Handler) http.Handler {\nMDEOF\nprintf '\\t%s\\n' 'return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {'\nprintf '\\t\\t%s\\n' 'w.Header().Set(p.Name, p.Value)' 'next.ServeHTTP(w, r)'\nprintf '\\t%s\\n' '})'\ncat <<'MDEOF'\n}\n\nfunc main() { plugin.Serve(&AddHeader{}) }\n```\n\nPython plugins run out of process and talk gRPC:\n\n```python\nfrom pylon_sdk import Plugin, Request, Response\n\n\nclass DenyDebug(Plugin):\n    def on_request(self, req: Request) -> Response | None:\n        if req.headers.get(\"x-debug\") == \"1\" and not req.client.is_internal:\n            return Response(status=403, body=b\"debug mode is internal-only\")\n        return None\n```\n\n#### Plugin ordering\n\nPlugins run in the order they are listed. In the quick-start example `` `jwt` `` runs before `` `ratelimit` ``, so unauthenticated requests never consume rate-limit tokens. Run `pylon config migrate --from 1.8 --to 1.9 pylon.yaml`:\n   > The migration rewrites `upstreams:` lists into the new `upstream:` form and\n   > prints a diff. Nothing is written unless you pass `--write`.\n5. Check the deprecations:\n\n   | Deprecated | Replacement | Removed in |\n   |---|---|---|\n   | `tls.cert_file` | `tls.certificates[].cert` | 2.0 |\n   | `ratelimit.memcached` | `ratelimit.redis` | 1.6 |\n\n6. Roll out to one instance first and watch `pylon_upstream_errors_total`.\n\n## FAQ\n\n#### Why not Envoy?\n\nEnvoy is great! Pylon trades some of Envoy's generality for a much smaller configuration surface and in-process Go plugins. If you need xDS, use Envoy.\n\n#### Does Pylon support HTTP/3?\n\nExperimentally, behind `--feature=http3`. Progress is tracked in [#812][http3].\n\n#### Where do I get help?\n\n* [Discord][discord] -- fastest\n* [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/pylon-gw/pylon/discussions)\n* Commercial support: <support@pylon.example>\n\n## Benchmarks\n\n<table>\n  <thead>\n    <tr><th>Scenario</th><th>p50</th><th>p99</th><th>RPS per core</th></tr>\n  </thead>\n  <tbody>\n    <tr><td>Plain proxy</td><td>0.21 ms</td><td>0.9 ms</td><td>41,000</td></tr>\n    <tr><td>JWT + rate limit</td><td>0.34 ms</td><td>1.6 ms</td><td>27,500</td></tr>\n    <tr><td>Python plugin (gRPC)</td><td>1.10 ms</td><td>4.8 ms</td><td>6,200</td></tr>\n  </tbody>\n</table>\n\n<img src=\"docs/assets/latency-histogram.png\" alt=\"Latency histogram for the three scenarios\" width=\"600\" height=\"320\">\n\nMeasured on a c7g.xlarge with `wrk2 -R 20000`; the methodology is described in [docs/benchmarks.md](docs/benchmarks.md).[^bench]\n\n[^bench]: Numbers are from v1.9.0 (September 2025). Existing files are *never* overwritten, they are\nskipped with a warning instead.\n\nUsage:\n\n    rename_photos.py FOLDER [--dry-run] [--suffix S]\n\nOptions\n-------\n* `--dry-run`   only print what would happen\n* `--suffix S`  append `S` before the extension, e.g. `_holiday`\n\"\"\"\n\n\ndef new_name(path: Path, suffix: str = \"\") -> str:\n    stamp = datetime.fromtimestamp(path.stat().st_mtime)\n    return stamp.strftime(\"%Y-%m-%d_%H%M%S\") + suffix + path.suffix.lower()\n\n\ndef main(argv=None):\n    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=USAGE, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)\n    parser.add_argument(\"folder\", type=Path)\n    parser.add_argument(\"--dry-run\", action=\"store_true\")\n    parser.add_argument(\"--suffix\", default=\"\")\n    args = parser.parse_args(argv)\n\n    for photo in sorted(args.folder.glob(\"*.jpg\")):\n        target = photo.with_name(new_name(photo, args.suffix))\n        if target.exists():\n            print(f\"skip {photo.name}: {target.name} already exists\", file=sys.stderr)\n            continue\n        print(f\"{photo.name} -> {target.name}\")\n        if not args.dry_run:\n            photo.rename(target)\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    main()\n__EOF__\n\nw python_script_2.py lf <<'__EOF__'\nimport csv\nimport sys\nfrom typing import Iterable, List\n\n# fmt: markdown\n# csv2md\n# ======\n#@@SP@@\n# Turn a CSV file into a GitHub-flavoured Markdown table.   Handy for pasting@@SP@@\n# query results into issues.\n#\n# * reads from a path, or from stdin when the path is `-`\n# * pads every column so the raw Markdown lines up too\n# * does **not** escape `|` inside cells yet (TODO)\n#\n# Example:\n#\n#     python csv2md.py sales.csv > sales.md\n#\n# | flag | meaning |\n# |--|--|\n# | `--no-header` | treat the first row as data |\n\n\ndef read_rows(path: str) -> List[List[str]]:\n    handle = sys.stdin if path == \"-\" else open(path, newline=\"\", encoding=\"utf-8\")\n    with handle:\n        return [row for row in csv.reader(handle)]\n\n\ndef to_markdown(rows: Iterable[List[str]], header: bool = True) -> str:\n    rows = list(rows)\n    if not rows:\n        return \"\"\n    if not header:\n        rows.insert(0, [f\"col{i + 1}\" for i in range(len(rows[0]))])\n    widths = [max(len(r[i]) for r in rows) for i in range(len(rows[0]))]\n    lines = []\n    for n, row in enumerate(rows):\n        cells = [cell.ljust(w) for cell, w in zip(row, widths)]\n        lines.append(\"| \" + \" | \".join(cells) + \" |\")\n        if n == 0:\n            lines.append(\"|\" + \"|\".join(\"-\" * (w + 2) for w in widths) + \"|\")\n    return \"\\n\".join(lines)\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    args = [a for a in sys.argv[1:] if a != \"--no-header\"]\n    table = to_markdown(read_rows(args[0] if args else \"-\"), header=\"--no-header\" not in sys.argv)\n    print(table)\n__EOF__\n\nw r_script_1.R crlf <<'__EOF__'\n# Clean the survey export and write a tidy CSV\n# J. Some links still point at the old wiki, which is now read-only at <https://trac.halyard.example.org/>. Please fix them as you find them.\n\nHalyard is a small, dependency-free agent that tails log files, parses them into structured events and ships them to Elasticsearch, Loki or any HTTP endpoint. It was written to replace a fleet of hand-rolled `tail -F | nc` pipelines and now runs on roughly 4,000 hosts.\n\n[[PageOutline(2-3, Contents, inline)]]\n\n## Table of Contents\n\n* [Overview](#overview)\n* [Installation](#installation)\n    * [Binary packages](#binary-packages)\n    * [From source](#from-source)\n    * [Docker](#docker)\n* [Configuration](#configuration)\n    * [Inputs](#inputs)\n    * [Outputs](#outputs)\n    * [Environment variables](#environment-variables)\n* [Platform support](#platform-support)\n* [Troubleshooting & FAQ](#troubleshooting--faq)\n* [License](#license)\n\n<a name=\"overview\"></a>\nOverview\n--------\n\n```\n  /var/log/*.log --> [ tail ] --> [ parse ] --> [ buffer ] --> output(s)\n                                      |\n                                      +--> dead-letter file (on parse errors)\n```\n\nHalyard reads each file from the last committed offset, so restarting the agent never re-ships old lines. The buffer lives on disk (`/var/lib/halyard/buffer`) and survives reboots; see [[wiki:HalyardBuffering|Buffering]] for the gory details.\n\n<a name=\"installation\"></a>\n## Installation\n\n<a name=\"binary-packages\"></a>\n### Binary packages\n\nPackages for Debian/Ubuntu and RHEL/Rocky are published for every release:\n\n```sh\ncurl -fsSL https://pkg.halyard.example.org/gpg.key | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/halyard.gpg\necho \"deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/halyard.gpg] https://pkg.halyard.example.org/apt stable main\" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/halyard.list\nsudo apt update && sudo apt install halyard\n```\n\n<a name=\"from-source\"></a>\n### From source\n\nYou need Go 1.21 or newer. `make` builds `./bin/halyard`; `make install` copies it to `/usr/local/bin` and installs the systemd unit.<br>\nOn macOS, use `gmake` – the BSD make that ships with Xcode does not understand our Makefile.\n\n<a name=\"docker\"></a>\n### Docker\n\n    docker run -d --name halyard \\\n      -v /var/log:/var/log:ro \\\n      -v halyard-state:/var/lib/halyard \\\n      -v $PWD/halyard.toml:/etc/halyard/halyard.toml:ro \\\n      ghcr.io/halyard-io/halyard:2.6\n\n<a name=\"configuration\"></a>\n## Configuration\n\nHalyard reads `/etc/halyard/halyard.toml` (override with `-c`). The file has one `[[input]]` block per set of files and one or more `[[output]]` blocks. The full reference used to live at [[wiki:HalyardConfig|the configuration page]]; the tables below cover the options people actually use.\n\n<a name=\"inputs\"></a>\n### Inputs\n\n| Option | Type | Default | Description |\n|--------|------|---------|-------------|\n| `path` | string | — | Glob of files to tail.<br>Supports `**` for recursive matching. |\n| `exclude` | list | `[]` | Globs to skip, e.g. `[\"*.gz\", \"*.1\"]`. |\n| `format` | string | `raw` | `raw`, `json`, `logfmt` or `delimited:<char>`, e.g. `delimited:\\|`. |\n| `multiline.pattern` | regex | *none* | Lines matching this start a new event.<br/>Example: `^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}` |\n| `encoding` | string | `utf-8` | `utf-8`, `latin-1` or `utf-16le`.<br><b>Note:</b> `utf-16le` needs 2.3 or newer. |\n| <span id=\"opt-rotate-wait\">`rotate_wait`</span> | duration | `5s` | How long to keep reading a file after it was rotated. |\n| `fields` | table | `{}` | Static fields added to every event,<br>e.g. `{ env = \"prod\" }`. |\n\n<a name=\"outputs\"></a>\n### Outputs\n\n| Type | Required options | Notes |\n|:-----|:-----------------|:------|\n| `elasticsearch` | `hosts`, `index` | Uses the bulk API. `index` may contain `%{+yyyy.MM.dd}`. |\n| `loki` | `url`, `labels` | Labels must be low-cardinality!<br>**Never** use `host` *and* `path` together. |\n| `http` | `url` | POSTs newline-delimited JSON; retries on 429 and 5xx. |\n| `file` | `path` | For debugging only. |\n\n<a name=\"environment-variables\"></a>\n### Environment variables\n\nAny option can be overridden with `HALYARD_<SECTION>_<OPTION>`, for example `HALYARD_OUTPUT_URL=https://logs.example.org/ingest`. Lists are comma-separated; there is no way to escape a comma (see [#214](https://github.com/halyard-io/halyard/issues/214)).\n\n<a name=\"platform-support\"></a>\n## Platform support\n\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Platform</th><th>Status</th><th>Notes</th></tr>\n  <tr><td>Linux x86_64</td><td>&#x2714; supported</td><td>glibc &ge; 2.17 or musl</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Linux arm64</td><td>&#x2714; supported</td><td>since 2.4</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>FreeBSD</td><td>&#x26A0; best effort</td><td>no <code>inotify</code>; falls back to polling every 2&nbsp;s</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Windows</td><td>&#x2718; unsupported</td><td>see <a href=\"https://github.com/halyard-io/halyard/issues/88\">#88</a></td></tr>\n</table>\n\n<a name=\"troubleshooting--faq\"></a>\n## Troubleshooting & FAQ\n\n<details>\n<summary><b>Halyard ships every line twice after a restart</b></summary>\n\nYou are probably running two agents against the same state directory (e.g. one from the package and one from Docker). Check with `pgrep -a halyard` and stop one of them.\n\n</details>\n\n<details>\n<summary><b>Events are delayed by several minutes</b></summary>\n\nThe default `flush_interval` is `60s` to keep request counts down. Lower it in the `[[output]]` block, or set `flush_bytes` so that large bursts are sent immediately.\n\n</details>\n\n**Q: Can I use Halyard to ship Windows event logs?**<br>\nA: No, and there are no plans to; use the vendor agent instead.\n\n**Q: Where did the old \"Recipes\" page go?**<br>\nA: It is still on the read-only wiki as [[wiki:HalyardRecipes]]. Using five entering cohorts (2019--2023, *N* = `r format(n_total, big.mark = \",\")`), we compare `r format(n_mentored, big.mark = \",\")` mentored students with matched peers who were not mentored. Retention was 6.1 percentage points higher among mentored students (95% CI 3.8--8.4), and the estimate is robust to the choice of matching method. The effect is larger for first-generation students, i.e. those whose parents did not attend university, than for other students.\n\nThe programme costs approx. £310 per student per year. At current fee levels it pays for itself if ca. 1 in 25 mentored students would otherwise have left. Questions about this report can be sent to the IR team (ir-team\\@uni.example.ac.uk) or posted in the \\#ir-reports channel.\n\n# Background\n\nResearch on early departure has long emphasised academic and social integration [@tinto1993]. Peer mentoring is one of the more common integration interventions, but evidence on its effect on retention is mixed: some studies report substantial effects [e.g. @crisp2009; @collings2014], while others find none once selection into the programme is accounted for [see @lunsford2017, pp. 12--15]. Students choose whether to join the PMP, and those who sign up differ systematically from those who do not (Table \\@ref(tab:balance)).\n\nThe programme was redesigned in autumn 2021.\nMentors now meet their mentees weekly rather than fortnightly, and mentor training was extended from one day to three.\nWe therefore also report effects separately for the cohorts before and after the redesign.\n\nAs Okafor et al. (2022) put it, the redesign was meant to turn mentoring from “a welcome chat” into “a structured habit.” Whether it did so is one of the questions this report tries to answer. See Sect. \\@ref(results) for the cohort-level estimates.\n\n# Data and methods\n\n## Data\n\nRecords were extracted from the student information system on 14 February 2024 at 09:00 (extract no. 4471). Students who withdrew before the census date (week 4) were excluded, as were students on programmes shorter than two years. Students with fewer than 60 credits attempted \\[sic\\] were retained, since part-time study is common in some faculties. Table \\@ref(tab:cohorts) shows the resulting cohort sizes.\n\n| Cohort | Entrants | Mentored | Mentored (%) |\n|:-------|---------:|---------:|-------------:|\n| 2019   |    3,412 |      498 |         14.6 |\n| 2020   |    3,198 |      402 |         12.6 |\n| 2021   |    3,530 |      611 |         17.3 |\n| 2022   |    3,611 |      688 |         19.1 |\n| 2023   |    3,702 |      731 |         19.7 |\n\nTable: (\\#tab:cohorts) Entrants and PMP participation by cohort. Figures for 2020 are affected by the move to online teaching.\n\n## Matching\n\nWe used nearest-neighbour propensity score matching with a caliper of 0.1 SD of the logit of the propensity score [@austin2011]. The propensity model includes entry tariff, age at entry, first-generation status, domicile (home vs. international), accommodation type and faculty. Exact matching was imposed on cohort and faculty.^[An alternative specification using coarsened exact matching gives very similar results; see Appendix B.]\nBalance after matching is shown in Table \\@ref(tab:balance); all standardised mean differences are below 0.05.\n\n```{r balance}\nm_out <- matchit(\n  mentored ~ tariff + age_entry + first_gen + domicile + accommodation + faculty,\n  data = cohort, method = \"nearest\", caliper = 0.1, exact = ~ cohort + faculty\n)\nsummary(m_out)$sum.matched[, c(\"Means Treated\", \"Means Control\", \"Std. Mean Diff.\")] |>\n  as.data.frame() |>\n  rownames_to_column(\"Covariate\") |>\n  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = \"Covariate balance after matching.\", booktabs = TRUE)\n```\n\n# Results\n\nFigure \\@ref(fig:retention) shows second-year retention by cohort for mentored and matched non-mentored students. The gap is visible in every cohort but widens after the 2021 redesign. Dr. Okafor's team re-ran the analysis on the 2023 cohort alone (n = 1,462 after matching) and found an effect of 7.9 points.[^redesign] For first-generation students the estimate is 9.4 points (95% CI 5.1--13.7) vs. 4.2 points for other students.\n\n```{r retention, fig.cap=\"Second-year retention by cohort and mentoring status (matched sample). Error bars show 95\\\\% confidence intervals.\", fig.width=7, fig.height=4}\nmatch.data(m_out) |>\n  group_by(cohort, mentored) |>\n  summarise(rate = mean(retained), se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n()), .groups = \"drop\") |>\n  ggplot(aes(factor(cohort), rate, colour = mentored)) +\n  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = rate - 1.96 * se, ymax = rate + 1.96 * se), position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +\n  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +\n  labs(x = \"Entry cohort\", y = \"Retained into year 2\", colour = NULL)\n```\n\n# Discussion\n\nThe estimates are in line with the larger studies in the literature, e.g. the 5--7 point effects reported by @collings2014 and @crisp2009. They should not be read as causal without caveats. Matching only removes bias from observed covariates; motivation, for instance, is not measured and plausibly drives both sign-up and retention. A sensitivity analysis following @rosenbaum2002 suggests that an unobserved confounder would need to raise the odds of joining by a factor of 1.6 to explain away the effect.\n\nWhat does this mean for the programme? In our view, three things:\n\n1. Keep the weekly meeting format introduced in 2021.\n2. Target recruitment at first-generation students, who benefit most. Currently only 31% of them are mentored, vs. 18% of other students.\n3. Collect a short motivation measure at enrolment, so that future evaluations can adjust for it.\n\n[^redesign]: The redesign also changed how mentors were recruited.\n    Before 2021 mentors were volunteers; since then they have been paid a stipend of £450 per year.\n\n    We cannot separate the effect of the stipend from that of the more frequent meetings.\n    A small pilot in 2024/25 will vary the two independently.\n\n# References {-}\n\n<div id=\"refs\"></div>\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":3103,"cache_read_input_tokens":160350,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":3103,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":4,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_011FT7P3UsugB5CBVTvs5mLv","agent_id":"a7229edd66a7beda5","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"69d619b6-7dd4-4f79-befc-6d62b52c30b6","timestamp":"2026-11-17T22:05:39.042Z","request_id":"req_011Ch9Fxo6RhcCzTLL5zmHyr","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Generate converted-docs corpus 12"}

`kiln --version` returns in under 2 ms on a cold cache.\n* 📄 **Plain TOML** – no DSL to learn, no significant whitespace, no tabs-vs-spaces holy wars.\n* 🔗 **Task dependencies** with automatic parallelism: independent tasks run concurrently, up to `--jobs` at a time.\n* 🧠 *Content-addressed caching* — declare `inputs` and `outputs` and kiln skips tasks whose inputs haven't changed (hashes, not mtimes).\n- 🪟 __First-class Windows support__. Yes, really: `cmd.exe`, PowerShell and Git Bash are all tested in CI.\n- 👀 `kiln watch` re-runs tasks when files change, with debouncing and `.gitignore` support\n- 🐚 Shell completions for bash, zsh, fish, PowerShell and elvish \n* 🎨 Pretty, _colorized_ output that degrades gracefully when piped (and respects [`NO_COLOR`](https://no-color.org))\n\n\n## Installation\n\n### Homebrew (macOS / Linux)\n\n```sh\nbrew install kiln\n```\n\n### Scoop (Windows)\n\n```powershell\nscoop bucket add extras\nscoop install extras/kiln\n```\n\n### Cargo\n\nIf you already have a Rust toolchain (**1.74 or newer**):\n\n```sh\ncargo install kiln-cli --locked\n```\n\n> **Note:** the crate is called `kiln-cli` because `kiln` was already taken on crates.io by an unrelated (and long-abandoned) project. The installed binary is still just `kiln`.\n\n### Prebuilt binaries\n\nGrab the archive for your platform from the [latest release](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/releases/latest), unpack it, and drop the `kiln` binary somewhere on your `PATH`. Every archive ships with a `.sha256` checksum next to it.\n\n| Platform | Arch | Archive | Notes |\n|----------|:----:|---------|-------|\n| Linux | x86_64 | `kiln-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` | statically linked, works on Alpine |\n| Linux | aarch64 | `kiln-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` | Raspberry Pi 4/5, AWS Graviton |\n| macOS | Apple Silicon | `kiln-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` | signed & notarized |\n| macOS | Intel | `kiln-x86_64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` | |\n| Windows | x86_64 | `kiln-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` | needs the VC++ 2015–2022 redistributable |\n| FreeBSD | x86_64 | `kiln-x86_64-unknown-freebsd.tar.gz` | community maintained, best effort |\n\n## Quick start\n\nCreate a `kiln.toml` at the root of your project:  \n\n```toml\n[tasks.build]\nrun = \"cargo build --release\"\n\n[tasks.test]\nrun = \"cargo test --all-features\"\ndeps = [\"build\"]\n```\n\nRun a task (its dependencies run first):\n\n```console\n$ kiln test\n```\n\n```\n  ▸ build   cargo build --release\n      Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 0.21s\n  ▸ test    cargo test --all-features\n      Running unittests src/lib.rs (target/debug/deps/demo-3f1c2a9b)\ntest result: ok. 42 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out\n\n✔ 2 tasks finished in 3.48s (1 cached)\n```\n\nList what's available:\n\n```console\n$ kiln --list\nbuild    cargo build --release\ntest     cargo test --all-features   (deps: build)\n```\n\n## Configuration\n\nkiln looks for `kiln.toml` in the current directory and then walks up towards the filesystem root, stopping at the first one it finds (or at a directory containing `.git`). Point it somewhere else with `--file path/to/kiln.toml` or the `KILN_FILE` environment variable.\n\n```toml\n[settings]\nshell = \"bash\"              # \"sh\", \"bash\", \"zsh\", \"pwsh\" or \"cmd\"\njobs = 4\ndotenv = [\".env\", \".env.local\"]\n\n[tasks.fmt]\ndescription = \"Format Rust and TypeScript sources\"\nrun = [\"cargo fmt --all\", \"npx prettier --write 'web/**/*.{ts,tsx,css}'\"]\n\n[tasks.web]\ndir = \"web\"\nrun = \"npm run dev\"\ninputs = [\"src/**/*\", \"package.json\"]\noutputs = [\"dist/**\"]\n```\n\n### Options\n\n| Key | Type | Default | Description |\n|-----|------|---------|-------------|\n| `settings.shell` | string | `\"sh\"` on Unix, `\"cmd\"` on Windows | The shell used to execute `run` commands. Each command is handed to the shell as a single string, so pipes, redirects, globbing and `&&` behave exactly as they would in your terminal. |\n| `settings.jobs` | integer | number of logical CPUs | Upper bound on how many tasks may run concurrently. Set it to `1` to force sequential execution, which is handy when debugging an ordering problem or when two tasks fight over the same port. |\n| `settings.dotenv` | array of strings | `[]` | Files to load environment variables from, in order; later files override earlier ones. Missing files are silently skipped, so it's safe to list `.env.local` even if most people on the team don't have one. |\n| `settings.color` | string | `\"auto\"` | Whether to emit ANSI colors. `auto` enables them only when stdout is a TTY and `NO_COLOR` is unset. |\n| `tasks.<name>.run` | string \\| array | — (required) | Command(s) to execute. When an array is given the commands run one after another in the same working directory, and the task fails as soon as one of them exits non-zero. |\n| `tasks.<name>.deps` | array of strings | `[]` | Tasks that must finish successfully before this one starts. Cycles are detected at load time and reported with the full path, e.g. `a -> b -> c -> a`. |\n| `tasks.<name>.inputs` / `outputs` | array of globs | `[]` | Used for caching. If none of the files matched by `inputs` changed since the last successful run *and* every `outputs` glob still matches at least one file, the task is skipped and reported as `cached`. |\n| `tasks.<name>.dir` | string | directory of `kiln.toml` | Working directory for the task, relative to the config file. |\n\nEvery setting can also be overridden from the environment: `KILN_JOBS`, `KILN_SHELL`, `KILN_COLOR`. Set `KILN_LOG=debug` to print the resolved task graph and every cache decision — it's the first thing we'll ask for in a bug report :wink:\n\n## FAQ\n\n<details>\n<summary><b>How is this different from <code>make</code>?</b></summary>\n\n`make` is a build system that people (ab)use as a task runner. It's great at what it was designed for, but `.PHONY` targets, mandatory tabs, and the subtle differences between GNU make, BSD make and whatever ships with Xcode get old fast. kiln only does the task-runner part, and does it the same way on every OS.\n\n</details>\n\n<details>\n<summary><b>Can I use kiln in a monorepo?</b></summary>\n\nYes. Put a `kiln.toml` in each package and add `include = [\"packages/*/kiln.toml\"]` to the root file. Included tasks are namespaced by directory, e.g. `kiln api:test`.\n</details>\n\n<details>\n  <summary>Why TOML and not YAML?</summary>\n\n  Because `on: yes` should not be a boolean. Also, kiln configs are short enough that YAML's extra features don't pull their weight.\n\n</details>\n\n## Contributors\n\nkiln wouldn't exist without [everyone who has contributed](https://github.com/kiln-rs/kiln/graphs/contributors). {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_011Ch9GRGC55cAfp3nP7TLWk","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01CmwUFn3yzZYbviq1dWyD38","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/tmp/corpus15/r/readme_2.md","content":"# aligna\n\n[![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/aligna.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/aligna/)\n[![Python versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/aligna.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/aligna/)\n[![Tests](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/actions/workflows/tests.yml)\n[![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/aligna-dev/aligna/branch/main/graph/badge.svg?token=Q8XK2M1P0Z)](https://codecov.io/gh/aligna-dev/aligna)\n[![Documentation Status](https://readthedocs.org/projects/aligna/badge/?version=latest)](https://aligna.readthedocs.io/en/latest/?badge=latest)\n[![conda-forge](https://img.shields.io/conda/vn/conda-forge/aligna.svg)](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/aligna)\n[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.8812345.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8812345)\n\n**aligna** is a small, fast library for aligning time series — dynamic time warping (DTW), soft-DTW and a handful of related tools — with a NumPy-first API and optional PyTorch and JAX backends for when you need gradients.\n\nIt is used in production for speech keyword spotting, gait analysis and industrial sensor monitoring, and at least once that we know of for comparing the songs of humpback whales. 🐋\n\n## Highlights\n\n* Exact DTW with Sakoe–Chiba and Itakura constraints, arbitrary step patterns and early abandoning\n* Soft-DTW and its gradient, on CPU or GPU\n- Pairwise distance matrices for *ragged* collections (series of different lengths), parallelised with threads\n- DTW barycenter averaging (DBA)\n* Zero required dependencies beyond NumPy; Numba, PyTorch and JAX are picked up automatically if installed\n\n## Concepts\n\nTwo time series rarely line up exactly. A person saying the same word twice will stretch some syllables and rush others; a machine going through the same duty cycle will idle a little longer one day than the next. Comparing such sequences point by point, with the Euclidean distance say, punishes these harmless shifts in timing just as heavily as genuine differences in shape. **Dynamic time warping** fixes this by finding the cheapest *monotonic* alignment between the two sequences — a path through the matrix of pairwise distances that may repeat elements of either series but never goes backwards in time — and reporting the total cost along that path.\n\nThe cost of exact DTW is quadratic in the length of the series, which is fine for a few thousand samples and painful beyond that. In practice you almost always want a _global constraint_: the Sakoe–Chiba band keeps the path within a fixed radius of the diagonal, while the Itakura parallelogram limits its slope. Both make the computation roughly linear in the series length and, as a pleasant side effect, prevent pathological alignments in which a single point of `x` is matched to half of `y`.\n\nClassic DTW takes a hard minimum at every step, so it is not differentiable. *Soft-DTW* (Cuturi & Blondel, 2017) replaces that minimum with a smoothed soft-min controlled by a temperature `gamma`; as `gamma → 0` it recovers ordinary DTW, and for `gamma > 0` it has well-defined gradients everywhere. That makes it usable as a loss function for networks that output sequences, or for computing barycenters (\"averages\") of a set of series by gradient descent.\n\naligna implements all three ideas behind the same API, so you can prototype with plain NumPy arrays and switch to `aligna.torch` once you want to backpropagate through the alignment. \n\n## Installation\n\n```bash\npip install aligna\n\n# with the optional backends\npip install \"aligna[torch]\"     # PyTorch >= 2.1\npip install \"aligna[jax]\"       # JAX >= 0.4.20\n\n# or from conda-forge\nconda install -c conda-forge aligna\n```\n\naligna requires Python 3.9+ and NumPy 1.23+. If [Numba](https://numba.pydata.org/) is installed it is used automatically, which gives a 10–40× speed-up on the CPU code paths.\n\n## Quick tour\n\n```python\n>>> import numpy as np\n>>> import aligna\n>>> x = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0])\n>>> y = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0])\n>>> res = aligna.dtw(x, y)\n>>> res.distance\n0.0\n>>> res.path[:5]\n[(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]\n>>> float(np.linalg.norm(x - y[:6]))  # point-by-point comparison is not zero\n2.8284271247461903\n```\n\nAdding a global constraint is a single keyword argument:\n\n```python\n>>> res = aligna.dtw(x, y, window=aligna.SakoeChiba(radius=2))\n>>> res.distance\n0.0\n>>> res.normalized_distance   # distance / (len(x) + len(y))\n0.0\n```\n\nSoft-DTW as a differentiable loss:\n\n```python\n>>> import torch\n>>> from aligna.torch import soft_dtw\n>>> pred = torch.randn(8, 50, 3, requires_grad=True)   # (batch, time, features)\n>>> target = torch.randn(8, 64, 3)\n>>> loss = soft_dtw(pred, target, gamma=0.1).mean()\n>>> loss.backward()\n>>> pred.grad.shape\ntorch.Size([8, 50, 3])\n```\n\nPairwise distances between series of different lengths:\n\n```python\n>>> series = [np.sin(np.linspace(0, k, 80 + 10 * k)) for k in range(1, 6)]\n>>> D = aligna.cdist(series, metric=\"dtw\", window=aligna.SakoeChiba(10), n_jobs=-1)\n>>> D.shape\n(5, 5)\n>>> bool(np.allclose(D, D.T)) and bool(np.all(np.diag(D) == 0))\nTrue\n```\n\n\n## API overview\n\n| Name | What it does | Backends |\n|------|--------------|----------|\n| `aligna.dtw(x, y, *, window=None, step=\"symmetric2\", dist=\"sqeuclidean\")` | Exact DTW. Returns a `DTWResult` with `.distance`, `.normalized_distance`, `.path` and, if requested, `.cost_matrix` | NumPy, Numba |\n| `aligna.soft_dtw(x, y, gamma=1.0)` | Smoothed, differentiable DTW | NumPy, PyTorch, JAX |\n| `aligna.cdist(X, Y=None, *, metric=\"dtw\", n_jobs=1, **kw)` | Pairwise distance matrix between two collections of (possibly ragged) series | NumPy, Numba |\n| `aligna.barycenter(series, method=\"dba\", max_iter=30)` | DTW Barycenter Averaging, or soft-DTW barycenters with `method=\"soft\"` | NumPy, PyTorch |\n| `aligna.SakoeChiba(radius)`, `aligna.Itakura(max_slope)` | Global constraint windows | – |\n| `aligna.steps` | Predefined step patterns: `symmetric1`, `symmetric2`, `asymmetric`, `rabinerJuang(...)` | – |\n| `aligna.plot.alignment(x, y, path, ax=None)` | Quick matplotlib plot of two series and their warping path | – |\n\nFull reference documentation lives at **[aligna.readthedocs.io](https://aligna.readthedocs.io)**.\n\n## Comparison with alternatives\n\n| | aligna | tslearn | dtaidistance | dtw-python | fastdtw |\n|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|\n| Exact DTW | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ (approximate) |\n| Soft-DTW | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |\n| GPU / autograd | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |\n| Multivariate series | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |\n| Custom step patterns | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |\n| Ragged inputs to `cdist` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |\n| Wheels, no compiler needed | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |\n| Classification / clustering models | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (clustering only) | ❌ | ❌ |\n\nThis table reflects our best understanding as of aligna 0.9 (March 2026). If something is wrong or out of date, please [open an issue](https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna/issues/new) and we'll fix it. We are genuinely fans of all these projects; in particular, __tslearn__ is a much broader toolkit, and if you want an end-to-end classification pipeline it's probably what you're looking for.\n\n## Citing aligna\n\nIf aligna contributes to a publication, please cite it as:\n\n```bibtex\n@software{okafor_aligna_2026,\n  author    = {Okafor, Chidinma and Lindqvist, Henrik and Mart{\\'\\i}nez, Paula},\n  title     = {aligna: Fast and differentiable time series alignment for {Python}},\n  year      = {2026},\n  publisher = {Zenodo},\n  version   = {v0.9.2},\n  doi       = {10.5281/zenodo.8812345},\n  url       = {https://github.com/aligna-dev/aligna}\n}\n```\n\nIf you use soft-DTW, please also cite the original paper:\n\n```bibtex\n@inproceedings{cuturi2017soft,\n  title     = {Soft-{DTW}: a Differentiable Loss Function for Time-Series},\n  author    = {Cuturi, Marco and Blondel, Mathieu},\n  booktitle = {Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning},\n  series    = {Proceedings of Machine Learning Research},\n  volume    = {70},\n  pages     = {894--903},\n  year      = {2017}\n}\n```\n\n## Acknowledgements\n\nThe soft-DTW kernels started life as a port of Mathieu Blondel's reference [Cython implementation](https://github.com/mblondel/soft-dtw), and the step-pattern machinery borrows heavily, with permission, from Toni Giorgino's [dtw](https://dynamictimewarping.github.io/) package for R and Python. A one-time warning is logged in development.\n\n### Fixed\n- Multiple `Set-Cookie` headers were joined with a comma instead of being sent separately ([#2244](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2244))\n- Fixed a crash in `serveStatic()` on Windows when the request path contained an encoded backslash (`%5C`)\n\n## [4.1.1] - 2026-09-15\n\n### Fixed\n* Type inference for route params broke when a path contained a regex segment like `/:id(\\\\d+)` ([#2231](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2231))\n* `brisk dev` no longer leaks a file watcher on every reload \n\n### Security\n* Upgraded `path-to-regexp` to address a ReDoS with two parameters in a single segment (e.g. `/:a-:b`). Upgrading is **strongly** recommended if you accept user-defined routes.\n\n## [4.1.0] - 2026-08-30\n\n### Added\n- `app.onError()` hooks can now be async\n- The CORS middleware accepts a function for `origin`: `cors({ origin: (o) => o.endsWith(\".example.com\") })` ([#2201](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2201))\n- Experimental Bun adapter, `@brisk/adapter-bun` — _please_ report issues!\n\n### Changed\n- `ctx.redirect()` now defaults to `302` instead of `301`. Permanent redirects are cached aggressively by browsers, which surprised a lot of people ([#2188](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2188))\n\n### Fixed\n- `HEAD` requests to routes that only define `GET` now return the correct `Content-Length`\n\n## [4.0.0] - 2026-07-01\n\nThis is a major release. The headline changes are that Brisk is now ESM-only and requires Node.js 22 or later.\n\n### Migration notes\n\nMost applications can upgrade by replacing `require(\"brisk\")` with `import { createApp } from \"brisk\"` and bumping their Node.js version. If you wrote custom middleware against the 3.x `(req, res, next)` signature, wrap it with `fromConnect()` from `@brisk/compat`, which adapts Connect/Express-style middleware to the new `(ctx, next)` model at a small performance cost; we recommend porting hot-path middleware by hand. The `config/` directory convention is gone — pass options to `createApp()` directly or load them with your favourite config library. The [upgrade guide](https://brisk.dev/docs/upgrading/v4) has a full checklist, and `npx @brisk/codemod v4 ./src` automates most of the mechanical changes.\n\n### Added\n- `(ctx, next)` middleware signature with full type inference for `ctx.state`\n- Built-in request validation via [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev), so it works with Zod, Valibot and ArkType\n- `brisk routes` CLI command that prints the route table\n\n### Changed\n- **BREAKING:** ESM-only; the CommonJS build has been removed ([#2050](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2050))\n- **BREAKING:** the minimum supported Node.js version is now 22.\n- **BREAKING:** the `ctx.body` setter is replaced by explicit helpers:\n  - `ctx.json()`, `ctx.text()` and `ctx.html()` for buffered responses\n  - `ctx.stream()` for streaming\n  - `ctx.empty(status)` for `204`/`304`\n\n### Removed\n- The `brisk/legacy` entry point\n- The `app.listen(port, callback)` overload — use `await app.listen({ port })`\n- Support for the `config/` directory convention\n\n## [3.9.2] - 2026-05-19\n\n### Fixed\n- Memory leak when a client aborted a request while a `ctx.stream()` was pending ([#2011](https://github.com/brisk-js/brisk/pull/2011))\n\n### Security\n- Session cookies now default to `SameSite=Lax` (previously the attribute was not set at all)\n- `serveStatic()` rejects paths containing null bytes\n\n\n## [3.9.1] - 2026-04-02\n\n### Fixed\n* Regression in 3.9.0 where trailing slashes were stripped from mounted sub-app paths\n    * `/admin/` returned 404 when the sub-app was mounted at `/admin`\n    * strict mode (`strictSlash: true`) was not affected\n\n## [3.9.0] - 2026-03-21\n\n### Added\n- `ctx.signal`, an `AbortSignal` that fires when the client disconnects\n- Per-route `timeout` option\n\n### Deprecated\n- The `(req, res, next)` middleware signature. We rewrote the result grid from scratch on top of a virtualized canvas renderer, which means scrolling through a million-row result set now feels the same as scrolling through a hundred rows, and memory usage for large results dropped by roughly 70% in our benchmarks. If you've ever watched Quarry freeze for a few seconds after running `SELECT * FROM events` against a production replica (we have, many times), this one's for you.\n\nThe other big change is that notebooks can now have *parameters*. Parameters are always sent to the database as bind variables, never spliced into the SQL text, so there's no injection risk even when the value comes from a free-text field.\n\n- New result grid with virtual scrolling, column pinning and per-column number formats\n- Notebook parameters: text, number, date, date range, and \"choice from query\"\n- `Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+E` exports the current result to CSV, Parquet or XLSX without opening a dialog\n- ClickHouse driver now supports the native `JSON` column type\n- **Breaking:** the `quarry.grid.maxRows` setting has been removed, since the new grid has no hard limit. When the shared definition changes, everyone picks up the update the next time they connect. If something here is unclear or out of date, please open an issue — or, even better, a PR that fixes it.\n\n## Repository layout\n\n```text\nnorthwind-ui/\n├── apps/\n│   ├── docs/            # Docusaurus documentation site\n│   └── playground/      # Vite sandbox for manual testing\n├── packages/\n│   ├── tokens/          # @northwind/tokens: design tokens (Style Dictionary)\n│   ├── icons/           # @northwind/icons: SVG icon set + React components\n│   ├── react/           # @northwind/react: the component library\n│   └── eslint-config/   # @northwind/eslint-config (internal)\n├── tooling/             # scripts, codemods, shared tsconfig\n├── turbo.json\n└── pnpm-workspace.yaml\n```\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n| Tool | Version | Notes |\n|------|---------|-------|\n| Node.js | 22.x (LTS) | `.nvmrc` is checked in; [fnm](https://github.com/Schniz/fnm) or [Volta](https://volta.sh) will pick it up automatically |\n| pnpm | ≥ 9.12 | Enable it with `corepack enable`. Please **don't** install pnpm globally with npm, the versions drift |\n| Git | ≥ 2.40 | |\n| Playwright browsers | whatever `@playwright/test` pins | `pnpm test:e2e:install` |\n| Docker | 24+ (optional) | Only needed to run the visual regression tests locally |\n\n## Getting set up\n\n1. Fork the repository and clone your fork:\n\n   ```sh\n   git clone git@github.com:<your-username>/northwind-ui.git\n   cd northwind-ui\n   ```\n\n2. Install dependencies. This also installs the Git hooks via `lefthook`.\n\n   ```sh\n   corepack enable\n   pnpm install\n   ```\n\n3. Build every package once so that cross-package imports resolve:\n   ```sh\n   pnpm build\n   ```\n\n4. Start the docs site and the playground in watch mode:\n\n   ```sh\n   pnpm dev --filter=docs --filter=playground\n   ```\n\n   The docs are served at http://localhost:3000 and the playground at http://localhost:5173.\n5. Before pushing, run the same checks CI runs:\n\n   ```sh\n   pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck && pnpm test\n   ```\n\n> **Tip:** Turborepo caches task outputs, so a second `pnpm build` without changes should finish in a couple of seconds. If something looks stale, `pnpm clean` deletes every `dist/` folder and the local Turbo cache.\n\n## Branch naming\n\nBranch off `main` and use `<type>/<short-description>`, optionally including the issue number:\n\n- `feat/combobox-async-options`\n- `fix/1423-tooltip-flicker`\n- `docs/theming-guide`\n- `chore/bump-storybook-9`\n\nThe allowed types are the same as for commit messages (see below). Lowercase and hyphens only, and no more than one slash please — a couple of our CI scripts split on it.\n\n## Commit messages\n\nWe use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/). The scope is the package name without the `@northwind/` prefix (or `docs`, `playground`, `repo` for changes outside the packages). Messages are checked by `commitlint` in a Git hook and again in CI.\n\n```text\nfeat(react): add `size` prop to <Avatar>\n\nfix(tokens): correct contrast of color.text.subtle in dark theme\n\nThe previous value (#8b8f98 on #1b1d22) had a contrast ratio of 4.1:1,\nwhich is below the WCAG AA threshold for body text.\n\nCloses #1502\n\nrefactor(icons)!: rename IconClose to IconX\n\nBREAKING CHANGE: IconClose has been removed. Run\n`pnpm dlx @northwind/codemods icons-v3 src/` to update imports.\n```\n\nAllowed types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore` and `revert`.\n\n## Pull request checklist\n\nBefore you request a review, please make sure that:\n\n- [ ] the PR title follows the commit convention — we squash-merge, so the title becomes the commit message\n- [ ] you've added a changeset (`pnpm changeset`) if the change affects a published package\n- [ ] new components have stories in `*.stories.tsx` and pass the Storybook a11y checks\n- [ ] tests cover the change (`pnpm test --filter=<package>`)\n- [ ] public API changes are documented in `apps/docs`\n- [ ] screenshots or a short screen recording are attached for visual changes\n- [x] you've read this document 🙂\n\nSmall PRs get reviewed *much* faster than big ones. If your change touches more than one package, consider splitting it up.\n\n## Style guide\n\n### TypeScript\n\n* Strict mode everywhere. Avoid `any`; prefer `unknown` and narrow it.\n* Export types with `export type { … }` so they're erased under `isolatedModules`.\n* Named exports only. The single exception is Storybook story files, which need a default export.\n\n### React components\n\n- Function components only; forward refs with `React.forwardRef` and set a `displayName`.\n- Props interfaces are called `<Component>Props` and are exported.\n- Style with CSS Modules and tokens from `@northwind/tokens` — never hard-coded colors or spacing. Stylelint _will_ complain if you try `color: #333`.\n- Every interactive component must be fully keyboard accessible and listed in the accessibility matrix in `apps/docs/docs/a11y.mdx`.\n\n### CSS\n\nUse logical properties (`margin-inline-start` rather than `margin-left`) so right-to-left layouts work out of the box. Class names in CSS Modules are `camelCase`.  \n\n### Tests\n\nUnit tests use Vitest and Testing Library. Query by role or label (`getByRole(\"button\", { name: /save/i })`) rather than by test ID wherever possible — test IDs are a last resort, not a default.\n\n\n## Release process\n\nMaintainers cut releases from `main` using [Changesets](https://github.com/changesets/changesets).\n\n1. Prepare\n   1. Make sure `main` is green and every PR intended for the release has been merged.\n   2. The changesets bot keeps a **Version Packages** PR open. Review the generated `CHANGELOG.md` entries and fix typos directly in that PR.\n   3. For a major version, check that the migration guide in `apps/docs/docs/migrations/` is complete and linked from the changelog.\n2. Publish\n   1. Merge the Version Packages PR.\n   2. The `release.yml` workflow builds every package, publishes to npm with provenance, and pushes tags such as `@northwind/react@3.2.0`.\n   3. If publishing fails halfway through, __don't__ re-run the whole workflow. Run `pnpm release:resume` locally instead, with an npm token that has publish rights (ask in #northwind-maintainers).\n3. OpenTrails exists because thousands of hikers, mappers, park rangers and software developers decided that good trail information should be free for everyone, and every contribution, no matter how small, makes the map a little more accurate and a little more useful for the next person heading out the door with a backpack. Whether you walked a trail last weekend and noticed the bridge is out, or you're a seasoned Rust developer looking for an interesting routing problem, there's a place for you here.\n\nThis document is intentionally short. It covers the main ways to get involved and where to ask questions; the technical details (building the app, running the tile server, the data model) live in the [developer docs](https://docs.opentrails.org/dev/) so that they can be kept up to date in one place.\n\n## Ways to contribute\n\nYou don't need to write code to make a big difference. Some of the most valuable contributions we get are:\n\n* **Reporting trail conditions.** Closures, washed-out sections, new reroutes and seasonal restrictions change faster than any official source can keep up with. Use the \"Report a condition\" button in the app, or file an issue using the *Trail condition* template.\n* **Improving the map data.** Our trail geometry comes from OpenStreetMap, so fixing a trail in OSM fixes it in OpenTrails within about a day. The [OSM hiking guide](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Hiking) is a great place to start.\n* **Translating** the app and the website on [Weblate](https://hosted.weblate.org/projects/opentrails/). We currently ship in 27 languages, and about a dozen more are partially done.\n* **Writing and editing documentation**, especially guides for first-time mappers.\n* Triaging issues: reproducing bugs, adding missing details and labelling duplicates.\n* **Code**, of course — the mobile apps (Kotlin and Swift), the routing engine (Rust), the web frontend (TypeScript and Svelte) and the data pipeline (Python).\n- Spreading the word: giving talks, writing blog posts, or organising a mapping party in your area.\n\n## Your first data fix in five minutes\n\nIf you've never edited OpenStreetMap before, here's the quickest way to fix a trail you know:\n\n1. Find the trail on the OpenTrails web map and click **Edit on OSM** in the sidebar. This opens the iD editor centred on the right spot.\n2. Log in, or create a free OSM account.\n3. Select the trail and correct whatever is wrong: the name, the `sac_scale` difficulty, or the geometry itself.\n4. Write a short changeset comment, such as \"Fix trail name per signage at trailhead\", and save.\n5. That's it! Your change will show up in OpenTrails after the next nightly import.\n\nPlease only map what you've seen on the ground or can verify from a source with a compatible license. Copying from Google Maps, AllTrails or official park maps is _not_ allowed unless they explicitly permit it — we've had to revert whole regions because of this, which is heartbreaking for everyone involved. \n\n## Good first issues\n\nIf you'd like to contribute code but don't know where to start, look for issues labelled [`good first issue`](https://github.com/opentrails/opentrails/labels/good%20first%20issue). These are deliberately small, well-scoped tasks, typically a few hours of work for someone new to the codebase, and each one has a short description of where the relevant code lives and what a good solution might look like. A maintainer has committed to reviewing PRs for these issues within a few days, so you won't be left waiting.\n\nBefore starting, leave a comment on the issue saying you'd like to work on it, so that we can assign it to you and avoid two people doing the same thing. If you get stuck, that's completely normal: push what you have as a draft pull request and ask for help. We would much rather see an unfinished PR with a question than have you struggle silently for a week.\n\nThere's also a [`help wanted`](https://github.com/opentrails/opentrails/labels/help%20wanted) label for bigger tasks where we'd especially welcome outside help, and a [`local knowledge`](https://github.com/opentrails/opentrails/labels/local%20knowledge) label for issues that need someone who knows an area rather than someone who knows how to program.\n\n## Making a pull request\n\nKeep pull requests focused on one change, explain *why* in the description (the diff already shows *what*), and link the issue it addresses. Every PR is reviewed by at least one maintainer and needs passing CI before it's merged. We squash-merge, so don't worry about tidying up your commit history.\n\n\n## Code of Conduct\n\nEveryone participating in OpenTrails — on GitHub, in the forum, on Matrix, or at in-person events — is expected to follow our [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), which is adapted from the Contributor Covenant, version 2.1. In short: be kind, be patient with newcomers, assume good intent, and remember that most people here contribute in their spare time. Harassment of any kind is not tolerated.\n\nIf you experience or witness unacceptable behaviour, please report it to **conduct@opentrails.org**. Reports are handled confidentially by the community health team, which is separate from the core maintainers.\n\n## Recognition\n\nWe use the [All Contributors](https://allcontributors.org) specification to recognise every kind of contribution, not just code. Once your first contribution has been merged, a maintainer will add you to the contributors list in the README; you can also ask the bot directly by commenting on any issue or pull request.\n\n## Licensing\n\nBy contributing code, you agree that it will be licensed under the project's [AGPL-3.0](LICENSE) license. Documentation is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0, and map data you add to OpenStreetMap is licensed under the ODbL by OSM itself.\n\n## Getting in touch\n\n- 💬 Chat: [#opentrails:matrix.org](https://matrix.to/#/#opentrails:matrix.org) (bridged to our Discord server)\n- 🗣️ Forum: <https://community.opentrails.org>\n- 🐘 Mastodon: [@opentrails@en.osm.town](https://en.osm.town/@opentrails)\n- 📧 Email: hello@opentrails.org, for anything that doesn't fit elsewhere, including press and partnership enquiries\n- 🔒 Security issues: please see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) instead of opening a public issue\n\nMaintainers are spread across time zones from Wellington to Vancouver, so please allow a day or two for a response.\n\nHappy trails! 🥾\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":135168,"cache_read_input_tokens":0,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":135168,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_01XE5rjet6uYehWEKYqXj7JS","agent_id":"a909b0d1a1c0df50d","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"24548ff7-778d-4ce3-b443-20305d0f2ef5","timestamp":"2026-11-17T22:28:55.350Z","request_id":"req_011Ch9Hin7VQQNasBf4WUqFZ","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Generate docs-heavy corpus 15"}

About two thirds of that growth came from the 600 pedal-assist e-bikes added in June, which now account for 38% of trips despite making up only 22% of the fleet.[^fleet]\n\nKey findings:\n\n- Ridership remains strongly weather-dependent: a day with 5 mm of rain sees roughly a third fewer trips than a comparable dry day.\n- E-bike trips are longer (median 14 min vs. 10 min) and more likely to start in the hillier eastern neighbourhoods.\n* Casual riders made 21% of trips but generated 46% of fare revenue.\n- The University and Riverside stations ran out of e-bikes before 08:15 on most weekday mornings.\n\n[^fleet]: Fleet composition as of 30 September 2026: 2,140 classic bikes and 600 e-bikes. Bikes out of service for more than seven consecutive days are excluded from the denominator.\n\n```{python}\n#| label: setup\nimport numpy as np\nimport pandas as pd\nimport matplotlib.pyplot as plt\nimport statsmodels.api as sm\nimport statsmodels.formula.api as smf\n\nplt.style.use(\"seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid\")\n\ntrips = pd.read_parquet(\"data/trips_2026q3.parquet\")\nweather = pd.read_csv(\"data/weather_daily_kwbk.csv\", parse_dates=[\"date\"])\n\ndaily = (\n    trips.assign(date=trips[\"started_at\"].dt.normalize())\n    .groupby(\"date\")\n    .agg(trips=(\"trip_id\", \"size\"), ebike_share=(\"is_ebike\", \"mean\"))\n    .reset_index()\n    .merge(weather, on=\"date\", how=\"left\")\n)\n```\n\n## Daily ridership\n\n```{python}\n#| label: fig-daily\n#| fig-cap: \"Daily trips, July–September 2026. Overdispersion was modest (Pearson $\\chi^2/\\text{df} = 1.8$), so the standard errors in @tbl-coefs come from a quasi-Poisson fit.\n\n```{python}\n#| label: model\nmodel = smf.glm(\n    \"trips ~ tmax + I(tmax**2) + np.log1p(precip_mm) + C(dow) + holiday\",\n    data=daily.assign(dow=daily[\"date\"].dt.dayofweek),\n    family=sm.families.Poisson(),\n).fit(scale=\"X2\")\n```\n\n| Term | Estimate | Std. error | Rate ratio |\n|------|---------:|-----------:|-----------:|\n| $T_t$ (°C) | 0.061 | 0.011 | 1.063 |\n| $T_t^2$ | −0.0012 | 0.0003 | 0.999 |\n| $\\log(1 + P_t)$ | −0.214 | 0.019 | 0.807 |\n| Holiday | −0.152 | 0.047 | 0.859 |\n\n: Selected coefficients from @eq-poisson; day-of-week effects omitted for brevity. {#tbl-coefs}\n\nThe temperature effect is concave, with expected ridership peaking at around 25 °C, consistent with earlier studies of North American systems [@gebhart2014impact; @noland2016bikeshare]. Holding everything else fixed, a day with 10 mm of rain has an expected count about $1 - 0.807^{\\ln 11} \\approx 40\\%$ lower than a dry day.[^rain]\n\n[^rain]: Because precipitation enters the model as $\\log(1 + P_t)$, each additional millimetre matters less than the one before. Riders who are already out in 10 mm of rain, apparently, don't much mind 15.\n\n## Recommendations\n\n1. Don't dwell on it — the people involved are in the room.\n:::\n\n## What `{targets}` gives you\n\n:::: {.columns}\n\n::: {.column width=\"50%\"}\n**A declarative pipeline**\n\n- each step is a *target*: a name plus a command\n- dependencies are found by static code analysis\n- only outdated targets re-run\n:::\n\n::: {.column width=\"50%\"}\n__More or less for free__\n\n* parallel workers via `{crew}`\n* targets stored in the cloud (S3, GCS)\n* a dependency graph: `tar_visnetwork()`\n:::\n\n::::\n\n## A minimal `_targets.R`\n\n```{.r code-line-numbers=\"2-3\"}\nlibrary(targets)\ntar_option_set(packages = c(\"dplyr\", \"readr\", \"fable\"))\ntar_source(\"R/\")\n\nlist(\n  tar_target(raw_file, \"data/sales.csv\", format = \"file\"),\n  tar_target(sales, read_sales(raw_file)),\n  tar_target(model, fit_models(sales)),\n  tar_target(forecast, make_forecast(model, h = \"8 weeks\"))\n)\n```\n\n::: {.notes}\nLines 2–3 first: packages, and sourcing our own functions from `R/`.\nThen the pipeline itself is just a list. Emphasise `format = \"file\"` — that's what makes the CSV a tracked dependency, so editing the file triggers a rebuild of everything downstream.\n:::\n\n## Running it\n\n```{.r code-line-numbers=\"1|3\"}\ntar_make()\n#> ▶ dispatched target sales\ntar_visnetwork(targets_only = TRUE)\n```\n\n![](images/visnetwork.png){.r-stretch fig-alt=\"Dependency graph rendered by tar_visnetwork, with outdated targets highlighted in blue\"}\n\n## Making it fast\n\n:::: {.columns}\n\n::: {.column width=\"40%\"}\n::: {.incremental}\n- branch over stores with `pattern = map()`\n- 8 local workers with `{crew}`\n- cache on a shared S3 bucket\n:::\n:::\n\n::: {.column width=\"60%\"}\n```{.r code-line-numbers=\"2|5-6\"}\ntar_option_set(\n  controller = crew::crew_controller_local(workers = 8)\n)\ntar_target(\n  model, fit_models(sales_by_store),\n  pattern = map(sales_by_store)\n)\n```\n:::\n\n::::\n\n::: {.notes}\nDynamic branching: one model per store, 212 stores. With 8 workers the model step goes from ~2 h to ~20 min.\n:::\n\n## Results\n\n| | Before | After |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| Full run | 3 h 10 min | 46 min |\n| Typical Monday run | 3 h 10 min | **4 min** |\n| Stale outputs in report | ¯\\\\\\_(ツ)\\_/¯ | 0 |\n\n::: {.notes}\n\"Typical Monday run\" = only the newest week of data changes, so most targets are skipped.\nThe shrug is deliberate. Wait for the laugh.\n:::\n\n\n## Lessons learned {.smaller}\n\n1. Write *functions* first. The pipeline is just glue.\n2. Hamblin et al. [-@hamblin2018physiological] found that large-bodied bees declined in abundance along an urban warming gradient in Raleigh, NC, whereas small-bodied taxa were largely unaffected; by contrast, a survey of 12 gardens in Berlin found no detectable effect of local temperature on visitation once floral abundance was accounted for [@vonkonigslow2022; but see @theodorou2020urban]. Most of this work has relied on temperature data from airport weather stations approx. 10--20 km from the study sites, which cannot capture the fine-scale variation that matters to a foraging bee [@hamblin2018physiological; @burdine2019, p. 4].\n\nHere we ask three questions:\n\n* Does garden-level UHI intensity predict pollinator visitation rates?\n* Is the relationship different for bees vs. hoverflies?\n* Does the effect depend on the time of day, e.g. is it stronger during the afternoon heat?\n\n# Methods\n\n## Study sites\n\nWe surveyed `r n_gardens` community gardens across Greater Manchester, UK, between 1 June and 31 August 2025.\nGardens were chosen to span a gradient of impervious surface cover (12.5--81.0 % within a 500 m buffer) while keeping garden size roughly constant (median 0.21 ha, range 0.08--0.46 ha).\nMean UHI intensity across gardens was `r round(mean_uhi, 2)` °C; see Fig. 1 for the full distribution.\n\n## Temperature measurements\n\nEach garden was fitted with two iButton DS1923 loggers in radiation shields at 1.5 m height, recording every 30 min. Loggers were calibrated against a reference thermometer before and after the field season, and drift was < 0.2 °C in all cases. UHI intensity was defined as the mean difference between garden temperature and a rural reference site at Abbots Moss^[Open heathland approx. 40 km SW of Manchester city centre, at a similar elevation to the study gardens.] between 10:00 and 16:00, i.e. the hours during which surveys took place.\n\n## Pollinator surveys\n\nVisitation was recorded in 10-min timed observations of a standardised 1 m² patch of *Borago officinalis* planted in each garden in April.\nObservers recorded every insect that contacted the anthers or stigma and identified it to the lowest practical taxonomic level (usually genus for bees, family for flies).\nEach garden was surveyed on 9 dates, three times per date (morning, midday, afternoon), giving `r n_obs` observation periods in total.\n\n## Statistical analysis\n\nWe modelled visit counts with a Poisson generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a log link [@bates2015lme4]. In brief:\n\n- response: number of visits per 10-min observation\n- fixed effects: UHI intensity (°C), pollinator group, survey period, and the group × UHI and period × UHI interactions\n+ offset: log number of open flowers in the patch\n- random intercepts: garden and survey date\n\nAll analyses were done in R version `r getRversion()` [@rcore2025].\n\n```{r model, echo=TRUE}\nm1 <- glmer(\n  visits ~ uhi_intensity * group + uhi_intensity * period + offset(log(n_flowers)) +\n    (1 | garden_id) + (1 | survey_date),\n  data = visits, family = poisson,\n  control = glmerControl(optimizer = \"bobyqa\")\n)\ncoefs <- tidy(m1, effects = \"fixed\", conf.int = TRUE)\nb_uhi <- coefs |> filter(term == \"uhi_intensity\") |> pull(estimate)\n```\n\n# Results\n\nWe recorded 4,318 flower visits, of which 61.4 % were by bees (mainly *Bombus* spp. and *Apis mellifera*) and 29.8 % by hoverflies (Syrphidae).\nThe remaining 8.8 % were by other flies, butterflies and the occasional wasp.\n\nVisitation increased with UHI intensity overall (β = `r round(b_uhi, 2)` per °C), but the effect differed strongly between groups (Fig. 2). For bees, each additional degree of UHI intensity was associated with approx. 14 % more visits per flower (rate ratio 1.14, 95 % CI 1.05--1.24), whereas for hoverflies the estimate was close to zero and slightly negative (RR 0.97, 95 % CI 0.86--1.09). The interaction with survey period was weak. If anything, the positive effect for bees was _smaller_ in the afternoon than in the morning, contrary to our expectation!\n\n```{r fig-visits, fig.cap=\"Fig. 2: Predicted visits per 100 flowers per 10 min vs. UHI intensity, by pollinator group (midday surveys). Ribbons show 95 % confidence intervals.\"}\nnewdat <- expand_grid(\n  uhi_intensity = seq(min(gardens$uhi_intensity), max(gardens$uhi_intensity), length.out = 50),\n  group = c(\"bee\", \"hoverfly\"), period = \"midday\", n_flowers = 100\n)\nnewdat$pred <- predict(m1, newdata = newdat, re.form = NA, type = \"response\")\nggplot(newdat, aes(uhi_intensity, pred, colour = group)) +\n  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +\n  labs(x = \"UHI intensity (°C)\", y = \"Visits per 100 flowers per 10 min\", colour = NULL) +\n  theme_minimal()\n```\n\n# Discussion\n\nOur results suggest that moderate urban warming may benefit bees in a temperate maritime climate, where cool and cloudy days frequently limit foraging.\nThis is consistent with the thermal-limitation hypothesis [@kuhsel2015high] and with observations of earlier activity onset in warmer microsites [@fisogni2020; @kammerer2021, pp. 3--5].\nHoverflies, in contrast, did not respond to warming, possibly because many syrphids tolerate low temperatures better than bees do.[^1]\n\nThere are several caveats. First, our temperature gradient (`r round(min(gardens$uhi_intensity), 1)`--`r round(max(gardens$uhi_intensity), 1)` °C) is modest compared with cities in continental or Mediterranean climates, and the relationship may well reverse above some threshold, e.g. once afternoon temperatures regularly exceed 30 °C. Second, we measured visitation, not pollination effectiveness or bee fitness. Third, 2025 was an unusually warm summer in the UK, which may have compressed the range of conditions we sampled.\n\nFuture work should combine fine-scale temperature monitoring with measurements of pollen deposition and pollinator body condition, ideally across several years and cities.\n\n\n[^1]: Several common UK hoverflies, e.g. *Episyrphus balteatus*, are active at air temperatures as low as 10 °C, whereas most bumblebees must warm their flight muscles to approx. 30 °C before take-off.\n\n# Acknowledgements {.unnumbered}\n\nWe thank the 23 garden groups who hosted loggers and borage patches, and the volunteers who spent approx. 300 hours watching flowers.\nFunded by NERC grant NE/X012345/1.\n\n# References {.unnumbered}\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":10325,"cache_read_input_tokens":135168,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":10325,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_01XE5rjet6uYehWEKYqXj7JS","agent_id":"a909b0d1a1c0df50d","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"d74c1532-4973-4240-8b84-e30810c0c56b","timestamp":"2026-11-17T22:29:50.169Z","request_id":"req_011Ch9HofZjLKuPKJc8QoM7S","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Generate docs-heavy corpus 15"}

It assumes you already have a Meridian workspace and at least one project; if not, start with the [installation guide](../getting-started/install.md) and come back here afterwards.\n\n> **Note**\n> Screenshots in this guide were taken with Meridian 2.8. Some labels may differ slightly in older versions, but the concepts are the same.\n\n## Concepts\n\nBefore diving in, it's worth getting the vocabulary straight. Meridian uses a few terms that mean slightly different things in other feature-flag tools.\n\n| Term | Meaning |\n|------|---------|\n| **Project** | A collection of flags that belong to one product or service. Each project has its own SDK keys. |\n| **Environment** | A deployment stage such as `development`, `staging` or `production`. Flags exist in every environment of a project, but their rules and on/off state are configured per environment. |\n| **Flag** | A named switch with two or more *variations*. Boolean flags have exactly two (`true` / `false`); multivariate flags can return strings, numbers or JSON. |\n| **Context** | The thing being evaluated — usually a user, but it can also be a device, an organization or a single request. |\n| **Segment** | A reusable list of contexts or a reusable set of rules, e.g. \"beta testers\" or \"EU customers\". |\n\n### How evaluation works\n\nWhen your application asks the SDK for the value of a flag, the SDK evaluates the flag's rules locally against the context you pass in. Rules are checked in order from top to bottom, and the first rule that matches determines the variation. If no rule matches, the *default rule* applies. If the flag is turned off in that environment, the *off variation* is returned regardless of the rules.\n\nBecause evaluation happens inside the SDK, it adds no network latency to your requests. The SDK keeps its copy of the flag configuration up to date over a streaming connection to the Meridian relay; see [Architecture](../reference/architecture.md#streaming) for the details, including what happens when the connection drops.\n\n## Creating a flag\n\n1. Open your project and select **Flags → New flag**.\n2. Enter a **name** (shown in the UI) and a **key** (used in code). Keys must be unique within a project and can contain letters, numbers, `.`, `-` and `_`.\n   - Keys can't be changed after creation, so pick something descriptive: `checkout.new-payment-form` is better than `test-flag-2`.\n   - We recommend an `<area>.<feature>` naming scheme; see [Naming conventions](#naming-conventions).\n3. Choose the flag type:\n   - *Boolean* — for simple on/off switches.\n   - *Multivariate* — for A/B/n experiments or configuration values.\n     - String, number and JSON variations are supported.\n     - JSON variations are limited to 32 KB each.\n4. Optionally add tags (e.g. `team:payments`, `temporary`) and a link to the ticket or design doc.\n5. Click **Create**. The new flag starts out *off* in every environment.\n\nYou can also create flags from the command line:\n\n```bash\nmeridian flags create checkout.new-payment-form \\\n  --project web-store \\\n  --type boolean \\\n  --tag team:payments --tag temporary \\\n  --description \"New Stripe Elements payment form (PAY-1182)\"\n```\n\n> **Warning**\n> Flags created with `--temporary=false` are excluded from the stale-flag report. Only use it for long-lived operational flags such as kill switches.\n\n## Targeting\n\n### Individual targeting\n\nThe simplest form of targeting is to list context keys explicitly. Open the flag, select the environment, and add keys under **Individual targets**. This is handy for QA accounts and for letting a specific customer try a feature early, but it doesn't scale beyond a few hundred keys — use a [segment](./segments.md) for that.\n\n### Rules\n\nRules let you match contexts by their attributes. Each rule has one or more *clauses*, which are combined with AND, and a variation (or percentage rollout) to serve when it matches. For example:\n\n* `country` **is one of** `DE`, `AT`, `CH` → serve `true`\n* `plan` **is** `enterprise` AND `seats` **greater than** `50` → serve `true`\n+ `email` **ends with** `@example.com` → serve `true`\n\nAttribute values are compared as strings unless the operator is numeric (`greater than`, `less than`) or semver-aware (`semver greater than` and friends). Missing attributes never match, except with the `is not one of` operator, which _does_ match when the attribute is missing — a subtle point that catches a lot of people out.\n\n### Percentage rollouts\n\nInstead of a single variation, a rule (or the default rule) can serve a percentage split, e.g. 10 % `true` / 90 % `false`. Meridian hashes the context key together with the flag key and a salt to assign each context to a bucket, so:\n\n- the same user always gets the same variation for a given flag, across sessions and devices, as long as the context key is stable;\n- increasing the percentage from 10 % to 20 % keeps the original 10 % in the `true` group;\n- different flags bucket independently, so being in the 10 % for one flag says nothing about another.\n\nTo bucket by something other than the context key — say, the organization, so that everyone in a company sees the same thing — set **Bucket by** to the attribute you want.\n\n> **Tip**\n> Try rollouts out in a staging environment that mirrors production targeting first. Once you're happy, `meridian flags copy-rules --from staging --to production` copies the rules across.\n\n## Gradual rollouts and guarded releases\n\nFor risky changes, use a **guarded rollout** instead of editing percentages by hand. Meridian increases the percentage on a schedule you define (for example 1 % → 5 % → 25 % → 50 % → 100 % over two days) and watches the metrics you attach. If error rate or latency regress beyond the thresholds you set, it rolls back automatically and notifies the flag's maintainers in Slack or via webhook.\n\n| Stage | Default duration | Default threshold |\n|------:|-----------------|-------------------|\n| 1 % | 1 hour | error rate +0.5 pp |\n| 5 % | 2 hours | error rate +0.5 pp, p95 latency +10 % |\n| 25 % | 6 hours | same as above |\n| 50 % | 12 hours | same as above |\n| 100 % | — | — |\n\nMetrics come from your existing observability stack. Meridian currently integrates with Datadog, Prometheus (via the remote-read API) and OpenTelemetry; see [Connecting metrics](./metrics.md) for setup instructions.  \n\n## Environments and approvals\n\nEach project starts with three environments — `development`, `staging` and `production` — but you can add as many as you like under **Project settings → Environments**. Environments can be marked as *critical*, which changes a few behaviours:\n\n- Changes require a confirmation dialog in the UI, and the CLI refuses to modify a critical environment without `--yes`.\n- If **approvals** are enabled, changes to a critical environment must be approved by someone other than the author:\n  - approvers are configured per environment, either as individual members or as a team\n  - an approval request expires after 72 hours\n  - workspace admins can bypass approvals in an emergency; bypasses are flagged in the audit log and every approver gets a notification\n- Flags can be *locked* in critical environments, so that only members with the `flag:admin` role can change them at all.\n\n| Role | View flags | Edit dev / staging | Edit critical envs | Approve changes | Manage members |\n|------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|\n| Viewer | ✓ | | | | |\n| Developer | ✓ | ✓ | with approval | | |\n| Maintainer | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | |\n| Admin | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |\n\nEvery change, approved or not, is recorded in the **audit log** together with its author, a timestamp, a diff of the flag configuration and an optional comment. You can stream the audit log to your SIEM via webhook, or export it as JSON Lines with `meridian audit export --since 30d`.\n\n## Flag lifecycle and cleanup\n\nEvery flag you add is a little bit of technical debt. Meridian helps you pay it back:\n\n1. When a flag has served the same variation to 100 % of contexts in production for 14 days, it's marked **Ready to archive**.\n2. The weekly stale-flag report (**Settings → Notifications**) lists these flags per team, based on the `team:` tag.\n3. `meridian flags code-refs` scans your repository and shows where each flag is still referenced. It understands the official SDKs' call patterns out of the box; add custom patterns in `.meridian/coderefs.yaml`.\n4. Once the code references are gone, archive the flag. Archived flags return their off variation and can be restored for 30 days.\n\n\n## Naming conventions\n\nThere's no single right answer, but consistent names make flags much easier to find and clean up. The convention we use internally, and recommend, is:\n\n```\n<area>.<feature>[.<variant>]\n```\n\n* `area` — the product area or service, e.g. `checkout`, `search`, `billing`\n* `feature` — a short kebab-case description\n* `variant` — optional, for related flags, e.g. `search.semantic-ranking.v2`\n\nAvoid putting team names in keys (teams get reorganized; flags outlive them) and avoid negative names like `disable-new-header`, which lead to double negatives in code.\n\n## Troubleshooting\n\n**The SDK always returns the default value.**\nCheck that you're using the SDK key for the right environment, that the flag key is spelled correctly (keys are case-sensitive), and that the SDK has finished initializing before the first evaluation. Most SDKs expose a `waitForInitialization()` method or a `ready` event; see the [API reference](./api.md#createclient).\n\n**A user sees a different variation than I expected.**\nUse the **Debugger** tab on the flag page: paste in the context JSON and Meridian shows which rule matched and why. Remember that rules are evaluated top to bottom and the first match wins.\n\n> **Note**\n> Still stuck? Ask in the [community forum](https://community.meridian.dev) or contact support@meridian.dev with your project key and the flag key.
