Everything is exported from the package root:\n\n```ts\nimport { createClient, MeridianError } from \"@meridian/js-sdk\";\n```\n\n## createClient()\n\n```ts\nfunction createClient(sdkKey: string, options?: ClientOptions): MeridianClient\n```\n\nCreates a client and starts connecting to Meridian in the background. Create **one client per process** and reuse it: each client holds a streaming connection and an in-memory copy of every flag in the environment.\n\n### Parameters\n\n| Name | Type | Required | Description |\n|------|------|:--------:|-------------|\n| `sdkKey` | `string` | yes | Server-side SDK key or client-side ID for the environment. When `false`, the SDK polls every `pollInterval` ms instead. |\n| `pollInterval` | `number` | `30000` | Polling interval in milliseconds. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_011Ch9HuLxhniEih4N66AkKH","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01VDJ1BxnWUZzFS8gaZnCRyA","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/tmp/corpus15/r/adr.md","content":"# ADR-0017: Publish domain events through a transactional outbox\n\n* **Status:** Accepted\n* **Date:** 2026-09-08\n* **Deciders:** Maya Chen (Orders), Jonas Petersen (Platform), Aiko Tanaka (SRE), Daniel Okoye (Payments)\n* **Supersedes:** [ADR-0009](0009-publish-events-after-commit.md)\n* **Technical story:** [ORD-2211](https://jira.example.com/browse/ORD-2211)\n\n## Context\n\nThe order service writes to its PostgreSQL database and then publishes domain events (`OrderPlaced`, `OrderPaid`, `OrderShipped`, …) to Kafka, so that downstream services — payments, fulfilment, notifications and the analytics pipeline — can react. Since [ADR-0009](0009-publish-events-after-commit.md) we have done this with a \"publish after commit\" approach: the request handler commits the database transaction and then calls the Kafka producer in the same code path.\n\nThis works most of the time, which is exactly the problem. Over the last two quarters we have had four incidents (INC-0412, INC-0438, INC-0471 and INC-0502) in which an order was committed but its event was never published, because the pod was killed during a deploy, the Kafka producer timed out, or the process ran out of memory between the commit and the publish. Each time the order got stuck in \"placed\" from the customer's point of view, support had to intervene manually, and reconciling state across services took hours. The opposite failure, publishing an event for a transaction that is later rolled back, is rarer but has happened once, when a well-meaning refactoring moved the publish call before the commit \"to make it faster\".\n\nWe need a way to publish events that is atomic with the database write, without making the request path depend on Kafka being available. \n\n### Options considered\n\n1. **Keep publish-after-commit and add a reconciliation job** that periodically compares orders with published events and republishes missing ones.\n2. **Distributed transactions** (XA / two-phase commit) spanning PostgreSQL and Kafka.\n3. **Transactional outbox:** write events to an `outbox` table in the same transaction as the business data, and have a separate relay publish them to Kafka.\n4. **Event sourcing**, making the event log the source of truth for orders.\n\nOption 2 isn't really on the table: Kafka doesn't participate in XA transactions, and we wouldn't want the operational complexity even if it did. Option 4 is a much bigger change than the problem warrants and would affect every team that reads from the orders database. That leaves options 1 and 3.\n\n#### Option 1: reconciliation job\n\n* Good, because it needs no new infrastructure\n* Good, because it's a small change to existing code\n* Bad, because events can still be delayed by up to the reconciliation interval (we'd run it every 5 minutes)\n* Bad, because it does nothing about events published for rolled-back transactions\n- Bad, because \"compare everything with everything\" gets slower as the tables grow\n\n#### Option 3: transactional outbox\n\n* Good, because atomicity comes from the database transaction we already have\n* Good, because the request path no longer talks to Kafka at all\n* Bad, because it adds a relay (Debezium) that has to be operated and monitored\n* Bad, because delivery becomes *at-least-once*, so every consumer must deduplicate\n\n## Decision\n\nWe will use the **transactional outbox pattern** (option 3) for all domain events emitted by the order service, with [Debezium](https://debezium.io/) reading the outbox table via PostgreSQL logical replication and publishing to Kafka through its outbox event router.\n\nConcretely:\n\n- Application code inserts a row into `outbox` in the same transaction as the business change. A small library, `orders-outbox`, provides `Outbox.record(event)` so that nobody writes the SQL by hand.\n- The outbox table has the columns `id` (UUIDv7), `aggregate_type`, `aggregate_id`, `event_type`, `payload` (JSONB), `headers` (JSONB) and `created_at`.\n- Debezium routes each row to the topic `orders.<aggregate_type>.events`, using `aggregate_id` as the message key so that per-order ordering is preserved.\n- A nightly job deletes rows older than 7 days. Debezium only needs the WAL, not the rows themselves, but keeping them for a week makes debugging much easier.\n- Consumers __must be idempotent__. The outbox gives us at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once; every event carries its outbox `id` in the `event-id` header for deduplication.\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n    autonumber\n    participant API as Order API\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\n    participant DBZ as Debezium (Kafka Connect)\n    participant K as Kafka\n    participant P as Payments service\n\n    API->>DB: BEGIN\n    API->>DB: INSERT INTO orders (...)\n    API->>DB: INSERT INTO outbox (OrderPlaced)\n    API->>DB: COMMIT\n    DB-->>DBZ: WAL change via logical replication\n    DBZ->>K: produce to orders.order.events (key = order_id)\n    K-->>P: OrderPlaced\n    P->>P: dedupe on event-id, then process\n```\n\n## Consequences\n\n### Positive\n\n* An event is published **if and only if** the transaction that produced it commits, which eliminates the whole class of incidents described above.\n* The request path no longer talks to Kafka, so p99 latency for `POST /orders` should drop; we measured roughly 35 ms of producer overhead at p99 in August.\n* A Kafka outage no longer causes API errors. Events simply queue up in the WAL until Debezium catches up.\n- The pattern is well understood and well documented, and Debezium's outbox router is widely used in production.\n\n### Negative\n\n* We take on Debezium and Kafka Connect as infrastructure for the Platform team to run. We already operate Kafka Connect for the analytics sinks, so this is an extra connector rather than a new cluster, but it still adds on-call surface.\n* End-to-end latency from commit to event increases slightly, typically by 50–200 ms depending on replication lag.\n* Logical replication slots retain WAL until it has been consumed. If Debezium is down for a long time, disk usage on the primary grows without bound, so **we must alert on replication slot lag** (more than 5 GB or more than 15 minutes).\n* Consumers that aren't idempotent yet must be fixed before the migration; an audit found two (notifications and the loyalty-points service).\n- Event schemas now live in the `payload` JSON rather than in shared code, so we'll need contract tests to keep producers and consumers in sync (see ADR-0018, currently in draft).\n\n### Neutral / follow-ups\n\n- The reconciliation job from option 1 will still be built, but as a monitoring tool that _alerts_ on discrepancies rather than republishing automatically.\n- Other services that publish events (payments, inventory) are encouraged to adopt the same library, but this ADR doesn't require it.\n\n\n## Rollout\n\nThe migration will happen behind a feature flag per event type, starting with `OrderShipped` (lowest volume, easiest to reconcile) and ending with `OrderPlaced`. During the transition both paths may run in parallel, with deduplication on the consumer side. Target completion is the end of Q4 2026; progress is tracked in [ORD-2211](https://jira.example.com/browse/ORD-2211).\n\n## References\n\n- Chris Richardson, [\"Pattern: Transactional outbox\"](https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html)\n- Debezium documentation, [\"Outbox Event Router\"](https://debezium.io/documentation/reference/stable/transformations/outbox-event-router.html)\n- Internal post-incident reviews: INC-0412, INC-0438, INC-0471, INC-0502\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":12053,"cache_read_input_tokens":145493,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":12053,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_01XE5rjet6uYehWEKYqXj7JS","agent_id":"a909b0d1a1c0df50d","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"42523b54-d882-4f27-9af6-a13e1937c21a","timestamp":"2026-11-17T22:31:21.659Z","request_id":"req_011Ch9HuLknvyYYSdBcptveB","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Generate docs-heavy corpus 15"}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_011Ch9HuLxhniEih4N66AkKH","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01CofTYu6Yx1sYb4MMkx9KnJ","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/tmp/corpus15/r/blog_post.md","content":"---\ntitle: \"The Week Our Cron Jobs Ran Twice\"\ndate: 2026-03-15T09:30:00-07:00\nlastmod: 2026-03-17T18:05:00-07:00\ndraft: false\nauthor: \"Sam Whitfield\"\nslug: \"cron-jobs-ran-twice\"\ntags:\n  - postmortem\n  - kubernetes\n  - scheduling\n  - \"time zones\"\n  - go\ncategories: [Engineering, Incidents]\ndescription: \"A daylight saving time transition, a Kubernetes CronJob with a time zone, and a billing job that charged 1,214 customers twice in one night. What happened, why none of our tests caught it, and the three changes we made so that it can't happen again.\"\nimages:\n  - /images/2026/cron-twice/cover.jpg\ntoc: true\n---\n\nAt 3:52 in the morning on Sunday, March 8th, our on-call engineer's phone lit up with an alert that had never fired in the four years we'd been running the billing system: `BillingRunDuplicate`. By the time Priya had found her laptop and her glasses, in that order, 1,214 customers had been charged twice for their monthly subscription, and the support inbox was starting to fill with messages ranging from *politely puzzled* to **extremely not polite**.\n\nThis is the story of how that happened. It's a story about daylight saving time, which means it's also a story about assumptions — in particular the assumption that any given wall-clock time happens at most once a day. It doesn't, of course; everyone knows about the autumn \"fall back\" hour that happens twice. What surprised us is that it was the _spring_ transition, the one where an hour disappears, that bit us.\n\n<!--more-->\n\n## Some background\n\nOur billing run is a Kubernetes `CronJob`. Once a day it finds every subscription whose renewal date is today and charges it. For most of its life it was scheduled in UTC, which was simple, boring, and correct. Last autumn we moved it to 2:30 a.m. *local* time in each region, so that failed charges would be retried during business hours in the customer's own time zone. CronJobs have supported a `timeZone` field since Kubernetes 1.27, so the change was essentially a one-liner:\n\n```yaml\napiVersion: batch/v1\nkind: CronJob\nmetadata:\n  name: billing-run-us-west\nspec:\n  schedule: \"30 2 * * *\"\n  timeZone: \"America/Los_Angeles\"   # <- this line\n  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid\n  startingDeadlineSeconds: 3600\n  jobTemplate:\n    spec:\n      backoffLimit: 0\n      template:\n        spec:\n          restartPolicy: Never\n          containers:\n            - name: billing\n              image: registry.internal/billing:2026.02.3\n              args: [\"run\", \"--region=us-west\"]\n```\n\nIf you know anything about DST in the United States, alarm bells may already be ringing. On the second Sunday in March, clocks in Los Angeles jump from 1:59:59 straight to 3:00:00, so 2:30 a.m. simply doesn't exist that day. We *knew* that. We'd even discussed it in the design review, and concluded that a skipped run would be harmless: the job charges everything due on or before today, so Monday's run would pick up Sunday's renewals. A one-day delay in charging is a non-event.\n\nWhat we didn't consider was that the run might not be skipped at all. Or rather, that it might be \"not skipped\" *twice*.\n\n## What actually happened\n\nThe first run started at 1:30 a.m. PST. The second started at 3:30 a.m. PDT — sixty real minutes later — and as far as the scheduler was concerned, both of them were the 2:30 a.m. run for March 8th. Somewhere between the cron parser, the controller's bookkeeping and Go's `time` package, \"2:30 a.m. on a day that has no 2:30 a.m.\" had been resolved one way when computing the next schedule and the other way when checking whether that schedule had already run.[^go-time] `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` didn't help, because the first job had finished long before the second one started.\n\n![Grafana panel showing two billing job runs an hour apart](/images/2026/cron-twice/grafana-two-runs.png \"Two runs, sixty minutes apart. Only one of them should exist.\")\n\nOn its own, a duplicate run shouldn't have been a disaster. The real bug was ours: the billing job assumed it would run *exactly once per day*. It selected subscriptions with `renewal_date = CURRENT_DATE` and charged each one, without checking whether a charge for that billing period already existed. That assumption had held for four years, which is exactly long enough for everyone to forget it was an assumption.\n\n> Every system has an invariant that nobody wrote down because it was \"obviously\" true.\n> You find out what it is when it stops being true at 3 a.m.\n\nPriya paused the CronJob at 4:06, and by 9:00 we had refunded every duplicate charge and emailed the affected customers. Total customer-visible impact: one confusing bank notification each, plus about six hours of support time. It could have been a lot worse.  \n\n## Why our tests didn't catch it\n\nWe did have tests for the time zone change, and good ones. They checked that the job ran at the right local time in summer and in winter, and that it did the right thing on the day of the autumn transition. What they didn't do was simulate the *controller* across the spring transition, because our tests called our own scheduling helper rather than the actual Kubernetes code. We were testing our model of the system, not the system.\n\n\n## What we changed\n\n1. **Idempotency at the charge level.** Every charge now carries an idempotency key of the form `sub_<id>:<period_start>`, enforced by a unique index in our database *and* passed through to the payment provider. Running the billing job ten times in a row is now boring, which is exactly what we want.\n2. **Back to UTC for scheduling.** The CronJob runs hourly in UTC, and the job itself decides which regions are due, using a proper time zone library and explicit rules for nonexistent and ambiguous local times.\n3. **A DST fixture in CI.** Our integration tests now spin up a `kind` cluster whose clock we control, and run the billing schedule across both transitions for each of the four time zones we operate in.\n\nWe also gave the `BillingRunDuplicate` alert a real runbook entry, replacing the \"this should never happen\" placeholder it had before.\n\n## The takeaway\n\nIf you remember one thing from this post, make it this: **anything that runs on a schedule should be safe to run twice.** Schedulers are distributed systems, and distributed systems deliver \"exactly once\" right up until the moment they don't. Time zones just make that moment arrive on a predictable date, which, if you think about it, is almost a courtesy.\n\n_Thanks to Priya Natarajan, Marcus Bell and Yuki Sato for reviewing drafts of this post, and to everyone who answered \"has this happened to you?\" on Mastodon with stories considerably worse than ours._[^stories]\n\n[^go-time]: Go's [`time.Date`](https://pkg.go.dev/time#Date) documentation says that for a local time that falls in a transition gap, it returns a time that is correct in one of the two zones involved, but it doesn't guarantee which. Which is fair! It's an impossible question. The trouble starts when two pieces of code ask it independently.\n\n[^stories]: My favourite involved a hospital pager system and a leap second. I am not allowed to say which hospital.\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":12053,"cache_read_input_tokens":145493,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":12053,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_01XE5rjet6uYehWEKYqXj7JS","agent_id":"a909b0d1a1c0df50d","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"c263d333-be14-4751-a68b-2e15bd7ac844","timestamp":"2026-11-17T22:31:58.074Z","request_id":"req_011Ch9HuLknvyYYSdBcptveB","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Generate docs-heavy corpus 15"}

Don't dwell on it — the people involved are in the room.\n:::\n\n## What `{targets}` gives you\n\n:::: {.columns}\n\n::: {.column width=\"50%\"}\n**A declarative pipeline**\n\n- each step is a *target*: a name plus a command\n- dependencies are found by static code analysis\n- only outdated targets re-run\n:::\n\n::: {.column width=\"50%\"}\n__More or less for free__\n\n* parallel workers via `{crew}`\n* targets stored in the cloud (S3, GCS)\n* a dependency graph: `tar_visnetwork()`\n:::\n\n::::\n\n## A minimal `_targets.R`\n\n```{.r code-line-numbers=\"2-3\"}\nlibrary(targets)\ntar_option_set(packages = c(\"dplyr\", \"readr\", \"fable\"))\ntar_source(\"R/\")\n\nlist(\n  tar_target(raw_file, \"data/sales.csv\", format = \"file\"),\n  tar_target(sales, read_sales(raw_file)),\n  tar_target(model, fit_models(sales)),\n  tar_target(forecast, make_forecast(model, h = \"8 weeks\"))\n)\n```\n\n::: {.notes}\nLines 2–3 first: packages, and sourcing our own functions from `R/`.\nThen the pipeline itself is just a list. Emphasise `format = \"file\"` — that's what makes the CSV a tracked dependency, so editing the file triggers a rebuild of everything downstream.\n:::\n\n## Running it\n\n```{.r code-line-numbers=\"1|3\"}\ntar_make()\n#> ▶ dispatched target sales\ntar_visnetwork(targets_only = TRUE)\n```\n\n![](images/visnetwork.png){.r-stretch fig-alt=\"Dependency graph rendered by tar_visnetwork, with outdated targets highlighted in blue\"}\n\n## Making it fast\n\n:::: {.columns}\n\n::: {.column width=\"40%\"}\n::: {.incremental}\n- branch over stores with `pattern = map()`\n- 8 local workers with `{crew}`\n- cache on a shared S3 bucket\n:::\n:::\n\n::: {.column width=\"60%\"}\n```{.r code-line-numbers=\"2|5-6\"}\ntar_option_set(\n  controller = crew::crew_controller_local(workers = 8)\n)\ntar_target(\n  model, fit_models(sales_by_store),\n  pattern = map(sales_by_store)\n)\n```\n:::\n\n::::\n\n::: {.notes}\nDynamic branching: one model per store, 212 stores. With 8 workers the model step goes from ~2 h to ~20 min.\n:::\n\n## Results\n\n| | Before | After |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| Full run | 3 h 10 min | 46 min |\n| Typical Monday run | 3 h 10 min | **4 min** |\n| Stale outputs in report | ¯\\\\\\_(ツ)\\_/¯ | 0 |\n\n::: {.notes}\n\"Typical Monday run\" = only the newest week of data changes, so most targets are skipped.\nThe shrug is deliberate. Hamblin et al. [-@hamblin2018physiological] found that large-bodied bees declined in abundance along an urban warming gradient in Raleigh, NC, whereas small-bodied taxa were largely unaffected; by contrast, a survey of 12 gardens in Berlin found no detectable effect of local temperature on visitation once floral abundance was accounted for [@vonkonigslow2022; but see @theodorou2020urban]. Most of this work has relied on temperature data from airport weather stations approx. 10--20 km from the study sites, which cannot capture the fine-scale variation that matters to a foraging bee [@hamblin2018physiological; @burdine2019, p. 4].\n\nHere we ask three questions: \n\n* Does garden-level UHI intensity predict pollinator visitation rates?\n* Is the relationship different for bees vs. hoverflies?\n* Does the effect depend on the time of day, e.g. is it stronger during the afternoon heat?\n\n# Methods\n\n## Study sites\n\nWe surveyed `r n_gardens` community gardens across Greater Manchester, UK, between 1 June and 31 August 2025.\nGardens were chosen to span a gradient of impervious surface cover (12.5--81.0 % within a 500 m buffer) while keeping garden size roughly constant (median 0.21 ha, range 0.08--0.46 ha).\nMean UHI intensity across gardens was `r round(mean_uhi, 2)` °C; see Fig. 1 for the full distribution.\n\n## Temperature measurements\n\nEach garden was fitted with two iButton DS1923 loggers in radiation shields at 1.5 m height, recording every 30 min. Loggers were calibrated against a reference thermometer before and after the field season, and drift was < 0.2 °C in all cases. UHI intensity was defined as the mean difference between garden temperature and a rural reference site at Abbots Moss^[Open heathland approx. 40 km SW of Manchester city centre, at a similar elevation to the study gardens.] between 10:00 and 16:00, i.e. the hours during which surveys took place.\n\n## Pollinator surveys\n\nVisitation was recorded in 10-min timed observations of a standardised 1 m² patch of *Borago officinalis* planted in each garden in April.\nObservers recorded every insect that contacted the anthers or stigma and identified it to the lowest practical taxonomic level (usually genus for bees, family for flies).  \nEach garden was surveyed on 9 dates, three times per date (morning, midday, afternoon), giving `r n_obs` observation periods in total.\n\n## Statistical analysis\n\nWe modelled visit counts with a Poisson generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a log link [@bates2015lme4]. In brief:\n\n- response: number of visits per 10-min observation\n- fixed effects: UHI intensity (°C), pollinator group, survey period, and the group × UHI and period × UHI interactions\n+ offset: log number of open flowers in the patch\n- random intercepts: garden and survey date\n\nAll analyses were done in R version `r getRversion()` [@rcore2025].\n\n```{r model, echo=TRUE}\nm1 <- glmer(\n  visits ~ uhi_intensity * group + uhi_intensity * period + offset(log(n_flowers)) +\n    (1 | garden_id) + (1 | survey_date),\n  data = visits, family = poisson,\n  control = glmerControl(optimizer = \"bobyqa\")\n)\ncoefs <- tidy(m1, effects = \"fixed\", conf.int = TRUE)\nb_uhi <- coefs |> filter(term == \"uhi_intensity\") |> pull(estimate)\n```\n\n# Results\n\nWe recorded 4,318 flower visits, of which 61.4 % were by bees (mainly *Bombus* spp. and *Apis mellifera*) and 29.8 % by hoverflies (Syrphidae).\nThe remaining 8.8 % were by other flies, butterflies and the occasional wasp.\n\nVisitation increased with UHI intensity overall (β = `r round(b_uhi, 2)` per °C), but the effect differed strongly between groups (Fig. 2). For bees, each additional degree of UHI intensity was associated with approx. 14 % more visits per flower (rate ratio 1.14, 95 % CI 1.05--1.24), whereas for hoverflies the estimate was close to zero and slightly negative (RR 0.97, 95 % CI 0.86--1.09). The interaction with survey period was weak. If anything, the positive effect for bees was _smaller_ in the afternoon than in the morning, contrary to our expectation!\n\n```{r fig-visits, fig.cap=\"Fig. 2: Predicted visits per 100 flowers per 10 min vs. UHI intensity, by pollinator group (midday surveys). Ribbons show 95 % confidence intervals.\"}\nnewdat <- expand_grid(\n  uhi_intensity = seq(min(gardens$uhi_intensity), max(gardens$uhi_intensity), length.out = 50),\n  group = c(\"bee\", \"hoverfly\"), period = \"midday\", n_flowers = 100\n)\nnewdat$pred <- predict(m1, newdata = newdat, re.form = NA, type = \"response\")\nggplot(newdat, aes(uhi_intensity, pred, colour = group)) +\n  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +\n  labs(x = \"UHI intensity (°C)\", y = \"Visits per 100 flowers per 10 min\", colour = NULL) +\n  theme_minimal()\n```\n\n# Discussion\n\nOur results suggest that moderate urban warming may benefit bees in a temperate maritime climate, where cool and cloudy days frequently limit foraging.\nThis is consistent with the thermal-limitation hypothesis [@kuhsel2015high] and with observations of earlier activity onset in warmer microsites [@fisogni2020; @kammerer2021, pp. 3--5].\nHoverflies, in contrast, did not respond to warming, possibly because many syrphids tolerate low temperatures better than bees do.[^1]\n\nThere are several caveats. First, our temperature gradient (`r round(min(gardens$uhi_intensity), 1)`--`r round(max(gardens$uhi_intensity), 1)` °C) is modest compared with cities in continental or Mediterranean climates, and the relationship may well reverse above some threshold, e.g. once afternoon temperatures regularly exceed 30 °C. Second, we measured visitation, not pollination effectiveness or bee fitness. Third, 2025 was an unusually warm summer in the UK, which may have compressed the range of conditions we sampled.\n\nFuture work should combine fine-scale temperature monitoring with measurements of pollen deposition and pollinator body condition, ideally across several years and cities.\n\n\n[^1]: Several common UK hoverflies, e.g. *Episyrphus balteatus*, are active at air temperatures as low as 10 °C, whereas most bumblebees must warm their flight muscles to approx. 30 °C before take-off.\n\n# Acknowledgements {.unnumbered}\n\nWe thank the 23 garden groups who hosted loggers and borage patches, and the volunteers who spent approx. 300 hours watching flowers.\nFunded by NERC grant NE/X012345/1.\n\n# References {.unnumbered}\nRMD_EOF","description":"Rewrite R Markdown article via heredoc with trailing spaces"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":2038,"cache_read_input_tokens":193447,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":2038,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_01XE5rjet6uYehWEKYqXj7JS","agent_id":"a909b0d1a1c0df50d","session_id":"0e7cfb1b-67a4-4c6e-bc49-6d823e4685c0","uuid":"9c0476fe-1e1f-4d0d-a2f0-695620503697","timestamp":"2026-11-17T22:35:21.987Z","request_id":"req_011Ch9JE8vw2ZroeeigUXHaN","subagent_type":"general-purpose","task_description":"Generate docs-heavy corpus 15"}
